The Vīraśaiva Commentary on the Śrīmad Bhagavad Gītā. Om. Salutations to Śiva, the Supreme Brahman.
Chapter One.

May the Conqueror of Death— who, ever shining by the power of his conscious nature, is the cause of bondage and liberation for the individual soul— joyfully protect those who are bowed in devotion as his servants through his release from the bonds of worldly existence.

Worshipped by the virtuous, served by yogis, delighted by the wielder of the sword (Kṛtti), smeared with ashes, graced by the Gaṅgā, encircled by the serpent, and propitiated by Nandin—may Śaṅkara protect you. || 2 ||

Just as the true nature of the *liṅga* is established in the world so that it may be grasped by all through exclusive devotion, even so did the Guru, the son of Eṇukā, constantly conduct its practice according to divine instruction. (3)
I bow to Śambhu, who assumes the form of the Guru, the eternal one who awakens the perpetual Dharma;
who is born from the Liṅga and possesses glory equal to the Liṅga, and who shines forever, pervading the entire universe.

He who, stabilizing Vīraśaivism upon the surface of the earth, shines even today within a perfectly pure heart—may that Lord now bring about a supreme succession of auspiciousness according to the direction pointed out by Agastya. || 5 ||
The noble Gurur Allama, whose root is dispassion, whose excellent seat is emptiness, who is attainable through right knowledge,
and who was established in the state of Guheśa, adorned the worlds while remaining amidst worldly phenomena.
May the Lord of Yogins, Śrī Guru Toṇṭadārya, who is of the nature of Śiva and shines upon his seat,
always protect his devotees through his grace and favor— he for whose sake this very God has descended.

The foremost of Śiva-yogins, whose form is untainted, who is of the nature of consciousness, and whose essence is pure light—he who wanders upon this earth in an incorporeal form—revealed his own form to her. (8)
If the reality of dispassion is fully established, it adorns the multitude of true devotees;
for the sake of strengthening that very [dispassion], Śambhu, though formless, assumed a physical form and wandered upon the earth.

That very Śambhu, under the name Murughēśa, ascended the stainless seat (pīṭha) at the great monastery; there, the Teacher of the World, immersed in yogic absorption, remained solely devoted to the welfare of the world. (10)

That which is called "stainlessness" (nirlepana) is the means for crossing the ocean of existence, the medicine that wards off the flood of sufferings such as passion, the excellent cleansing of the power known as Māyā, and the ornament of the investigation into the knowledge of the true meaning of reality. || 11 ||
The Lord known as Carajaṅgama shines forth with the seal of pure detachment, capable of bestowing such divine medicine—the fruit of asceticism—which is able to destroy the disease of the heart. 12.
The illustrious Murugheśa-varya, who has girded his loins against the terror of the flood of sins,
having assumed a divine body through yoga, constantly bestows grace upon all devotees.
This Lord Murugheśa shines upon the earth at the Śūnya-pīṭha, resplendent in a stainless body of pure consciousness;
I bow to that true Guru, Allikārjuna, whose lotus feet are the sole abode of my mind. (14)

I praise the mobile Liṅga, whose divine feet are served by the wise, who is accessible through true devotion, endowed with eternal peace, fixed in his aim upon the purification of the meaning of the scriptures, and a hero of dispassion. 15.

Constantly devoted to the multitude of virtuous deeds that bring benefit to the world and please the Lord of Murughā, he shines upon this earth with a broad vision, having abandoned all worldly desire for rewards. (16)
This very Jagadguru, out of his noble disposition, has revealed this *Gurubhāṣya* titled *Samanvaya* for the sake of discerning the meaning of the *Śrī Kṛṣṇa Gītā*, for the welfare of the world. (17)
Dwelling within my very heart, he—possessing pure intellect—has composed this *Siddhāryabhāṣya*, the excellent Vīraśaiva work that is dear to Śiva and fulfills all desires. 18.
May this commentary now serve to please Murugheśa and his father;
this command of the Teacher of the World has been fulfilled through the grace of His full compassion. (19)
May this commentary unfold the meaningful purpose; may the mind eternally attain identity with consciousness;
may the intellect, being serene, delight in the Lord of the Cave (Śiva); and by the grace of Śiva, may there be the blossoming of power. 20.
May this Lord Murughēśa, whose nature is consciousness, having beheld me, his servant, with a gaze moistened by compassion,
bestow upon me the unfailing yoga of *samādhi* on the stage of the task of purifying the meaning of the *Gītā*. (21)

It has been established in the Śaktiviśiṣṭādvaita philosophy that the Supreme Brahman alone—which is characterized by diverse and infinite powers and is designated by such terms as Paramaśiva, Sadāśiva, Rudra, and so forth—undergoes transformation into the form of the universe.
The one and only Supreme Brahman accomplishes its various effects by being qualified by this or that particular power. Thus...

The Supreme Brahman, Paraśiva, shines forth as one who delights in the Self through the experience of His own bliss, effortlessly accomplishing the cosmic activities of creation, maintenance, dissolution, and so forth. Among these, He alone, characterized by the power of knowledge (jñānaśakti) conducive to creation and the power of action (kriyāśakti) conducive to preservation, is called Viṣṇu. Likewise...

That very [Lord], characterized by the power consisting of the union of knowledge and action conducive to withdrawal (*saṃhāra*), is designated as Kālarudra; for Kālarudra is the one authorized over dissolution (*pralaya*), at the time of whose passing even the three forms (*trimūrti*)—Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva—are likewise withdrawn. Furthermore, even the three forms are indeed manifestations (*vibhūti*) of Paraśiva-Brahman. Therefore, Brahmā, Viṣṇu, and Śiva...
Beyond Kālarudra; thus, having existed in the form of the threefold manifestation (trimūrti) and carrying out creation, maintenance, and dissolution,

when and whenever the world itself becomes inclined toward destruction due to the weight of unrighteousness (adharma), then and there the Supreme Self, descending into the world Himself in the form of Viṣṇu— who holds the office of protection— effects the preservation of the universe.

Thus, for the sake of protecting the world, the formless Supreme Self alone descends as Viṣṇu, assuming a divine form. In this way, even the ten incarnations of Viṣṇu are merely the playful manifestations (*līlāvibhūti*) of the compassionate Lord Parameśvara (Paraśiva), who is endowed with His supreme power (*parāśakti*). This Viṣṇu is one among the three deities (*trimūrti*).

In the *Rudrasūkta* of the *Sāmaveda*, it is declared that [Viṣṇu] is a portion of the supreme power (*parāśakti*) which is established in Paraśiva. "The single power of the Supreme Lord becomes fourfold at the time of its application: as Bhavānī in enjoyment, as Durgā in battles, as Kālī in anger, and indeed as Viṣṇu in protection. Thus, regarding Viṣṇu therein—

It has been taught that [Viṣṇu] is a portion of the Supreme Power (parā-śakti). Therefore, Viṣṇu, who is appointed for the purpose of protection, is indeed the very form of Śiva’s vital power (prāṇa-śakti).
And this Supreme Śiva (paraśiva), although transcending the Trinity (trimūrti), carries out the activity of the world while existing as the essence of the Trinity.

"In the world, however, [the Lord's activity] is mere sport (līlākaivalya)," as has been established by the venerable Paṇḍitārādhya in his commentary on the *Brahmasūtra* (p. 4). For Śiva alone has transformed himself into the form of the three deities (trimūrti).

Because he, having come into being, accomplishes the welfare of the world, he alone is reckoned as Mahādeva. Now, why is he called Mahādeva? Because he is magnified (*mahīyate*) in the great through the sovereignty of self-knowledge and yoga, therefore he is designated as Mahādeva; by this designation, his status as the Lord of all and his nature as the inner controller of all [is established].
Furthermore, it is established in the *Śrīkarabhāṣya* that the quality of being the bestower of all fruits resides solely in Mahādeva Śiva, the supreme cause;

thus it is rightly stated that the performance of the world's activities through the three forms (*trimūrti*) is the playful sport (*līlāvinoda*) of the formless Śiva. Among these incarnations of the three forms, two are particularly renowned:
The incarnations of Rāma and Kṛṣṇa.

Of these two, the incarnation of Rāma shines forth, firmly established in the path of performing virtuous deeds through qualities such as righteous conduct and moral discipline. The incarnation of Kṛṣṇa, however, exists specifically for the purpose of imparting instruction on the ultimate reality (tattva).

He is renowned as the Divine Mirror. And by this teaching, Kṛṣṇa, under the pretext of Arjuna, purifies all living beings who are composed of the three *guṇas*. It is beyond dispute that for this teaching as well, the very *Gītā* taught by Śiva during his incarnation as Rāma is the foundational source (*mūlādhāra*). Long ago, in the Tretā Yuga, during the separation from Sītā—

In order to settle him—who was his own partial manifestation—Śiva, who had arrived at the Daṇḍaka forest with his three forms in full majesty, graced him with compassion through his divine and auspicious form;
[the place] shines [there]. Having heard the Śiva-tattva taught at that time with faith, Śrī Rāmacandra...

He attained unsurpassed concentration of mind. At that time, this ancient instruction, which had remained within Śrī Rāma in the form of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*), was able to dispel Arjuna’s despondency during the Kṛṣṇa incarnation and establish him in his duty. This divine instruction arrived through the mouth of Kṛṣṇa.

It is well known that, taking Arjuna as the occasion, He remains manifesting divine radiance and the remembrance of His own true nature within all living beings— just as they all conduct themselves in the world for the sake of pleasing the Lord so that they may experience eternal bliss. In the Tretā Yuga, His mind was composed by the nectar of the *Śivagītā*.

Just as Rāma purified himself through his conduct of truth, so too did he, having descended in the Dvāpara age under the name of Kṛṣṇa by means of that very same self-refinement, succeed in instructing all afflicted living beings through the pretext of Arjuna. This is the intended meaning; furthermore, this is what is recorded in the commentary on the aforementioned sūtra.
It is recorded that even the Gītā-śāstra was taught by Kṛṣṇa to Arjuna solely under the authority of the Lord’s command; the introduction therein proceeds as follows:
"This knowledge has been spoken by me for the benefit of those who discourse on Brahman.

It must always be given by you to disciples whose minds are tranquil. Thus Śiva instructed Rāma. Likewise, the Blessed Lord Nārāyaṇa, Hari, the son of Devakī, gave it directly and personally to Arjuna.
It declares the fulfillment of Śiva’s command: "This very Vyāsa [is he]; for in the *Śivagītā* contained within the *Padmapurāṇa*, it is said:

'In ancient times, in the Daṇḍaka forest, that which was spoken by the Lord of Pārvatī to Rāma is indeed called the *Śivagītā*, the most secret of all secrets. Thus, regarding the *Gītā* taught by Śiva during the incarnation of Rāma.

It perfectly reveals its secrecy and antiquity. That very teaching, which became renowned during the time of the Mahābhārata at the incarnation of Kṛṣṇa, attained great popularity; for it was precisely in this incarnation that, for the benefit of all the world, the lost knowledge of the supreme self (adhyātma-jñāna) was [revealed] by taking Arjuna as the occasion.

Furthermore, that which was taught by the Supreme Self through Śrī Kṛṣṇa is itself called "instruction directed toward the Blessed Lord. This is stated in the *Śrīkarabhāṣya* during the exposition of the meaning of the sūtra: "Or [the instruction is] by means of the vision of the scripture, as in the case of Vāmadeva," wherein Śrī Kṛṣṇa [is the teacher].
The intention is that Śiva, having attained identity with Paraśiva through the contemplation "I am Śiva," teaches the Śiva-principle;
this is clearly demonstrated by the example of Vāmadeva. At the time of his instruction, the great seer Vāmadeva points out his own universal nature at every step, saying, "I was Manu," and so forth.
In the same way, on the occasion of his instruction, Kṛṣṇa also reveals that all of this is indeed his own instruction:
"In the Daṇḍaka forest, the Blessed Lord Paramaśiva [taught] Śrī Rāmacandra: 'All is indeed Rudra;
there is only one Rudra, and he does not stand for a second. Śiva alone is to be meditated upon, the maker of auspiciousness; having completely abandoned all else.'"

"Renouncing all duties, take refuge in Me alone"—by such words, the knowledge of Śiva, which is the essence of all the Vedāntas, was indeed taught. That very Rāma, in his incarnation as Kṛṣṇa, said to Arjuna, "Vāsudeva is everything"; that Great Soul is truly difficult to attain.

Statements such as "A portion of My very self, having become a living soul in the world of the living, is eternal" were taught through the vision of identity with Śiva. The very Śruti, "He who knows Brahman becomes Brahman indeed," teaches the oneness of the disciple with the Guru within the state of the disciple's intellect. This was taught by Śiva.
Just as Rāma, having realized the Śiva-principle, became Śiva while remaining self-contented, so too he who had descended in the form of Kṛṣṇa obtained that very same refinement.

Therefore, even Kṛṣṇa, being Śiva himself, employs the term "we" (*asmad-pada*) in numerous contexts during the occasion of instruction, following the sequence: "I alone am the doer, the causer of action, the enjoyer, and the impeller," and so forth. And this is indeed consistent with the authority of the Vedas (*śruti*), logical reasoning (*yukti*), and direct experience (*anubhava*). For this very reason, even though there are many versions of the *Gītā* existing...

This alone is honored by all. By designating it by the name *Bhagavadgītā* rather than *Viṣṇugītā*, its universal preeminence is indicated. For this very reason, it has been commented upon by all the teachers, such as Śaṅkara, Rāmānuja, and others, according to their respective philosophical systems; however—
According to the Śaktiviśiṣṭādvaita school, no commentary on this [text] has been composed by anyone up to this time;

for in the Śaktiviśiṣṭādvaita philosophy, it is established that liberation arises from knowledge alone, which is an auxiliary to action. It is for this very reason that the Blessed Lord taught this scripture precisely on the battlefield of Kurukṣetra, in the context of sustaining his life through the performance of duty.
Through deceitful means such as gambling, Duryodhana seized the kingdom of the Pāṇḍavas. Following his command, the Pāṇḍavas lived in forest exile for twelve years and one year in concealment.
Consumed by wicked ambition, he declared, "I will not give even five villages; if you have the power, [take them]."

"Accept the kingdom by displaying your strength," he spoke thus out of audacity. In the end, they departed because there was no other course of action. Those Brahmins who are knowers of the Vedas and those people who are knowers of the supreme self (adhyātma) declare that the high-souled Kṛṣṇa is the eternal Dharma. Thus, Śrī Kṛṣṇa, whose very nature is Dharma, stood on the side of the Pāṇḍavas.

Out of affection for those who depend on him, the aged Dhṛtarāṣṭra— the father of hundreds of Kauravas, including Duryodhana and others, and himself born blind and unable to witness the battle— accepted the role of charioteer for Arjuna and desired to know about it from time to time so that he might establish righteousness.

And he requested the means for that from the great sage Śrī Vyāsa. Vyāsa, out of compassion, summoned Sañjaya and, having granted him divine vision, instructed him: "Whatever occurs on the field of battle every day must be told by you to him. Thus appointed was Sañjaya.
Dhṛtarāṣṭra, desiring to hear news of the battle, made inquiries. (p.
7) Thus, in this sequence, the Bhagavadgītā begins; thus [it sets forth] the path of the integration of knowledge and action.

Experts believe that the Śaktiviśiṣṭādvaita philosophy is highly esteemed as it accords with worldly practice (*vyavahāra*). Indeed, the *Gītā* instructs: "He who performs actions, having offered them to Brahman and abandoned attachment, is not tainted by sin, just as a lotus leaf is not wetted by water. According to this principle, whoever...

For one who acts without attachment to the fruits of action, having united with the Lord dwelling in the heart, no taint of sin occurs. He who knows that the Lord dwells in the heart is able to offer his own karmic fruit to Him. Thus, by the very offering of the fruit, karma does not bind him.
It binds. This very thing is designated as *karmayoga* in the *Gītā*.

And this yoga indicates the equal primacy of both knowledge (*jñāna*) and action (*karman*). In the state of equilibrium in the form of non-duality (*advaita*), which is to be realized through Śaktiviśiṣṭādvaita, there is great significance for the path of the integration of knowledge and action.

There is a necessity. When the individual soul (jīva), having realized the Supreme Śiva (paraśiva) existing within itself, offers all its own fruits of action with devotion to Him, only then does its mental faculty (citta-śakti) transform into the nature of consciousness (cid-rūpa). This very process is what is termed there as the "evolution of power" (śakti-vikāsa), another name for liberation (mukti).

It has been calculated. Thus, since the reality of Śaktiviśiṣṭādvaita (Qualified Non-dualism with Power) perfectly accords with the *Gītā*, an effort has been made today to provide an exposition of it along this very line of thought.
Although there is scope for an exposition of this [text] according to the method of that [other] system, certain [points] therein—
Whenever there is a decline of righteousness, O Bhārata,
and a rise of unrighteousness, then I manifest myself.
For the protection of the virtuous, for the destruction of the wicked,
and for the sake of establishing righteousness, I manifest myself age after age.

Thus, in the Bhagavad Gītā, Śrī Kṛṣṇa describes the purpose of his own incarnation through the vision of the Supreme Self as a point of comparison. Here, in the passage beginning with "I come into being," the word *asmad* (the first-person pronoun) does not, for its part—

8) [The word "Kṛṣṇa"] denotes merely the form of the incarnation; because such a human form is perishable and because it is impossible for it to be the cause of all beings, that word likewise does not denote Viṣṇu, who is the source of that form.

Furthermore, because [the Lord] lacks the status of being the agent of creation and dissolution, there would arise the contingency of contradiction with such statements as "I am the origin and likewise the dissolution of the entire universe," which speak of Him as the agent of creation and dissolution. Therefore,
[this applies] even to the three forms (trimūrti) who are the agents of the threefold effects consisting of creation, maintenance, and withdrawal.
It is beyond dispute that the word "we" (asmat) refers exclusively to the Supreme Śiva-Brahman, who is the fundamental source;

therefore, Śrī Kṛṣṇa is indeed an incarnation of the Supreme Śiva-Brahman. For the three deities (Trimūrtis) are merely divine manifestations (*divya-vibhūtis*) serving as the fields for the playful pastimes (*līlā-vinoda*) of Paraśiva. Now, one might object: if that is so, then [how can he be considered] an incarnation of Viṣṇu?

The objection arises as to how such renown could have come about. For Viṣṇu is indeed none other than Paraśiva-Brahman, characterized by the power of action conducive to protection; regarding this, no disagreement can possibly exist for anyone. Furthermore, by Kṛṣṇa, through the subduing of the demonic powers of Duryodhana and others—
Because he accomplishes the task of protecting the world by bringing about the excellence of divine power in the Pāṇḍavas and others,

he is also called an incarnation (avatāra) of Viṣṇu. Whatever action is performed and whatever word is spoken by Kṛṣṇa— who is that incarnation of Viṣṇu— all of that is [the work] of the Supreme Light who dwells within him as the inner controller (antaryāmin).

Meanwhile, those who are mere reciters, having not attained the experience of direct realization, defile their hearts with mutual envy, malice, and the like, and thus they hate Śrī Kṛṣṇa— the Supreme Self in essence—
who is the form of divine nectar, as well as His instruction. For among the three forms [of the Divine], there is no such thing for the discerning.
A perception of gradation among the three forms might arise, or else the notion that they are distinct from Paraśiva might emerge;

such a perception of gradation and the conception of their difference are seen in the scriptures to be utterly condemned. As it is stated in the source texts, such as the Brahmāṇḍa Purāṇa: "Bhavān and I..."
"O Soul of the Universe, you alone are indeed the cause of this world; for the sake of the world, we two are established in distinct forms.
Whatever was given by you has been given entirely by me. You ought not to perceive yourself as separate from me, O Śaṅkara. Thus spoke Viṣṇu to Śaṅkara in the *Bhaviṣyottara Purāṇa*.

"Those fools of perverse reasoning who perceive me or Brahmā as other than Viṣṇu are cooked in the lower hells. And those deluded, evil-minded ones who perceive me or Brahmā as distinct from Hari—their sin is equal to that of killing an embryo. Thus [the Lord spoke] to his devotees.
The words of Śaṅkara: "I am you, O omnipresent God; you alone am I, O Janārdana. There is no difference between us, whether in terms of words or meanings, O Lord of the World. (p. 9)
Whatever great names you have in this world, O Govinda, those indeed are my names as well; there is no need for deliberation on this point.
O Lord of the World, O Lord of the Cowherds, let that very devotion to you be mine;
and whoever hates you, O God, he undoubtedly hates me as well.

Thus ends the speech of Śaṅkara to Viṣṇu in the Mahābhārata. In this manner, the identity of Śiva and Viṣṇu is thoroughly established in the authoritative scriptures (*pramāṇagrantha*). However, although the Bhagavadgītā was spoken by Kṛṣṇa, who is a partial incarnation (*aṃśabhūta*) of Śiva, its true instructor is [Śiva].
Like a wooden puppet strung on a thread, Kṛṣṇa manifests only that disposition impelled by Śiva.
At the time of manifesting his universal form, he shows Arjuna only the great majesty of the Lord shining within his own inner self, saying, "Behold my divine yoga."

"The Lord dwells in the heart-region of all beings, O Arjuna; by His grace you shall attain supreme peace and the highest abode. Thus, indicating that the perfection resulting from the grace of the Lord is necessarily to be obtained by Arjuna, [the Lord] points out that He Himself is the enjoyer of the fruit of sacrifice, directing [Arjuna] toward His own Self alone in the words "whatever you do" (yatkaroṣi).

When He instructs Arjuna, "Whatever you eat— that, offer all to Me"— nevertheless, by employing the word *tat* (that) alone in numerous contexts such as "with their minds fixed on That" (*taccittāḥ*) and "with their lives absorbed in That" (*tadgataprāṇāḥ*), Kṛṣṇa generates the very same intellect of offering everything to the Lord in all instances. Wherever the word *asmat* (we/us) occurs...

When it is employed at the time of instruction, that word should be understood as not being natural (*prākṛtika*), but rather belonging to the Supreme Lord (*pārameśvarīya*). For the egoity (*ahaṅkāra*) related to *prakṛti* is already well known;
this [other] is the supreme I-consciousness (*parāhantā*) for the purpose of carrying out the play of grace toward devotees.

It is utilized by all who possess experience; those who are merged in the state of equanimity within the Supreme Self attain such a condition. Kṛṣṇa, abiding in the state beyond the highest limit, acts as if unattached—though his desires are fulfilled—out of sincere love for the sake of gathering the world together. For:
Although Kṛṣṇa was a human being, by means of Śiva-yoga he abided in the state of Śiva and perceived the world [from that perspective];
therefore, in his instruction, the use of the word "we" (asmad-śabda) does not involve a mutual contradiction.
Furthermore, by examining the meaning of the Gītā, it is evident that Kṛṣṇa’s realization of identity with Śiva was present within his heart.
It appears clearly.
Even for the Supreme Lord, his affection for Kṛṣṇa— who was an incarnation of Viṣṇu— was likewise unsurpassed; likewise,
in the Śivagītā contained within the Kūrma Purāṇa, Śiva also [expresses it] regarding Viṣṇu in the same way.

He reveals his own intention as if it were his own: Śiva instructs Rāma in this very way: "The supreme form of mine is called Nārāyaṇa; it abides within the self of all beings, is peaceful, and is designated as the Imperishable (Akṣara)."

"Therefore, this great yogi, my devotee, the supreme person, is indeed to be worshipped and saluted for the sake of generating my pleasure. In this way, Śiva manifests such reverence toward Nārāyaṇa. He who censures Viṣṇu... [is... (Note: The provided source text ends abruptly; the translation reflects the available portion.)

"Such a person does not obtain my grace," thus Śiva himself teaches in the *Śivagītā* contained within the *Padmapurāṇa*. Furthermore, the Vedic scripture itself teaches the identity of Śiva and Keśava, stating: "Obeisance to the Blessed Rudra-Viṣṇu; protect me from death. And in the *Ādityapurāṇa*, [it says] regarding Viṣṇu...
The word of Śiva shines forth in this excellent discourse: "O best of gods, you are Prakṛti and I am Puruṣa;
of this there is no doubt. Everything consists of you and me, having the nature of the unmanifest Puruṣa.
Such a sweet kinship exists between those two by virtue of their innate nature. Prakṛti is the supreme Viṣṇu.

In the *Kūrma Purāṇa*, it is stated that "the Supreme Person is Śiva. In the Vedic scripture (*Śruti*), in the passage beginning "To you, the King of the sacrifice, the Hotṛ-priest, Rudra," the status of being the Lord of Sacrifice is assigned specifically to Mahādeva, the inner controller of all, the cause of all, who is designated by the name Rudra—that is, Śiva himself. For this very reason, the *Atharvaṇika* scripture states:

By the statement, "Rudra, the great seer, is superior to all," his supremacy over the universe is established. In the Śruti, "O Rudra, this animal is yours; accept it; O Rudra, this is your portion along with your sister Ambikā," it is Rudra himself who is invoked at the sacrificial ground for the purpose of accepting the first honor. For this very reason, in the Kaivalya [Upaniṣad], he is described as accompanied by Umā.

Beginning with the words "the Supreme Lord, the Master," and continuing with "He alone is Viṣṇu, He is Prāṇa, He is Time, He is Fire, He is the Moon," and so forth, it is correctly taught that Paramaśiva alone is the essence of all deities such as Viṣṇu and others. This is established in the commentary on the sūtra "From the distinction of the word" (*śabdaviśeṣāt*), regarding the worship of Śiva.
It is clearly stated that the attributes such as omnipresence and being the inner controller— qualities not shared by others— are seen in Nārāyaṇa as well, once he has attained the state of Śiva.
O fair-faced one, there is no devotee superior to Nārāyaṇa for me;
in former times, he attained the state of being my wife, the state of being my bull, and the state of being Bāṇa.
Thus shines the word of Śiva in the Skanda Purāṇa. In the Droṇaparvan, the word of Śiva concerning Aśvatthāman is as follows:
"I have been duly propitiated by Kṛṣṇa of unwearied deeds."
Therefore, no one other than Kṛṣṇa is found by me to be more beloved.
The relationship between Śiva and Viṣṇu manifests in this way:
having personally realized the meaning of the supreme reality (paratattva), Śiva spoke thus to Viṣṇu; and Viṣṇu, in turn, proclaimed it to the one within the lotus-womb (Brahmā).

By means of such passages, [the text] correctly teaches the relationship of the worshipped and the worshipper, as well as the relationship of teacher and disciple, between Śiva and Viṣṇu. In the Skanda Purāṇa, after the paralyzing of Vyāsa’s arms, Viṣṇu speaks to Vyāsa:
"I alone am the creator of the world; Maheśvara is my creator"—thus it proceeds. One who follows the Veda should perform all actions dedicated to Śiva.
Thus it is clearly prescribed in the Śaiva Purāṇa: at the commencement of the śrāddha,
may the Lord Īśāna, Mahādeva, Maheśvara, the Blessed Īśa, the Supreme Self, Sadāśiva, be pleased in the form of the ancestors.

Thus, it has been taught that the Vedic practitioners should perform the *śrāddha* rite— which consists of the gratification of the Guru and the *Jaṅgama*, and takes the form of worshiping Śiva— because it brings pleasure to Śiva. For this very reason, what is indicated in the *Skanda Purāṇa* by the statement "I bow to him who is dear to Sukunda," namely that Śiva is the beloved of Viṣṇu and is dear to him, is entirely consistent.

"He shines; I meditate upon Kālabhairava, born from Śiva and Keśava"—thus, in the *Śaktipurāṇa*, Kālabhairava is designated as the beloved son of both Śiva and Keśava. In this manner, there are hundreds of statements that demonstrate the identity of Śiva and Nārāyaṇa.
Not only was Kṛṣṇa the expounder of the formless Śiva-tattva, but furthermore, impelled by his prior latent impressions,
he was graced with the purificatory rite of Śiva-initiation (śivadīkṣā) by Upamanyu, the most eminent of the great Śaiva sages.

He also thoroughly understood the greatness of the worship of Mūrta-Śiva. When asked by him, "What indeed is the propitiation of Śiva? that great sage replied as follows: "The granting of fearlessness to all, as well as the bestowing of grace upon all, and the performing of assistance for all—these they know to be the propitiation of Śiva. [He taught] the Śiva-tattva to himself...
In order to awaken him, Śrī Kṛṣṇa requested the great sage Upamanyu, as stated in the Vāyusaṃhitā: "O Blessed One, I desire to hear the knowledge of Śiva,
the essence of the Vedas, which was expounded by Śiva for the liberation of those who take refuge in Him" (Chapter 40.1).
Thus it is said.
In the *Kūrma Purāṇa*, it is stated that the great sage Upamanyu bestowed the initiation of Śiva (*śivadīkṣā*) upon Śrī Kṛṣṇa. (p. 12)

Having spoken thus, the great sage Upamanyu bestowed upon Kṛṣṇa, whose actions are effortless, the knowledge of the Pāśupata vow and yoga. Addressed by that best of sages, Madhusūdana propitiated the Lord Rudra right there through austerity. Thus it was performed by Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna.

The worship of the Śiva-liṅga is pointed out in the Droṇaparvan; it is stated there quite clearly that the efforts of Aśvatthāman were frustrated solely because of the worship of the Śiva-liṅga by those two who belonged to the enemy's side.
In this context, the epithet "of unblemished deeds" (*akliṣṭakarma*) applied to Kṛṣṇa is seen to be significant; he [Kṛṣṇa] [neutralized] everything...
By this, it is illuminated that he was able to accomplish [his goal] even without [the need for] karma and afflictions (*kleśa*).

Consequently, it is suggested that this Kṛṣṇa was indeed a *karmayogin* who had become like a mirror. Since this Kṛṣṇa is the male form of the Supreme Power (*parāśakti*), he is therefore honored not only by Śiva, but especially by all the gods as well.

He is thus praised. And so, it is repeatedly stated in the Mahābhārata that he was exceedingly skillful in carrying out his worldly activity in the form of protecting [the world]. Since he was a practitioner of *karmayoga*, even while being a knower of reality (*tattvajña*), he became capable of instructing others in that reality. Therefore, this—

It is beyond dispute that Kṛṣṇa was a devotee of Paramaśiva and that he was indeed the vital energy (prāṇa-śakti) who is the very heart of Śiva. Because such a vast realization is born from latent impressions (saṃskāra), Kṛṣṇa— having attained complete sovereignty through the grace of Śiva— [bestowed] even the entirety [of his power] upon one like Arjuna.
He perceived the world with a mind intent solely on its welfare; a delight in the benefit of all beings arose within him as his very innate nature.
[He beheld] that stainless Supreme Brahman, which consists of the supreme ether, eternal, whose form is truth, and which is the bliss of consciousness in every aspect.
Of the yogis who have attained oneness with the Supreme Self.

Thus, among those sovereigns of Śiva-yogins pointed out by the eminent Reṇukācārya, Śrī Kṛṣṇa became worthy of being addressed by the very term "Supreme Self" (Paramātman). Having dissolved into the formless, supreme Reality— the Universal Self which is free from any suspicion of duality— and remaining like the sky through a state of non-conceptualization, who indeed [could not recognize] Kṛṣṇa?

Could the Supreme Self not be composed of light? To whom would the Blessed Lord Śrī Kṛṣṇa—not having attained oneness with the Liṅga of Light, which is self-luminous, uninterrupted, and of the nature of consciousness—not be worthy of honor?
Thus, having dissolved into the Supreme Brahman, that Blessed One, because he has directly realized Dharma and because he transcends the three qualities (guṇas), [is beyond all doubt].
He has become honored by all; having realized Paraśiva, the yogi, dissolved in that state of equal flavor (samarasa), becomes Paraśiva himself.
The venerable Śruti itself, which is the embodiment of all means of valid knowledge, clearly teaches that [the Lord] becomes [all things].

Since Śrī Kṛṣṇa himself was the Lord of Guha (Guheśvara) as experienced by his own realization and the stage-manager for the drama of his divine play (līlā), he taught while abiding in the state of the Lord through identity with the Lord; thus, there is no inconsistency whatsoever in this.
Through the vision of the Lord, all indeed become of one single nature; and that nature is renowned as "internal" (*ādhyātmika*).

This nature, purified by the fire of initiation (*dīkṣā*), is reckoned as the "new" and "transcendent of the castes and stages of life" (*ativarṇāśrama*). Those great souls who are born again into this extraordinary nature attain the wondrous, supreme state of the Lord.

Having attained this power, they remain ever vigilant solely with a view toward the welfare of the world. Indeed, Kṛṣṇa, being one among such extraordinary great beings, taught the divine, formless reality for the sake of the benefit of the world alone; and this reality has been extracted from the ocean of the Upaniṣads.
It is indeed divine nectar. By drinking this, a human being becomes a god; even a mortal is born immortal.
A *jīva* bound by the three *guṇas* and resembling a tethered animal (*paśu*) becomes a Lord (*īśvara*) transcending the three *guṇas*.
Thus, because the venerable *Kṛṣṇa-gītā*, which is the very essence of the inner self (*adhyātma*), consists of the synthesis of knowledge and action, [it grants this result].
It is a cause for great joy that all the eminent scholars, having long since believed and been striving toward it, consider a commentary elucidating that [text] to be absolutely essential.

Divine instruction may come from any man or any woman; it must certainly be accepted with increasing devotion. Casting aside envy and reflecting upon what ought to be done, let the noble ones speak with propriety—such indeed is the path of the wise that spreads as an ideal. That very [path]...

Following the path, we have come to fully understand the reality of the manifest Supreme Śiva as taught by the Blessed One, the Supreme Soul Kṛṣṇa in his divine form, as well as the secret of the worship of His manifest form which is conducive to attaining Him; [we do this] in order to pacify our material nature, which is shrouded in darkness and like ashes.

In accordance with the instruction of the Blessed One, let us strive by whatever means possible. Let us overcome the demonic nature (*āsurī-saṃpat*). We, who have been consumed by the fire of desire, shall be thoroughly sprinkled by the divine rain of nectar ordained by the Blessed One;
thus we shall become satisfied and peaceful. For there is no wisdom for one who is undisciplined.
There is no cultivation for one who is unsteady, and for one who does not cultivate, there is no peace; for one who is not at peace, how can there be happiness?
14) Thus the Blessed One himself teaches in the Gītā: "Therefore, O Arjuna, be ever disciplined in yoga at all times."

Thus, he himself teaches the culmination of Yoga: all human beings, at all times, must remain steadfastly devoted to Śiva-yoga. Even those immersed in worldly affairs must always contemplate with a pure mind Guheśvara, who shines resplendent within their own hearts. This alone is Yoga.

The Gītā points out that such persons—whether men or women—even while engaged in worldly affairs, are not afflicted by the qualities and defects [of nature]. Karma never clings to such individuals. Thus, leading a life untainted, possessing supreme dispassion, and sporting in the sky of consciousness, they are one who finds delight in the Self (ātmārāma).
How could Śrī Kṛṣṇa not attain that which is characterized by the yoga of Śiva, consisting of the expansion of power?
While sporting with the Gopikā women through his divine opulence and yet experiencing the bliss of supreme detachment,
how could he not demonstrate to all the necessity of both of these states?
How could he not prevail? For that very reason, to whom would the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva—the supreme power (*parā-śakti*) who moves everywhere with total detachment—not grant his grace?
It is for the purpose of manifesting Śiva, who dwells unmanifestly within this world consisting of Śiva (*śivamaya*).

To which practitioner would the divine path revealed by Kṛṣṇa Paramātman, the foremost among the devotees of Śiva, not be pleasing? Therefore, although the Bhagavad Gītā was spoken by Kṛṣṇa, it shines forth as being held in the highest esteem not only by Vaiṣṇavas or Śaivas, but by Vīraśaivas as well.
This is for the benefit of all people.

It appears that the authority of such a scripture, consisting of the words of a trustworthy person (āptavākya) spoken by the Supreme Self itself, is self-evident and unavoidable. Regarding the *Gītā*, which is included within the threefold path (*prasthānatraya*) and consists of the paths of knowledge and action:
those who desire to set forth toward the Supreme Lord residing within the body, having abandoned the identification with the body [should take refuge in it].

Experienced practitioners state that for all of them, the integration of knowledge and action is indispensable. Likewise, according to the words of the learned, "For all aspirants desiring to set forth, the Commentary on the Gītā ought to be a treatise that provides rest"; thus, it is indeed appropriate to engage with this work.

If the divine yoga of Kṛṣṇa—who is endowed with devotion to Śiva and who delights in the small ether (daharākāśa) consisting of consciousness and bliss—were not revealed, then by [the great... p. 15).

May we all, though born as portions of the Blessed One, remain shrouded in *tamas*; while the *prāṇaliṅga* shines within our hearts, may Kṛṣṇa experience the bliss of deep sleep (*suṣupti*), and likewise, may our contracted nature never attain expansion. And so, we—
We would not be able to experience the supreme sovereignty that is of the nature of Being and all-pervading;

though it exists, the light of the Heart would never flash forth in our lives. Although we are of the very essence of stainless knowledge, through forgetfulness we would suffer like those blinded by delusion in the darkness of ignorance—such is the extent of this [bondage].

The divine message shall not enter our hearts; therefore, the exposition of the meaning of the Gītā should be investigated by the discerning with a spirit free from envy. To which practitioner would the Blessed Lord Kṛṣṇa, the supreme master of yoga, not be pleasing, regardless of caste, stage of life, outward marks, age, or learning? Therefore, this—

If we were like blind men led by the blind, falling into the darkness of delusion, we would fail to attain the meaningful purpose of our birth. In human life, fulfillment must indeed be achieved at every moment; and this achievement depends solely upon the grace of God.
The grace of the Lord also depends upon the expansiveness of the heart and self-confidence.
If we were not thus graced, then nature would enjoin us;
and if, bound by nature, we were to become enjoyers like beasts, then [there would be no attainment] of the bliss of Yoga.

Otherwise, there would be no fragrance even in us. Therefore, we must certainly resort to the path of living known as the union of renunciation and enjoyment (*tyāga-bhoga-yoga-samanvaya*). Indeed, worldly people maintain that one who is capable, compassionate, and powerful is worthy of being a refuge; and Kṛṣṇa is truly endowed with both of these characteristics.
Therefore, for the sake of sustaining our lives through spiritual lineage, the song of Kṛṣṇa alone must be our divine elixir of life. Consequently,
this commentary in the form of an exposition upon its meaning— which we have long desired and which has now appeared by the grace of the Lord— is a cause for supreme joy.

The individual soul, having acquired a body according to its own karma, abandons the limitations of birth, opinion, family, and lineage; by knowing its own true nature, it discards the finite measure bestowed by *prakṛti* and [realizes] that which exists within itself. (p. 16)
Having worshipped Guheśvara both internally and externally, one should dissolve into that very state of equanimity (*samarasa*) and conduct oneself in the world.
This alone is the essential message of the Bhagavad Gītā. To whom could such a divine instruction not be dear?
In that regard, where would there be any room for calculating the superiority or inferiority of caste and stage of life (*varṇāśrama*)?

In that case, they would not attain the meaningfulness of that birth; how then could it be realized? Those who do not experience the bliss of the Self (*ātman*) in this life will always remain possessed of a dualistic vision (*bhedadṛṣṭi*). Indeed, by them the welfare of the Self can never be accomplished, and the means for accomplishing the welfare of the world is far removed from them.

They would not be able to understand the meaning of the Bhagavad Gītā. Only those among the realized knowers who have directly perceived Dharma and do not take account of the distinctions of caste and stage of life (varṇāśrama) would be liberated from the bond consisting of the three qualities (guṇas).
The knowers who perceive reality, being unconditioned by space, time, and so forth, are beyond the stages of caste and order (ativarṇāśramiṇaḥ) and [attain] the supreme state.

Free from desire and conducting themselves with detachment, these very ones who delight in the Self accomplish the welfare of the world through a marvelous manner and without effort, thereby becoming mirrors for the universe. These beings of pure essence,
having ascertained the ultimate meaning through inquiry into Vedānta, experience the bliss of the Self while remaining in the stainless state.
Even toward human beings bound by the three qualities (*triguṇa*), they produce an expansion of the heart through sincere love.

Devoted to the welfare of all beings, these high-souled ones, being truly the Supreme Lord himself through the direct realization of the Supreme Lord, are designated by the word "Guru" because they attract all; and by means of their excellent instruction, they [lead] all...
Wandering everywhere for the sake of attaining the highest good, these moving and unmoving beings, whose forms are stainless, are designated as Śiva-yogins.
Thus, the Supreme Lord, assuming the form of a wandering teacher, dwelling everywhere with detachment for the sake of protecting and preserving all practitioners,
and performing every action as mere sport,
manifested from the form of Kṛṣṇa a spiritual discourse to present to all a divine model of Karma Yoga.
He who does not approve of this divine instruction, considering it to have been uttered by a human being in the form of Kṛṣṇa, shall never attain the bliss of the supreme self.

One may even attain such contact. Who would Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the revealer of such divine reality, not remove both mental and physical anguish? According to the etymology "He who restrains the *guṇas* is the Guru," and following the direction set forth in the *Kriyāsāra*, He stands beyond the three *guṇas*—sattva, rajas, and tamas—in a state free from the three qualities (*nistraiguṇya*).
Whom would Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the supreme lord of yogis, not endear by his resplendent state of detachment?

What discerning person would not honor him as the ideal practitioner of Karma Yoga in the form of Kṛṣṇa? However, the teaching of the Gītā is not merely technical; it concerns the very sphere of universal human conduct.
All the reflections therein expound nothing but daily affairs.

The sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, moreover, are considered to be of evil counsel—filled with demonic qualities (*āsurī-sampad*), abounding in the qualities of passion (*rajas*) and darkness (*tamas*), and manifesting wicked pride and arrogance. In the same way...

The sons of Pāṇḍu are considered to be endowed with both knowledge and action, characterized by a predominance of *sattva*, filled with divine fortune, and possessed of right discernment; likewise, Śrī Kṛṣṇa is revered as the embodied form of the formless Supreme Brahman, Paraśiva.

Experiencers conceive that the Mahābhārata is indeed a battle between right reflection and wrong reflection, which proceeded by the will of the Lord in his dark form (Kṛṣṇa). By the grace of the Lord, the Kauravas— who represent wrong reflection— suffer defeat, while the Pāṇḍavas— who represent right reflection— attain universal victory.
Having attained [it], they become eternally happy.

In accordance with the Gītā, this word *sat* is employed for the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), the pure individual soul (*jīva*), and its praiseworthy actions. There is no contradiction whatsoever in applying the word *sat* to Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Self; likewise, its application to Arjuna, the pure individual soul, is also appropriate. In that same sequence—

For the sake of establishing Dharma, by means of the path spoken by Īśvara, the Mahābhārata war— serving merely as a pretext— is accomplished through Arjuna as a pure *jīva*; it is a praiseworthy endeavor consisting of the eradication of unrighteousness (*adharma*) and the stabilization of Dharma, carried out in the form of the quest for the Supreme Brahman (*parabrahman*).

Karma is designated by the word "sat" (the existent). This Śrī Kṛṣṇa Gītā, which generates the desire for renunciation (*jihāsā*) regarding such investigations into the real, is called the Bhagavad Gītā precisely because it takes the form of an instruction on Paraśiva-Brahman as its inner controller; thus, it is addressed by that sacred name which signifies the realization of the formless reality.

It dwells in the mental temple of all practitioners. It is a matter for regret that, until now, no commentary devoted to the Vīraśaiva doctrine of such a sacred Gītā— attained through the grace of the Supreme Lord— has appeared.

What is the true nature of the Vīraśaiva doctrine? And what is the necessity for this commentary, which is in agreement with that doctrine? These questions must be examined here. First, as for the Vīraśaiva doctrine:

He approves of the natural duality between the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman in the state of bondage, and the natural non-duality in the state of liberation. Therefore, it has been stated by the presiding authorities of the Śrīśaila Pīṭha that "the reconciliation of all the Vedas is found in the pure doctrine of Dvaitādvaita, known exclusively as Vīraśaivism. Thus [says] Jagadguru...

This doctrine, renowned everywhere under the name of *Samanvaya*, is established through the harmonization (*samanvaya*) of both types of scriptural texts—those teaching duality and those teaching non-duality. In this view, the distinction between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*) stated in the scriptures is considered innate; the postulation of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) is not tenable therein. [The two] are the Knower and the Unknower.

Scriptural passages such as "Two unborn ones, the Lord and the non-Lord," "Two birds, companions and friends, cling to the same tree," and others, as well as Brahma-sūtras such as "The two selves have entered the cave, for that is seen," clearly teach the distinction between the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara) as something innate. It is not otherwise.

They indicate that [the difference] is due to limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*). Therefore, the Vīraśaiva doctrine established its Vedic authority by accepting the natural distinction between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*). Likewise, such scriptural passages as "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*), "This self is Brahman" (*ayam ātmā brahma*), and "All this is indeed Rudra" (*sarvo hy eṣa rudraḥ*) establish the identity between the individual soul and the Lord.

They teach non-duality (*advaita*), which is another name for *sāmarasya* (perfect equilibrium). This too is properly practiced in the Vīraśaiva system: the individual soul (*jīva*), being a portion of Śiva, although distinct from Śiva, worships Śiva incessantly;
gradually abandoning its own sense of difference, it becomes dissolved in Śiva, its own source. This very dissolution is [the goal].
Through the absolute cessation of bonds, it establishes *sāmarasya*, which is the state of equilibrium consisting of the union of the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*).

Those who possess direct experience declare that this very bliss of unity is the *sāmarasya* known as "the Stainless" (*nirañjana*). This occurs when one, having received the purificatory rite of initiation (*dīkṣā-saṃskāra*) from a Guru, increases the experience of His *liṅga* through the living embodiment (*jaṅgama*).

He who is established in the *liṅga* indeed becomes that which is denoted by the word *aṅga*. It is called *aṅga* because it goes (*gacchati*) to the *Aṃ*, the Supreme Self (*paramātman*). Such a well-refined individual soul (*jīva*) is capable of becoming dissolved in the Supreme Self through the state of being of one flavor (*samarasatā*); this is what is called *aṅga* in the Vīraśaiva doctrine.

For the sake of being in conformity with that [Self], even the Lord (Īśvara) who shines within one’s own heart becomes denoted by the word *liṅga*. It is precisely the Lord taught in the verse, "The Lord dwells in the region of the heart of all beings, O Arjuna," who, in the Vīraśaiva system, is designated as the *iṣṭaliṅga*, dearer than life itself. The individual soul (*jīva*) is called *aṅga*.
Through the door of uninterrupted worship, one attains the expansion of the heart by the grace of the Lord;
in such a pure, luminous heart, the individual soul, dissolved in equanimity,
experiences the bliss of the Lord itself.

19) He is also capable of carrying out worldly affairs with total detachment. This very [text], because it is a means of achieving liberation in the form of eternal bliss through the limbs of its characteristic marks, is the *Bhagavadgītā* among the threefold path (*prasthānatraya*).

It shines forth as a highly renowned and reckoned system. This very approach of the Gītā establishes the truth of both difference and non-difference— according to time and according to state— by means of a path consisting of the synthesis of knowledge and action, which is itself a mode of harmonizing all the Śrutis.
This commentary, esteemed by all schools of thought, has been scrutinized over a long period by eminent scholars, the great masters, and the public alike.
Announcing it to those of refined taste with self-confidence, we declare: "That very same work has now arrived."
This Bhāṣya is not merely characterized by the synthesis of difference and non-difference; rather, it is the essence of Paraśiva himself,

because in the Śruti, Paraśiva-Brahman is presented in many ways— as sometimes with attributes (saguṇa) and sometimes without attributes (nirguṇa), as sometimes having form (sākāra) and sometimes formless (nirākāra), and as sometimes with distinctions (saviśeṣa) and sometimes without distinctions (nirviśeṣa).

A mutual contradiction appears to exist; however, such a contradiction can never be appropriate within the Śruti, which is accepted by all as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Therefore, these conflicting views must be harmonized according to the difference in the qualifications (*adhikāri-bheda*) of the seekers. It is for this very purpose that the section on Harmonization (*samanvayādhikaraṇa*) has been undertaken.
In the *Sūtraprasthāna*: otherwise, the authority of the Śruti, which is accepted by all, would be contradicted.

First, in the Vīraśaiva doctrine, both a formal (mūrta) and a formless (amūrta) aspect are admitted regarding the Supreme Self; however, only its formlessness is accepted as the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*). This is also the case in the Dvaita and Viśiṣṭādvaita doctrines.
Only the embodied nature of the Supreme Self is accepted; for the Śruti states, "Verily, there are two forms of Brahman:
the embodied and the unembodied," and it describes both of these forms as being truly real.
Therefore, the Vīraśaiva doctrine [teaches] the embodied form of the Supreme Self for those of duller faculties.

He also accepts that for those of the highest qualification (*uttamādhikārī*), the formless aspect (*amūrtarūpa*) is necessary; and this acceptance relies precisely upon the manifoldness of the Supreme Self’s powers (*śaktivaicitrya*). Without contact with these powers, such a comprehensive integration (*samanvaya*) within the Supreme Self would not be possible. Of the Supreme Self...

In the Advaita system, it would be easy to reconcile the scriptures concerning the absence of qualities (*nirguṇa-śruti*) and the scriptures concerning the absence of distinctions (*nirviśeṣa-śruti*) with the state of the contraction of power (*śakti-saṃkoca-avasthā*). Likewise, it would be easy to reconcile the scriptures concerning the possession of qualities (*saguṇa-śruti*) and the scriptures concerning the presence of distinctions (*saviśeṣa-śruti*) with the state of the expansion of the Supreme Self’s power (*paramātman-śakti-vikāsa-avasthā*).

In that case, there would be no room at all for such a systematic coherence (samanvaya). Furthermore, to deny the reality of the world-activity being brought about by the Supreme Self (paramātman) would result in a contradiction with direct experience (anubhava).

A real entity can never become false. Even the worship and other rites performed by the living soul within the body cannot be said to be false. If a person carries out all worldly transactions with a sense of reality, yet conceives of them as being merely conventional (*kevalavyāvahārika*), then in his mind—

Whatever contradiction may be conceivable is indeed possible; therefore, whatever is performed through the contemplation of duality (dvaitabhāvanā) must be understood as being entirely real. Thus, the acceptance of the reality of duality is simply not possible without the presence of a specific power (śakti), because it is Śiva himself who transforms into the form of the individual soul (jīva).

In this marvelous state of transformation, wherein Śiva’s power is unrestrained, any kind of limitation must necessarily be admitted even by the non-dualists (advaitins). Although the individual soul (jīva) is a portion of Śiva,
it has fallen into delusion regarding its true nature solely due to the contraction of power, and thus continues to wander within the wheel of saṃsāra.

In this state, what discriminating person could say that he is indeed the Supreme Brahman? Likewise, no one can say that he can never become the Supreme Brahman, because he remains connected to the Supreme Self;
however, through the power of Māyā residing in the Supreme Self, he is naturally divided by non-discrimination (aviveka).
Having forgotten the Supreme Self, who is its own kinsman, it functions independently by itself.

Regarding such a living being (jīva), it cannot be said that it is Brahman alone, nor can it be said that it is not Brahman. Therefore, its state as a jīva during its bound condition must be accepted as real. That very [state]...

In the state of discernment (*viveka*), through full acquaintance with one's own kinsman—the Supreme Self consisting of bliss—one attains the expansion of power by merging into Him in a state of equanimity (*samarasa*). This expansion of power is indeed the awakened state of the intellect (*buddhi*) of the individual soul (*jīva*). Thus, it is precisely by accepting the contraction and expansion of power that the distinction between the individual soul and the Supreme Self is established.

Only by accepting that the state of the expansion of that [power] is itself the state of Śiva does worldly discourse become consistent, and thus the scripture also becomes fruitful. If, while being a *jīva* due to the contraction of power, one shines as Paramaśiva at the very same moment through the expansion of power— that is, in the state of Śiva— only then does he possess the status of Lord of the Universe.

And sovereignty would be established. Thus, the acceptance of the distinction of power (*śakti-vaiśiṣṭya*) in the Supreme Self is both proven by universal experience and accessible through the authority of the scriptures. For this very reason, in the Vīraśaiva system, that relationship which is described between Śakti, Śiva, and the individual soul (*jīva*) [is established].
That very same [state] is also designated as the Vīraśama state according to its true meaning.
Taking this very excellence of power as the basis, the harmony of the Vedas with respect to the Supreme Self is established in the *Śivapurāṇa*:

"He who is stainless, without support, and untainted is called Śiva; the Lord who is a single mass of infinite and endless auspicious qualities is called Śiva by the virtuous who know the true meaning of the principle of Śiva," so it is stated in the Smṛti.

In the *Ubhayaliṅgādhikaraṇa* of the *Śrīkarabhāṣya*, Śrīpati Paṇḍitārādhya has explained that the Supreme Brahman, which is denoted by the word "Śiva," possesses both characteristics (*ubhayaliṅga*).
This is stated in the commentary on the sūtra: "Because it is so declared when [the topic] is present" (3.3.40).

It is stated that the masters Revanasiddha, Marulasiddha, Udbhaṭa, and others—who were knowers of the primary meaning of all the Vedāntas—determined and established the principle that the Śrutis concerning the Nirguṇa Brahman have as their scope the contraction of Śakti.
This is based on the Sūtra: "But [His] sport is like that of the world; [it is] for the sake of His own isolation," which explains that the Supreme Brahman, Śiva, possesses an abundance of Śakti.

In the *Śrīkarabhāṣya*, it is stated that while the Lord remains poised for creation, his state of being the locus of divine play (*līlāśrayatva*) is taught; however, following dissolution until the next creation, he is taught to exist in a state of absolute oneness (*kevalatva*) through the contraction of his powers by his own will.
This has also been affirmed by the eminent *nirañjana* and leader of the moving beings, the Lord Allama Prabhu, who said: "O Lord of Umā, your play is at Yādoḍe."

By the passage beginning with "tappidoḍe svayaṃbhu," it must necessarily be admitted that within the one Supreme Self alone, there is a contraction of power during the state of the individual soul (jīva) even after the creation of the world for the sake of the devotees' enjoyment; yet, for the purpose of carrying out the divine play of grace toward devotees, there is also an expansion of power.

Thus, by establishing the Vīraśaiva doctrine as a system of Śaktiviśiṣṭādvaita through the reconciliation of all scriptural texts, it shines forth— being common to all philosophical systems, bringing about the highest good for all practitioners, and being desired by everyone.

It is indeed beyond dispute that this path of reconciliation (*samanvaya-mārga*), which is accepted by our school of thought, is consistent with the *Bhagavadgītā*. For, in reality, there exists a state of essential identity (*sāmarasya*) within the formless Supreme Śiva, who is immanent within the three deities (*trimūrti*). It is precisely this perspective of reconciliation that is reiterated in the *Bhagavadgītā*. Kṛṣṇa is an incarnation of Viṣṇu.

It teaches the reality of Śiva precisely through identity with Śiva. By the recitation of this [text], all worshippers of the embodied forms, having obtained the grace of the formless Supreme Śiva through those respective forms, remove the pervasive impurity and defects within the temple of the body and become stainless.
(Thus, p.

22) the Bhagavadgītā offers consolation to all practitioners: "Only those practitioners who are pure [attain] the state of Brahman, which shines forth through the path of yoga in the head, the heart, and between the eyebrows."

While conducting their worldly affairs, they should gladden all living beings by regarding them as their own selves. Such practitioners, through the grace of this principle of "regarding others as oneself" (*ātmaupamya*), become eternally contented and peaceful. Thus, this *Vīraśaiva-bhāṣya*, which reveals the universal intent of the *Bhagavad-gītā*, is not merely—

However, for all Vīraśaivas who live a spiritual life, Mahādeva resides within their own hearts; just as Dhṛtarāṣṭra, though born blind, obtained the grace of the Lord through the purity of his mind and attained the eye of knowledge by His favor, so too do living beings who are bound by egoism [attain liberation].
Even though they were blinded by ignorance, by the sight of the Bhagavad Gītā their karmas were consumed by the fire of knowledge.

This very body, which is the abode of the Lord, becomes a field of dharma (*dharmakṣetra*). As it is said, "One should know the heart to be the great abode of the universe," here in the human body, the heart is [the seat] of the Universal Self.

It is designated as the place for the playful diversion of divine sport. If such a heart were to be thoroughly purified so that it becomes stainless, then the vital breath (*prāṇa*), which is of the nature of light and shines therein, would be perceived by all practitioners. Bound by the three qualities (*guṇas*) in the form of fetters, the individual soul (*jīva*) is bound by objects consisting of those three qualities.
One necessarily exists in constant conflict with form, taste, smell, touch, and sound.
For a human being enveloped by these five objects of enjoyment, a battle of dualities proceeds perpetually. The Mahābhārata war is something practiced constantly throughout the lifetime of everyone.

The individual soul (*jīva*), whose essential nature is *dharma* and which consists of existence, consciousness, and bliss (*saccidānanda*), exists eternally and invariably associated with *adharma*, which consists of the qualities of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*. Now, a great doubt arises as to whether the *jīva* should resort to the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*) or resort to the power of the mind (*cittaśakti*). As for the power of consciousness:

The vital energy (*prāṇa-śakti*) is indeed of the nature of the splendor of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), consisting of existence, consciousness, and bliss (*saccidānanda*). For this very reason, it is heard in the Upanishads that the Supreme Brahman, Paraśiva, "delights in the vital breath" (*prāṇārāma*). This vital energy, which is established in the Supreme Self, when contracted, exists here in the body together with the individual soul (*jīva*). And thus, what is the [nature] of the individual soul?

"Should one go for refuge to the power of consciousness (*cic-chakti*), or should one take recourse in the objects of enjoyment that cause delusion— which are transformations of the power of the mind (*citta-śakti*)?"— in such a state of doubt, [the following occurs].

The living soul dwells [within]. To resolve this doubt, the external eye is indeed not capable [of perceiving it]; nor would it be able to enter within. Therefore, the purity of the mind is itself the internal eye.
If one partakes [of food] with the thought of offering it to the Lord, then all of that is transformed into the form of grace.

Śiva himself properly instructed Śrī Rāma during the Kṛtayuga that this very life of devotion is the means for all to achieve eternal happiness: "O Rāma, whatever you do, whatever you eat, whatever you offer in sacrifice, whatever you give, and whatever austerity you perform—perform that as an offering unto Me; there is no devotion higher than that toward Me."

O Best of the Raghus! This very state of total self-surrender (*sarvārpaṇabhāva*) taught here is also reiterated in the *Bhagavad-gītā*. By means of this life of grace, may we all become clear-minded;
and may our youths and maidens likewise become serene and pure, casting aside the darkness of their own ignorance.

They shall shine with the eye of wisdom. Although in the Purāṇas, here and there, one observes descriptions of the gradations in the Supreme Self’s existence as both manifest and unmanifest, and although in some places the superiority of Śiva is indicated and in others the supremacy of Viṣṇu, nevertheless, all of that is not [ultimately real].

The knowers of Brahman understand that, according to the maxim "even when criticism sets out to criticize, it actually praises that which is worthy of praise," such censure is intended solely for the purpose of praising the relevant portion; indeed,
such criticism does not proceed to condemn the censurable part, but rather [praises] the portion appropriate to the context and worthy of eulogy.

It should be understood by the discerning that she acts there solely for the purpose of praise. Therefore, upon observing the apparent censure seen therein, this temple-like body must not be defiled. Consequently, even through the worship of the embodied form, a human being may attain the bliss of union with the unembodied Śiva in this very life.

The Gītā bestows a divine message upon the human community submerged in the ocean of suffering, enabling them to experience it within their own bodies of faith. And this message, having come directly from the Supreme Self, shines forth consoling all practitioners according to their respective natures.

More will be said later in accordance with the requirements of the context. Now, having indicated the fourfold preliminary elements (anubandha-catuṣṭaya) appropriate to the composition, we shall proceed with the subject at hand.

Although the individual soul (jīva), shining within the heart, is indeed formless, it is not perceived by anyone on its own. Being a portion of the Supreme Self (paramātman), even though it is of extremely minute dimension, it is [perceived] through the Supreme Self.
The conscious self (*cetana*) is the substratum for the powers of will, knowledge, action, and agency; likewise, the individual soul (*jīva*) also exists as such a substratum.

Nevertheless, the power of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) is of a different nature—immeasurable and infinite—whereas the power of the individual soul is common to all [souls], limited, and finite. In terms of consciousness, the individual soul belongs to the same genus [as the Supreme Self].

Through the expansion of one's power, one necessarily attains a state of equilibrium (*sāmarasya*) with the Supreme Self. For this very purpose, the union of oneself with the Supreme Self must be realized within this very body of grace.
And through this union, one is able to experience here and now the vision of equality (*samadarśana*), which consists in regarding all beings as one's own self.

For a human being, the Bhagavad Gītā ought to be our primary refuge for such yogic practice. This very path is designated as Śivayoga in the Śiva Āgamas. Regardless of the name by which it is designated, that reality results in happiness for everyone.

The Bhagavad Gītā reveals the true nature of such Śivayoga with ease and teaches numerous paths for its realization. Therefore, the subject matter here is precisely the exposition of the state of *sāmarasya* (perfect equilibrium), which is the union of the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Supreme (*parama*), designated as the *aṅga* and the *liṅga*. By means of such...

The purpose here is everything included in this: the soul’s realization of its own true nature through union; the experience of Śiva—who dwells within it as the inner controller (antaryāmin) and whose essence consists of the desired state of vital breath; and the soul’s abiding in self-delight, being satisfied by such nectar of knowledge.

The relationship of this treatise with its subject matter is well known as that between the means of exposition and the object to be expounded. As for the qualified students here, they are those who have studied the sciences of logic, grammar, and poetics;
who have properly experienced the aesthetic flavors (*rasa*) of poetry and drama; and who have attained purity of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*).
Those who are adept at discerning the body from the self, who are endowed with the presence of right understanding,
and who are devoted to the knowledge of the nature of the manifold and variegated phenomenal world— all practitioners, whether in the form of men or women,
[are qualified]. Thus, when the fourfold prerequisites have been described, a certain objection may arise from the perspective of the qualified candidate.

Now, one might object: since the scriptures establish that women are unfit for instruction in the ultimate truth (*tattva*), how can they also be eligible for the *Gītā*? Although this inquiry is indeed profound and subtle, nevertheless, when examined with an impartial perspective, their—

Opportunities for the realization of the science of reality (*tattva-śāstra*) are indeed seen even from ancient times. It is known that during the period of the Upaniṣads, women such as Maitreyī not only personally realized the truth of the Self (*ātman*), but also imparted such instruction to men. — Yājñavalkya.
He wished to divide and bestow his inheritance upon his own wife; then she asked him, "If [there were] immortality..."

"Do you hope for immortality through wealth? He replied, "I do not hope for immortality through wealth. Then she said, "What could I possibly do with that, if I were not immortal? Oh, what a wise, profound, and deep-seated statement this is! What kind of heroism and splendor it possesses!

In this regard, it is illuminated: whatever is performed, spoken, or contemplated with faith, knowledge, and the secret doctrine (upaniṣad) becomes more powerful. Why should such speech and action not be appropriate even for young women of today? It exists in both women and men.

Brahman is indeed of a single kind. This point is also correctly restated by Basavārya: "Just as fire is hidden in water, as sap is contained within crops, and as fragrance is established in flowers, even so is the Supreme concealed within living beings; it is hidden like affection in young girls."

Maheśvara, though omnipresent, remains hidden. Thus, in order to describe the abiding of the Supreme Self within the body, the venerable Basavārya points specifically to a daughter’s affection as the illustrative analogy. And so, since the Supreme Self exists in the same singular form within women and men alike, one may seek to realize Him just as men do [in their daughters].

The same opportunity for women also shines forth by virtue of their innate nature; therefore, they too become qualified. The venerable Vyāsa states in the Mahābhārata that it was precisely with women, Śūdras, and others in mind that the Gītā scripture was set forth: "For women, Śūdras, and the twice-born who are mere kinsmen, the three Vedas (Trayī) are not within the range of hearing."

The narrative of the Bhārata was composed by the sage out of compassion. Thus, the great seer Vyāsa composed the Gītā scripture within the Mahābhārata specifically for women, Śūdras, those fallen from their duties, and Brāhmaṇas. Having said, "Women, Vaiśyas, and likewise Śūdras," Śrī Kṛṣṇa also [addressed] women...

It provides an opportunity for Vaiśyas and even Śūdras to attain the realization of the nature of the Supreme Self. Therefore, there is a great distinction here: that without any distinction of gender or age, there is eligibility even for any seeker in general. As the saying of the learned goes: "There is no person who is unfit; rather, it is the guide therein who is difficult to find."
Indeed, all those designated as *puruṣas*—whether in male form or female form—are included within the term *gītā*.

In the human body, the conscious individual soul (*jīva*) is called *puruṣa*; even when residing in women, that same *jīva* is denoted by the word *puruṣa*. Therefore, since women are in reality *puruṣas*, [they are included].
Thus, it is entirely clear that there is indeed scope for the Gītā system [of thought].
Thus, commencing the Gītā system which is set forth to uplift the commonality of humanity, [the author] provides the occasion for its manifestation.

By means of Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s question, beginning with "Dhṛtarāṣṭra said," and so forth: "O Sañjaya, what did my sons and the Pāṇḍavas do when they had assembled on the field of dharma, Kurukṣetra, desiring to fight? (1)

On the field of dharma, which has become a field of merit, at Kurukṣetra, my men—my sons Duryodhana and the others—and the Pāṇḍavas—the sons of Pāṇḍu, Yudhiṣṭhira and the others—all assembled together, desiring to fight, wishing to wage war; what did they do? [First,] those on our side...
Having observed that his army was powerful and superior, and having realized its preponderance and great strength, did Dhṛtarāṣṭra—
out of pride for his son and curiosity— wonder whether the Pāṇḍavas had desisted from battle due to doubt regarding their own victory, or whether they had indeed commenced fighting with them?
He asks Sañjaya for news of the battle. || 1 ||
Having seen the Pandava army drawn up in battle array, King Duryodhana approached his teacher and spoke these words.
Sañjaya said: The cessation of the fear of the Pāṇḍavas is expressed by the word *tu* (but).

The sense is that they had no fear at all; rather, it was Duryodhana himself who became afraid. Then, at the encounter of both sides, King Duryodhana, having formed his battle array and performed the other necessary arrangements, [proceeded].
Having seen the Pāṇḍava army stationed there, he approached the teacher Droṇa, went very close to him, and spoke these words— that speech which is about to be told. || 2 ||
Behold, O Teacher, this vast army of the sons of Pāṇḍu, drawn up in battle array by the wise son of Drupada, your own disciple. (3)
The previously mentioned intention is now elaborated upon: by the son of Drupada— that is, by the son of King Drupada,

who is your disciple and who has acquired the science of archery from you alone— the wise and intelligent Dhṛṣṭadyumna has arranged [the army] through the formation of battle arrays and other such dispositions.
Behold, look upon this great army of vast proportions standing before you—the host of the sons of Pāṇḍu, the Pāṇḍavas.
By stating that it is a "great army" despite being inferior in number, the fear rooted in Duryodhana’s underlying lack of confidence is indicated. || 3 ||
He reveals this very fear that has arisen in his heart in detail:
"In this [army] are heroes, great archers equal to Bhīma and Arjuna in battle—
Yuyudhāna, Virāṭa, and Drupada, the great chariot-warrior."
Dhṛṣṭaketu, Cekitāna, the heroic King of Kāśī, Purujit, Kuntibhoja, and Śaivya, that bull among men; || 5 ||
And the valiant Yudhāmanyu, the heroic Uttamaujas, the son of Subhadrā, and the sons of Draupadī—all of them were indeed great chariot-warriors (mahārathas). || 6 ||

In this case, on the side of the Pāṇḍavas, there are heroes, full of valor, and great archers whose fame is exceedingly renowned. Arjuna is celebrated for his strength in weaponry. All those from Yuyudhāna down to the sons of Draupadī are equal to these two; indeed, they are all great car-warriors (*mahārathas*) who [protect] themselves, their charioteers, and their own armies.
Furthermore, "A man who protects [his side] and fights in every respect is called a mahāratha.

Since they are endowed with these previously described characteristics of a full-fledged hero, and since all those existing on that side are likewise mahārathas, it was said earlier that there was a "vast army" with this intention in mind.
Having thus described the superiority of the enemy's force despite its small numbers, he speaks of the inferiority of his own side in terms of strength despite its numerical superiority:
"But as for those among us who are distinguished, learn of them, O best of the twice-born."
I speak of them for the sake of signaling the leaders of my army.

By the word "tu" (but), a distinction from the opposing side is indicated. For while all those on their side are indeed *mahārathas*, all those on our side are experts in battle; yet, though they are somewhat superior to ordinary heroes, they are not *mahārathas* by that alone. Even though there are *mahārathas* here such as Bhīṣma, Droṇa, and others, nevertheless—

Not all [on our side] are great chariot-warriors (*mahāratha*s), but on his side, however, all are indeed great chariot-warriors. This distinction is indicated by the word "but" (*tu*). O best of the twice-born, those who are distinguished on our side—[p.
28]—are as follows:
Listen and hear of those who are endowed with virtues such as valor; although you already know all this, I nevertheless name those who are the foremost in my army for the sake of enumeration.
Yourself, Bhīṣma, Karṇa, Kṛpa the victor in assembly, Aśvatthāman, Vikarṇa, the son of Somadatta, and Jayadratha; || 8 ||
And there are many other heroes who have renounced their lives for my sake;
they carry various weapons and missiles, and all are experts in warfare.
Moreover, there are many other heroes besides you who have renounced their lives for my sake and are ready to offer up their very breaths;
they possess various weapons and implements of war, such as maces, clubs, and the like. All of them are indeed experts in combat. || 9 ||
Thus, having weighed the enemy's force against his own, he states his conclusion: "That army of ours, though protected by Bhīṣma, is insufficient;
