but this army of theirs, protected by Bhīma, is sufficient. (10)

Therefore, in comparison with our own side, because of the superiority of the great chariot-warriors (*mahāratha*) on the enemy's side, this army—the force of the Pāṇḍavas protected by Bhīma—is sufficient for its own task; whereas that of the others is insufficient, immeasurable, yet excessive, being capable of insulting us and thus overwhelming. It is sufficient [for them].
They explain it as being extremely limited and incapable of our victory; however, the natural sense remains exactly as stated previously. || 10 ||
Thus, recognizing the weakness of his own side, Duryodhana said that everyone must remain vigilant in the protection of the aged grandfather Bhīṣma, the commander-in-chief:
"And in all the strategic positions (*ayana*), stationed according to your respective assignments..."
Therefore, let all of you indeed protect Bhīṣma alone.

*Ayana* refers to the position on the battlefield occupied by warriors during the intensity of combat, corresponding to their respective individual forms. Therefore, in all *ayanas*, one should remain in one's own fixed position according to one's allotted share.

"Indeed, all of you remaining here must protect our commander-in-chief Bhīṣma by every possible means; you must guard him thoroughly. Since the army is dependent upon its commander-in-chief, when he is protected, the entire army will be protected—this is the meaning. || 11 ||

Thus, in order to encourage King Duryodhana who was speaking thus to the preceptor Droṇa out of a lack of fortitude, the commander-in-chief and the grandfather Bhīṣma exerted himself; so it is said: "The grandfather of the Kurus, the grandsire, [spoke], generating joy in him."
Having uttered a lion’s roar loudly, the powerful one blew his conch shell.
Bringing forth— that is, perfectly generating— joy and satisfaction for King Duryodhana,

the powerful Bhīṣma, the elder of the Kurus, who was increased in the Kuru lineage and possessed great strength and prowess, let out a lion’s roar to dispel his fear and [strike] terror into those of the enemy.

Having let out a roar like the lion's roar— uttered by heroes to strike fear into their enemies and to inspire courage in their own— the meaning is that he made a "lion's roar" (the usage is like *pākaṃ pacati*, "he cooks the cooking"); he blew his own conch shell, that is, he filled it with sound.
Thus, having been encouraged by the commander-in-chief, all the others did exactly the same; so he says:
"Then conchs, kettledrums, *praṇavas*, *ānakas*, and *gomukhas* were suddenly sounded, and that sound became tumultuous. (13)

Then, immediately thereafter, conchs, *praṇava* drums, *gomukhas*, and kettledrums were suddenly struck; and that sound produced by them was all-pervading, causing fear to the opposing side. Thus, as the Pandava armies witnessed this encouragement of Duryodhana’s faction, their lack of fortitude [became apparent].

To show that the partisans of the Pāṇḍavas likewise strove to encourage their own army so that such a thing might not happen, he says: "Then, stationed upon a great chariot yoked with white horses..."
Mādhava and the Pāṇḍava likewise blew their two divine conchs.
Then, after the sounding of kettledrums and other instruments by the enemy's side, Mādhava— Śrī Kṛṣṇa— and Pāṇḍu— Arjuna— were seated together in a great, massive chariot yoked with white horses.
(30) They both blew their divine conchs— conchs distinguished by their own divine power— and filled them [with sound]. || 14 ||
Hṛṣīkeśa blew the Pāñcajanya, Dhanañjaya the Devadatta, and Vṛkodara, the doer of terrible deeds, blew the great conch Pauṇḍra. || 15 ||
King Yudhiṣṭhira, the son of Kuntī, took Anantavijaya;
Nakula and Sahadeva took Suṣeṇa and Maṇipuṣpaka respectively.
Kāśya, the supreme archer, and Śikhaṇḍin, the great chariot-warrior;
Dhṛṣṭadyumna, Virāṭa, and the unconquered Sātyaki. || 17 ||
O lord of the earth, Drupada, the sons of Draupadī, and the mighty-armed son of Subhadrā, all blew their conchs individually from every side.
"Pāñcajanya" is the name of Śrī Kṛṣṇa’s conch; "Devadatta" is the name of Arjuna’s conch.

The same applies to those mentioned further on. Thus, encouraged by the blowing of the conchs by the principal heroes, all the other warriors as well—beginning with the King of Kāśī (Kāśya), the ruler of Kāśī—[prepared for battle].
Each one blew his own conch shell individually, filling it with sound.
Thus, when the Pandava army was emboldened by Śrī Kṛṣṇa and others with the sounds of divine conchs, a great fear arose in the army of Duryodhana upon hearing this; so it is said:
"That roar tore apart the hearts of the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra."
The tumultuous sound caused both the sky and the earth to resound. || 19 ||

Making the sky and the earth resound, especially by producing echoes, that tumultuous and all-pervading sound— the blast of the conch— tore asunder, that is, split apart, the ranks of Dhṛtarāṣṭra’s sons, headed by Duryodhana. || 19 ||
Thus, although the hearts of Duryodhana and the others were shaken by this outward appearance, he created an opportunity to bring about a manifold transformation through some pretext:
"Then, seeing the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra standing there, the one whose banner bears the monkey..."
When the discharge of weapons had begun, the son of Pāṇḍu raised his bow. (20)
O lord of the earth, he then spoke these words to Hṛṣīkeśa.

The address "O lord of the earth" is Sañjaya’s way of addressing Dhṛtarāṣṭra. Then [he saw] all the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Duryodhana and the others, stationed in their respective positions, well-prepared for battle.
Then, having seen that, the son of Pāṇḍu, Arjuna— whose banner bears the monkey (kapidhvaja)— when the clash of weapons (śastrasaṃpāta),
meaning the mutual discharge of missiles, had begun, [he acted] through such encouragement as the sounds of conchs from both sides and by signaling the commencement of the battle.
When the mutual discharge of arrows had begun— meaning that having raised his own bow and held it in his hand,
he made himself ready to discharge an arrow— he spoke these words about to be mentioned to Hṛṣīkeśa, Śrī Kṛṣṇa. Here, by the use of the word *hṛṣīkeśa*, there is this particular significance.

It is indicated that this was done by the Blessed Lord himself. *Hṛṣīka* means a sense organ; Amara states, "The sense organ is the instrument for objects. He is the Lord (*īśa*), the impeller of those [senses]. For that Blessed Lord is the master of all the senses; indeed, he himself will say much later, "From Me come memory, knowledge, and their removal" (15.15). Therefore, this is *adhyātma*.

This is indicated by the term *Hṛṣīkeśa*. Now, one might ask: for what purpose was this instruction given on the battlefield of war? Surely, the science of reality (*tattva-śāstra*) ought to be taught while sitting somewhere in seclusion. This is true; however, the science of the self (*adhyātma-śāstra*)...

All people are immersed in delusion, thinking in such ways as: "That which accomplishes mere dry detachment is useless for worldly conduct and is, in fact, contrary to it; therefore, it serves no purpose for the world and instead causes only conflict. Thus, they withdraw from all efforts toward the study of the spiritual scriptures (*adhyātma-śāstra*).

Some even wander into the error of thinking it must be "accomplished. They say that only those whose youth has faded—the elderly—are qualified for the spiritual science (*adhyātma-śāstra*); that science is not for the young.
Furthermore, they claim that only those who are incapacitated in body, mind, and intellect [are fit] for the mere passing of time.

Some dull-witted people think that they should study the inner science (adhyātmaśāstra); others think that men and women occupied with royal affairs will be able to study the inner science immediately after the completion of their own duties.
In order to dispel such delusions,
the Lord begins the instruction on Vedānta right in the midst of the army; this is the nature of the science of the inner self (adhyātma-śāstra).

In order to demonstrate the utility of both spiritual and worldly activity, the instruction was begun on the very field of battle; conversely, in order to demonstrate how spiritual knowledge produces engagement in one's own duty among those who are sluggish with pride, possessed of false conceit, and self-conceited, the teaching was given right within the sphere of action.

With the intention that [the teaching] might be successfully accomplished, the Lord created the opportunity for its instruction on the very field of battle, in order to directly demonstrate the such-like potency of that scripture through action itself. For Arjuna had already [slain] all those on his own side as well as those on the enemy's side.
It was simply out of ignorance; his desire to see them arose as if from novelty, and by seeing them he became disillusioned,

which led him to desist from battle, saying "I will not fight"— that speech of his, and finally the proclamation that "his delusion is destroyed," all of this would not have occurred spontaneously without the impulsion of the Blessed Lord.

Such matters as the Lord’s role as the impeller of all the senses, the dependence of the senses upon Him, and the fact that the spiritual science culminates in practice— all these points are clearly indicated by the term *Hṛṣīkeśa*. Therefore, [the Lord] [emphasizes] the culmination of the scripture in practice for the sake of all.

In order to demonstrate [the truth] through direct perception itself, the instruction on the inner self (adhyātma) and its scriptures, given under some pretext on the very field of battle, would not be a fault. The remaining subject matter will be presented elsewhere as the occasion arises. || 20 ||
He then states what Arjuna, impelled by the Lord residing in his heart, said:
"O Acyuta, station my chariot between the two armies. (21)
"Let me observe these who have arrived desiring to fight;
with whom must I contend in this martial endeavor? (22)
I shall observe those who have gathered here,
desiring to do what is pleasing in battle to the evil-minded son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, as they prepare for combat.

O Acyuta Kṛṣṇa! From the use of the term "Acyuta," it is understood that Kṛṣṇa, though a human being, is free from destruction and is indeed the Supreme Self itself. Thus, he is devoid of birth and destruction—the Supreme...

The Blessed One, Mahādeva himself, whose form is divinely auspicious, stood before Arjuna under the name of Kṛṣṇa. Arjuna, the pure soul, with a sincere heart, manifested his own intention— which was to achieve future welfare— directly before the Supreme Self in the midst of both armies.
"Stop my chariot and remain stationary for the duration of a few moments. To the question "For what purpose?", he says:

"Until," and so forth. "Until I have observed"—meaning, in such a way that I may see—"those who stand firm, desiring to fight," that is, those who are stationed there wishing to engage in battle; stop the chariot so that I may behold them.

"Station them so that they may be easily observed. The explanation of "who are those to be observed" is given by the words "by whom," and so forth; that is to say, "by whom. This is intended to indicate despondency: "In this undertaking of war, considering me to be a mere child, who would wish to engage in battle with me in opposition?"
By the word "by whom" (yaiḥ), it was implied "by which [people]"; he clarifies this very point in detail with the words beginning "those about to fight," and so forth.

It refers to the son of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, who possesses a wicked mind—that is, a mind intent on malice—and who desires to commit full treachery against us, even though we might desire peace for any reason whatsoever, such as for the sake of five villages.

While that battle of Duryodhana was thus proceeding, those who have assembled here on this field of combat— desiring to do what is pleasing to such a brother by means of our own slaughter, and wishing to act accordingly— I observe them well; I look closely at those who are about to fight.

Thus addressed by Arjuna, Śrī Kṛṣṇa, although the Lord of all, remained as his charioteer out of affection for those who have taken refuge in Him; and He fulfilled the specific command of His master at that time exactly as requested— so Sañjaya said to Dhṛtarāṣṭra:
Thus addressed by Guḍākeśa, O Bhārata, Hṛṣīkeśa, having stationed that best of chariots between the two armies, [said]: || 24 ||
In the presence of Bhīṣma, Droṇa, and all the lords of the earth,
he said, "O Pārtha, behold these Kurus assembled here."
"O Bhārata" is an address to Dhṛtarāṣṭra. Hṛṣīkeśa is the impeller of the internal and external organs.
By this, it is indicated that such an awakening of the intellect in Arjuna was brought about by Him alone.
Such [is He].
(On page 34:

Śrī Kṛṣṇa, who is an incarnation of the Supreme Self (paramātman), having been thus addressed by Guḍākeśa—namely Arjuna—in this manner, [the meaning is] "having caused [them] to be stationed. O Pārtha, [he spoke to] the many Kurus who had assembled for the sake of battle.

"Behold those who belong to the faction of Duryodhana," he said. Here, the use of the term *guḍākeśa* is appropriate as it is significant in meaning and etymologically justified. *Guḍākā* means sleep; its *īśa* (lord) means one who has conquered sleep. Now, sleep is indeed a harmful transformation of *tamas* (darkness), and that was conquered by Arjuna, whose nature is wakefulness.

Indeed, for the sake of attaining the Pāśupata state, he performed extraordinary austerities; it is well known that at that time he completely abandoned sleep, laziness, and the like, and thus he was of a purely sattvic nature. However, by the prompting of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, delusion regarding his kinsmen arose in his mind.
For the sake of the world's welfare and for the purpose of providing instruction, this opportunity was thus fashioned by the Supreme Self alone.

In reality, Arjuna was of a pure nature; therefore, the word *guḍākeśa* (the one with matted locks) indicates the intention that he had become worthy of instruction. This is what is fitting here and brings beauty to the context.
What happened then? What did Arjuna see? To this he says:
"There Partha saw standing his fathers, then his grandfathers, teachers, maternal uncles, brothers, sons, grandsons, and friends as well. (26)
Arjuna saw his fathers-in-law and friends, as well as his fathers and grandfathers, stationed in both armies. Having observed all those kinsmen standing there, that son of Kuntī— || 27 ||
Overcome by supreme compassion and despondent, he spoke this;

having looked at them and observed them thoroughly, being despondent, he thought, "My fathers, grandfathers, and others are indeed to be slain"—Arjuna realized that one must fight with one's own kin. Nevertheless, even though he knew through his intellect that [this was so], on the one hand...
The meaning is that as he beheld them assembled together, grief arose in his heart solely through the impulsion of the Blessed Lord. || 27 ||
(35) To the one thus despondent, he said: "O Kṛṣṇa, having seen these kinsmen standing here eager for battle... (28)
My limbs fail me and my mouth is parched.
O Kṛṣṇa, seeing these kinsmen standing here eager for battle, my limbs fail— that is, they grow weary— and my mouth is parched, becoming lusterless due to grief.
Trembling arises in my body and my hair stands on end. || 29 ||
The Gāṇḍīva bow slips from my hand, and my skin burns;
a trembling arises in my body, as well as horripilation born of fear, loathing, and the like. Even the Gāṇḍīva bow falls from my hand, and my skin and flesh are scorched. (29)
And I am unable to remain steady; my mind, as it were, reels.
And I see omens that have turned adverse, O Keśava;
nor do I foresee any good in slaying my own kinsmen in battle. (31)
I do not desire victory, O Kṛṣṇa, nor kingdom, nor pleasures.

I have no wish to stand before these men who are enemies without cause. Having reflected, "For what purpose must I fight with these people who seek only their own self-interest? a delusion has arisen in my mind.
Even as I have come to fight with these, adverse omens are appearing;
by slaying these kinsmen in battle, no fruit whatsoever is obtained by me, nor is victory even desired in this war. What is to be gained from such a sinful deed?
Let there be no kingdom for me either.
To the question, "Why do you not desire victory and the like in battle? he says:
"O Govinda, what have we to do with kingdom, what with enjoyments, or even with life? (32)
For whose sake we desired kingdom, enjoyments, and pleasures—
those very people now stand here in battle, having renounced both their lives and their wealth.

I do not desire this kingdom out of a mere devotion to my own self-interest; rather, I desire it only with the thought that I might be happy together with my kinsmen. If my kinsmen themselves should perish in this battle, then what would be the use of it for me?

What use would I have for this kingdom? Those for whose sake I shall fight—such kinsmen, wealth, and gold—are already present here. And I shall certainly kill them; but having killed them, what purpose would such a kingdom serve?
With whom should the pleasure of sovereignty be shared? And who are those who must be bound by me? To this [he says]:
"The teachers, fathers, sons, and likewise grandfathers;
maternal uncles, fathers-in-law, grandsons, brothers-in-law, and other kinsmen. (34)
Arjuna’s intention was that these teachers, being his kinsmen, are worthy of worship and must certainly not be killed.
If it be argued that since they are prepared to kill you, they too ought to be killed by you for the sake of self-protection— to this I reply:
"O Madhusūdana, I do not wish to kill these men, even though they are killing me."
How much less, then, for the sake of sovereignty over the three worlds, or even for the sake of the earth? || 35 ||

"Even if, by killing these men, I were to attain sovereignty over the three worlds, let that not be mine; this indeed is my resolve. In such a situation, for the sake of mere earthly power or for the sake of a kingdom in this world, why indeed should I engage in battle? It would be better even if I were slain by them. As for me—"
I do not wish to kill them in this battle under any circumstances. || 35 ||
To the question, "Why do you not wish to kill even those who are intent on slaying you? he says:
"O Janārdana, what joy could come to us by killing the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra?
By killing these aggressors, only sin would take hold of us. (36)

Thus, since there is no expectation even for the sovereignty of the three worlds, what joy or satisfaction (*prīti-santoṣa*) would there be for us after killing these sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra? The meaning is: none at all. Having harbored hatred toward us without cause, these men are indeed *ātatāyins* (assassins), being even prepared to kill us; and *ātatāyins* are perpetrators of great sins (*mahāpātakin*).
If I were to kill such people as those, even greater sin than that would accrue to me;
for it is by wise men like us that it is held that sinners must themselves experience the fruit of their own committed sins—therefore, we should remain silent.
One must remain steadfast. If we were to abandon such a path and slay them out of desire, anger, and the like, their sin would recoil upon us alone. Therefore, it is not right to kill these men;
consequently, we ought not to slay the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra along with their kinsmen.
For how, O Mādhava, could we be happy after having slain our own kin? (37)
Who indeed could become happy after killing his own kinsmen? Such a person would be nothing but a fool;
he shall never find happiness in this world.
To the question, "In that case, how did those relatives of yours become prepared to kill you?", he says:
"Even though these people, their minds afflicted by greed, do not perceive the evil resulting from the destruction of the family, nor the sin in betraying friends. (38)
O Janārdana, how could we not know how to turn away from this sin, when we clearly perceive the evil brought about by the destruction of our own kin? (39)

These men, Duryodhana and the others, have lost their sense through greed for the kingdom; out of such greed, they are utterly unaware of the destruction of their lineage and other evils. Knowing this full well, how could I commit such a sin?
We, who clearly perceive and fully experience the fault caused by the ruin of the family—[how could we do so?]
How is it not known how to turn away from this sin? How is such cessation from sin not contemplated? Therefore, some means must indeed be devised for the cessation of sin.

Regarding the question, "What is that great evil in the destruction of a family?", the great evil that arises here is the intermingling of castes (*varṇasaṃkara*). [Gītā 1.41]: "Upon the destruction of a family, the eternal family traditions perish.
When dharma is lost, indeed, unrighteousness (*adharma*) overcomes everything. (40)
O Kṛṣṇa, through the overwhelming power of unrighteousness, the women of the family become corrupt;
O Vārṣṇeya, when women are corrupted, the intermixture of castes arises. (41)

Upon the extinction of a lineage, the self-destruction of even those customs and practices transmitted through traditional succession becomes unavoidable. Thus, when the boundaries of right conduct (*sadācāra*) and other norms are destroyed, human beings, being inherently weak, [will themselves...]
Or, due to the insistence of others, they might be defiled by those belonging to other [castes]; and because of that, [the status of] Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, and Vaiśyas would be compromised.
Let there be an intermixture of castes. If it is asked, "What loss is there in this?", he declares its great evil nature:
"The intermixture leads only to hell for both the destroyers of the lineage and for the lineage itself;
for their ancestors fall, deprived of the offerings of rice-balls and water. (42)
Confusion means the intermixture of castes (*varṇasaṃkara*). For those destroyers of the family, the destruction of the family becomes the cause of the confusion of castes;

it is not merely that their own dharma is lost when the family is ruined, but rather, even those who are the perpetrators of that family's destruction—the very causes of this fault—are themselves gradually destroyed by the power of that sin.
It has been stated that they will surely exist. Having said "only for hell," he says "they fall.

For this reason—because the ancestors of these destroyers of their lineage and those whose lineages have perished would fall, that is, they would descend, with the funeral offerings of rice balls and water lost, and the ancestral rites destroyed.

The very birth of a son is renowned as the means for discharging such debts. Since all men die in battle, there would be no men left to perform the *śrāddha* rites; and when even the ancestral rites (*paitṛka-kriyā*) are abandoned, the ancestors (*pitṛ-devatā*) would become enraged. Therefore—
By abandoning the virtuous act of worshipping Maheśvara, which is dedicated to Mahādeva in his form as the Father (Pitṛ),
the fruit thereof— the suffering of hell and other realms— will surely accrue to everyone.
If it is argued that the mere mixture of castes does not preclude the possibility of a son being born— on the grounds that whoever is born will,
for the sake of his father’s ancestors, perform the propitiation of the devotees of Maheśvara with food—
that too is impossible; thus he says:
By these faults of the destroyers of the family, which cause the intermixture of castes, the eternal laws of the classes and the laws of the families are destroyed. (43)
O Janārdana, we have heard it said that for those men whose family traditions are destroyed, residence in hell is inevitable.

O Janārdana, because of these faults—namely, the destruction of the lineage and the intermixture of castes—the eternal duties of those who protect the world have perished through the decay of their families.

If these [castes] continue for such a length of time, they will be eradicated and perish. Would a son born through such intermixture not be born devoid of caste, family, and so forth? And how could he know the duties (dharma) inherited through his own caste and family lineage? Therefore, in the case of intermixture, there is the destruction of dharma.

This is unavoidable. Therefore, we have heard from the Śruti and Smṛti that for those humans whose family traditions are destroyed and whose caste and family traditions are lost, a residence in hell inevitably arises;
hence, it is impossible to deny that such social confusion leads only to hell.
With his mind trembling at the mere thought that he alone might be the cause of such a great sin—the intermingling of castes—Arjuna, out of fear of evil, spoke thus:
"Alas! Oh, we have resolved to commit a great sin!"
Those who, out of greed for the pleasures of sovereignty, have prepared to kill their own kinsmen. || 45 ||

The two indeclinables *aho bata* indicate astonishment, distress, shame, and so forth, suggesting the thought: "Alas! How has such a mind of mine arisen—one that causes the intermingling of castes? For, out of greed for the pleasures of sovereignty—that is, the desire for the happiness dependent upon attaining a kingdom—we have, through wicked ambition, [abandoned] our own kin.

They were prepared and equipped to kill their very own kinsmen, such as fathers and brothers; thus, they had resolved and determined to commit a great sin. In this way, it is shown that the duties of the castes and stages of life are established by the Vedas and traditional conduct, and that their confusion leads to hell.

In order to fully demonstrate this succession of calamities—including the attainment of hell and other such states even for those who cause such confusion—Vyāsa composed the introductory passage beginning with "Alas! (aho bata).
Furthermore, the Blessed One will state later: "I would become the author of confusion and I would destroy these creatures."

In this [verse], the fact that confusion (*saṅkara*) causes the destruction of everything is shown; and in the verse, "The fourfold order of castes was created by me according to the division of qualities and actions," the fact that the duties of the castes and stages of life (*varṇāśramadharma*) were created by Him is shown. Now, one might object: by the phrase "according to the division of qualities and actions," is it not implied that being a Brāhmaṇa and so forth depends solely upon qualities and actions?

If it is argued that [the relationship] is known through cognition, then every quality or every action would not necessarily be able to connect with all [things] equally; for it is not possible for everything to be performed by everyone. For example, qualities such as forbearance and generosity belong to Brāhmaṇas, while qualities such as vigor and heroism belong to Kṣatriyas, being connected to them by way of their respective castes (*varṇa*).

Furthermore, those [qualities] that follow along would not be achievable through mere effort; rather, the nourishment of these qualities already existing by their very root is what must be accomplished through effort. Therefore, the castes such as Brahminhood and so forth, which reside in the seed, must necessarily be accepted.

40) For this very reason, the word "jāti" (birth/class) is employed here with the thought that "the characteristics of birth are also eradicated. Therefore, the [distinctions of] caste and stage of life (*varṇāśrama*) are established. Furthermore, if the duties of caste and stage of life were not accepted, everyone would be able to perform everything.

In that regard, even if one does not accept the establishment of dharma based on the distinction of caste (*jāti*), its acceptance based on the distinction of stages of life (*āśrama*) is absolutely necessary. Otherwise, even the systematic arrangement of the stages of life— such as that sexual enjoyment with a woman is *dharma* for a householder but constitutes a great *adharma* for a renunciant— would not have to be accepted.

Consequently, there would also be a confusion among the four stages of life (āśramas)—namely, the student (brahmacārin), the householder (gṛhastha), the forest-dweller (vānaprastha), and the renunciant (saṃnyāsin). Even for the student, there would be the enjoyment of sense objects and so forth. As a result, even human beings would become like animals. And if the duties of the stages of life are accepted, then [the consequences] recited along with them...

The duties of the social classes (varṇadharma) must also be accepted; therefore, it is not proper for the duties of the classes and stages of life (varṇāśramadharma) to be denied by those who are discerning and well-refined. Those who are completely dispassionate, immersed in the bliss of knowledge, and experience Śiva, are called "beyond the classes and stages of life" (ativarṇāśramin).

Even though they have transcended the duties of the castes and stages of life (*varṇāśrama-dharma*), they abide practicing the most exalted dharma characterized by the vision of equality, out of a perspective for the welfare of the world. Having entered the path of absolute knowledge (*kevalajñāna*) and being dissolved in equanimity (*samarasa*), such persons are indeed those who have transcended the castes and stages of life. Of them—
This deliberation is never to be scrutinized by others. This point was perfectly revealed by Basavārya:

"May those who are solely devoted to Śiva and have taken refuge [in Him] dwell eternally in this world in whatever form they may; may those noble souls whose minds are fixed on Śiva alone dwell upon the earth in whatever manner possible; for they are of a virtuous nature."

Let those whose desires have ceased dwell in the world by whatever means of livelihood; let this jewel, though rough, be a purifier, for it still purifies iron in this world. Let those oceans of nectar, who are devoted to the Supreme Lord, dwell in the world according to their own inclination; for the state of such wise ones is of a different and extraordinary kind.

[The world] continues. For now, let them abandon the duties of caste and stage of life (*varṇāśramadharma*); there would be no loss whatsoever by that much. Nevertheless, not everyone has attained such a state. Since those duties of caste and stage of life were created by the Lord and are therefore unavoidable, they must certainly be observed. Only when this is done will they [also]...

Gradually, they will be able to obtain the grace of Śiva. Even by all those submerged in the ocean of worldly existence, the duties of the stages of life (āśramadharma) and so forth must indeed be practiced.

This intention is restated in my *Śaraṇagītā*: "If everything were condensed into its own essence like a pearl, how could the ocean carry water? Likewise, if all living beings were fallen due to behaving like beasts, how could they attain the realization of the Supreme Self? And if by all of them that [realization]..."

When existence on this earth is thus attained, where could one find further growth? Therefore, devotees have indeed become rare, just as [the presence of] the god at Kūḍalacannasaṅgam is rare; likewise, among a hundred thousand there is but one saint, while among ten million there is but one true refuge-seeker. In this way, all human beings strive only to attain the state of a devotee.
They would not have been able [to prevail]. Therefore, if they should become *ativarṇāśramins*, you must remain steadfast against their increasing transformations. More on this is unnecessary here.
Now, if you do not engage in battle, then the enemies will [overcome] you as you sit in silence.

Anticipating the objection that they might kill me, he states his acceptance of the consequence: "If the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, with weapons in hand, were to slay me in battle while I am unresisting and unarmed, that would be better for me. (46)

If the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the partisans of Duryodhana, with weapons in hand, were to kill me in this battle while I stand silent— having been disarmed, having cast away my weapons, and for that very reason being unable to offer resistance even though they have set out to slay me—
that alone would be more secure for me than saving myself from falling into hell and other such fates.
It shall be conducive to welfare. || 46 ||
Having spoken thus on the battlefield, Arjuna, his mind agitated by grief, cast aside his bow and arrows and sat down upon the seat of the chariot.

Pointing out Arjuna’s despondency in this manner, Sañjaya said: Having manifested grief, world-weariness, and so forth in the manner described, Arjuna— whose mind was agitated by grief, that is, distressed— stood upon the battlefield (*saṃkhye*), on that very field of combat.
Casting aside his bow with the arrow and leaving it far behind, he sat down right at the edge of the chariot— on the seat, the rim, or even in the middle of the chariot—
out of loathing; thus Arjuna, fallen under the sway of nature, forgot his duty and succumbed to his own despondency.
He reported: "In that very same way, all living beings are deluded during the time of worldly activity. To remove that delusion, Arjuna’s despondency was [addressed] by means of divine... (p. 42)
They obtain.
Now begins the second chapter.
Then, to Dhṛtarāṣṭra, who desired to hear what happened next out of curiosity, Sañjaya reported the Lord’s commencement of the effort to dispel Arjuna’s despondency:
To him who was thus overcome with compassion, whose eyes were clouded and filled with tears, and who was despondent, Madhusūdana spoke these words: || 1 ||

Thus, permeated—that is, filled—with such compassion and pity, and for that very reason [overcome] by the slaughter of his kinsmen, Madhusūdana spoke these words. The construction is like "he cooks the cooking" (*pākaṃ pacati*). By saying "he spoke these words," it is indicated that Kṛṣṇa is the one who prevents [the world from falling into ruin]. || 1 ||
Whence has this dejection come upon you in this hour of crisis, O Arjuna? It is unworthy of the noble, it leads away from heaven, and it brings infamy.

The Blessed One said: O Arjuna, this degrading impurity—which is resorted to by ignoble, foolish people who do not understand the meaning of the scriptures, and which is practiced only by the vulgar—is therefore unfit for heaven, unworthy of the next world, disgraceful, bringing ill-repute, and unsuitable for this world; it is a corruption in times of crisis.
In this time of adversity, when it is your duty to act, why have you arrived here at this moment? If you knew that war was unrighteous, then it should have been avoided from the very beginning.
Even though an effort was made to avoid it, since this war has now occurred as something unavoidable, a Kshatriya must not—
One must flee at some point; however, fleeing from the field of battle is certainly not the duty of a Kṣatriya.

Since you speak of the great sin of the intermixture of castes (*varṇasaṅkara*), you must necessarily observe the duties of your own caste. By abandoning one's own duty, the intermixture of castes will surely come to pass.

43) For a Kṣatriya, the duty (*dharma*) in battle is indeed the subduing of enemies. Even in that regard, this battle has come about quite involuntarily. If you say, "Even so, it shall not be done," then first of all, you yourself must [abide by] the duty of your social class (*varṇadharma*).
"not fleeing from battle; generosity and lordliness are the duties of a Kṣatriya born of his own nature.

Thus, not fleeing from battle is the duty ordained for you as a Kṣatriya. For you, who speak of the excellence of the castes and stages of life (varṇāśrama), this [fleeing] would constitute an abandonment of the duties of your own caste.

Since you are unworthy of committing such a great unrighteousness, how has this kind of defilement—this turbidity of mind—come upon you? If you are dispassionate, then you should go to the forest only after completing the task you have undertaken. Moreover, not fleeing from battle is indeed your duty; for this very reason it is said:
"By the words 'when danger has arisen' and so forth... [Verse 2]

Thus, for a Kṣatriya, desisting from a battle that must necessarily be fought is indeed the mark of a eunuch, and not the mark of a heroic Kṣatriya. Therefore, you must certainly stand with enthusiasm on the field of battle— do not fall into unmanliness, O Pārtha, for this is not worthy of you.
Casting aside this petty weakness of heart, arise, O scorcher of the foe!
O Pārtha Arjuna, do not yield to unmanliness or weakness; do not fall into it.

For one such as you—a heroic Kṣatriya who has fought even with Maheśvara and possesses stainless power—this kind of timidity is neither appropriate nor fitting. This [weakness] does not become one born of a great lineage.
Such a statement is not appropriate; therefore, this is merely a base weakness of heart born of a petty mind.

This is not dispassion (*vairāgya*), but rather simply a frailty of the mind. The sense is that even compassion and other such qualities, when misplaced, arise solely from a weakness of mind. Abandoning this, arise and prepare for battle.
Act! The display of compassion on the field of battle does not befit you. || 3 ||

Thus, when the Blessed One had induced in Arjuna both cowardice and weakness of mind, Arjuna said— intending that "there is no weakness of mind in me, nor am I a eunuch; rather, this battle we are about to engage in is not a righteous war (dharmayuddha), but an unrighteous war (adharmayuddha)"— as follows:
O Madhusūdana, O slayer of enemies, how shall I fight back against Bhīṣma and Droṇa in battle with my arrows, they who are worthy of worship?
"O Madhusūdana, how shall I fight with arrows in battle against my grandfather Bhīṣma and my preceptor Droṇa, who are both worthy of worship by me and most venerable?"
I shall fight back; even when struck by them, I must behave with respect toward their domain.
Therefore, it is my resolve that I should remain silent [in retaliation]. For they are indeed worthy of my reverence; thus, the meaning is that I do not desist from the fight out of fear. || 4 ||
He says that even compared to such unrighteousness, the practice of begging for alms is better for me:
"Indeed, it is better to live on alms in this world than to slay these high-souled teachers;
for by slaying my teachers—who are driven by the desire for wealth—I would only enjoy pleasures stained with blood right here. (5)

It is indeed better (śreyaḥ) to enjoy even the sustenance obtained by wandering for alms in this world, without killing—that is, without committing the slaughter of—teachers who possess great power and are most worthy of worship; for wandering for alms is truly more beneficial than the killing of teachers. But having killed teachers...

"I would enjoy—that is, experience—here, in this very world, pleasures consisting of wealth and desire that are smeared with blood, stained red, and utterly contemptible. Such is Arjuna's intention: that for one who desires such wealth and sensual enjoyment, the practice of begging alone is in every way conducive to the highest good in this world. || 5 ||
Indeed, for a Kṣatriya, because it is his own duty, battle alone is better than wandering for alms;
nor do we know which is weightier for us: whether we should conquer them, or whether they should conquer us.
Those very sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, after killing whom we would not wish to live, stand arrayed before us.
We do not know which is better for us:

whether we shall conquer the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, or whether the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra shall conquer us. Furthermore, we do not know how we shall fare after having slain our own brothers, such as Duryodhana and the others.
"We wish to live; we desire to remain alive. Those sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra stand right before us, face to face. And thus, I would not desire a kingdom to be obtained by killing my brothers and others."
Arjuna presented his own intention: "Due to my delusion regarding my kinsmen, I have forgotten my very duty.
Although Duryodhana and the others have caused me great suffering out of malice since childhood, they certainly do not deserve compassion; nevertheless, Arjuna [felt] toward them..."

One who desires to practice compassion abandons one's own duty in the form of slaying the wicked. In the very same way, all worldly people, while practicing compassion toward the unworthy and though aware of their own weakness, do not strive to acquire the appropriate fitness necessary for the fulfillment of their own duties. He who acts thus...

They bring about fitness; therein, yoga in the form of the Lord’s grace becomes possible. This very harmony between such [grace] and fitness accomplishes the welfare of the world through the welfare of humanity.
Yoga, for its part, depends solely upon fitness; fitness, in turn, depends upon a disciplined way of life.

Even established livelihood depends upon faith in the Supreme Self. Only for one who possesses such faith will all their desires be fulfilled; otherwise, they shall surely perish. Therefore, the learned declare that faith alone is the root of all happiness. The Great Soul Basavarya, for the sake of human welfare—

It clearly elucidates the necessity of faith: people do not indeed trust in God, yet they constantly invoke Him; and though the dull-witted are unable to exercise faith, they nevertheless wander about out of delusion. If one were to invoke Him preceded by faith, why would He not respond?
The Lord said: "If one devoid of self-confidence were to invoke the Divine, he would immediately fall, restrained by the goad of the Divine's punishment.
If this teaching were always remembered, then the thought of committing sin would never arise.
Thus, due to the poverty of self-confidence, Arjuna forgot his duty through delusion.
Thus, declaring on the field of battle, "I shall not fight," Arjuna— due to being born of a noble lineage—
fell into doubt as to whether his own conclusion was right or wrong, having resorted to delusion; then,
impelled by that very Hṛṣīkeśa residing within his heart, he [approached] for the sake of determining his duty.
He goes for refuge to the Blessed One alone. Then, in order to ask what ought to be done, he asks:
"With my nature afflicted by the fault of envy and my mind utterly bewildered regarding the Dharma, I ask you."
Tell me decisively that which is the highest good; I am your disciple, teach me who have taken refuge in you.
46) He who is unable to endure even a slight injury to himself is a wretch; his state of being is *kārpaṇya*.
Miserliness is wretchedness. Afflicted by that defect, my own nature—that is, my mind—is corrupted;
for this very reason, I am one whose mind is utterly deluded regarding dharma. What is dharma? Or what is adharma?
Thus, devoid of discernment, I ask you alone:
tell me clearly and decisively which is the better path—the one to be adopted between engaging in battle or not—to that which is my ultimate good; I am your disciple, I have sought refuge in you.
"Instruct me, who have come for refuge; teach me. The root *śās* means "to instruct. The meaning is: "Teach the Dharma to me, your disciple. (2)
Thus, Arjuna informs [the Blessed One] that he himself possesses the detachment from all sense-objects, which is the root of taking refuge in the Blessed One through the desire to know the Dharma:
"Indeed, I do not see what could dispel this grief of mine, which withers the senses."
Having obtained on earth a prosperous kingdom without rival, and even sovereignty over the gods.

Having obtained on this earth in this world a kingdom free from rivals— that is, devoid of enemies— and prosperous and flourishing, or even the sovereignty over the gods, whatever it may be, that which might dispel or destroy the grief that causes the withering and drying up of my senses, beginning with the mind.

Therefore, I do not see it; I have no certainty that my grief would be dispelled either by the attainment of earthly sovereignty or by the attainment of the kingdom of heaven. Consequently, I seek the means for the cessation of my grief—though the desire to know one’s own true nature certainly arises at times during the course of worldly activity, since all [beings]...

They exist as the Self alone; however, their power remains in a state of contraction. It is precisely for the sake of attaining the expansion of this power that they must engage in worldly activity (*vyavahāra*). The spiritual science (*adhyātma-śāstra*) teaches that all activities whatsoever should be undertaken solely for the expansion of power. And this expansion of power—
That [truth] would be realized by human beings only when every form of worldly activity were conducted through the medium of the body.
And the *Śaraṇagītā* perfectly reveals the greatness of the body; therein, Basavārya (p.
47) states:
He reveals that greatness through his own example: "I would indeed practice agriculture for the sake of worshipping my guru;
I would engage in trade for the sake of worshipping the Liṅga; and I would perform service for the sake of pleasing Śiva while practicing [his teachings].
I know that [all this] will be accomplished. O noble one, I shall offer to you the wealth given by you for the sake of union with the Guru."

Thus, by acting solely for the sake of pleasing the Supreme Lord—who manifests as the Guru, the Liṅga, and the Jaṅgama—a human being becomes eternally happy. This alone constitutes the fulfillment of human birth.
Having attained this state, whether they be men or women, individuals no longer fall under the sway of *prakṛti*.

They delight this universe, which is composed of Śiva, through the vision of the inner self (adhyātma-dṛṣṭi), and they accomplish the welfare of all. Their conduct is illustrated as an ideal in the *Śaraṇagītā*.
Basavārya, the foremost among devotees, says: "I do not desire even the status of the lotus-born Brahmā..."

"Neither the station of Viṣṇu nor even his path here, nor likewise the path of Śambhu or any other, do I desire, O God of Union, for I seek eternally the status of a servant devoted to worshipping the feet of Your devotees; grant me that station by Your decree. Such a petition alone is conducive to the welfare of both women and men; however—

By what means and for what purpose a task is to be accomplished—this matter must be determined by the Supreme Self alone. No one whatsoever is able to transcend such a determination. If, out of such incapacity, they were to become bewildered and seek refuge in that very Supreme Self within themselves, then this world...

It shall be the place of rest for one who finds bliss in yoga. Thus, through Arjuna, the great seer Vyāsa reveals to the world the ideal that taking refuge in the Supreme Self must necessarily be practiced: "He who performs actions by placing them in Brahman and abandoning attachment is not tainted."

"He is not touched by evil, just as a lotus leaf is untouched by water"—such is the instruction of the Blessed One, which universally elucidates the most profound mystery of humanity. Due to the absence of such discernment, Arjuna became deluded; nevertheless, he remained in the company of the virtuous.
He desired to attain discernment. In this very way, the Blessed One expects that all living beings should strive to abandon their own delusion and acquire discernment. || 8 ||
To Dhṛtarāṣṭra, who was asking what had occurred previously, Sañjaya said:
48) Having spoken thus to Hṛṣīkeśa, Guḍākeśa, the scorcher of foes—
Having said to Govinda, "I will not fight," he indeed became silent.

Having spoken to Hṛṣīkeśa, Śrī Kṛṣṇa, in this manner, Gudākeśa Arjuna—the scorcher of foes and possessor of prowess—having said to Govinda, Śrī Kṛṣṇa, "I will not fight; I shall not engage in battle," became silent and inactive; indeed, he became so, as the sense is. || 9 ||
O descendant of Bharata, Hṛṣīkeśa, as if smiling, spoke these words to him who was despondent in the midst of the two armies.
O Bhārata, O Dhṛtarāṣṭra, Hṛṣīkeśa— Śrī Kṛṣṇa— as if laughing, that is,
as if mocking Arjuna, but not manifesting anger; for the use of the word *hṛṣīkeśa* and the statement "as if laughing" in these two verses indicate that all this [is the work] of the Blessed Lord.
His own conduct has thus been indicated. To that Arjuna, who was despondent—feeling dejection—in the midst of those two armies, he spoke these words, the speech about to be described. || 10 ||
You have grieved for those who should not be grieved for, yet you speak words of wisdom;
the wise do not mourn for the dead or for the living.

You have grieved for those who should not be grieved for—Bhīṣma, Droṇa, and the others—for whom you felt sorrow. Yet at that very same time, you spoke words of wisdom, uttering the discourses of the wise and intelligent. These two things are mutually contradictory.

Indeed, self-knowledge has arisen in them; they are wise, knowers of the Self. They do not grieve for those who have departed their life-breaths—that is, for the dead—nor for those whose life-breaths have not departed—that is, for the living.
In that regard, they simply do not feel sorrow. But you, though appearing to be a knower of the Self, are [bound by] dharma and adharma...

It is a ground for lamentation that you do not know this fact: even those who cast off their bodies in battle do not, in reality, die. Is this not the prattle of a madman to grieve for Bhīṣma and others who are free from death? Such is the intention suggested here. || 11 ||
(On page 49:
To the question, "How can they be beyond grief?", he states that in reality they are indeed eternal:
"Never was I not, nor you, nor these rulers of men."
And yet, we shall all certainly not cease to exist hereafter. (12)

I, who am the divine-formed Self of the formless Supreme Self, have never at any time indeed not been; rather, I have always existed. Just as I exist now in this body, so did I exist previously in another body, and likewise shall I exist in the future as well. In the same way, you also were not non-existent—this is the modification [of the verse].

But rather, they were indeed near. Likewise, these lords of men—not only Bhīṣma, Droṇa, and the others, but all the kings present here as well—were not that they were not there; rather, the change is that they were indeed near.
All of us, even after this, following the destruction of this body, shall certainly not cease to exist; rather, [we shall continue].
"We shall indeed exist. Thus, in all three periods of time, we are all by our very nature eternal and everlasting.
How can there be our destruction? Or whence could there be grief? Therefore, by grieving for those who should not be grieved for, you do not know your true nature according to reality.
If it be argued, "But surely I am grieving now specifically regarding the destruction of the body," that too is not tenable; thus He says:
"As in this very body the embodied one passes through childhood, youth, and old age, so too does he attain another body. The wise man is not deluded by this. (12)

Just as for an embodied being (*dehin*), childhood—the state of infancy—and youth—the state of adolescence—naturally occur within this very body, so too does old age—the state of decrepitude; yet no one grieves over these, nor ought anyone to grieve. In the same way, death is also merely a certain state consisting of the attainment of another body. Therefore...
Knowing this, the wise man, possessing self-dependent intellect, is not deluded even regarding death.

He who experiences fear, grief, and delusion does not truly become a man of knowledge. You, however, speak of knowledge yet experience grief; the coexistence of knowledge and grief in one place is not fitting.

The union of those two, like that of light and darkness, is never possible. As long as you grieve for Bhisma and the others, for that long you do not know their true nature. He who grieves for the unworthy—
The vessel does not know at all. He alone who feels sorrow for the worthy recipient knows its true nature as it really is.
Thus, the states of the body have been described here. (12)

Surely I do indeed know that the self is eternal and the body alone is impermanent; nevertheless, the experience of pleasure, pain, and so forth in the world, which is occasioned by connection with and separation from such a body, cannot be denied. Therefore, for me who perceives such suffering and the causes of suffering—

Anticipating the doubt as to why there should not be sorrow, he says: "But the contacts with the sense-objects, O son of Kuntī, which give rise to cold, heat, pleasure, and pain, are fleeting, coming and going, and impermanent; endure them, O Bhārata. (14)

The "contacts with the senses" (*mātrāsparśāḥ*) are as follows: the "senses" (*mātrāḥ*) are so called because objects such as sound are measured by them; they are the sense organs, beginning with the ear. Their "contacts" (*sparśāḥ*) are the connections of these [organs] with their respective objects, such as sound. These contacts between the objects and the sense organs—giving rise to cold, heat, pleasure, and pain—are sometimes cold and sometimes hot.

And because it is the opposite of that, it is also hot. Thus, those contacts between the sense objects and the senses indeed bestow pleasure at one time and pain at another; for such is their very nature, and that is indeed difficult to overcome. Therefore, those contacts, being difficult to abandon, always occur. What then [is the solution] in this regard?
Regarding what ought to be done in this matter, he says: "The self. For those [senses] are by nature subject to coming and going;
they come of their own accord and go away of their own accord, and do not remain anywhere with stability.
Thus, endure and bear them until they themselves perish, because they are unavoidable.

In this matter, endurance must be practiced. He who endures, knowing that pleasure or pain is merely temporary, attains knowledge of the true Self (svarūpa-jñāna) and becomes eternally happy. The sense is that men should acquire that very knowledge by which one may avoid sorrow. "O Bhārata"—this is addressed to Arjuna.
Thus, for one who endures the pairs of opposites such as cold and heat, pleasure and pain, a great fruit may arise;

however, for one who does not endure them and remains under their sway, the afflictions of saṃsāra will exist eternally. With this in mind, he says: "O bull among men, that person whom these do not distress..."
The steadfast one who is equal toward pain and pleasure is fit for immortality. || 15 ||

O bull among men, O best of men Arjuna, one who is equal in pain and pleasure—that is, one who does not fall under the sway of joy, despair, and the like when encountering happiness or sorrow—is indeed a person (or woman) who, through delusion and other such states, attains [the true state].
For delusion is the destroyer of the power of the intellect (*buddhi*). Therefore, the intellect of a living being who is equal in pain and pleasure is always [steadfast].

It remains indeed serene. That person whom these states of pleasure, pain, and so forth do not distress, do not afflict, and do not disturb— he, possessing such an unchanging mind, is the living being (*jīva*) who exists for the sake of immortality,
that is, for liberation (*mokṣa*), in order to attain liberation in the form of great bliss preceded by the cessation of eternal dualities and the like.

It is capable; it becomes competent. But he who is under the sway of pleasure and pain would indeed have his intellect destroyed. Therefore, for him, the attainment of grief and so forth will certainly occur again and again. He would remain perpetually wandering in saṃsāra;
he would never abide steadily in one place. And thus, for him—
The meaning is that liberation from delusion, which takes the form of a snare, would not be possible. || 15 ||
Out of a desire for the welfare of living beings, the Supreme Self teaches another reason to prevent grief and delusion:
"The unreal has no being; the real never ceases to be.
The truth regarding both of these has been perceived by those who see the essence. (2.16)

The existence—that is, the being—of a non-existent thing, which does not exist, is not found. Likewise, the non-existence—that is, the absence—of an existent thing is also not found. Thus, the conclusion regarding both of these, existence and non-existence, has been directly realized by those who see reality and those who have attained the direct perception of truth. And so it is said:
No one can effect a change through human effort; this established order cannot be transgressed by anyone. Why then indulge in vain anxiety, grief, delusion, and the like?
For whatever the inherent nature of things may be, such indeed is their state everywhere.
The meaning is that the discerning should conduct themselves solely in accordance with the true nature [of things]. || 16 ||
What is the true nature of the existent and the non-existent? And who is that "Being" which exists eternally? To this he says: "But know that to be indestructible by which all this is pervaded.
No one is able to effect the destruction of this imperishable. (17)

Know— that which by which this entire world is stretched out, pervaded— to be that very same imperishable, having the nature of non-destruction. Know that it is Brahman alone, the pervader of the world, which exists forever, uncontradicted throughout the three periods of time.
It is designated as "Sat" (Being). The universe, being pervaded by that [Brahman] yet distinct from it and consisting of insentient matter (*jaḍa*), is called "Asat" (Non-being).

The Supreme Brahman, whose nature is consciousness, by the power of its own wonderful and majestic *śakti*, sustains the entire universe itself and remains as the support of all. The universe, composed of the five elements, because of its insentience...

Transforming in manifold ways, it is reckoned as "non-existent. And this transformation proceeds solely through the proximity of the existent Supreme Self. Therefore, no one whatsoever can effect the destruction or dissolution of this Paraśiva-Brahman, which is the root cause, immutable, and devoid of decay.

It is neither fitting nor possible. Since it has been stated that "the non-existence of the existent does not occur," how could the destruction of the existent Brahman— the support of all, the cause of all, the impeller of all, the all-pervading, indivisible mark— be accomplished?
Having thus given the answer to the question "What is existent?", he now states the answer to the question "What is non-existent?":
"These bodies are said to have an end, belonging to the eternal embodied self, which is indestructible and immeasurable; therefore, fight, O Bharata! (18)

Of this eternal, ever-present, and for that very reason indestructible— meaning free from destruction— immeasurable Self (ātman), which is not an object of perception and other means of knowledge and is the embodied one (śarīrin), the master of the body, these bodies that exist, consisting of an aggregate of the five elements,
are indeed finite, meaning subject to destruction. Although the conscious being acting within this body...
That [soul] is indeed the Lord himself. Due to contact with the body, he becomes subject to the attributes of the touched body and, becoming miserable, grieves.
And this grief is rooted solely in delusion and ignorance.
The conscious being has acquired a body precisely in order to realize the vastness of its own Self; nevertheless, it thinks, "I am the body."

And such being the case, there is no non-existence of the Self; its destruction can never occur. Likewise, it is stated that there is no existence of the body which is non-existent [in essence]. Here, even the body, by way of its subtle form, remains within the Supreme Self during dissolution, and at the time of creation, emerging outwardly in accordance with His will, it belongs to Him alone.
Because it is employed for the purpose of diversion, it cannot be asserted that even the body is eternal; nevertheless, since the body reaches the state of the five elements, it is finite.

When it is properly applied, then, through its very assistance, the true nature of the embodied being is realized. If the defect residing within the body were to be eradicated from its root, then that very [defect] becomes the means for achieving the soul's own welfare. This point is clearly elucidated in the *Śaraṇagītā*: "If the row of fangs of the serpent is uprooted..."

And at that time, a person should take delight in that very [state]. Likewise, when poison and sin are being expelled from the body, it is indeed better to dwell there. If a mother herself were possessed by a demonic nature, the child would not be protected by her in this world;
similarly, a corruption that has arisen within the body will not protect the life-force—this is the truth. That which is in the body...
O Gurumālli-Kārjuna, he alone who is favored by you is truly blessed.

Thus, through the cessation of the defect consisting of delusion regarding the body, the Self becomes solitary and pure; this is the intended meaning. For this very reason, the Śiva-yogins, out of a vision for the welfare of all people, instruct as follows: "You..."

"For what purpose do you strive to gather together merely to turn away the sidelong glances of people? First purify your own respective bodies and seek to concentrate your own minds; do not concern yourselves with others. You will grieve in vain for the sake of suffering—this is the truth—and because of it, the Lord will not grant his favor. Thus [he spoke].

Not only those who have taken refuge in Śiva, but even the great sages urge humanity to attain the purification of the self through the purification of the body. Thus, because the nature and essential form of both the body and the self are fixed, O Bhārata Arjuna, you cannot act in any new way whatsoever.

For the very purpose of accomplishing dharma, by means of this body which has come into being through the grace of the Lord, one must necessarily perform the duty consisting of the destruction of enemies as its auxiliary. Therefore, fight;
engage in battle. There is no fault in performing battle. This is for the sake of that purpose for which this body has come into being.

That duty must certainly be performed; otherwise, a great ruin may occur. Through your disregard for the Lord who is latent within your own body, you will perish. Those who desire their own spiritual welfare must never disparage the body; however—

First, the discrimination between the body and the self must be realized; it is precisely due to the absence of such discrimination that you have become a sufferer—thus, under the guise of Arjuna, the Supreme Self enlightens all those in the world. 18.

The object being thus established in its true nature, he says that whoever, lacking the discrimination between the body and the self, should think "I am killing someone" or "I am killed by him," is indeed deluded:
He who thinks this [Self] is a slayer, and he who thinks it is slain—both of them do not understand; this does not slay, nor is it slain. (19)

Whosoever, being undiscriminating, knows this aforementioned eternal embodied one—the living self (jīva) existing within the body—to be a slayer, that is, the agent of the act of killing; and whosoever else, being undiscriminating, knows this eternal embodied living self to be slain, that is, the object of the act of killing—this is to be supplied from the context. Both of these...

"They do not understand the reality of the Self" means they are not possessed of knowledge; that is to say, they are undiscriminating. To the question "Why?", he says: "This one does not kill. This embodied being is not the agent of killing. Likewise, "he is not killed," meaning he is also not the object of killing. Neither of these two states can ever possibly apply to the Self, the individual soul (*jīva*). Now, [an objection]: *Note: The provided text ends with "nanu" (now/if it be objected), indicating the beginning of a further argument or objection.*

Because the *jīva* is eternal, the prohibition against it being the object of killing is logical. But how could the prohibition against its being the agent of killing also be possible? For there is no contradiction between eternity and agency. If it is argued that although an eternal conscious being cannot be bound, it is nonetheless capable of being the agent of killing, [we reply] that this is not so regarding the self (*ātman*).

The general property of agency is being negated; however, [what is negated] is the agency of killing, and even therein, the agency of killing that has the self as its object. Since the self is eternal, killing it is simply non-existent. And when the very act of killing the self is non-existent, then—

Or rather, to whom could such agency of killing belong? Since a rabbit’s horn is itself unestablished, no one can possibly possess the agency of making a rabbit’s horn. Therefore, there is no fault whatsoever in negating the agency of one who kills oneself as the object of that act. || 19 ||
He establishes very clearly that the self cannot be the object of the act of killing:
"It is never born, nor does it ever die; having come into being, it will not cease to be hereafter.
Unborn, eternal, everlasting is this ancient Self; it is not slain when the body is slain. (2.20)

This self, the lord of the body, the *jīva*, is not born and does not arise; for this very reason, it never dies. For the learned say, "Death is certain for that which is born"; only that which arises can perish. Since there is no arising for the *jīva*, its destruction is impossible. Therefore, having come into being, it is subject to the activity of existing.
Having remained, it would never again cease to exist; for that which is empty of the activity of becoming would simply be that which always exists, and thus it would never at any time not exist.

For its origination would be established only through the conventional usage "it exists at some time. How could origination be possible for that which exists eternally? That which exists at all times could never have been non-existent;
rather, it simply always exists. Thus, as to what its essential nature is, he says: "unborn" (aja), meaning it is not born.

Thus, the Unborn (*aja*) is devoid of origination; for that very reason, he is eternal (*nitya*), being devoid of destruction. Being thus devoid of both origination and destruction, he is beginningless (*anādi*). This Self (*ātman*) is certainly not slain even when the body is slain. In this regard, what was said concerning the body does not apply to the living being (*jīva*), because such a configuration [of parts] does not exist in the case of the Self; likewise, even dissection is not applicable. And so, it is only of the body—
Thus, it is stated that the state of being the object of the act of killing does not belong to the self. || 20 ||
Thus, because the essential natures of the body and the self are distinct, the statement "this one neither kills nor is killed" is established; he says:
"He who knows this as indestructible, eternal, unborn, and immutable..."
O Pārtha, how does that man cause anyone to be killed, or kill anyone? (21)

O Pārtha, that person who knows this Self— which is distinct from the body, unborn (devoid of origination), and for that very reason imperishable (devoid of destruction), and for that very reason eternal (existing at all times), and consequently immutable (free from modification)— how can such a person cause any other person to be slain? Who can slay whom?

Or how could one kill a person? How could such a discerning person perceive himself as "I am his killer" or "he has been killed by me"? Only one who is deluded by egoism (*ahaṃkāra*) and the like through identifying the body with the self or with Brahman would perceive "I am the killer" or "this one is killed. For this very reason:

It will be said: "He whose state is not characterized by egoism, whose intellect is not tainted—even having slain these worlds, he does not slay and is not bound. He who employs the body, senses, and so forth for the sake of serving the Lord residing within the body certainly becomes eternally happy; whereas he who conducts himself from the perspective of the body [is otherwise].

He alone experiences suffering. That noble and great-souled one points out the method for the utilization of the body by means of his own example: "Having clearly perceived the suffering of the body, being afraid, never pray to the Lord [for its preservation]."

Seeking a single means for the protection of his body, the servant here remains fearful; he shall never beg of the Lord, "Give me a body. Let that which is destined to happen here be so eternally; for let even censure follow after praise.

"Indeed, for that servant, both [happiness and suffering] would be truly beneficial; he neither begs for happiness nor for suffering, nor does he even strive to reject them. In the same way, O Lord Gurusaṅgameśa, I shall never beg from you, nor from others. And thus, the seekers [endure] bodily suffering with contentment.

Enduring all, they employ the body in a disciplined manner solely for the sake of accomplishing their purpose. In this very way, the great sages, protecting the body only for the sake of their own spiritual welfare and having abandoned the delusion regarding the body, remained ever-blissful. They maintained a truly positive disposition toward the body. May it be well.

"O Gods, may we hear with our ears what is auspicious; O Holy Ones, may we see with our eyes what is auspicious. With firm limbs and bodies, praising [you], may we attain that lifespan ordained by the Gods. Thus it is clearly understood that they possessed firm bodies and long lives, thereby accomplishing what was ordained by the Gods. In the same way...
The great seers (maharṣis) also praise bodily health above all else, saying:
"May we see a hundred autumns; may we live a hundred autumns; may we rejoice a hundred autumns; may we delight a hundred autumns;
may we remain unconquered for a hundred autumns. In such ways, they fully extol the greatness of the body.

They establish this: thus, a person of discrimination, performing every action brought about by the body as being devoid of self-interest, should remain entirely unattached. Such discrimination was necessary for the embodied Arjuna;
the Blessed Lord stated that this very quality is required by all during the time of worldly activity.

Now, even though the selves are eternal, it is observed in the world that birth is merely the connection with a body and death is merely the separation from a body; thus, the abandonment of the body and so forth are indeed seen as causes of suffering. Therefore, how can such [death] be a cause of satisfaction? Consequently, how could there be any fear of suffering from death, which actually bestows eternal bliss?
Just as a person, casting off worn-out garments, takes others that are new, so the embodied soul, casting off worn-out bodies, enters into others that are new. 22.
A person, having cast off— having abandoned— worn-out garments that have become weak and ancient, puts on other, different, new, fresh, and strong clothes. Thus [it is said].

Bodies are afflicted by old age and are weak; they are called "bodies" (*śarīrāṇi*) because they disintegrate. Having abandoned—meaning having cast off—such bodies which are themselves perishable, he goes to, that is, attains, others that are new, fresh, and very firm; this [word *śarīrāṇi*] is also to be repeated [in the verse]. Thus, there is the abandonment of old garments.

The meaning is that one must suffer. For the sake of protecting such a perishable body, the undiscriminating commit great sins. Even when standing at the very mouth of death, a human being does not realize the suffering of the body;
thus, the *Śaraṇagītā* perfectly reveals this folly. As it is said: "Just as a frog [falls] into the mouth of the wind-eater..."

Just as one who is stung by a bee might violently shake it off, so too this life, clinging to the jaws of death, clings only to a mere fragment of worldly enjoyment. And as for the thief who, out of sheer hunger, consumes ghee and milk only to mount the stake—
tell me, who am seeking refuge with you, for how much longer will he live?

"Relying here upon this perishable body and employing false means, if the embodied soul constantly nourishes only his own belly, a noble person should certainly never place trust in him. Thus, he who follows the path of untruth for the sake of protecting the body does not [attain] the grace of the Lord.

One certainly attains it; however, the most excellent Śiva-yogins, perceiving even this transient body as a temple of the Divine, experience their own bliss of Śiva right there. Allamārya, by means of his own body alone, through faith and focused attention, cultivated the crop of the Supreme Self and [attained] its...

Just as he experienced the fruit in the form of bliss through the grace of the Guru, so too may other practitioners not defile their bodies with the notion that they are perishable; thus, he instructs them by means of his own example:
"Having made one's own body a garden and having dug it with the spade of the mind, [one should uproot] delusion along with its roots."

Having discarded the clod of worldly existence from my mind and having broken it apart through reasoning, I have planted the seed of the Supreme Self within my own heart. Having properly irrigated it with water drawn from the mechanism called *prāṇa* via the *suṣumṇā* channel, it has been thoroughly nourished by me; indeed, even the five senses would not be able to undo this.

Reflecting thus upon its destruction, O Lord of the Cave, through devotion and by applying the mental state known as equanimity and forgiveness with focused attention toward that very crop, they caused it to flourish by your grace.

"For indeed, all this is your play. Thus, those possessed of discernment should reflect that this body, obtained through the grace of the Blessed One, is a means for the practice [of yoga] within it. If this body, which has come together for the attainment of such yoga, were to be employed solely for the sake of worldly enjoyment, then a great loss would arise. Therefore, the body—

The Blessed One observes that as long as one remains strong, for that duration human beings should strive to know and experience the reality existing therein. For such a person, death is merely the assumption of a new body; however, for the wise, death is—

The opening of the house that is eternal, blissful, and of the nature of the Self is indeed [the goal]. The bliss experienced within one's own body is experienced eternally even after death. And thus, humans should practice spiritual discipline (*adhyātma-yoga*)—for it is only bodies that undergo birth and decay, not the Self—as he says:
Weapons do not cut this, nor does fire burn it;
water does not moisten it, nor does the wind wither it. (23)

"Though residing within the body, this individual soul (jīvātman) is the absolute, pure Śiva, eternally stainless, eternal, untainted, and peaceful; therefore, the self is itself Śiva. Thus, through experience, [it is realized that] the self exists as pure, unattached, and peaceful; yet, when covered by impurities, it revolves in the cycle of birth and death.

Although transmigrating, the individual soul (*jīva*) is in reality *Śiva*; therefore, through the worship of Śiva, it is capable of becoming Śiva. Just as Śiva is formless, so too the individual soul, which is a portion of Him, remains entirely untainted even while situated within the body.
Fear, grief, delusion, and the like do not exist in him in reality. And weapons and arms [cannot harm] that embodied one...

They do not cut, nor do they perform the act of cutting; rather, it is the body alone that they cut. Likewise, fire (*pāvaka*) does not burn the embodied one, nor does it reduce him to ashes; rather, it is the body alone that fire reduces to ashes. Similarly, water (*āpaḥ*) does not moisten this embodied self (*dehinaṃ ātmānam*), nor does it make it wet; rather, it is the waters [that moisten the body].

They would only moisten the body itself. In this way, the vital air (māruto vāyuḥ) does not dry up this self (ātmānam), nor does it make it parched. And likewise in the world, there are causes for cutting, burning, moistening, and drying.
Weapons, fire, water, and wind are unable to produce even the slightest modification in the Self.

Not knowing such a pure nature of the Self, a person, identifying the Self with the body, becomes tainted by the suffering of the body. And this self-inflicted transgression must be experienced by oneself alone.
This is the meaning. || 23 ||
To the question, "Why does this Self not undergo modification even while residing in the body? he says:
"This [Self] is neither cut, nor burned, nor moistened, nor dried away;
it is eternal, all-pervading, stable, immovable, and ancient. (24)

Since this Self is "uncuttable," it cannot be cut by weapons and the like; it is "indestructible by fire," meaning it cannot be burned by fire; it is "unmoistenable," meaning it cannot be made wet by water; and it is "indeed un-dryable," meaning it cannot be dried up by wind. Therefore, it is said: "Weapons do not cut this," and so forth.

How is it that the self possesses such qualities as being indivisible? For only upon the establishment of that [self] would statements such as "weapons do not cut this" be consistent; to this, he says "eternal," and so forth. Since the self is eternal—devoid of origination and destruction—it is therefore omnipresent and all-pervasive, like space. Indeed, not...
No one is able to perform acts such as cutting through space; therefore, it is a pillar (sthāṇu), meaning stable.

For that very reason, it is immovable (acala), for it cannot be moved by anyone. Thus, due to reasons such as its eternity, it is eternal (sanātana), existing forever. Bodies, however, are seen to be perishable by direct perception itself.

Therefore, the meaning is that cutting and so forth belong only to the body, not to the Self (*ātman*). It is the individual soul (*jīvātman*), acting through its identification with the body, that continues to experience cutting and so forth even now. If that very soul were to transform, through discernment, the worldly activity proceeding from the perspective of the body into the perspective of the inner Self (*ādhyātmadṛṣṭi*), then—

No affliction whatsoever shall arise for him through his body. Thus, for one who discriminates between the body and the self, because the body itself is transformed through the contemplation of it as Śiva, its modifications are not experienced by him. This alone is the distinction between the wise man and the fool: the fool perceives the modifications of the body, whereas the wise man does not take them into account. Nevertheless...
Alterations such as disease certainly exist therein; those who are learned say that bodies are possessed of disease.

Being the locus of disease is the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*) of the body, while freedom from disease is the defining characteristic of the self (*ātman*). Health alone is its mark (*lāñchana*). Due to contact with the body, through lack of discrimination, he [the self]...
