p.

60) By virtue of being innate, one is perceived as diseased. However, by knowing the Śiva that exists within oneself and practicing its worship, the individual soul (jīva), having itself become Śiva, becomes stainless and free from disease. Thus, regarding the body...

Constantly remembering his own transformation and [the Lord’s] eternity, a human being should employ the body for the sake of eternal union and perpetual contact with the eternal Supreme Śiva. Since the body possesses its essence only through the Lord, this worldly existence becomes meaningful only for the embodied soul. And thus, all who possess bodies—

If they were to become knowers of the Self, then and only then would eternal happiness arise for them. In its absence, the mutual relationship between human beings could never be auspicious; rather, only misfortune would arise.
Among all embodied beings, it is only the Lord within the cave (guheshvara), the inner witness of the soul, who is worthy of trust. This is the point.
Basavārya spoke correctly: "The ocean rises at the rising of the moon and subsides at its setting. When the sage drank the waters of the ocean, did the moon come to assist him?
But when Rāhu swallows the moon, does the ocean go into the midst of it? No one [does so], O Lord."

"You alone grant protection; you are the sole kinsman of the world. Thus, among embodied beings, Paramaśiva alone—eternal and stainless—is the one who is to be trusted and revered by all. It was precisely due to ignorance of Him that Arjuna, through delusion, forgot his own duty. *Arir-doḍe śaraṇam*.
The liberation from fear expressed as "O mortal, do not fear" shines forth, constantly impelling all practitioners toward right conduct.

Therefore, he who proceeds with the discrimination between the body and the Self remains untouched by the modifications of the body and performs every action with the perspective that it is his duty to do so.

And this is accomplished through the contemplation of worshipping the Blessed Lord. The Lord teaches that such conduct, endowed with knowledge, is not only necessary for Arjuna but is indeed essential for everyone. || 24 ||
This Self is said to be unmanifest, inconceivable, and immutable;
therefore, knowing it to be such, you ought not to grieve.
The characteristic of the self is not merely eternality and so forth; rather, it also possesses qualities such as being unmanifest (*avyaktatva*).
Therefore, he says: "Unmanifest. This self is unmanifest; it is never manifest to anyone in the manner of a jar or similar objects.
Consequently, by whom could such a thing be cut or otherwise acted upon? Since it belongs to no one, [it cannot be destroyed].
Manifest for this very reason, it is inconceivable— that is, impossible to conceive as "this is such-and-such.
On the other hand, that which is manifest, such as a jar and so forth, being perceptible by the senses, can indeed be conceived as "this is such-and-such."

The self (ātman), however, is not manifest; for that very reason, it is not an object of thought. How could the cutting of such an incorporeal embodied being by means of weapons and the like be possible? Only an entity possessing a material form can be cut by a weapon. How, then, and by what means could the incorporeal self ever be cut?

Thus it is said by those who possess direct experience. Therefore, having known and understood this Self in the manner described—namely, as being distinct from the body and so forth—you ought not to grieve or suffer, thinking, "How can these [beings] be slain by me? Only one who knows the Self becomes free from fear, grief, and delusion; setting that [Self-knowledge] aside, [you do not].
All others, too, always spend their time in nothing but grieving. Therefore, you should not feel sorrow in this battle. || 25 ||

Thus, for you who know the eternity of the self, grief resulting from their slaughter would not arise. And even if, through delusion, you do not know it thus but instead know the self to be perishable, even then there is no occasion for grief; so he says:
Moreover, O mighty-armed one, even if you consider this self to be constantly born or constantly dying, even so, you ought not to grieve in this manner.
(26) Furthermore—or rather—this aforementioned self is "constantly born," meaning it is perpetually subject to birth; [birth is its very nature].

Or if you think that this self has the very nature of arising and perishing— if you consider it so, then you should understand that such a notion of yours is merely temporary and not real. Nevertheless, O mighty-armed Arjuna, possessed of valor, even if you accept it as such— having been addressed thus:

The meaning is: if you understand that birth has the nature of birth and death has the nature of death, then, according to the principle that "the nature of things is difficult to transcend" because they are inherent natures, these two are unavoidable; therefore, how could sorrow arise?
For death is certain for one who is born, and birth is certain for one who has died;
therefore, you ought not to grieve over this inevitable matter.
62) [The text] establishes that birth and death are indeed the very nature of the body:
for death—that is, dying—is certain and inevitable for a body that has been born, that is, produced; likewise, there is again birth for one who has died.

Arising is certain and fixed; thus, you consider arising and destruction to be its inherent natures. For that reason, regarding this matter which is unavoidable—that is, impossible for anyone to avoid—you ought not to grieve, nor should you feel sorrow. This body has come only to depart; how then could it be otherwise?

"Should one remain? For what confidence can there be in life when death stands as an adversary? Thus Aśvaghoṣa speaks in the *Buddhacarita*. For this very reason, the statement of Kālidāsa is also consistent: "If a living being remains for even a moment according to its own will, it is indeed a gain. This refers to the momentary duration of the body.
"Why should primacy be given to that very [conduct]?"—this point was addressed by Basavārya:

"Conduct alone is the abode of the gods; the neglect of conduct is indeed a miserable state. "In my own practice, O noble one, association with the Guru is the authority"—such was his firm conviction. Thus, by the authority of his own experience...

Basavārya elucidates the greatness of purity in conduct (*śīla-śuddhi*) and the sanctity of the body employed for that purpose. He maintains that only that embodied being who achieves the welfare of the world through the proper use of his body and always contemplates the benefit of all is truly considered one born of a noble lineage (*satkula*). [Not] for one's own sake...

The body of one who lives solely for the sake of others, having forgotten their own self-interest, truly becomes fruitful. Even the body of one who accomplishes the welfare of others only after first achieving their own ends should never be negligent; however, as for one who causes suffering to others for the sake of achieving their own ends—

For one who produces [such thoughts], his body shall always remain in bondage; experienced people censure such a person as a "body-possessor. He who constantly destroys living beings is to be considered an outcaste forever; likewise, he who eats only the food of others is to be considered an outcaste forever. By those very [acts]...

"The welfare of all should be considered; their lineage is not to be scrutinized at all. Those who wish for the welfare of all living beings and are devoted to the noble ones are proclaimed as those of true birth.
Thus, embodied beings, in cooperation with their bodies, must properly accomplish the public good. Otherwise, it is not pure—
His life would become meaningless; therefore, even this perishable body [should be used] for the sake of one's own welfare.
The intention conveyed here is that this should be properly employed by those possessed of discernment.
Beings are unmanifest in their origin, manifest in their middle state, O Bhārata, and unmanifest again at their end; what cause for lamentation is there in this? (28)

Now, one might raise the objection: "Even if it is improper to grieve for oneself, is it not indeed appropriate to grieve for the living beings residing in bodies, who are subject to birth and death? To this, the following resolution is stated:
"The unmanifested is the beginning"—those beings whose beginning (the prior time) is unmanifested (unperceived).

Indeed, the pre-natal state of living beings—such as sons, wives, and others—is not known by anyone at all; their perception lasts for only a certain limited period after birth. Therefore, they are "those whose middle is manifest," meaning those whose middle period (madhya-kāla) is seen as manifest.

Beings, moreover, at the end have the unmanifest as their dissolution; that is, those whose dissolution—meaning death—and the state immediately following it are the unmanifest (avyakta), which is unseen. Even after death, their destination is simply not known. And thus, the prior state or the immediate subsequent state of sons, friends, and others is likewise not known at all.

In the interim, there is merely a brief mutual encounter; even regarding those who were sons, friends, and so forth today, there is no confidence that they will remain the same even when they return to their former state. He who was an enemy in a previous time may now, in his manifest condition, act in accordance with his own interests.

Having been a friend for a time, one may become harmful by acting contrary to one's own interests. Thus, the conditions of living beings are unstable. Therefore, what lamentation, what idle chatter—that is to say, what distress—is there in that regard? Beings were not seen before, nor are they seen at the end; of them—
One should never feel sorrow regarding sense objects; indeed, sorrow is not appropriate here at all.
But he says that the true nature of the Self, which resides within the body, is extremely difficult to know:
"Someone beholds this [Self] as a marvel; likewise, another speaks of it as a marvel;
and another hears of it as a marvel; yet even having heard of it, no one at all knows it. (29)

The individual soul (jīvātman), dwelling within the body, can never be perceived through direct sensory observation. Yet, a certain person perceives this self as something wondrous, as something truly marvelous; and likewise, another certain person does so as well.
He speaks as if it were a marvel, as if it were something truly extraordinary. Likewise, some other person hears of this Self as if it were a marvelous and most wonderful thing;
yet another person, even after hearing from those who have experienced it that the Self exists in such a way, does not truly know it.
He has realized the true nature of the self; thus, the meaning is that the knowledge of the self is exceedingly difficult to attain. || 29 ||
Having thus taught the true nature of the Self, the instruction relevant to the present topic is now commenced: "O Bharata, this embodied being in the body of everyone is eternally indestructible;
therefore, you ought not to grieve for any living beings. (30)

This embodied Self (dehī), which exists within the very body of every single living being without exception, is eternal and at all times indestructible—incapable of being slain. For that reason, you ought not to grieve for any beings, referring to the entire class of living entities beginning with Bhīṣma; they are far removed from birth and death.

It is entirely improper to feel grief on their account; nevertheless, he who grieves is indeed a fool. You must not act in this way. Since you have descended into the Kṣatriya lineage for the protection of the world through the suppression of the wicked, it is truly unfitting for you to grieve over Bhīṣma and the others, who are not objects of lamentation.

Having thus stated that, from the perspective of ultimate truth (*paramārtha*), it is simply not fitting to feel grief or delusion, he now says that it is not only from the perspective of ultimate truth, but even from the perspective of the Dharma (*dharma*), that it is not fitting for you to grieve:
Moreover, considering your own duty, you ought not to waver;
for there exists nothing better for a Kshatriya than a righteous war. 31.

Moreover, even after considering and reflecting upon your own duty—that is, the nature of your duty as a Kṣatriya—you ought not to waver or flee from battle. For it is well known that the duty of a Kṣatriya, arising from his own caste, is "not fleeing in battle"; therefore, [you must act] because it is obtained through dharma.
"For a Kṣatriya, no merit greater than battle exists. Therefore, you ought not to waver from battle;
on the contrary, by failing to fight, you would incur great sin through the loss of your own duty.
If it were so grasped, then even human birth would not be obtained again;

rather, the birth of some four-footed animal might occur. In such a state, for the welfare of the world—or indeed for the sake of humanity itself—you alone [must act] on this field of battle, yet by all human beings in this world which has become a field of action.
One's own duty must necessarily be performed; there is no room for consideration of merit or demerit therein.
Likewise, if his own people also perform their duty while reflecting that both [sides] are equal, they would receive his favor. And thus, by all those who are striving to grow...
The vision of duty must be respected in every way; by this very path, you must certainly engage in battle—thus the Blessed One instructs Arjuna. 31.

On the contrary, it is truly strange that you grieve over a matter for which you ought to rejoice; thus he says: "O Pārtha, happy are the Kṣatriyas who obtain such a battle as this, which comes of its own accord and is an open door to heaven. (32)
O Pārtha, such a battle— a righteous war that has arrived by chance, unasked for, and stands open like the very gateway to heaven— is obtained only by fortunate Kṣatriyas who possess merit. Thus...
The meaning is: what Kṣatriya would abandon such a battle, which has been obtained spontaneously and without effort, and which is a certain means for attaining heaven? || 32 ||
Having thus taught the necessity of fighting through various modes, he now states that if one does not do so, undesirable consequences will also ensue:
"But if you will not engage in this righteous battle..."
Then, having abandoned your own duty and your reputation, you will incur sin.

Moreover, even though you thus recognize that this battle must necessarily be fought, if you do not engage in this righteous war— which is obtained through dharma— then you will abandon the duty of your own class (svavarṇadharma) and,
by its very root, abandon fame and glory, thereby incurring the sin of falling away from your own duty.
"You shall incur sin; you shall obtain it. (p.
66) Thus, for one who abandons the duty that ought to be performed, there is not only a loss of dharma, but also sin.
This may come to pass. Having understood this, the Supreme Self expects that men should become practitioners of *karmayoga*.

The intention is that men who do not perform their duties merely become a burden to the earth. The *Śaraṇagītā* describes the miserable condition of those who abandon their duties quite clearly. [This is] by means of truth and purity.

For as much wealth as a person obtains through bodily effort, the mind remains attached to that very extent; yet one should not seek a separation from it out of greed for riches. One should not desire more than what can be obtained by bodily means—surely one may obtain what is obtainable through the body. But if gold is distinct from the wealth produced by bodily labor, then it is established as something separate.
"The ignorant man desires it; then his service perishes, for through the hope of such service he finds only a snare.
Thus, by the mere performance of their own duties through the body alone—not only the Kṣatriya, but all human beings—having become blessed, may they obtain the grace of God.

It is not merely a loss of reputation; on the contrary, you will incur even great infamy. Thus he says: "And people will speak of your undying infamy; and for one who has been esteemed, infamy is worse than death. (34)

All living beings—that is, all species of creatures—will speak of that [infamy] as imperishable and stable, meaning it will not perish even after the lapse of time; they will speak of such infamy, even ill-repute, regarding you. Thus, all men everywhere shall propagate this eternal infamy concerning you. You have abandoned—

Regarding the word "loss" (*hāni*), he says "of one who is honored," and so forth. For you—who have been highly esteemed by all people in various ways as "Arjuna, the great hero, the most righteous," and so on—this infamy, rooted in such things as the loss of dharma, outweighs even death itself. Such a disgrace...
"Now, what loss is there to my valor? My innate valor certainly exists.
Even so, if you say, 'I will not fight out of compassion,' to that he says:
'The great chariot-warriors will think that you have withdrawn from the battle out of fear.'"
And having been highly esteemed by them, you will fall into contempt. || 35 ||

67) Even though you are brave, when you came to the field of battle and withdrew from the fight, all the great chariot-warriors and heroes standing before you, such as Duryodhana and the others, [fled] from you out of sheer fear of combat.

They will consider him who has desisted from battle as having retreated, and they will censure him for his lack of prowess. One should have desisted out of compassion even before entering the field of battle; if one desists only after arriving on the battlefield and seeing all the combatants, then it is a retreat made out of fear.
The meaning is that they would think thus. To the question "Who are these who are called 'great chariot-warriors' (mahārathas)? he says:
"Of whom..."—referring to Duryodhana and the others—of whom you were highly esteemed and honored for your heroism, yet now you will incur *lāghava*, which is a loss of dignity. || 35 ||

He says that it will not merely result in a loss of internal respect, but there will also be public censure: "Your enemies will utter many unspeakable words, reviling your capability; what indeed could be more painful than that? (36)

Your enemies, those who are unfriendly to you, such as Duryodhana and others, will— while actually disparaging your capability, which truly exists, as well as your prowess and other qualities— utter many kinds of unspeakable words, insults that are unworthy even to be spoken,
such as "this Arjuna is a mere eunuch," and so forth.
They will say: "What indeed could be more painful than this? There is no suffering more grievous even than that. You alone would be the root of every misfortune. (36)
Therefore, the Blessed One states the conclusion: "In this matter, you must do only this:
either slain, you will attain heaven; or victorious, you will enjoy the earth. Therefore arise, O son of Kuntī, resolved for battle. (37)

If you are slain and struck down by enemies, you will attain or go to heaven; you will experience the gateway to heaven. Therefore, O Kaunteya Arjuna, for a Kṣatriya, battle yields gain in either case. For this reason, having made a firm resolve—thinking "I shall conquer my enemies" or "I shall surely die"—[engage in battle], O son of Pṛthā. Thus spoke the Blessed One.
Having previously declared, "I shall wage war," it is by no means appropriate to flee now out of fear.

By the Lord who is the inner controller within you, if there is uniformity between His word and His action, then that noble one dwells within; thus, by the authority of the words of refuge, I observe Your presence in my heart—
otherwise, even here in this phenomenal world, which is the playground for the divine sport of the Supreme Lord, he would be abandoned.

Living by any means whatsoever out of wretchedness, you will not attain dignity; likewise, in the end, you will not even meet death without effort. In this context, the teaching of the great soul Basavārya, the ornament of devotion, shines forth as something to be remembered by all: "For the mortal world belongs to the Supreme Lord."

"This house was constructed for the sake of playful diversion. Those who are seen here today as worthy are indeed worthy of union there, O noble one. But those men who were not fit here are not capable of being fit there. Thus, it is only those men and women who are steadfast in their duty that are [fit] both here and hereafter.
They become praiseworthy; therefore, this righteous battle must certainly be fought by you—thus the Blessed One instructs Arjuna with sincere affection. 37.
Now, to provide a resolution to the thought, "Could it be that the sin arising from the slaughter of my kinsmen would not befall me?", he says:
"Having made pleasure and pain, gain and loss, victory and defeat the same, then engage in battle; thus you shall incur no sin whatsoever. (38)

Since fighting is the specific duty (*svadharma*) of a Kṣatriya, a Kṣatriya should engage in battle with the sole intention of that duty; having rendered victory and defeat, or winning and losing, equal—that is, having contemplated them with equanimity—one should thereafter "be joined for battle," which means set forth for it. Thus...

By performing battle as your very own duty (*svadharma*), you shall incur no sin; that is, you will not obtain [sin]. By this, the intended meaning (*āśaya*) suggested here is that all human beings must likewise avoid sin through the practice of their own respective duties. || 38 ||

In the middle [of the discourse], the necessity of performing battle was taught as a consequence of attachment, wrong views, and the notion that it is one's own duty; however, concluding that the ultimate reality has been taught by such statements as "Never was I not," he prepares the introductory framework for what is to be explained further on.
(69) This wisdom has been declared to you in the context of Sāṃkhya; now hear this [wisdom] regarding Yoga, O Pārtha, by which wisdom joined, you shall cast off the bondage of action. 39.

In the Sāṃkhya, "saṃkhyā" means knowledge; this [instruction] pertains to that which relates to it, namely the subject matter of the discrimination of ultimate reality. To this extent, this wisdom has been taught to you and spoken with sincere affection. But as for Yoga, which serves as the means for such knowledge of the ultimate reality—
Listen now to this wisdom concerning the yoga of action which is being described immediately hereafter; endowed with this wisdom—

the knowledge regarding the subject of the yoga of action— you, O Pārtha Arjuna, shall cast off the bondage of action, that is, the bondage consisting of karma, by performing action preceded by the knowledge of action about to be taught.
The praise of *karmayoga* is offered here with the view that the cessation of the bonds of *saṃsāra* ought to come about.

He who performs action in conjunction with knowledge of the supreme self (*adhyātma-jñāna*) is alone called a *karmayogin*. When action is performed after realizing that all action is of the nature of worshiping the Blessed Lord, then—

Such performance is called *karmayoga*. That very same [yoga] is praised by the *Śaraṇas* under the name "action of the body. Action in the form of the body alone does not bind human beings; otherwise, this world would certainly be bound by action. [This applies to] performing action without knowing, as well as performing it with knowledge.

Both of these—the non-performance of duty and the performance of forbidden acts—would be improper. Therefore, in this section, the Supreme Self teaches this point: that human beings should joyfully perform whatever actions are beneficial to their own nation for the sake of pleasing the Supreme Lord who dwells within all.
He speaks further regarding the excellence of karma-yoga itself:
"In this [path], there is no loss of effort, nor does any obstacle exist;
even a very little of this dharma protects one from great fear. (40)

In this yoga of action, which serves as the means to liberation, there is no loss of the effort undertaken; that which is begun never perishes. It will certainly yield its fruit. Furthermore, whatever action is undertaken with the desire for the welfare of the world will, by the grace of the Lord, surely reach completion. Not...

It is indeed that same action; however, even that which is performed with a view toward self-interest will certainly yield its specified fruit, yet it binds human beings. Such persons are called "doers" (karmīs).
Arjuna should become a practitioner of Karma-yoga through the performance of his own duty, and not merely a doer (karmī)—this is the Lord’s [intention].
The intention is this: in the performance of such action, no transgression or sin exists, nor would it arise;
for even the slightest [defect] in this dharma— [page 70]
When practiced, it protects and guards you from great fear—that is, from the great fear that is the nature of *saṃsāra*.
However, ritual action such as agriculture yields fruit only when it is fully completed. Regarding *karmayoga*:
"In this world, O joy of the Kurus, the intellect characterized by resolute determination is one."
For the intellects of those lacking resolve are indeed many-branched and infinite.

O descendant of Kuru, the intellect characterized by resolve—resolve being certainty—is indeed established as a single intellect alone that shines forth here in this world. For there can be no duality in a conclusion;

the path established by certainty is one and only one. As for that which is distinct from it, the unsettled [intellect]— *Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the available portion.*

They exist as infinite, distinguished by many kinds of divisions. Because they possess infinite modes, there is simply no end to such classifications. However, for those who lack knowledge of the ultimate reality (*paramārthatattva*), whose intellects have not attained [realization], and who are unsettled, they become infinite; for a single person, [these objects] consist of cattle, sons, and so forth.

The supreme goal of human endeavor (puruṣārtha) is that [liberation]; he lives solely for its sake. For another, however, wealth alone is the supreme goal of human endeavor; for yet another, worldly fame alone is the supreme goal of human endeavor. Therefore, it is said that the intellects of the undiscriminating and the deluded have many branches—that is, they are of many kinds. But as for those who are resolute...
Those possessing certain knowledge correctly understand the supreme purpose of human birth and so forth;

because their purpose is singular, it is said that their intellect is likewise one. Praising the conduct of those whose minds are thus established, the Śaraṇas [criticize] those who are unsettled for their being preceded by false pride.

They declare that action is far removed from truth; this must always be remembered by all. Having done and done again, they are frustrated by dejection; having given and given again, they are frustrated by the loss of truth. For whatever they might do or give, through union with truth, they would be united with you alone, O Lord of the Confluence. Thus they are established.

The meaning is that those who, with a stainless mind, for the sake of pleasing Lokeśvara and with the vision of the world’s welfare, are always engaged in action, are not bound by that action. || 41 ||
With three verses, he censures those who lack a resolute intellect: "That flowery speech which the unwise proclaim... (p. 71).
O Pārtha, those who delight in the mere recitation of the Vedas argue that there is no other world.

Those whose nature is desire and who look toward heaven follow [this path], which yields birth as the fruit of action and abounds in various ritual performances, leading toward the attainment of enjoyment and power. (43)
For those who are deeply attached to enjoyments and power, whose minds have been carried away by that [attachment],
the intellect characterized by worldly exertion is not established in meditative absorption.
O Pārtha, those who are unwise—meaning ignorant and lacking discrimination—are possessed by desire. "Desires" (*kāma*) are so called because they are desired;
these include fame, gain, honor, and the like. Having such a nature, their minds are constantly inclined toward them.
Transcending some worldly fruit, they are attached to heaven—that is, their minds are inclined toward the happiness of heaven. Thus...

And it has been stated that for these [people], both types of results—those pertaining to this world and those pertaining to the next—are indeed to be abandoned. They are "devoted to Vedic discourse" (*vedavādaratāḥ*), but not devoted to the reality of Vedānta. "Vedic discourse" (*vedavāda*) is well known as referring to the ritual section (*karmakāṇḍa*).
And in the ritual section, for the sake of satisfying those of limited intellect, there are [teachings] regarding results such as cattle, sons, heaven, and fame.

Actions are taught [in the Vedas], and as will be stated right here: "The Vedas have the three qualities (guṇas) as their subject matter. Thus, those who delight in and are attached to the Vedic doctrines that teach only results pertaining to this world and the next—speaking with the conceit that there is nothing else beyond these, asserting that there is indeed nothing such as liberation (mokṣa) other than these—are referred to by the word "others" (anye).

If rebirth exists only for those who perform actions for the sake of heaven—as it is said: "Having enjoyed that vast heavenly world, they enter the mortal world when their merit is exhausted; [that wheel] which bestows birth, action, and fruit, granting birth again and again"—then what need is there to speak of fame, profit, and the like?
It bestows the fruits of action again and again, but does not bestow liberation from action.
Thus, because the intellect of those lacking resolve possesses many branches—that is, it is of many kinds—it abounds in various specific activities;
it consists of manifold actions and is "flowering," like a flowering tree, in every respect.

The sense is that it is merely beautiful to look at, like a tree in bloom but not yet bearing fruit; it is not truly delightful. Regarding this aforementioned speech, which they speak in favor of the attainment of enjoyment and power—that is, the acquisition of minor human goals such as heaven, cattle, and sons—the ignorant ones [speak thus]. Of them—

For those who are intensely attached precisely to enjoyments and lordly powers— whose minds have been carried away by that extreme attachment to enjoyments and lordly powers, meaning whose intellects are lost—

The intellect characterized by resoluteness does not exist—that is, it does not function—in *samādhi*, which consists of the cessation of the fluctuations of the mind. *Samādhi* means the steady concentration of the mind; the intellect characterized by resoluteness is the cause of that.
The meaning is that in the absence of such an intellect, the concentration of the mind upon those [objects] never occurs.

The meaning is that for those whose minds are inclined toward various minor human goals, neither mental composure nor peace ever arises; as he will later state: "He attains peace, not the seeker of desires" (4.39). || 42-44 ||
"Do not be one who is intent on such a trifling human goal," the Blessed One said to Arjuna:

"The Vedas have as their domain the three qualities; be free from the three qualities, O Arjuna! Be free from the pairs of opposites, eternally established in purity, devoid of the concern for acquisition and preservation, and self-possessed. (45)

The state of the three qualities (*traiguṇya*) is the worldly existence (*saṃsāra*) consisting of the three qualities (*triguṇātmaka*), which is material (*prākṛta*). Those whose objects are that [existence] and whose activities are directed toward its production are characterized by the three qualities (*traiguṇya*). Such individuals are distinct from the conscious being (*cetana*) who is free from the three qualities (*nistraiguṇya*) and whose sole aim is the supreme goal of man (*paramapuruṣārtha*). Only those who are subject to pleasure, pain, and so forth would be thus; however, those seeking liberation (*mumukṣu*), being distinct from them, would not be so. For this very reason:

"Be ever established in goodness, always relying solely on the quality of *sattva*; likewise, be free from acquisition (*yoga*) and preservation (*kṣema*). Acquisition is the gaining of what has not been gained; preservation is the guarding of what has been gained. The meaning is that you should be devoid of both. Those engaged in ritual action (*karmin*) imagine thus: 'Everything in this world is being done by Me alone.'"

The wise, however, engaging in worldly affairs as mere instruments, know that their acquisition and preservation are carried out by the Supreme Self alone; thus, remaining silent, they fix their gaze upon their own duty.
Even the gain highly expected by those engaged in ritual action arrives only in accordance with the will of the Lord.

Human beings obtain only that which is destined to be obtained; indeed, those who take refuge in Him describe this realm through their own direct experience. Just as canals rush toward a lake to fill it completely, so too, by His grace, one should run swiftly toward whatever wealth the Lord shall bestow at any time.

"Knowing that the attainment of the unattainable occurs, place your mind at the lotus feet of the Guru. Then, through the grace of Śiva, all forms of happiness will come to you. If this stainless one should forget you, he would be struck down like a pot by the falling of a stone. Thus, it is solely by the will of the Lord.
The Śiva-yogins are certain that our effort shall bear fruit; and thus,
let there be neither engagement for the sake of worldly results nor engagement for the sake of protecting them.
Be content with whatever you obtain; for it is only by being so that you will possess self-mastery. Otherwise, the destruction of the self itself would occur—this is the meaning. || 45 ||
If it be objected that since actions yielding fruits such as cattle and sons are also enjoined by the Veda, what fault is there in performing them?
[The Lord] says that there is no insistence that every action prescribed in the Veda must be performed by everyone:
"Whatever purpose is served by a small reservoir of water when there is a flood of water everywhere..."
Such is the extent [of his knowledge] among all the Vedas for a learned Brāhmaṇa. || 46 ||

For the wise man who knows, the seeker of liberation, the Brāhmaṇa who possesses knowledge of Brahman, for whom [the world] is flooded on all sides—[it follows that] this much alone is the purpose in all the Vedas; this is the remainder [of the sense]. Just as a Brāhmaṇa obtains from a lake filled with water only the results of bathing and drinking, but not the mud and such things found therein.

Or he takes fish and so forth; in the same way, merely because they are prescribed in the Vedas, the worldly and otherworldly rites of a Brāhmaṇa are not at all to be undertaken. However, since the wise, acting with an equal vision toward everything, perceive only Paraśiva—the very nature of equanimity—therefore they [behave accordingly].

Those whose nature is knowledge and bliss do not remain relying solely on the Vedas and other scriptures; for the Supreme Self is neither one who delights only in knowledge nor one who delights only in mere ritual action, but rather it is action conjoined with knowledge that pleases Him. "The Great Lord is pleased by knowledge accompanied by right conduct."
The *Siddhāntaśikhāmaṇi* states: This very path, which is the union of knowledge and action, is designated as "devotion" (*bhakti*).
Those who possess knowledge recognize that Supreme Śiva is fond of devotion; therefore, they would not remain solely intent upon scriptural knowledge. Regarding this matter, the *Śaraṇagītā*...

He explains it correctly: "Śambhu is said by people to be fond of sound (nāda)," yet Śiva is not satisfied by sound alone; "Śambhu is said by people to be fond of the Vedas," yet Śiva is not satisfied by the Vedas alone.
Indeed, the Lord of Laṅkā, though he practiced the Veda, lived only half his lifespan because, alas, he was devoid of devotion. But [the one who] practices the Veda...

He who sat upon a lotus became indeed devoid of a head; therefore, Śiva is not merely another form of Nāda, nor is he one who loves only the Vedas. For devotion is what truly comes together with the Lord; thus, "I shall surely become a devotee for the sake of union. In this way, the greatness of devotion is perfectly established.
Having understood this, those possessing true knowledge— who are steadfast in virtuous conduct— do not act by relying solely on their scriptural learning;
therefore, no great fruit arises for them from the Vedas and other scriptures.

To Arjuna, who asks, "Since actions are not to be undertaken by the man of knowledge, how should I perform action?", [the Lord replies]: "For you, whose intellect is as yet immature, action must indeed be performed for the sake of purifying the mind, preceded by the renunciation of attachment to results and the sense of agency. Thus...
But he says that action performed with a desireless disposition leads only to liberation:
"Your right is to action alone, never to its fruits;
let not the fruit of action be your motive, nor let your attachment be to inaction. (47)

Because they are not yet mature and because they are fit to attain maturity, their engagement in action—such as battle—is appropriate; let there be no association with them. And when there is thirst for the fruit of action, you alone would be the cause for the attainment of such a fruit of action; therefore, you are also the cause of the fruit of action.

Do not be [attached]; abandon the notion of agency. For this very reason, let there be no attachment—that is, no connection—to *akarma*, the non-performance of action. Even cessation from action is not appropriate for you; rather, devotion to action must certainly remain within you. And if action is performed with a view toward its respective fruits—

That shall become the means for attaining each respective fruit. Furthermore, he whose intellect is characterized by resolute determination performs action solely with the aim of liberation, without depending even slightly on fame, gain, or the like, but rather out of the conviction that it is simply his duty. Moreover, having abandoned attachment to these actions as well—

And he will state later that "the fruits" are indeed the Supreme Self. Thus, through the performance of action with the view that it is one's duty, the purification of the human mind arises. Then the mind, which consists of the three *guṇas*, transforms into the nature of consciousness (*cid-rūpa*).
This very transformation is reckoned as the universal expansion of power (*śakti-vikāsa*).

It is for this very purpose that human beings have obtained the means such as the body; therefore, embodied beings must certainly perform their own duty for the sake of their own spiritual welfare. Otherwise, a great loss will arise. As the Śruti itself says: "Performing actions here indeed, one should desire to live a hundred years."

It properly impels human beings to engage in action. As it has been said by the learned: "When the impurities have been ripened through actions, then knowledge arises. Therefore, your own duty called battle must certainly be performed.

Thus the Blessed One instructs Arjuna: if action were not to be performed in this manner, then human beings would become objects of the Lord’s displeasure; by this method, humans are not even to abandon action.
They will prevail; for the Lord Himself instructs that at that time Nature (prakṛti) will impel you. Therefore, the sense is that you must certainly engage in battle. || 47 ||
If one should not have regard for the fruit, then how is this battle to be performed? To this he says:
"Established in yoga, perform actions, O Dhanañjaya, having abandoned attachment;
becoming the same in success and failure, equanimity is called yoga. (48)

Therefore, O Dhanañjaya Arjuna, being established in yoga—meaning existing in a state of yoga—and having become equanimous by abandoning attachment to the fruits of action, remain unchanging and perform your duties such as battle. But what is the meaning of "perform [your duties] while established in yoga"? How is that accomplished? How can one who is established in yoga perform action?

In response to the doubt as to whether one would be able to act at that time, the word *yoga* does not refer to meditative absorption (*samādhi*) and the like, but rather to equanimity (*samatva*). That which is equanimity toward success and failure is here called *yoga*. Here, *yoga* is said to be the acceptance of results and non-results with an attitude of equanimity.

In this context, *yoga* is the acceptance of both success and failure with equanimity. He in whom neither joy exists in prosperity nor sorrow in adversity is alone designated here as a *yogin*. To abide without perturbation amidst pleasure and pain is what is called *yoga* here; and thus, regarding the term "established in *yoga*" (*yogastha*), [it refers to this].

The meaning is that one is distinguished by such a cultivation of equanimity. If defeat should occur in battle, then one should remain silent with contentment, through the realization that one’s duty has been fulfilled.
If victory should occur, then likewise one should remain with contentment alone, through the contemplation that one’s duty has been accomplished. Such is [the state].

Yoga is indeed the state of remaining free from modification. This yoga stands by relying upon these two: steadfastness in duty and the renunciation of attachment to fruits. Established in this yoga, one becomes eternally happy and always abides in contentment. As the saying of the learned goes: "If success is not achieved despite effort being made, what fault is there in this?"

For effort does not become fruitless. In that case, this offense committed by oneself must be experienced by oneself alone. Therefore, one's own duty must never be abandoned under any circumstances. || 48 ||

76) He states that action performed for one's own sake with expectation of fruit is to be utterly abandoned, in comparison to selfless action performed after first relinquishing attachment to its fruits:
For action performed through the lower path is far inferior to the yoga of wisdom, O Dhanañjaya.
Seek refuge in wisdom; those motivated by the fruits of action are pitiable.

O Dhanañjaya Pārtha, action performed with an expectation of results is far inferior to action performed through the yoga of the intellect characterized by equanimity. This is because those men who have the fruits as their motive— whose very activity is driven by the pursuit of results— are considered wretched, for they are of a highly contracted nature.

Alternatively, those actions in which the attainment of the fruit itself has become the means are reckoned as "miserable" (kṛpaṇāḥ) and extremely insignificant. Thus, in comparison with the fruit, both the conscious agents who perform them and the actions being performed would be devoid of greatness. Therefore, in the intellect—that is, in the aforementioned state of equanimity—[one should act].

Seek refuge; pray for it. For your own protection, take refuge in that very state of equanimity. By this yoga of the intellect alone, your ignorance shall perish. Those who have taken refuge rightly praise the greatness of such association.

"Ignorance is destroyed by the power of knowledge, just as darkness is destroyed by the strength of light; untruth is destroyed by the power of truth, and likewise iron [is overcome] by the power of a diamond. My very existence, O Lord, has indeed been destroyed through association with those of great majesty who are my refuges. Thus [he spoke]. In this manner...

Only through association with right understanding does a human being attain composure; for this very reason, it is rightly stated here that one should seek refuge in the intellect. It is precisely through the yoga of the intellect that a human being achieves success in his own duty. With such an even-mindedness, one should engage in battle.
The Blessed One commands Arjuna.
Thus, he says that for a person performing worldly action, there may be a great fruit:
"One endowed with wisdom casts off here both good and evil deeds;
therefore, apply yourself to yoga; yoga is skill in actions. (50)

One who is endowed with *buddhi*—that is, established in the yoga of the aforementioned equanimity of intellect, well-refined, perfected through the initiation (*dīkṣā*) of Śiva, and who has learned from the mouth of the Guru the greatness of Śiva’s divine play—is Paraśiva within the body, [realized] through devotion, the vital breaths, and the beloved [deity].
Knowing that [the Self] abides between the eyebrows,

one abandons both the good and evil deeds performed by oneself in this world; one dwells together with the Supreme Self and at that very moment offers [all actions] with devotion, without any expectation of fame, gain, heaven, or the like.
For a living being performing an action that has necessarily arisen as a duty,
there will certainly be no merit, demerit, or the like resulting from such an action. Therefore,
since you must engage in battle which has necessarily arisen as your own duty (svadharma), even though the killing of your brothers and others may occur.

For evil cannot possibly arise. Therefore, since merit and demerit are thus inapplicable here, you too should apply yourself to yoga—that is, to the cultivation of equanimity—and exert effort; for when actions are performed, yoga—skill in the aforementioned cultivation of equanimity—becomes the bringer of security and the means to achieve the welfare of the self. Therefore:
"Apply yourself to yoga. Furthermore, He will say later: "Therefore, O Arjuna, be ever united with yoga.

The intention is that the individual soul (*jīva*) must strive by all means to unite with the Supreme Self (*paramātman*)—who exists in the form of the *bhāva-liṅga*, *prāṇa-liṅga*, and *iṣṭa-liṅga*—through the state of *samarasatā* (equilibrium of flavor). This is achieved through the renunciation of the fruits of all actions unto the Supreme Self in His aspect as the Desired (*iṣṭa-rūpin*).

The soul (*jīva*) is designated as the limb of renunciation (*tyāga*). Because it experiences the enjoyment of all fruits within the heart together with the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), who is of the nature of *prāṇa*, the soul is called the limb of enjoyment (*bhoga*). Thus, after the self-surrender (*samarpaṇa*), the individual soul enjoys that very [fruit] together with Śiva. In this way, through the service of grace (*prasāda*), the soul—

Being conjoined with the *bhāvaliṅga* of true form shining upon the head, it is designated as a limb of yoga (*yogāṅga*). According to the perspective stated in the *Siddhāntaśikhāmaṇi*: "Just as a sprout is already established within a seed, so Śiva resides within the self," Śiva indeed dwells within the individual soul (*jīva*) as its inner controller (*antaryāmin*). And he...

He shines in the form of the beloved (in the form of bliss) between the eyebrows, in the form of vital breath (prāṇa) in the heart, and in the form of pure being (sat-rūpa) in the head. Thus, because he serves as the locus for the playful sport of the Supreme Self, the individual soul (jīva) is called a "limb" (aṅga). This soul, named "the limb," [is the enjoyer] of the fruits of all actions.

From enjoyment (*bhoga*) comes the limb of enjoyment (*bhogāṅga*); by the greatness of this enjoyment of grace (*prasāda*), the individual soul (*jīva*) becomes radiant upon the head in the thousand-petaled lotus (*sahasrāra-kamala*).

Through the very renunciation of fruits, the soul ought to become the limb of renunciation (*tyāgāṅga*); likewise, through the enjoyment of grace alone, it ought to become the limb of enjoyment. He who is both a renouncer and an enjoyer is indeed the limb of yoga (*yogāṅga*).

[The practitioner] should become [a yogi]. A person of discrimination should always exert effort to attain such yoga; this very intention is revealed here by the words "yoke yourself for yoga. || 50 ||
For one who acts in this manner, there is not only the attainment of the fruit, but rather the attainment of liberation; thus he says:
"For the wise, endowed with discernment, having abandoned the fruit born of action..."
Freed from the bondage of birth, they go to the state that is free from suffering.

Those endowed with discernment (*buddhiyuktāḥ*), who are possessed of the aforementioned cultivation of equanimity and are wise (*manīṣiṇaḥ*) discriminators, having abandoned the fruit born of action—

consisting of cattle, sons, heaven, and so forth, but not having abandoned action itself— they [attain] liberation from the bondage of birth through the destruction of the fetters of impurity (*malapāśa*) by virtue of association with auspicious yogis, right here in this very body of grace (*prasādakāya*).
Upon the dissolution of the body, liberation—which consists of the absolute cessation of suffering and is eternal and infinite—is experienced.

This, however, is the extraordinary majesty of Śivayoga alone, to be experienced only by those possessed of discernment. Those who seek refuge describe the greatness of yoga correctly; indeed, all mountains are joined by the Gaṅgā and other rivers.
They are destroyed by being uprooted. Indeed, through contact with fire, wood perishes along with its very roots;
behold, O living soul! Through contact with one who possesses true knowledge, a creature indeed dissolves into Śiva by the destruction of ignorance.
In the same way, O Śambhu, Mallikārjuna, it is through union with you alone that the world attains happiness. Thus, it is solely through Śiva-yoga...
The practitioner-soul is capable of attaining liberation, which is of the nature of eternal bliss. || 51 ||
Regarding when such an intellect characterized by equanimity will arise in the practitioner, he says:
"When your intellect shall transcend the thicket of delusion, then you will attain indifference toward what has been heard and what is yet to be heard. (52)

When— meaning at which time— your intellect shall cross beyond the mire of delusion (moha), that is, the turbidity consisting of non-discrimination; at that time, you will realize that there is nothing more to be heard regarding the objects of this world and the next, concerning which you have determined what ought to be heard and have already heard so much.
Only for the self that lacks discrimination between the beneficial and the harmful would there be engagement in activities yielding meager results.

However, for a living being possessing such discrimination, detachment from such activities that yield meager results arises spontaneously. Therefore, having first firmly established discrimination, one should remain devoted to one's own duty.
The meaning is "it would be. || 52 ||
79) Thus, he also describes the higher fruit for one who possesses discrimination and is established in yoga:
"Then your intellect, which has been perplexed by various scriptural teachings, will stand firm and unshakable."
When your intellect becomes unshakable in concentration, then you will attain yoga. || 53 ||

Their intellect, having been confounded by the hearing of such words over this much time— words spoken by those ignorant of the truth who are intent on worldly existence, who are devoted to fame and gain, and who declare through various statements that "this alone is the fruit of birth"— has become confused; "confounded" means having fallen into a misconception, that is, a contrary understanding.

The meaning is that she has fallen into, or reached, the state of having the notion of what is to be abandoned regarding what is to be accepted, and the notion of what is to be accepted regarding what is to be abandoned.

When such an intellect—by the power of discrimination—becomes steady, resolute, and very firm, it shall remain fixed for the duration of my birth; for fame, gain, and the like are not its goal, but rather [the highest good].

When the firm conviction arises that "this is indeed liberation from the bonds of saṃsāra," then, because the intellect no longer engages with things of little fruit, it does not become defiled— that is, corrupted— in manifold ways. At that time, with the cessation of such restlessness, that intellect, being of the nature of certainty, becomes concentrated in *samādhi*— that is, the mind is absorbed therein.

Samādhi: When you are established in that state of equanimity of mind which is called samādhi—in which the soul’s intellect becomes concentrated, free from turbidity, and attains peace—your mind will become unshakable and firmly established. Through that, you will attain yoga, which consists of equanimity toward all things.

If the cultivation of equanimity were to arise spontaneously when the intellect is concentrated, then when the intellect is not concentrated, that cultivation of equanimity would not occur because of its turbidity; such is the meaning. || 53 ||

When it has been stated that by thus completely renouncing attachment to the fruits [of action], a person’s intellect becomes steady and established, Arjuna asks about the characteristics of such a person of certain realization:
"O Keśava, what is the description of one whose wisdom is steady, who is established in samādhi?"
What would one of steady wisdom speak? How would he sit? How would he move? (54)

Arjuna said: O Keśava, Kṛṣṇa, what is the description of one who is established in samādhi—that is, one who is steadfast in the wisdom described above? What indeed is his speech, and of what nature is it? And how does that person of steady intellect behave toward others?
What kind of speech would he utter? How did he speak? In what manner did he sit? In what manner did he walk?
"Where would he go? What would be the nature of his movement, his station, and so forth?"—thus Arjuna asked. (54) To Arjuna who had thus questioned him, the Blessed One gave this reply:
"O Pārtha, when one completely abandons all desires residing in the mind..."
But when one is satisfied in the self alone by means of the self, then one is called "steadfast in wisdom. (55)

The Blessed Lord said: O Pārtha Arjuna, when one completely abandons—casts off—all desires existing in the mind, whether pertaining to this world or the next, such as fame, gain, heaven, and the like, which are objects of limited human ends; but rather, remains established in the Self alone—then he attains peace.

When he dwells satisfied within himself alone by means of the mere experience of the Self through the power of yoga, then he is called one whose wisdom is established (*sthitaprajña*). Considering sensory pleasures and the like to be utterly insignificant, he is content with the bliss of the Self alone; however, as long as there is no possibility of withdrawing the mind from its objects, his wisdom can never truly become well-established.
One whose mind is unperturbed in the midst of sorrows, who is free from longing amidst pleasures, and from whom passion, fear, and anger have departed—he is called a sage of steady wisdom. 56.

When sufferings have arisen, one whose mind is undisturbed—meaning one whose mind is not agitated or perturbed—is one whose heart remains unaltered. Likewise, regarding pleasures, one is free from longing, being devoid of any expectation for them. Just as fire is not extinguished by fuel, the desire for sense objects is not quenched by enjoyment; indeed, desire for sensual pleasures is never satiated by the indulgence of those pleasures.

They say: likewise, because he is unchanging even in suffering and because he is free from longing even in pleasure, he is one whose passion, fear, and anger have departed; such a person is called a sage, a yogi, one of steady mind, and one of steady wisdom.
During his lifetime, whatever sufferings may arise at various times, he regards them with contentment as being obtained through the grace of the Blessed One.
This person of steady wisdom accepts [this]. The *Śaraṇas* describe his way of life in a manner that touches the heart.

"Having observed the suffering of the body, one who is afraid should never pray to the Lord for its protection. Rather, one should pray that the body may be cast away; let whatever is destined to happen here be so eternally. Let both censure and praise follow the servant; indeed, it is true that both will be beneficial for him. Such is the steadfastness found in one whose wisdom is established.

We observe this very fact. Therefore, for such a person, everything—including pleasure, pain, and so forth—transforms into the form of the Lord’s grace. In one who possesses such experience, even desire and the like abandon their own crookedness; employed toward the Lord and becoming dear to Him, they adorn the experiencer. What could desire possibly do here?
"What would anger avail one who desires the *liṅga*? What would greed avail one who longs for refuge?

And what would delusion avail one who yearns for grace? Thus, Basavārya [declared] that desire, anger, and the like should be employed in the service of Śiva, who is embodied as the Guru and the *Jaṅgama*.

He explains: likewise, even though desire, anger, and the like exist, if they are employed for the sake of serving Śiva, they do not produce any harm whatsoever. However, the *Śaraṇas* warn practitioners that no room must be given to pride and envy, because through those two, the very purity of consciousness would be lost.

O Lord of Saṃgam, the purity of consciousness cannot be observed in those whose nature is characterized by intoxication and envy; for it is a well-known conviction that the Divine dwells only among those who strive in virtuous conduct. Thus does the venerable Basavārya praise virtuous conduct in those free from envy. A yogi of this very kind is designated as one of "steady wisdom" (sthitaprajña).
Kṛṣṇa observes that Arjuna shall become such a yogin.
He who has no attachment anywhere, and who neither rejoices nor feels aversion upon encountering whatever is auspicious or inauspicious—his wisdom is firmly established. 57.

That yogi who is entirely free from attachment toward all worldly objects—attachment being clinging—and who, having encountered anything whatsoever, neither rejoices nor feels aversion; who, upon encountering the auspicious, does not exult, reflecting that such exultation is itself the cause of inauspiciousness, and thus does not disparage anyone; for such a person as this...
The wisdom of the sage practitioner is established and remains well-settled (p. 82). He is called one whose wisdom is steady. For the sake of protecting the body, [he endures] that suffering...
However, it must be understood that a person of virtuous nature, who is indeed dear to Śiva, may dwell in this world for even a single day; thus is the meaning of the words of refuge. || 57 ||
And when he withdraws his senses from the objects of the senses, as a tortoise draws in its limbs from all sides, his wisdom is firmly established. 58.
When this yogi completely and entirely withdraws his own senses— the mind and the rest— from their respective objects, just as a tortoise draws in its limbs,
and remains free from even the slightest expectation, being self-witnessed [in that state], then the wisdom of that sage [shines forth].

He is firmly established; he alone is called one whose wisdom is steady. And thus, knowing pleasure or pain—attained by chance through the power of karma—to be equal, and being satisfied within himself by means of the self alone, he is to be understood as one whose wisdom is steady. 58.

Regarding how the withdrawal of the senses from their objects should be performed, he says: "The objects turn away from the embodied one who abstains from food, except for the taste; even that taste turns away from him once he has seen the Supreme. (59)
For a person whose body is without food and who does not enjoy sense objects, the objects— namely form, taste, smell, and so forth—

which constitute the fundamental seed, cease upon their removal. However, because the nature of the senses is to grasp objects and because that nature is difficult to abandon, such a nature remains within them in the form of a latent seed.

However, for a person who does not indulge in objects one after another, his senses would remain silent as if realizing, "My power does not operate in his presence. Therefore, the desire for the enjoyment of sense-objects must first be abandoned; and these objects, such as sound and the rest, belong to the external senses.

It is well known that intentions for wealth such as fame and profit belong to the mind; therefore, all of these must be abandoned from afar by one who possesses discernment. Furthermore, the "taste" (rasa) that exists as the seed within the senses is of a nature of supreme bliss, which exceeds the pleasure derived from the objects of the senses.
Having seen and experienced the reality that is the supreme essence (*paratattva*), one ceases [from worldly existence] by oneself. Through the experience of the Supreme Self, one attains liberation;
for that purpose, neither individual effort nor any worldly activities whatsoever are required.

When a human being proceeds by contemplating Śiva, at that very moment his mental disposition undergoes a transformation; from that point forward, he attains the state of Brahman. Remaining thus, one’s desires do not arise—however, the conquest of the senses is not easy, as he says:
For the turbulent senses, O son of Kuntī, violently carry away the mind of even a wise man who is striving for self-control.

O son of Kuntī, for even of a wise man—one who strives, indeed making every effort, and who knows all this—the turbulent senses, which are by nature destructive and cause instability of the mind, forcibly and suddenly carry away the mind; they would turn it outward. And thus, first—
One must achieve mastery over the external senses; otherwise, even the mind will become defiled.

"The powerful host of senses drags away even a wise man," thus the great seer Vyāsa declares the capacity of the senses to attract the mind. Therefore, by means of a regulated method regarding the senses—
Human beings should strive with the power of their intellect for its proper application.
Restraining all these, one should sit disciplined, intent upon Me;
for he whose senses are under control, his wisdom is firmly established. (61)

Therefore, having fully restrained— that is, properly controlled and regulated according to the established rule— all those senses which are so turbulent and productive of harm, being disciplined through equanimity toward all things and composed with your mind intent on Me alone—
meaning your heart is solely inclined toward Me— you must become one who is certain that the Supreme Self alone is to be attained by you.

Remain in one-pointed meditation alone. For that person who remains thus, under whose control the senses abide, his wisdom becomes established and unwavering. The method for restraining the senses taught here is simply their employment in their proper task. By the individual soul (jīva) joined with the intellect...
If the sense faculties were employed for the practice of Dharma, then they would not be causes of bondage.
84) Thus, by accomplishing his duty through the very cooperation of the sense faculties, a human being achieves his own spiritual welfare.

The Blessed One expects that one should accomplish this. However, the Śaraṇas establish this subject based on their own experience, providing illustrative examples. A statement by Basavārya shines forth here as a worthy illustration:
"If the senses are indeed restrained by mortals, then there would be freedom from being defiled by faults."

"O Lord Gurukūḍalārya! Did Siriyālabhakta, who was solely addicted to enjoyments, renounce the pleasure of those enjoyments once he became detached? Or did this Ballāla renounce his fortune of enjoyment? For one who, having taken refuge in you, desires another's wife or another's property, is indeed always cast away. Thus, the senses [should be employed] for the sake of service to the Blessed One.

What the noble Basava says—that one should act for one's own welfare only after having disciplined [the senses]—is indeed to be accepted by all at all times. The path for the discipline of the senses is also correctly taught by that great soul. O noble one who has met with the Guru, look upon me as your servant; I entreat you with firm devotion.

"Make me, out of mere compassion, a cripple so that I do not wander here and there; and out of mere compassion, make me mute so that I hear nothing else but this very place. Likewise, look upon me today such that, having abandoned your feet, nothing else is thought of by me. Thus [he prayed] at all times.
The application of the senses solely for the purpose of serving the meditation on the Blessed One is indeed the means by which they are diverted from evil paths.
He describes the method of restraining the senses and the harm that arises from their lack of restraint in two verses: "In a person who dwells upon sense objects, attachment to them arises."
From attachment arises desire; from desire, anger is born. || 62 ||
From anger arises delusion; from delusion, the confusion of memory;
from the loss of memory comes the destruction of discernment; and from the destruction of discernment, one perishes.
By contemplating external objects such as forms and touches, as well as internal ones such as fame and gain, attachment arises toward them;

from the obstruction of those [objects], anger is born. When anger has arisen, delusion—that is, a lack of discernment—is produced. For the well-known maxim holds that "an angry man might even kill his own teachers. Thus, it is from this lack of discernment [that [evil follows]].

Confusion of memory—such as [the thought] "Who am I? or "What ought to be done?"—results in the destruction of the discrimination between what should and should not be done. By that, there is the destruction of the intellect. And from that, one perishes; the human being becomes completely ruined.

For right understanding indeed becomes the cause of all prosperity; the meaning is that upon its destruction, the ruin of the person is inevitable. The Śaraṇas illustrate the disastrous consequence of anger through its heart-wrenching nature: for him who, through lack of discernment, takes up anger, there is no [prosperity].
They maintain that it is not merely a loss of status and honor, but rather a total destruction of everything that may occur.

Why do you become angry? Even when a person is angry, what fruit would that yield for you or for others? Anger toward the body destroys honor; anger of the mind destroys wisdom. A householder might burn his own home...

"The house itself is the forest; it is as if no other house burns [the self], O Lord. Thus, the refuge Basavārya correctly demonstrates the adverse consequence being turned away by anger. In this way, since it is heard in scripture that desire, anger, and so forth arise from attachment to sense objects, practitioners should always remain in the company of the virtuous.

It is observed that by directing desire, anger, and the like toward the Supreme Self—the Great Object—one shall attain the fulfillment of birth through His very grace alone. Only after attaining such maturation of the mind do practitioners become established in their duty; it is only then that they become eternally beautiful.
Indeed, for as long as a human being dwells in the world, for that long he experiences objects such as forms and touches through his senses;
yet, by engaging with these objects through senses free from attachment and aversion, one who has self-control and a disciplined mind attains tranquility. (64)

Being free from passion and hatred by means of the method previously described— thereby abandoning attachment to pleasant things and aversion or delusion toward unpleasant things— they are thus self-controlled; while experiencing or enjoying the objects of touch and so forth that have arrived at that particular time through the power of karma, they [perceive] their own internal body as consisting of the desired life-force and its states.

Having then offered those very objects of sense enjoyment with devotion to the Supreme Lord, and partaking of them as His remnants, the individual soul— submissive in spirit, steady in mind, well-purified by Śiva-initiation, and stainless— attains *prasāda*, that is, the purity of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), regarding the objects of enjoyment such as touch and the rest.
In each and every [form], there exist three categories: form (*rūpa*), taste (*ruci*), and satisfaction (*tṛpti*). If these are offered with devotion, then the Supreme Lord [is pleased].

The one and only Supreme Self manifests for the sake of bestowing grace upon devotees in the form of the *prāṇaliṅga* in the head and in the form of the *bhāvaliṅga*. Having understood all this from the gurus, if the practitioner— the individual soul— were to offer even a single edible object with devotion to the Supreme Self, then that form belongs to the *iṣṭaliṅga*.
The *rasa* (essence) is offered to that which resides between the eyebrows as the *prāṇaliṅga*; *tṛpti* (satisfaction) is offered to that which resides in the heart as the *bhāvaliṅga*;

and [the offering] is dedicated to that which shines upon the head. Through such dedication, the qualities of *rajas* and *tamas* are eliminated from the objects of perception, and only the quality of *sattva* remains. Thus...

Through the increase of *sattva* and by acting with *sāttvika* conduct, clarity of mind arises for the practitioner. Those who have experienced reality say that this clarity is indeed serenity. Renunciation (*tyāga*) is defined as the giving of whatever one possesses with contentment to some worthy recipient before enjoying the object oneself. It is through this very renunciation that the Supreme Self is pleased, and not otherwise.

"Neither by enjoyment, nor by ritual action, nor by progeny, nor by wealth, but by renunciation alone have some attained immortality"—thus the venerable Śruti itself describes the greatness of renunciation. By renunciation alone, a human being becomes dear to Śiva and, through the unfolding of Śakti, becomes Śiva Himself. This indeed is the state of immortality; not by enjoyment.

The animalistic mode of existence increases; however, if that very same object of enjoyment is consumed after renunciation, it becomes transformed into *prasāda* (divine grace) and purifies the practitioner. It is the Lord’s intention that human beings should never be consumers of material objects, but rather consumers of *prasāda*.

"By that which has been renounced, you shall enjoy; do not covet the wealth of anyone"—thus it is heard in the *Īśāvāsya Upaniṣad*. By the offering of objects whose nature consists of desired forms and tastes, and which are themselves satisfied by the essential form [of the deity], those very things are enjoyed by the Supreme Self through its very invisibility and are then relinquished.

Out of affection, they are returned in order to bestow grace upon the devotees. This very substance remaining after consumption is conceived as *śeṣa* (the remnant) in the Vaiṣṇava tradition, and as *tyakta* (the abandoned) in the Vīraśaiva tradition.
It is everything—be it pleasure, pain, or anything else—that has been offered with devotion to the Supreme Self at that very moment.

He who accepts what has been renounced by another, considering it as such, becomes eternally happy. He alone is a *brāhmaṇa* who experiences such eternal happiness even in the midst of suffering. This indeed is the equalization of pleasure and pain. He who possesses this vision of equality is a *brāhmaṇa* in every respect. He who is thus...
Having contemplated the Supreme Self— who dwells within one's own heart for its own benefit, who is dearer than life itself, and who is the eightfold deity—
as such,
one should offer all of one's own food with devotion to Him.

He alone is a Vīraśaiva who embraces the singular vow of the hero (vīravratam). Having realized that the Brahman-consciousness, which pervades all as the form of the universe, is the undivided Liṅga, he who contemplates his own abiding within that very [Liṅga] and considers himself to be entirely dependent upon it— he alone, because his mind is surrendered to the Liṅga, [is a Vīraśaiva].

Thus, it is designated as "liṅgāyata. In this way, discerning individuals should understand that the terms *brāhmaṇa*, *vīraśaiva*, and *liṅgāyata* do not merely denote castes, but rather signify the realization of the state of Brahman.
Everyone of virtuous conduct has the right to attain such a state of Brahman. Thus...

Having become a brāhmaṇa and having completely abandoned the notions of "I" and "mine" regarding the state of Brahman, and having become pure through the enjoyment of His grace, the Supreme Self, Śrī Kṛṣṇa, impels Arjuna to carry out the battle with the contemplation that it is an act of worshiping Śiva. || 64 ||
For one who has attained serenity, the destruction of all sufferings arises;
for the intellect of one whose mind is serene quickly becomes firmly established. 65.

When the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) has become serene through such serenity and the enjoyment of that serenity, the cessation of all sufferings arises for the person (*puruṣa*). For indeed, the root of all sufferings is the turbidity of the mind alone.
The mind itself is the cause of bondage and liberation for human beings; it leads to bondage when attached to sense-objects, and to liberation [when detached].

"The mind has no object"—thus it is said by those who possess direct experience. For the intellect of a person whose mind is thus serene quickly, indeed very swiftly, becomes firmly established. The meaning is that such a practitioner, possessing unwavering devotion, soon becomes one whose wisdom is steady (sthitaprajña). || 65 ||
For one who is undisciplined, there is no discernment, nor is there meditative cultivation for the undisciplined;
for one who does not cultivate, there is no peace, and for the one without peace, how can there be happiness? (66)
For one who is undisciplined and whose mind is not composed, correct understanding does not exist and cannot arise.

Likewise, for such an individual soul— a person who has not taken refuge in the Supreme Self through the spirit of total surrender— there exists no [correct understanding] even during the time of worldly activity, despite [the Lord] shining upon his head.

For one who has not attained identity with the observer (prekṣaka) through the mark of being (bhāvaliṅga), meditation—namely, the constant contemplation of the Self—is not possible. For such a person, the vision of self-similarity (*ātmaupamya*) does not yet shine forth.
He who performs actions by placing them in Brahman, having abandoned attachment, [is liberated].
He is not stained by evil, just as a lotus leaf is not wetted by water.
Thus the Blessed One himself will say. In this way, for all actions as well, yoga is precisely their performance with the vision of equality through the state of Brahman. That...
Thus, that in which [such qualities] are not found is understood to be "unfit" (ayukta). For one who is unfit, the cultivation of existence does not occur.

In this way, for one devoid of internal cultivation, peace—that is, tranquility—is not possible. For one who is not peaceful and is defiled by sense objects, how can happiness be obtained? [Such is] the happiness obtainable through the senses.

That it is indeed mixed with suffering is known by all; for the Blessed One himself said, "Those enjoyments born of contact are verily the source of suffering. Therefore, only for one who is united [with yoga] through worldly activity (*vyavahāra*) could there be eternal happiness. Those by whom such a yoga is not attained, they alone experience suffering through worldly activities.

They attain [this]. This very intention is revealed in the statement, "Yoga is skill in actions. He who, for his own sake and for his own benefit, conducts himself through that very egoism becomes a partaker of suffering. But he who, along with all his senses, [offers] even his own self to the Liṅga of Prāṇa shining within his own heart...

Having surrendered herself for the sake of his satisfaction, she acts solely in accordance with his prompting and never experiences suffering. She who is centered on him, devoted to him, whose life-breath is absorbed in him, and who, having become composed, constantly acts only for the pleasure of her husband, remains forever eternally happy. Peace and contentment.
As he transforms through his own inherent nature, the Supreme Self teaches that such conduct in a state of wakefulness is itself Yoga. Familiarity with such Yoga is necessary for everyone;
it is precisely through the non-attainment of this Yoga that human beings become miserable. 66.
To the question of why the intellect of one who is undisciplined does not become steady, he says:
"For when the mind follows after the wandering senses, it carries away his wisdom, just as the wind sweeps a boat upon the waters. (37)
The mind that follows the senses— that is,
the mind which acts in accordance with the senses as they operate within their respective domains—
carries away the wisdom of this person, just as the wind carries away a boat upon the waters of a river's current.

Just as the wind forcibly drives even a boat in whichever direction it blows, so too, when the objects of the senses are powerful, the mind also functions in accordance with them, and consequently, wisdom itself becomes conformable to that— this is the meaning. || 68 ||
Therefore, O mighty-armed one, for him whose senses are completely restrained from the objects of the senses, his wisdom is firmly established. (69)

O mighty-armed one, for that reason, the wisdom of that discerning person whose senses are restrained in every way from their respective objects— the domains of the senses— becomes established and unshakable. || 67 ||

Thus, the engagement with the objects of the senses occurs through the power of ignorance (*avidyā*). And ignorance is the opposite of knowledge (*vidyā*); therefore, this ignorance would destroy knowledge—that is, wisdom. Likewise, once knowledge has arisen, it would destroy ignorance.
That knowledge is the destroyer of ignorance is well-established. Such is the relationship between knowledge and ignorance.
He explains how they are mutually destructive:
"That which is night for all beings, therein the self-controlled man is awake;
that wherein beings are awake is night for the sage who sees. (69)
Just as night becomes day for night-stalkers and day becomes night for them,
