so too, that which is night for all beings— that darkness which is the cause of non-discrimination and the reason for the non-perception of all objects— in that very darkness the self-controlled yogi remains awake.

He perceives everything; yet the world proceeds in a manner entirely contrary to that. Therefore, for them, discernment itself is called "darkness" because it opposes their own desires. As for the yogi, although he does not perceive the external forms of objects in the darkness, he indeed perceives the luminous, Brahmanic nature of consciousness.

At that time, however, those lacking discrimination do not perceive the external forms of objects due to the absence of external light; yet, they are likewise unable to behold the form of consciousness (cidrūpa) shining within. Therefore, that which is the state of waking for the wise becomes the state of night for the ignorant. When...

When an ignorant person perceives all things through an external vision, the wise person does not perceive them at all; on the contrary, he sees everywhere only the radiance of the Supreme Self. Even external forms are seen by him solely as the nature of Brahman. For those lacking discrimination, that which is opposed to their own desires— [is perceived otherwise].

Discrimination is darkness for the yogis because it is the means to achieve their own desired goal; thus, that very state in which beings— other living creatures— wake up and perceive everything becomes day for the sage who sees,
the yogi who perceives the reality of the supreme truth.
p.

90) It becomes night. For in a state of non-discrimination, a human being performs everything; yet for the knower, that state is like night because it is opposed to his own desired object. And thus, that in which the undiscriminating man delights—
It becomes an object of loathing for the discerning; it is said that whatever is loathed by the discerning is precisely what is most beloved by the foolish. || 69 ||

And thus, in the manner described, he establishes with an illustration that peace or liberation can belong only to the discerning one who is free from thirst for objects other than the Self, and not to one who thirsts after trivial and utterly contemptible things other than the Self:
Just as the waters enter the ocean, which is being filled yet remains established in immovability, even so all desires enter him; he attains peace, but not the one who hankers after desires.

Just as the waters reaching from all sides enter the ocean— which, though constantly being filled by the waters of rivers and other sources, remains unmoved and of one uniform nature— so too, that Person who is eternally of one uniform nature and remains unmodified whether by attainment or non-attainment, into whom all objects of desire (kāmāḥ) enter involuntarily; [him the wise do not grieve].
They enter [into him], yet they do not cause even the slightest modification; he alone attains peace—the composure of the mind in this world—and subsequently, liberation in the form of eternal peace.
One who desires objects of desire—desires being those worldly objects other than the Self that are sought after—in order to desire them...
He whose conduct is such that he desires sensual pleasures—that kind of living being does not attain peace at all; this is the meaning. || 70 ||
Having abandoned all desires, the man who moves about free from longing, without the sense of "mine" and without egoism, attains peace. 71.

Therefore, he who has abandoned—meaning, completely renounced—the desires mentioned as worldly objects; that is to say, one who is devoid of the notion that these possess the status of human goals; for this very reason, one who is free from longing (niḥspṛhaḥ), lacking any expectation toward anything; and for this same reason, one who is without "mine-ness" (nirmamaḥ) and without egoism (nirahaṅkāraḥ), being devoid of the sense of "I" and "mine"—he who is thus constituted [is fit].
He attains, that is, reaches peace. || 71 ||
This is the state of Brahman, O Pārtha; having attained this, you shall not be deluded.
Abiding even at the time of death in this state, one attains the nirvāṇa of Brahman.
p.

91) O Pārtha, this is the aforementioned state of being established in Brahman (*brāhmī sthiti*), which is conducive to the attainment of Supreme Śiva. Having attained this state, no one is ever deluded. Abiding in this state, even at the time of death—that is, even in the final stage of life—
He attains—that is, reaches—the Brahman-nirvāṇa, the liberation that is the very form of Brahman; therefore, the meaning is: "Strive by some means to achieve such a state."
In the third chapter,
beginning with the words, "For action is far inferior to the yoga of wisdom, O Dhanañjaya;
seek refuge in wisdom," the text establishes the discardability of actions and the superiority of knowledge alone.
Thus it was said. Here Arjuna asks:
"If you consider wisdom to be superior to action, O Janārdana, then why do you urge me toward this terrible deed, O Keśava? (1)

O Janārdana Kṛṣṇa, if it be Your opinion— that is, if You consider— that wisdom alone, which is knowledge, is superior to action by comparison with action, then, O Keśava Kṛṣṇa, why do You urge me toward this terrible deed called battle, this horrific task? Therefore, rise up!

"O son of Kuntī, having resolved upon battle," and so forth. However, the mere knowledge that "the Supreme Śiva exists within you in three ways" is not sufficient; rather, He Himself exists carrying out all worldly transactions through His own senses and by means of His servants. At that time, Nature (Prakṛti) draws Him away and forcibly [detaches Him] from their presence.

He causes [the disciple] to perform action. Therefore, if he performs every action for the sake of pleasing the Blessed One, without self-interest, then he becomes a vessel for the Blessed One’s grace and, by His favor, attains happiness. Thus, with the intention that every worldly activity should be performed as an offering for the satisfaction of Śiva who shines within the body—

At that time, Kṛṣṇa instructed Arjuna that every action to be accomplished must be performed by all with the sense of duty; for if a person were to abide solely in the knowledge of his own true nature, he would not perceive the presence of Śiva within the body nor the divine play of the world-activity being carried out through him.
His intention was: "That alone is sufficient; why must this terrible deed called battle be performed? For this very reason, he asks. || 1 ||
(92) With words that seem as if contradictory, you appear to bewilder my intellect.
Therefore, tell me with certainty that one path by which I may attain the highest good.

By means of these previously spoken words— which, as it were, confuse my understanding through their mutual contradictions regarding actions and by praising knowledge while making it impossible to determine the true meaning— you seem to delude my intellect; indeed, you have made me appear as if devoid of the discrimination between what ought to be done and what ought not to be done.
The use of the word "as if" (*iva*) in both instances indicates that this appears so only to one of dull intellect like myself.

You state at one point that for a human being, knowledge of Śiva alone is essential, and by that alone does the knowledge of his own true nature arise; subsequently, having realized that all action is his [Śiva's] alone—

And you say that it should be practiced with faith. A doubt has arisen in me as to whether I should rely on knowledge alone, or whether I should always remain performing action. Therefore, having determined one of these two—either action or knowledge—by means of which I may attain the highest good and a favorable state, [please instruct me].
Tell me how I might attain that; please speak.
O sinless one, I have previously declared that in this world there are two kinds of steadfastness:
that of the Sāṃkhyas by means of the yoga of knowledge, and that of the Yogis by means of the yoga of action.

Thus questioned, the Blessed Lord said: "O sinless Arjuna, two kinds of steadfastness have been previously declared by me in this world—by me taught—namely, the steadfastness of the Sāṅkhyas, the knowers of wisdom, through the yoga of knowledge; and that of the Yogis, the performers of action, through the yoga of action. And likewise, there are some who are qualified for the yoga of knowledge alone."
It is thus stated that others are indeed qualified for the yoga of action (karmayoga). || 3 ||
Having thus spoken, He describes the nature of these two types of perfection:
"A person does not attain freedom from action by merely refraining from the commencement of actions, nor does he achieve perfection simply through renunciation. (4)

By the mere non-commencement of actions, a person does not attain *naiṣkarmya*—renunciation in the form of cessation from action; nor does he achieve perfection, which is the supreme human goal known as liberation, merely through the abandonment of actions, that is, by renunciation alone. And so it is said:
The yoga of knowledge would not be accomplished through the mere renunciation of action alone;
rather, it occurs when, as actions are performed, purification of the mind gradually arises.
The meaning is that, because of the possibility of being established [in yoga], there is an opportunity for the yoga of knowledge at that very moment, and not only at the initial commencement.
In response to the doubt as to why actions are necessary, he states their inevitability:
"For no one ever remains even for a moment without performing action;
indeed, everyone is driven helplessly to act by the qualities born of material nature. (4)

For no person whatsoever can ever, even for a moment or for any length of time, remain without performing action—that is, exist while not acting at all. Indeed, everyone must always perform some kind of action.
There is no living being who abandons action; however, it is by the qualities born of *prakṛti*—that is, those connected with *prakṛti*—that one acts.

Driven by *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*, every single person, being entirely powerless and even unaware of it, performs some action or other until the fall of the body; for since the connection with *prakṛti* is unavoidable, everyone is necessarily compelled to perform some kind of action. Therefore, [liberation does not come] merely by the renunciation of actions.
One must not be deluded by the thought that the yoga of knowledge succeeds; for the meaning is that actions are simply impossible to abandon. || 5 ||
He who sits restraining the organs of action but continues to remember the objects of the senses with his mind, being deluded in soul, is called a hypocrite.

This being the case, he who remains thinking of and contemplating the objects of the senses— the domains of the senses— while forcibly restraining and binding the organs of action, such as the hands and feet, is a person of deluded soul; being utterly afflicted by infatuation, he is a hypocrite, one of false conduct who wears a deceptive guise.

It is said: In this way, the yoga of knowledge would not be accomplished merely by the external renunciation of actions. Thus, the mere restraint of the senses is not sufficient; rather, the meaning is that the withdrawal of the mind from all objects is also required. || 6 ||
He says that one who is fit for action is indeed superior to such a deceitful knower:
"But he who, O Arjuna, having restrained the senses with the mind, engages in the yoga of action through the organs of action while remaining unattached—he is distinguished. (7)

But he who, knowing thus that the complete abandonment of actions is not possible, restrains— by means of the mind, that is, the internal organ— the senses, such as the eyes and so forth, having controlled them from their respective objects;

One who, being unattached through the organs of action such as the hands and so forth, and being free from attachment to the fruits [of action], undertakes the yoga of action—he alone is distinguished. The meaning is that, compared to the previously mentioned one who is fit for deceptive knowledge, this very person who is fit for such action is superior; namely, he who employs the senses according to their proper order and, by means of them alone, remains devoid of any desire for results.
The meaning is that such a practitioner of action, who undertakes action solely for the sake of pleasing the Lord who impels him, is praiseworthy. || 7 ||
Therefore, the Blessed One urges Arjuna to remain steadfast in action:
"Perform your prescribed duty, for action is indeed superior to inaction;
even the maintenance of your body would not be possible through inaction. (8)

Perform the action that has come to you as something necessarily to be done; for, compared to *akarma*—that is, the renunciation of such action—the performance of action alone is superior (*jyāyaḥ*). To the question "Why so?", he says: "Because of the maintenance of the body's course. Without *akarma*, meaning the complete renunciation of action, your maintenance of the body's course (*śarīrayātrā*) [would be impossible].

Even the preservation of the body would not be accomplished; indeed, it could not be achieved at all. When all actions are abandoned, how can the protection of the body be performed? For animals do not enter the mouth of a sleeping lion. Indeed, all desires are fulfilled through exertion—so say the wise.
They say this; therefore, to indicate that action must certainly be performed at least for that purpose, it was said: "Action is indeed superior to inaction. (8)
Now, since action is a means for merit and demerit and is thus a cause of bondage, how can it be superior? To this he says:
"Other than action performed for the sake of sacrifice, this world is bound by action;
therefore, O son of Kuntī, perform action for that purpose, free from attachment. (9)
This world [exists] for the sake of sacrifice. Sacrifice is activity performed for the purpose of pleasing the Lord. From "yaj" (to worship), [sacrifice is] the worship of the gods.
This world—meaning the people here—is bound by action, characterized by the bondage of action in its various forms.
However, when one performs the actions that have necessarily arisen simply as an offering to please the Lord, such action does not [bind].
The meaning is that it becomes a bond. He who contemplates that whatever is performed is entirely an act of worshiping Īśvara is not bound by action; on the contrary, he who [considers] his own...
One performs action solely for one's own happiness, and that very action binds him.

However, he who recognizes the playful activity (*līlā*) of Śiva pervading the universe as being spontaneously manifest within his own body perceives even the functioning of the senses as nothing other than the play of Śiva; therefore, no bondage whatsoever arises from his action.

There would be the possibility of decline. For that reason, therefore, O Kaunteya Arjuna, being free from attachment—having abandoned attachment to the fruit and having relinquished expectation of results—perform action. Attachment to the fruit alone is the cause of misfortune. Therefore, for all actions whatsoever performed by human beings with the body, [attachment to the fruit is the obstacle].
The fruits [of one's actions] must then be offered with devotion to the Lord, who shines within one's very self;

the meaning is that when this is done, there will be no bondage whatsoever in them. Since it is the Lord alone who causes merit or sin to be performed by the living being who is His own servant, therefore this soul has performed everything solely through Him.
Having understood this according to its true nature, one should engage in action with faith, acting merely as an instrument.

Performing action while remaining untainted and not even mentally recollecting one's own agency, one accepts all things, including pleasure and pain, as the grace of the Lord. This alone is the path to liberation from bondage.

Instructed by the Blessed One for the welfare of humanity, Śrī Kṛṣṇa commands Arjuna to undertake the battle that must inevitably come through this contemplation, so that he may experience its fruit as the grace of the Lord, [realizing] that all action resides within the body.
And by dwelling in peace, one becomes eternally happy. For this very purpose, that human being who performs actions with body and senses is never bound by those actions. (9)
In the beginning, Prajāpati, having created living beings together with sacrifice, said:
"By this you shall propagate; let this be the cow of plenty that grants all your desires."
He explains precisely the manner in which a person is released from bondage: In ancient times, Prajāpati—the Creator Brahmā—having created beings together with sacrifice (*yajña*), spoke thus:
"By means of this sacrifice, you shall propagate; that is, attain growth. This...
Sacrifice (*yajña*) is for you—the yielder of desired objects (*iṣṭakāmadhuk*), meaning it milks and bestows upon you all desired and immeasurable objects.
And thus, at the time of the creation of living beings, ritual actions were created along with them, as well as the means for accomplishing their intended purposes. Therefore...
p.

96) One must never abandon actions; indeed, they are impossible to abandon. Furthermore, those residing on the land of Bhārata must necessarily perform action. For this earth is *karmabhūmi* (the field of action), whereas other lands are otherwise.

The masters of supernormal knowledge (abhijñā) call these "lands of enjoyment" (bhogabhūmi). The meaning is that everyone born in the "land of action" (karmabhūmi) must necessarily perform action through the perspective of the body. || 10 ||
Nourish the gods with this; let those gods nourish you.
Nourishing one another, you shall attain the highest good. 11.

Regarding how ritual action in the form of sacrifice accomplishes the desired goal, he says: "The gods. By this sacrifice, which causes the gods—Indra and the others—to be nourished, that is, to be pleased; by your performed work, those gods, being pleased, shall nourish you—that is, they shall satisfy you by granting what you desire. Being honored by you...

The gods will grant you every fruit. Thus, cultivating one another and accomplishing each other's desires, you shall all gradually attain the highest good and even the supreme goal of human life. By performing actions in this manner, every fruit [shall be attained].

Since it is capable of granting all desired objects, it has been declared by the Supreme Self to be "sacrifice" (yajña). Furthermore, this sacrifice is described by the venerable Reṇukācāryas as being of the nature of the worship of Śiva.
Moreover, that very worship is said by the virtuous to be fivefold.
Austerity, ritual action, recitation, meditation, and knowledge— this is the sequence.
He who worships Śaṅkara with these five sacrifices,
endowed with supreme devotion, is indeed remembered as a true devotee.

Thus, he who worships Śiva—who consists of both the manifest and the unmanifest—by means of this fivefold Śiva-sacrifice (śivayajña), obtains every fruit pertaining to both this world and the next through the grace of Śiva. || 11 ||
Thus, he says that even sin would accrue if one does not perform this mutual cultivation:
"For the gods, nourished by sacrifice, will indeed grant you desired enjoyments;
he who enjoys what is given by them without giving to them in return is verily a thief. (12)

For the gods, Indra and the others, who have been nourished, gratified, and propitiated by sacrifices, will indeed bestow and distribute upon you the desired enjoyments—women, cattle, children, and so forth. Thus, whatever means of bodily pleasure is obtained, all of that should be regarded as given by the gods. In this way...
Having taken those things given by them, he who—without giving them to these gods, that is, without providing satisfaction for them—[consumes them] alone;
He who consumes [the offerings] for his own sake alone, merely satisfying his own body and senses, would indeed be a thief, a robber.

For him who turns that sacrificial means—which was granted by the gods in the form of worship for their sake—into an instrument for his own enjoyment, a great sin in the nature of theft certainly arises. This is because by not performing the ritual action, he fails to fulfill his duty.
They properly direct their own minds toward the performance of such pure sacrifices:

"O my mind, listen to these auspicious words, having invoked 'Śiva, O Guru! Likewise, by worshipping Śiva even once, become Śiva yourself through the contemplation of Śiva. Having thus invoked him but once—
"O pervasive Lord Hara, having worshipped with devotion, become Bhava; having summoned this Liṅga by His name—
the Guru Mallikārjuna, who is of the nature of consciousness— and having worshipped Bhava even once,
bestow [the fruit] and remain eternally as that very Liṅga, O mind!"— thus say those who have sought refuge in Him who is the soul of all the gods.
They demonstrate that through the worship of Śiva in the form of the *liṅga*, a human being indeed becomes Śiva himself.

Their firm self-confidence— expressed as, "From contact with you, who are the *liṅga* of consciousness and the moving soul, may there be for me the destruction of the disease of worldly existence"— is something we must remember for a long time.
The virtuous who eat the remnants of the sacrifice are liberated from all sins;
but those sinful ones who cook for their own sake, they indeed consume only sin. 13.

Therefore, those who eat the remnants of sacrifice— sacrifice being the worship of the deities— are those who, having performed that [worship], consume what remains there, namely women, cattle, children, food, and so forth, which they have obtained as a form of divine grace.
By thus utilizing only that, people are liberated from all sins— that is, from all kinds of evils— precisely through the contemplation of divine grace.

The meaning is that no sin arises from the consumption of anything. Even regarding the grace (*prasāda*) consisting of the remnants of sacrifice (*yajña-śiṣṭa*), the sequence must be observed with reverence: whatever edible substance is offered to one's own deity, that very thing, having been consumed by him, is bestowed upon oneself as grace. In one's own deity...

He who does not trust in His own grace would have no trust anywhere. Regarding this matter, Śaraṇā expresses her own intention with frankness: "If one were to abandon the God he worships and worship another instead, he would become fallen; but what do the learned say of one who abandons many gods and eats [the offerings]?"
"Speak for yourself, O Lord!"—thus those who consider themselves devotees restrain you impartially. He who enjoys grace through such firm conviction...

The Blessed One consoles all practitioners by assuring them that they shall be liberated from all kinds of obstacles. However, those who are deluded act out of self-interest, performing all actions such as cooking and the like solely for the sake of satisfying their own bodies, senses, and so forth; they are indeed sinful and possess a sinful nature. It is only sin.
They consume [the fruits of] evil deeds and they bring them about. || 13 ||
Since action is the cause for the continued turning of the wheel of the world, it must necessarily be performed; thus he says:
"From food beings come into existence; from rain comes the production of food;
from sacrifice rain comes into being; sacrifice originates from action. (14)
Know that action originates from Brahman, and Brahman originates from the Imperishable (Akṣara).
Therefore, Brahman is all-pervading and is eternally established in sacrifice.

From food—that is, from the nourishment that has been eaten—beings, the classes of living creatures, come into existence; they are born. For the food that has been consumed is transformed into the nature of blood and other bodily constituents. From the rain-cloud, that is, from the rain, arises the production of food; the origin of food is thus described: "The oblation properly offered reaches the sun; from the sun rain is produced, and from rain comes food."
From that come the subjects; thus it is heard in the scriptures. Therefore, from sacrifice comes Parjanya (the rain-god), and sacrifice arises from action.

Even the Śiva-sacrifice consists essentially of the bringing of materials for worship and so forth. Thus, both types of sacrifice arise solely from action. And action, which is of the nature of activity, arises from Brahman—Brahman being the Veda.

That which has its origin or cause [in this]—namely, ritual action such as sacrifice prescribed by the Vedas—the Śiva-sacrifice (*śivayajña*) is also indeed prescribed in the Veda in the form of the threefold worship (*trividhopāsana*). This is heard in the *Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad*: "From meditation upon that, from union with it, and from becoming one with its true nature" (1.10). Regarding the threefold nature of the officiating priest (*ṛtvij*), see the *Brahmasūtra*... [text truncated].
Know this. Thus does the Blessed One instruct one to know: that Brahman and the Veda are born from the Imperishable (*akṣara*).

The Imperishable is the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), and He alone is the ultimate cause of the Veda. The origin of the Vedas from Paraśiva is well known from the scriptural statement: "This Veda is the breath of that Great Being."
Thus, because it is the cause of all, the Supreme Śiva-Brahman, although omnipresent and existing everywhere, is eternally present at the sacrifice. (p. 99)

It is established that among all activities, sacrifices and the like ordained by the Vedas hold primacy. As he will state later, "Sacrifice, charity, and austerity—these actions purify the wise" (4.28), thus establishing the sanctity of sacrifice and the rest;
therefore, it is said that Brahman is established in sacrifice. (14–15)
O Pārtha, he who does not follow this sacrifice thus set in motion lives in vain here— evil-minded, delighting only in the senses.

Thus, this wheel—the wheel of the universe—set in motion and established by the Lord himself, he who does not follow it lives in vain and fruitlessly, his life consisting of sin. This is because his very delight and place of play are the senses; such a person is one whose life is composed of evil. They describe the wretched life of such people in this way: *indriyārāmo hi yo 'syāntarbahirmukhatayā viṣayeṣveva ramate, na tu ātmani, sa indriyārāmaḥ | sa ca aghāyuḥ pāpamayajīvitaḥ san moghaṃ vyarthameva jīvati |* For he who delights in the senses, being oriented toward objects both internally and externally, finds pleasure only in sense-objects and not in the Self; he is one whose life is sinful and who lives in vain and for no purpose. Thus they point out the miserable existence of those of such a nature.
In the past, hundreds have died for the sake of shelter, and likewise, millions have indeed died for the sake of food;
thousands have died for the sake of women and gold, all afflicted by the disease of worldly existence.
Yet, O Lord of Guha, when examined from many perspectives, not even a single person is seen to have died for your sake. Thus it is said.
They reveal their intention that only he who lives solely for the sake of serving the Blessed One is truly blessed. 16.
But for that person who delights only in the Self, who is satisfied with the Self, and who finds contentment in the Self alone, there exists no duty to be performed. (17)

But that practitioner known as Piṇḍa—a human being distinct from the former type, whose sins have been exhausted by the power of merit acquired through the worship of deities and other virtuous acts performed over many lifetimes—he should find delight only in the Self and not in the objects of the senses;
he should be satisfied with the Self alone and not with sons, wife, and so forth. For such a knower, however, there is this duty:

There is nothing whatsoever that remains to be done here; indeed, there is none. The *Siddhānta-śikhāmaṇi* describes such a practitioner as follows: "When the cage of sins has been destroyed by merits accumulated over many lifetimes, the embodied being with a purified inner organ is designated by the term 'piṇḍa' (the body), having arisen from the power of Śiva."
"In this phenomenal world, he is distinguished as one whose merit is preeminent, whose sins are exhausted, and who is a pure-souled *piṇḍa*.
Thus, this very *piṇḍa* is designated by Śiva as "the devotee" (*bhakta*) and by Kṛṣṇa as "a portion of myself" (*mamivāṃśa*).
(100) For him there is no purpose served by action, nor any at all by inaction here;
nor does he have any dependence on any being for any object whatsoever. || 18 ||

For that knower who delights in the Self, there is no purpose or objective whatsoever to be gained by action; likewise, there is nothing gained by non-action. Nor is there any loss of purpose or the like here through the non-performance of action.
For this knower, whatever purpose might exist among all beings—from Brahmā down to the stationary objects—among all living creatures, [is not affected].
Therefore, always perform the action that must be done without attachment;
for by performing action without attachment, a person attains perfection.

Therefore, because there is an absence of fault through the performance of action without regard for its fruit, one who is unattached— that is, free from attachment— attains, reaches, the Supreme, which is the Supreme Self itself.

By performing action in such a manner, through the purification of the *sattva* [constituent], the dawn of the knowledge of Śiva occurs, resulting in the destruction of the bonds of impurity (*mala-pāśa*).
The meaning is that liberation is accomplished. || 19 ||
For Janaka and others attained perfection through action alone;
you should likewise act, having regard for the maintenance of the world.

He also provides an illustration regarding the necessity of performing action: even kings such as Janaka attained perfection—that is, liberation—through action alone, specifically through the protection of their kingdom and other duties obtained by virtue of their own caste and stage of life (*varṇāśrama-dharma*). This is so even though those such as Janaka were possessed of complete knowledge.

If you think that [the Blessed One] performed such acts as the protection of the kingdom solely for the sake of the welfare of the world, then you too, likewise perceiving the need for the gathering of people, ought to perform action itself for the purpose of preventing the world from following the wrong path according to its own whims. (20)
Whatever a superior person practices, that very same thing other people do;
whatever standard he sets, the world follows it. (21)

If it is argued that this is "for the sake of the welfare of the world" (*lokasaṃgraha*), the meaning of this is now explained: whatever a superior person— that is, a preeminent or leading individual—
practices, whatever action he performs, the other person— the common or ordinary folk— does exactly that.

Furthermore, whatever standard he—the best among men—establishes, whether it be worldly or Vedic, that very standard shall be considered authoritative by me as well. Thinking, "Therefore, I too must do exactly that," everyone would act accordingly. Thus, the meaning is that you, being a person of high standing, should not abandon your duty. || 21 ||
O Pārtha, there is nothing whatsoever in the three worlds that must be done by me;
there is nothing unattained to be attained, yet I continue to engage in action.

He establishes here the meaning previously stated through his own practice: "O Pārtha, for Me, who have attained all perfection, no action remains even in the slightest degree. For, throughout this entire time, there is indeed no unaccomplished task for Me;
I remain engaged in the duty of preserving My own varṇa and āśrama dharma."

By the statement, "Even in the absence of a fruit to be accomplished, I am always intent upon action," it is suggested that the Blessed One himself is the exemplar of the practitioner of Karma-yoga. || 22 ||
For if I were not to engage in action tirelessly at any time,
O Pārtha, men would follow my path in every respect.
O Pārtha, listen to this: for what purpose am I always occupied with the performance of duties?

If I, being untiring and free from laziness, should ever—at any time—not engage in action due to indolence or the like, that is, if I were not to perform action, then all men in every way would surely follow my path alone.

They would follow only my own path and continue to do so; yet, if I were not to perform action, everyone in the world would cease to perform any action at all, and they would merely become a burden upon the earth. (23)
These worlds would perish if I were not to perform action;
I would be the cause of confusion and would destroy these beings. (24)

To the question, "If people in the world were to abandon their duties, what would be the loss? he says: "If I were not to perform action, these worlds, following my example, would also fail to perform their respective duties. (p. 102)

Since all desires have been attained, there would be no loss whatsoever for them; however, because they are not such [as those who have attained their desires], I alone would be the author of the confusion—that is, the confusion of castes and stages of life (varṇāśrama-sāṅkarya). Therefore, the meaning is: "I alone would destroy these creatures," or rather, "I alone, having arrived for the sake of favoring the creatures, would destroy them. || 24 ||
Just as the ignorant act with attachment to action, O Bhārata,
so should the wise man act without attachment, desiring the welfare of the world.

O Bhārata, just as the ignorant and unenlightened, being attached to action, perform various deeds for the sake of their respective fruits, even so the enlightened one, though possessing knowledge, desiring the welfare of the world and following the conduct of the world, performs action with the sense of duty; nevertheless, the knower remains unattached to the fruit of action while performing it.

The ignorant person, however, performs action out of expectation for its fruit and out of self-conceit. Of these two, one becomes liberated from the bond, while the other remains bound by the bond. This alone is the internal distinction between them. || 25 ||
One who knows should not create a disturbance in the minds of the ignorant who are attached to action; rather, remaining disciplined, he should engage them in all actions by performing them himself.

Here he elucidates the very same intention stated previously: for those performers of action who are attached to actions, whose minds are not yet matured, and who are therefore ignorant, there is no "division of the intellect"— that is, no destruction of the intellect characterized by the thought, "This must necessarily be done."

One should produce—that is, one should perform. If you do not perform action, they too, by not performing action, would become fallen. Therefore, the wise person, being disciplined (*yukta*)—that is, united with the Lord who shines within the heart in the form of the *prāṇaliṅga*—himself [should perform] all actions that must necessarily be done.

Even while performing action in accordance with the impulsion of the Lord, one should remain silent; without indicating even in the slightest degree one's own state of knowledge or one's own non-performance of action, even the man of knowledge should perform everything just as the ignorant perform their actions,
for the purpose of generating faith in them regarding those actions.
Being free from attachment to the fruits of action, agency, and so forth, one should indeed act. || 26 ||
All actions performed in every way by the qualities of material nature,
one whose self is deluded by egoism thinks, "I am the doer. (27)

He states the cause for the attachment of the ignorant to actions: "Of nature" (prakṛteḥ) means of Pradhāna, the Unmanifest, the root cause of the entire universe, a substance consisting of the three qualities (guṇas). "By its qualities"—by Sattva, Rajas, and Tamas—"in every way," that is, in all possible manners, are the actions performed.

Sattva is the cause of right action; rajas is the cause of passion and the like; tamas is the cause of ignorance. Therefore, all these three types of effects are entirely dependent upon *prakṛti*. Deluded in mind by the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*), thinking "I alone perform all such actions," the individual soul (*jīva*) considers itself the doer.

Thus one considers oneself [the agent]. In reality, however, the meaning is that agency belongs to *prakṛti* alone. Furthermore, the meaning is that delusion (*moha*)—consisting of the notions of "I" (*ahaṅkāra*) and "mine" (*mamakāra*) and so forth—is the cause of attachment (*saṅga*) in all actions. || 27 ||

But he who knows the truth, O mighty-armed one, regarding the divisions of the qualities and their functions, does not become attached, realizing that "it is the qualities acting upon the qualities. (28)

O mighty-armed one, the knower of the truth regarding the division of qualities (*guṇa*) and actions (*karman*)— that is, knowing that the division of qualities is the root of actions and that the senses,

being naturally engaged in their respective objects which are merely qualities, operate therein— does not harbor even a trace of attachment, thinking, "I have no involvement in this. Thus, knowing this, he does not become attached and does not form an attachment toward any worldly activities whatsoever.
However, he carries out every action with a commitment to duty and a sense of physical detachment;

therefore, he remains in happiness and peace both before and after the performance of that action. The Śaraṇas praise such a practitioner of Karma-yoga, provided that the action is performed in the form of bodily service.

At that very moment, they correctly demonstrate that suffering shall not arise for the doer [of the act]. Agriculture then attains the state of being performed by the body only when it is resorted to by those truly devoted [to the Lord]. When [the mantra] "The dust of the feet of the gurus is upon my head"—thus, for the benefit of the universe whose nature is Śiva—[one acts] with the body as an auxiliary.
Whatever is performed, even all of that does not bind the doer. The meaning is that young men and women should perform their own duties with such a true disposition. || 28 ||
Those who are deluded by the qualities of material nature become attached to the actions of those qualities.
One who knows the whole should not unsettle those dull-witted people who do not know the whole. (29)

Those who are deluded by the qualities (guṇas) of the aforementioned Prakṛti—the substance consisting of the three qualities—become attached, that is, they become bound, to actions through those qualities of sattva, rajas, and tamas. One who knows the whole, the knower of reality, should not cause them—who are knowers of only a part and are ignorant of reality—to waver; he should not produce a confusion of their intellect, for [this applies to] those whose minds are not yet matured.

Actions are indeed unavoidable. If a person of realized knowledge (*jñānī*) whose intellect is fully matured were not to perform action, then others, seeing him, would likewise refrain from acting. Therefore, even one who possesses such knowledge must certainly perform action for the sake of maintaining social order (*lokasaṃgraha*).
Those who have taken refuge in Him praise the greatness of such a knower as an ideal; his words are as follows:

I understand that the supreme purifier is likewise the purity of one's conduct, and he who taught that truth to him is alone the divine Guru. Considering such a house of a devotee to be none other than Kailāsa itself, if a wandering ascetic (*jaṅgama*) should perform the worship of the Liṅga there, he—

"O Lord, I offer my salutation to him who is worthy of worship, the sole purifier of the world, for he is indeed such a moving image of the universe. If the life of a true devotee, which is thus worthy of praise,
were to be upheld by young men and women, then they would be eternally satisfied, eternally happy, and eternally beautiful.
They would exist. || 29 ||
Renouncing all actions in Me with a mind focused on the Supreme Self,
become free from desire and the sense of "mine," and fight, rid of all feverish anxiety.

In that case, what is the destiny of ignorant ritualists? How might they be liberated from the bonds? To this, Kṛṣṇa speaks as follows: having renounced—that is, surrendered—all actions such as battle and the like, which have become incumbent as duties, with an internal mind endowed with discrimination (*viveka*), like a servant for the pleasure of a king.

Thinking, "I perform this solely for the pleasure of the Lord, and not with a view toward its fruit," one should thus abandon the connection with results; being thus free from desire (nirāśīḥ), devoid of longing for results, and consequently free from possessiveness (nirmama)—
lacking the sense of "mine" such that "this should be mine"— and being free from feverish distress (vigatajvara), devoid of mental anguish.
"Fight; perform the battle. In this way, when action is performed without regard for the fruit, no misfortune will arise from it. His very life would become worthy of respect by everyone.
He would not seek any gain beyond the prescribed fruit.
105) He never looks to another nor does he beg; his holy life is thus described by Basavārya:
"Whatever may come to me tomorrow, let that very thing be attained by me this very day."

"Whatever is destined to happen today, let it come immediately; who would fear this, or who would shed tears? For one who is born, death is certain, occurring solely according to the weight of one's own karma. Whatever is written upon the forehead by the Creator cannot be wiped away. Thus [he spoke].
To whom would a man of such utterly shameless nature not be repulsive? For him, there is never any thought of sense objects except for constant contemplation of the Supreme Lord.
And wherever he directs his gaze, there he beholds you; and whatever comes before his eyes—
"Indeed, everything is truly Your form. Thus, the wise perceive the Supreme Self alone everywhere.
The *cakora* bird gazes upon the rising of the moon and gazes upon the light of the sun;
the bee desires the fragrance of the flower. "I have this longing for the Lord who is the assembly of my gurus"—thus [he thinks].

Through his own example, Basavārya points out that for all practitioners, the vision of God alone is a necessity. Thus, under the guise of Arjuna, he instructs all aspirants that the performance of duty must be accomplished through practice by those who desire spiritual growth.
Kṛṣṇa || 60 ||
Those men who constantly follow this teaching of mine,
full of faith and free from cavil, they too are liberated from the bonds of action.

Stating the excellence of the aforementioned meaning and the censure of its opposite, He says: Those men who follow—that is, conform to—this declared opinion and determination of Mine; or, if they are unable to practice it, those who remain full of faith; and even if unable in that regard as well, those who do not find fault with Me—at the very least, [they remain] in Me.

Or, even those who remain without showing malice toward Me are gradually liberated from their actions—both meritorious and sinful—and shall become free. Thus, Lord Kṛṣṇa teaches many paths for the sake of liberation. But those who, being envious of this, do not follow My teaching...
Know them to be utterly deluded regarding all knowledge, ruined, and devoid of consciousness. || 32 ||
But those men who, filled with envy and censuring this teaching of mine, do not follow it—
know them alone to be lost, having fallen into destruction by their own accord; for they fail to perform such action.
Those devoid of discernment will ultimately meet only with destruction; therefore, the Blessed One instructs Arjuna on the true reality so that he may not become like that. 32.
If that is so, why then do not all people in the world follow your teaching?
On the contrary, why do they, being inclined toward meager human effort, bring about their own destruction in this way? To this he says:
"Even the man of knowledge acts in accordance with his own nature."
All beings follow their own nature; what can restraint accomplish?
Even one who possesses knowledge and is discerning acts and proceeds only in accordance with his own nature (prakṛti), that is, his own inherent disposition, according to the maxim:

"One's nature is difficult to overcome. For this reason, living beings—that is, sentient creatures—follow their nature, which is their own inherent disposition. Restraint is considered to be the suppression [of these tendencies] through discernment and other means.
"What will he do? means "What indeed could he possibly do? The meaning is: if such is the course of action for those who possess discernment, what more need be said regarding others? || 33 ||
Attachment and aversion are established toward the objects of the senses;
one should not come under their sway, for they are his adversaries.

When the restraint of the mind is impossible, what should be done? To answer the question of how a human being should strive to achieve self-perfection, he says: "In regard to the object of each respective sense—such as the eye and so forth—namely, in the objects such as sound and touch, attachment and aversion (liking and disliking) are firmly established."

These two are inevitable; therefore, a human being should not fall under the sway of attachment and aversion rooted in dependence on the senses and their objects, nor should he become subject to them. For these two—attachment and aversion—are the adversaries of this conscious being, standing in the place of its primary enemies. Therefore, [one should first subdue] attachment and aversion.
Having renounced [these], with a concentrated mind, you should be intent on what ought to be done; thus the Blessed One, under the pretext of addressing Arjuna, impels everyone.
One’s own duty, though deficient, is better than the duty of another well-performed.
Death in one’s own duty is better; the duty of another is fraught with fear. 35.

He says that for those possessed of passion and hatred, even the meaning of the scriptures appears perverted: "From one's own duty performed with discrimination rooted in passion, hatred, and so forth, [it is better] than the duty of another—that is, the duty belonging to another—even if it is well-performed, yet deficient in its constituent qualities. (p. 107)

Even if devoid of merit, one's own duty alone is better and supreme; for even death while established in one's own duty is indeed conducive to welfare. For one who follows another's duty, even life is better than death while practicing one's own duty, because another's duty is alien to oneself.

One must never abandon one's own duty (*svadharma*) nor practice the duty of another (*paradharma*). It was already explained at the outset that the human being is not merely the perishable body, but rather the imperishable Self (*ātman*); therefore, a person who has become the Self must necessarily perform the duty of the Self. That alone is his *svadharma*.
It is said: if he were to abandon that established, righteous sequence and always follow only the nature of the body, then a great loss would inevitably befall him.
He should consider the nature of the body to be alien to himself; nevertheless, [regarding] the body...

The expansion of one's own qualities must be accomplished through cooperation alone; those who have experienced this truth declare that this is his very own duty (*svadharma*). If the expansion of power were not attained by human beings, then a great succession of calamities would surely arise. (35)
Now, by what impelled does this person commit sin, O Vārṣṇeya, even against his will, as if constrained by force? (36)

In that case, Arjuna asks: "Why does every person in the world commit sin? He continues: "If this is so, O Vārṣṇeya—O Kṛṣṇa, born of the Vṛṣṇi clan—by whom is this man impelled or driven, even though he himself does not desire it, and even while knowing full well, 'This unrighteousness must not be done by me,' yet acts by force, through compulsion?"
Arjuna asks about the cause of the wicked conduct of those who are arrogant, thinking, "Being impelled, one performs and commits evil. (36)
This is desire, this is anger, born of the quality of rajas;
know that it is a great devourer, a great sinner, and the enemy here in this world. (37)

The Blessed One spoke the answer to Arjuna’s question: "This desire, born of the quality of passion (*rajas*), arising from the quality of passion, impels men toward the commission of sin; this alone is the cause for the practice of evil. Likewise, anger rooted in that [desire] impels a human being toward the practice of sin. That desire..."

p. 108) *Mahāśanaḥ*: one for whom there is great eating—that is, one whose food consists of vast objects of enjoyment. For in the world, because objects of enjoyment are infinite, no satisfaction occurs even through constant experience; desire is never quenched.
"By the enjoyment of desires, one does not find peace; rather, like a fire fed with oblations, it increases all the more.

This is indeed a well-known principle. Therefore, desire is a great eater. For this very reason, it is known as a great evil, for it is the instigator even of great sins. Indeed, one whose heart is overcome by desire [is driven to commit] everything.

One becomes prepared to commit evil; therefore, know and recognize this desire (*kāma*) in this cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*) as a foe, an enemy, and a destroyer of all. Having correctly established the miserable state of desire and anger—[the latter] being like a stream of blood—if one who is evil-minded offers an oblation of flowers, [he falls].

One might incur a wound from the edge of a sword; yet, O Lord, anger destroys one's honor, and mental agitation destroys one's wisdom. A forest fire burns down the very house it dwells in, for it does not burn another's house. Thus is the evil influence of desire and anger.
They announce it in a manner that reaches the heart. || 37 ||
As fire is covered by smoke, as a mirror by dust, and as an embryo is enveloped by the amnion, so is this [Self] covered by that. 38.

Just as fire is covered and pervaded by smoke, just as a mirror is covered by impurity, and just as a fetus is enveloped and concealed by the placenta (ulba), even so is this entire universe covered and pervaded by that desire. 38.
Knowledge is veiled by this eternal enemy of the wise,
O son of Kuntī— by desire in the form of fire, which is impossible to satiate.

For the wise man who possesses discernment, desire—which is like a constant enemy, ever-present as an adversary, insatiable, and like a fire—never subsides. Desire is never appeased by the enjoyment of the objects of desire; rather, it increases all the more. By such a fire of desire, a person’s knowledge of reality is destroyed.
A human being does not indeed investigate dharma, adharma, and so forth; therefore, so that a human being does not fall under the sway of desire, association with the virtuous alone [is the means].

One should strive to remain [in such a state] whenever the opportunity arises. Therefore, with the intention that he whose mind is rooted in desire and anger might become well-established if it were to dwell in the company of the virtuous, the Śaraṇas have prepared a singular medicine that destroys the seed of worldly existence. They describe it as follows:

O you of great majesty! It is true that this mind of mine wanders like a monkey leaping from branch to branch. It is so deeply attached to the enjoyment of sense objects that it does not remain even for a moment in the assembly of the virtuous. Likewise, it allows me no entry into the inner heart for the practice of meditative absorption (*samādhi-yoga*). I pray to you [for its restraint].

O Lord Gurusaṅgameśa, have mercy upon this servant who has become a portion of You; place my mind forever in Your lotus feet like a bee. Through contact with You—the moving Self who is the Liṅga of pure Consciousness—there is the destruction of the disease of worldly existence; this cannot be achieved by any other means except through association with the virtuous.
Those who have experienced [the truth] declare that this mind, whose seed is desire and anger, is restrained;

therefore, if a person remains in the company of the virtuous and is devoted to their own duty, then no evil tendency can possibly arise in the mind. For by virtue of association with those of true knowledge, a living being destroys ignorance.
It dissolves into Śiva. In the very same way, O Śambhu, through your yoga alone, O Guru Mallikārjuna, the world attains happiness.

Thus the Lord Siddharāmaśivayogī employs the company of the virtuous (*satsaṅga*) itself as a medicine for the disease of the mind. Knowing this, a person should, to the best of their ability, exert themselves toward the restraint of the mind, which is rooted in desire.
One should strive. || 39 ||
The senses, the mind, and the intellect are said to be its seat;
by these it deludes the embodied soul, veiling its knowledge. (40)
Regarding how desire veils knowledge, he describes its sequence here:

the locus and support of this desire are the senses—the five organs of perception and the five organs of action—as well as the mind (*manas*), the intellect (*cetas*), and the faculty of deliberation (*buddhi*); these are the supports of desire.
This desire arises from restlessness toward objects such as sound, from delusion regarding fame, gain, honor, and the like, and from defects of the intellect. This desire,
through these aforementioned doors of the senses and so forth, obscures knowledge and discrimination, and thereby deludes the embodied conscious being.
It renders one subject to delusion. || 40 ||
Therefore, O bull among the Bharatas, first restrain your senses and utterly destroy this evil which destroys knowledge and realization. 41.
Therefore, O bull of the Bharatas, O Arjuna, for that reason— because the senses and so forth destroy the light of the Self (ātman) of the person— you must first, at the outset, restrain the senses.

Having brought it under control through systematic discipline and having employed it for worthy purposes, abandon— cast away— this evil, this desire which is the cause of sin and which destroys both knowledge and realization;
"knowledge" here refers to that wisdom born of scripture, while "realization" specifically refers to the knowledge consisting of direct experience,
and [desire] is the destroyer of both of these.

Thus, human beings should strive according to their capacity to draw away desire—the root of all misfortune—by withdrawing from the grasping for sense objects, and to apply it instead toward association with the virtuous. Only he who exerts himself to the best of his ability through meditation on the Lord dwelling within the heart is capable of restraining the mind. He who, by means of his own ego...
If one strives by oneself alone, having forgotten the Lord, he will never succeed in restraining the mind. || 41 ||
They say that the senses are superior; the mind is superior to the senses; the intellect is superior to the mind; and he who is beyond the intellect is the Supreme.

He teaches the abiding of the Supreme Self within the body: The wise say that the senses—the ears and so forth—are "higher" (para), because they are more subtle and thus more powerful than the gross body. The mind is higher than the senses, as it is even subtler than they. Likewise, [it is higher] even in comparison to the intellect (buddhi), which is well-known for its subtlety.
The meaning is that he who exists beyond [the universe] is indeed Paraśiva-Brahman. || 42 ||

Thus, having understood that which is beyond the intellect and having steadied the self by means of the self, slay the enemy, O mighty-armed one, who takes the form of desire and is difficult to overcome. 43.

O mighty-armed one, having thus understood— that is, known— the reality that is even higher than the intellect (buddhi), and having steadied the unrefined mind (ātman) by means of a well-refined self (ātman)— that is, the mind— through complete restraint,
destroy, that is, annihilate, the enemy who is difficult to approach, difficult to perceive, and whose form is desire, by means of this yoga of action (karmayoga).

In order to generate mindfulness and enthusiasm so that the excellence of his bodily actions might be firmly established in the hearts of all, the Blessed One has here truly revealed the noble intention of his own incarnation with sincere love. (43)
The Fourth Chapter:

Having thus concluded the connection explained in the two preceding chapters, the Blessed Lord Himself praises yoga, which consists of the performance of action, by means of describing the lineage of its transmission.
(111) I taught this imperishable yoga to Vivasvat;
Vivasvat told it to Manu, and Manu declared it to Ikṣvāku.

This eternal yoga—which is imperishable because its fruit is imperishable—I formerly proclaimed and taught to Vivasvat, the Sun, at the beginning of creation. And that Vivasvat spoke it to Manu, his own descendant;
he, in turn, declared and instructed it to Ikṣvāku, who was born of his own lineage. || 1 ||
Thus, the royal sages knew this [yoga] as handed down through tradition;
but over a long period of time here, O scorcher of the foe, that yoga was lost.

O scorcher of the foe! Thus, this Yoga—which has been handed down in succession and reached us through a lineage of instruction—was lost, its transmission severed, among the royal sages (*rājarṣis*), who were both kings and sages; that is, those who, though being kings, were also sages. It gradually vanished due to the state of lack of discernment on the part of Manu’s descendants.
And because of the difficulty in impelling their inherent nature (prakṛti), this yoga of action has become lost; such is the meaning. || 2 ||
This very same ancient yoga has been declared by Me to you today;
for you are My devotee and My friend, and this is indeed the most supreme secret. || 3 ||
This very same ancient, primordial yoga has been declared and taught by Me to you today for this reason: "You are My devotee and you are My friend. What kind of excellence is that? To this He says:
"It is a secret," because such a secret is so exceedingly supreme and excellent. Such is [the nature of the teaching].

This yoga has been taught to you; therefore, it is not fit to be taught to everyone. Out of affection, it was taught specifically to you, who are both a devotee and a friend. The meaning is that this yoga must be understood and practiced by you with faith. || 3 ||

When the Blessed One had spoken thus, Arjuna, suspecting a contradiction in these statements, asks: "Your birth was later, while the birth of Vivasvat was earlier. How am I to understand this, that You taught [this] in the beginning? (4)

The birth and manifestation of you, who possess the form of Kṛṣṇa, is a later occurrence; for you were born in the house of Vasudeva at a very recent time. However, the birth and manifestation of Vivasvat, the Sun, is extremely ancient.

Indeed, it is said that the birth of the sun occurred at the very beginning of the creation of the world. Therefore, how can I understand this—that you, having been born now, spoke this to the sun at the commencement of the first creation?
How could this possibly be consistent? There is simply no compatibility between those two. || 4 ||
Thus, to Arjuna— who had questioned Him while regarding Śrī Kṛṣṇa as an ordinary man— Kṛṣṇa begins to instruct him on His true nature: "Many births of Mine have passed, as well as yours, O Arjuna."
I know all of them, but you do not know them, O scorcher of the foe.
To provide an introduction for answering Arjuna’s question, the Blessed One said:
"O Arjuna, many births of mine have passed away; many births of yours also have passed away. O scorcher of foes, nevertheless, I know all those births, whereas you do not know them. Thus...
I, who am now the son of Vasudeva, was that very same one who existed at the beginning of the creation of the universe and taught this Yoga to Āditya; because I know all my births,
it was I alone who then taught this Yoga to Āditya, and now I teach it to you.
The listeners, however, are many individual souls. What is the nature of the one and of the many?

And what is their relationship? This very point must now be understood; through the knowledge of this alone, your doubt will be removed. This is indeed the great subject matter in the science of reality (tattva-śāstra).
It is worthy of inquiry; through familiarity with this, you will become established in yoga. || 5 ||

Thus, having stated his own omniscience, [the author] addresses the doubt: "If the Blessed One alone is omniscient and not subject to karma, for what purpose does he take on many births? In response, he states that even though he is not subject to karma, births are taken up by him of his own free will.
Though unborn and of imperishable nature, and though the Lord of all beings, He, presiding over His own material nature, manifests Himself through His own power of illusion (māyā).
Though unborn (*aja*), being himself devoid of origination, and likewise though of an immutable nature (*avyayātman*), being free from decay (*vyaya*)— that is,
the exhaustion of the powers of knowledge and so forth— he remains one whose powers of knowledge, action, and will are undiminished.
Although he is the Lord and the controller of all living beings, from Brahmā down to a blade of grass,
he presides over his own nature— having brought his own dependent nature consisting of the three qualities (guṇas) under his own control— and not like other people who are subject to their nature.
"Having become subject to another's will, I manifest—I shall be born—by means of my own diverse power of *māyā*.
Here, some are deluded into thinking that the incarnations (*avatāras*) of the Blessed One are unreal merely because of the mention of *māyā*;
however, immediately following [this verse], [the Lord] clearly states regarding His own birth: 'Both my birth and my action are divine.'"

In the *Śrīkarabhāṣya*, it is stated that because of the mention of its divine nature (*divyatva*), the meaning of the word *māyā* is precisely "possessing manifold powers" (*vicitraśakti*), and not "falsity" (*mithyātva*);

for it is impossible for the word *māyā* to have falsity as its meaning. It is said: "That which by its very nature attains (*ayati*) Maḥ—Śiva, the Supreme Brahman—is called *māyā* in the world; it is the devotion to Brahman."
The etymological derivation of the word *māyā* as "the eternal" (*sanātanī*) is also well-known and shines forth in the Śiva Āgamas.

This meaning has been clearly elucidated in the Vīraśaiva commentary on the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad. Thus, even though the Supreme Self is unborn, the fact that He appears to be born is entirely consistent through His possession of diverse powers; this very point is what is intended here.

The meaning of the word "māyā" is to be understood [as such]. Furthermore, in the Brahma-sūtra, "And she is endowed with all [powers], for that is seen," and in the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad, "His supreme power is indeed heard to be manifold and innate," the inherent nature of the Supreme Self's possession of powers is thus described. (6)
Whenever there is a decline of righteousness, O Bhārata,
and a rise of unrighteousness, then I manifest myself.

Regarding the question of what time my descent occurs, he says: "O Bhārata, whenever there is a decline—that is, a state of exhaustion—of dharma, which is the cause of the world's stability and is being taught in such words as 'be devoted to your own duty' and so forth, specifically the dharma of the social classes and stages of life (varṇāśrama-dharma); however, there is no fixed rule regarding the specific time for that."

This is the meaning. Thus, when there is the decline of dharma and the simultaneous rise—that is, the emergence—of its opposite, adharma, then I manifest myself through my own māyā, by means of the application of my power of illusion; that is to say, I descend into the world. || 7 ||
For the protection of the virtuous, for the destruction of the wicked,
and for the sake of establishing righteousness, I manifest myself age after age.
(114) For what purpose is the descent of the Supreme Self, and what is His teaching? To this He gives the answer: [for the sake of] the virtuous who are devoted to dharma and are innocent.

For the protection and preservation of the devotees of the Blessed One who are oppressed by unrighteousness, and likewise, as an ancillary to that, for the destruction and eradication of the wicked deeds of those who harm the virtuous and are devoted to unrighteousness, and for the purpose of establishing dharma, which is rooted in that [destruction], for the sake of dharma—

For the purpose of establishing and firmly stabilizing—by means of making them perfectly unmixed—the system of the duties of the castes and stages of life (*varṇāśramadharma*) created by me as the support of the world; for it has been stated in such passages as "mixture leads only to hell" that the confusion of castes (*jātisaṃkara*) is a cause for hell. Therefore, having avoided such confusion and the like, [I have acted].
In order to establish the Dharma according to its true state, in every age—whenever and wherever there is a decline of the Dharma—I manifest myself and descend [into the world] at all times. || 8 ||
He who knows in truth this divine birth and action of Mine, O Arjuna, having abandoned the body, does not undergo rebirth; he comes to Me.

To anyone who does not perceive my birth as illusory or as being like that of an ordinary person—for such a person, the attainment of the supreme goal of human life is indicated here. O Arjuna, my birth and all my actions are, in the manner described, divine; they are eternally beautiful, voluntarily assumed for the sake of blessing the worlds.

He who knows and understands "form" (rūpa) according to reality and the actual state of things, having abandoned this physical body which is a product of nature (prākṛta), becomes a possessor of a divine body and does not undergo this material birth again; the principle that "birth is certain for one who has died" does not apply to him. But he who [knows] Mahādeva residing in the heart...

He knows and unites with that [Mahādeva], and thus Mahādeva alone is seen everywhere within his body. The limbs and senses undergo a transformation into the form of the *liṅga* (the subtle body) and the *indriya* (the faculties). Likewise, the body composed of *prakṛti* becomes a divine body through contact with Mahādeva. To an external observer, he appears like an ordinary living being.

Even while remaining in the physical body, one who has abandoned delusion becomes free from affliction and attains divine life. This very divine life is considered to be the "casting off of the body. Such a person of divine life, experiencing eternal bliss right here and liberated from the bonds of worldly existence, does not undergo rebirth. Therefore, at the conclusion of the body—

Regarding the question "Where does he go?", it is said here: "He comes to me. He attains me, the Supreme Self, who is free from birth and death, the formless Śiva. However, he who does not know this remains subject to repeated birth and death.

It is indeed so. Liberation from wandering in the wheel of *saṃsāra* occurs only through acquaintance with the Lord residing within the body; even there, it arises from performing service to Him, and everywhere, it is clearly evident that it comes solely from the realization of Him. Such...

Taking refuge in the possessor of divine knowledge, they meditate upon him as "unborn. For although such a devotee is born like an ordinary being from the perspective of the body, he is indeed unborn. Indeed, this unborn one does not beg of another nor does he desire anything at will; thus the practitioner, through the power of yoga, remains unborn.

Perceiving only Śiva everywhere and experiencing union with Śiva (*śivasāyujya*) even here in this divine body, one shall dwell in a state of uninterruptedness and continuity following the separation from the body; thus the Lord instructs all through Arjuna. 9.
Free from passion, fear, and anger, absorbed in Me, and taking refuge in Me— many, purified by the austerity of knowledge, have attained My state of being.
"By taking refuge in Me, having transformed the human nature into a divine nature, they attain life"—thus he says:

"Those whose passion, fear, and anger have departed (vīta-rāga-bhaya-krodhāḥ)—that is, those beings from whom passion, fear, and anger have gone away—become absorbed in Me (man-mayāḥ) through meditation on Me, and thereby attain My state. For this very reason:

Many practitioners and devotees who have taken refuge in me and serve me—purified by knowledge and austerity; here, "knowledge" refers specifically to the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*), while "austerity" refers to the means that disciplines the body and senses—and by this they are cleansed and thoroughly purified, meaning they have attained the destruction of impurities and karma. They attain my state, the state of Godhood.
They have attained—that is, reached—the state of being the Paraśiva-liṅga, which is the very nature of the Liṅga and whose essence is equanimity.

Therefore, the dissolution through becoming one in flavor (*samarasatā*) of the individual soul (*jīva*), which is a portion of Brahman, into the undivided Liṅga-form of the supreme Brahman Paraśiva, is not said to be something new. For a long time...

From ancient times, numerous great sages, preeminent Śiva-yogis such as the venerable teachers Reṇukācārya and others, and the refuge-seekers of Allama and others, have been seen to remain absorbed in that Great Liṅga latent within their own hearts; being thus one with it, they have, out of exclusive affection, inspired other practitioners as well to become likewise absorbed. Śrī Basavārya—

He thus describes the process of his own deliverance: When the Guru had grown upon the ground called devotion, having attained the state of a *liṅga*, and when the flower called wisdom had blossomed above it, the ritual action was like a green fruit;
and when that fruit reached maturity, he lifted him up as it fell, loosened from its stalk. He was full of affection.

"I have become one whose fruit is the affection of Gurusaṅgamārya. Thus, through the grace of Gurusaṅgamārya, Basavārya realized the true nature of the internal *liṅga* within himself and then merged into it.

It impels even the practitioners; not only He Himself, but others as well—those who have found fulfillment in life by taking refuge [in Him]—exert themselves with deliberate intent to inspire everyone toward the fruitfulness of their birth.
Therefore, from ancient times, many great souls, having personally realized the reality of Śiva, [have likewise inspired] others.
Even now, beholding only Śiva through their own mirror, they shine forth, still inspiring practitioners toward spiritual bliss. || 10 ||

Now, why is it said that "many" [have attained this]? Is it not the case that all people lack the capacity to see and experience the Lord who resides within themselves? If they do possess this capacity, why is there such partiality, whereby only some have attained the state of Brahman? To address this doubt, he says: "This fault is not mine, but theirs alone. [Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.21]
In whatever way people approach me, in that same way do I reward them;
O Pārtha, human beings follow my path in every respect.

In whatever manner, by whatever means, and with what kind of fruit in view human beings take refuge in me—that is, resort to me—I honor them in that very same way, according to their respective dispositions; I fulfill that which they desire. And likewise, for those who take refuge in me with the aim of a small fruit, I grant them that very fruit.

I give [worldly benefits] to those who seek them; however, to those who take refuge in Me solely for the sake of liberation, I give liberation itself. Therefore, I have no partiality toward anyone. Thus, the Śruti describes Me as "the Impartial One" (Sama), because I conduct Myself with an equal vision toward all. And so, O Pārtha, men [should follow] My path in every respect.
They follow—that is, they pursue—precisely the path of *karmayoga*, which was ordained by Me and is permeated by both knowledge and action.

To the question, "What is this path ordained by You?", the answer will be stated immediately hereafter in the verse beginning with, "The fourfold order of society (*cāturvarṇya*) was created by Me. We are Your devotees; therefore, according to our own natures, whatever [action] we perform—

Whatever fruit pertaining to the next world is desired, all of that is attained by the Supreme Lord at that very moment; thus the saying is beautifully illustrated: "Even one who has mounted the chariot, this dog-like person, having been made to adopt a new state of being, does not abandon his own nature when he beholds the objects of sense acquired in a previous birth"—so it is with me.
O Lord Mṛḍa, let the mind’s wandering elsewhere be utterly consumed;
for my ignorant inner mind does not even grant me the power to remember you here. O my Master!

"Instruct me so that I may remember the pair of your feet; for even one who begs by spreading out the hem of his garment—such a high-souled person instructs all those attached to worldly fruits correctly, so that they may attain the Blessed One alone and become happy through its ultimate result. All [beings] [should follow] his word.

It conduces to one's welfare. If a devotee should desire a woman for himself, then indeed, by the command of Śiva, he should marry that woman; if his mind is set upon clay, then he should construct his dwelling there—thus, by the grace of the Lord alone, even the fruits in the form of land, women, and gold are obtained by human beings.

Because it is obtainable through the grace of the Blessed One, it is never to be censured. Whether enjoyment (*bhoga*) or yoga, everything is obtainable from the Blessed One alone. Therefore, all people indeed follow the Supreme Lord by whatever path.
Those, however, who censure His path would surely go to hell. For this reason, Arjuna...
The intention indicated here is that one shall become happy by following precisely the path shown by the Blessed One. || 11 ||
Desiring the fulfillment of their actions, people here worship the deities;
for in the world of men, success born of action is quickly attained.
Now, one might ask: why do not all people take refuge in you solely for the sake of liberation?
Even when worldly fruits are attained, because they are transitory, they inevitably result in the very noose of saṃsāra.
To the question of how these people could possibly desire the bondage of existence itself, he says:
Desiring— that is, expecting— the accomplishment, which is the attainment of results, of actions pertaining to this world and the next,

human beings in this world worship— that is, honor— the deities, such as Indra and other gods; for, in the human world, the accomplishment born of action— the attainment of results pertaining to this world and the next dependent upon action— is swift.

It becomes swift. And thus, men and women, looking toward the attainment of such swift results, worship various deities corresponding to those [results] for the sake of those specific aims; they do not take refuge in me for the sake of liberation. He whose destruction of impurity (mala) and karma is imminent—he alone [attains] that which is of the nature of immortality.

One aspires for liberation, attains it, and experiences it; yet not everyone behaves in this way within this variegated and manifold phenomenal world—[regarding] the earth, gold, and a beautiful woman. (p.

Fools even sacrifice their lives for the sake of acquisition alone; bound by the fetters of worldly existence, they speak thus. He declares with an impartial vision that the granting of fruits depends upon the will of Manu. 12.
The fourfold order of society was created by me according to the distinction of qualities and actions;
know me to be its creator, yet also its non-creator and immutable.

It has been stated, "They follow my path. To the question "What is your path?", he says: *cāturvarṇyam* (the fourfold order) refers to the four *varṇas*; the suffix is used in its own sense (*svārthika*). By me alone—the Supreme Self—according to the division of qualities (*guṇa*) and actions (*karman*): the qualities are *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*; and the actions are those corresponding to them.

These will be explained in the eighteenth chapter. For the Brāhmaṇa, whose nature is dominated by *sattva* and who is eager for the knowledge of Brahman, there are duties such as austerity (*tapas*) and so forth. For the Kṣatriya, whose nature is dominated by *rajas* mixed with *sattva*, there are duties such as the protection of the kingdom and so forth. For the Vaiśya, whose nature is dominated by *rajas* mixed with *tamas*—

The occupations of trade and so forth [belong to the Vaiśyas]; the occupations of service and so forth belong to the Śūdra, for whom Tamas is predominant and mixed with Rajas. In this manner, the fourfold order of castes (cāturvarṇya) was created by Me alone at the beginning of creation for the sake of maintaining the world's order, in accordance with the differentiation of the qualities (guṇas) and their corresponding duties (karmas). Regarding these duties prescribed for each caste:

Not even a single one [of these] can be considered insignificant or contemptible. Even each individual person is worthy of praise if they carry out their own duty with faith and with the very intention of worshipping the Lord; then, by that alone, he obtains the grace of the Lord. Thus, it was already stated by me previously that [the fruits] correspond precisely to those respective qualities and actions.

Because of the creation of such an arrangement, know Me—its author—to be a non-agent, and therefore immutable and inherently changeless. What is said regarding being both "the agent" and "the non-agent" is highly meaningful: the portion stating that "I alone am its agent" is indeed true; nevertheless, this...

I have performed this solely for the welfare of humanity; indeed, there is no fruit whatsoever for me to be achieved through it. In this world, all four kinds of action are necessary for the happiness of everyone.
Therefore, setting aside notions of high and low regarding one's own duties, [all should act] with mutual love.
With the expectation that all actions may be carried out for the benefit of the public with the vision of seeing everyone as one's own brother,

the Supreme Self manifests its own state of detachment. Although He is the author of the distribution of qualities and actions for the sake of the world’s order, by means of the realization of His own non-agency, He remains far removed from all defects.
He establishes [this].
