119) If such a distinction did not exist, a state of total lack of order would arise everywhere. For thus is the world—

Experiencers declare that although He abides within all living beings, He is distinct from them. For this very reason, the Blessed One remains eternally beautiful as a divine mirror; from beginningless time, and not merely for this day alone, He has been acting for the welfare of the world, while inwardly and verbally relinquishing all sense of agency.

The Blessed One, intending to abandon this [notion], enlightens [the seeker] by means of his own example. The *Śaraṇagītā* thoroughly establishes the necessity of cultivating the sense of non-agency from the perspective of the welfare of the individual soul who has sought refuge. Indeed, one who reflects, "This work was done by me here," [attains the opposite].

That which is offered to the *liṅga* should not be spoken of by one who desires to increase [merit] and aspires to the state of the *liṅga*; likewise, that which is offered with devotion to a *jaṅgama* (human representative) should also not be spoken of by one who desires devotion to Śiva. For if this [offering] is indeed something that ought to be done, it should certainly not be entertained in the mind as "this is an improper act."

"Saṅgameśa shall surely grant what is desired to the disciplined, the striving, and the active. Thus, the high-souled Basavārya reveals his noble disposition, declaring that one should abandon the notion of being an agent and instead perform everything with the desire for the welfare of others. The same applies to others as well.

Making devotion to Śiva alone their primary focus and carrying out all their worldly activities solely for the sake of pleasing Śiva, the Śaraṇas even today reinforce that very same intention among modern youths as well. Similarly, Reṇukācārya also, in the context of the offering of one's inner being (*bhāvārpaṇa*), [states]:
They instruct practitioners to carry out all sensory activity solely for the sake of Śiva.
All philosophers also accept that people who conduct their affairs with the thought of offering them to Śiva shall become eternally happy. 13.
"Actions do not taint me, nor do I have a desire for the fruits of action;
he who understands me thus is not bound by actions. (14)

Thus, he says that even one who knows Me, the doer of all, as being a non-doer and as not sharing in the fruits produced by those actions, also gradually becomes liberated from the bondage of karma: "Those actions do not smear Me; I have no contact with those actions. Thus it is with Me regarding the fruit of action—that is, such a fruit of action."
There is not even a desire or longing for it. Thus, he who knows me, understands me correctly;
such a person is not bound by actions, whether meritorious or sinful. In this way, he who [knows me] according to reality...

He knows that he is not bound by any action whatsoever. However, it is said that those who, conversely, maintain the view that "I alone am the direct agent of every action, and therefore the enjoyer of its fruit, and therefore the one who possesses the merit or demerit"— even though I have performed everything for the welfare of the world, in that regard [they remain bound].

Agency never exists [in Me]. Nevertheless, the intention is this: he who knows Me alone as the agent of everything, as the enjoyer of all sacrifices and penances, and as the very form of Consciousness and Bliss according to reality—he alone shall become eternally happy.
Knowing this, even the ancient seekers of liberation performed action;
therefore, you too perform action, as it was performed by the ancients of old.
Thus, because the system of the castes and stages of life was established by Me alone, human beings who are My own portions must necessarily protect its dharma; with this in mind, He says:
"Having thus understood the true nature of action, which consists of the duties of the castes and stages of life, even the ancients..."

Even by the ancient seekers of liberation, such as Janaka and others, action was performed— that is, practiced— as their own duty. For it has already been stated more than once that action, when performed preceded by the renunciation of attachment to results and the sense of agency, becomes the bestower of the fruit of liberation.

In the verse, "For Janaka and others attained perfection through action alone," this very intention has been made clear. Therefore, for that reason, you too should perform only that which was performed by those of old—
namely, action established since beginningless time— and you ought not to abandon action.
As long as one remains in the body, the failure to protect the duties of one's caste (*varṇadharma*) is considered a great fault.

In that regard, he who feels aversion toward it will not be able to achieve his own spiritual welfare. Therefore, knowing that your duty is entirely bound to the body, you must certainly perform it with faith; otherwise—
A great loss would arise and a succession of calamities would descend.
Now, if action were to be performed by me, then— since not every action can be performed by a single person alone—

the discernment of what kind of action should be performed and what kind should not be performed would be difficult for those like me to understand. Therefore, how should I act, or what should I do, and when?
In response to the thought "I shall act," the Lord himself, in the form of the Supreme Power (Parāśakti), prepares the introductory foundation for discernment:
"Even the wise are deluded in this matter as to what is action and what is inaction" (p. 121).
I shall declare that action to you, by knowing which you will be liberated from evil.

If action is to be performed, what is it and of what nature? Likewise, regarding that which is non-action—what is it and of what nature—that action which is not to be performed and is to be abandoned? Even the wise, even the learned, are deluded, having fallen into confusion on this point. Therefore, for that reason, I myself shall declare to you the true nature of action.
Having understood that such delusion regarding the impure leads to bondage in existence rooted therein, and to rebirths of that same nature—[one might ask:
"Is it not the case that the scriptures themselves clearly show what action is prescribed as 'to be done' and what is prohibited as 'not to be done'?
Therefore, the portion of reality to be known in this regard can be understood simply by consulting the scriptures. To address this doubt:

Demonstrating that the true nature of action and the other categories cannot easily be understood, the Blessed One teaches that very analysis with absolute clarity: "For one must understand what is action, and one must also understand what is forbidden action (vikarman)."
And one must understand the state of non-action; for the course of action is profound. || 17 ||
For indeed, even regarding action—that is, concerning the very nature of action—there is a secret to be understood, something that must be known.
Likewise, there is a secret to be understood even regarding "vikarman," or contrary action, concerning its true nature.
Similarly, even regarding "akarman," which consists of the abandonment of action or remaining silent, there is some secret to be understood.

For the course of action—of deeds that ought to be done and those that ought not—is profound, exceedingly deep, and subtle. If everything were to be done, then every single action would indeed have to be performed;
yet, since it is impossible to perform every action, if one were to abandon them all, then everything would indeed have to be abandoned. Therefore, regarding this...
The subtle secret of karma is extremely difficult to comprehend; therefore, my intention is that I alone shall explain that secret after having analyzed it.
He who sees inaction in action, and action in inaction, he is wise among men; he is disciplined and a performer of all actions.
That very secret of the performance of action is first presented in brief for the sake of praise:
122) "One who, while action is being performed, should perceive non-action—the absence of action—within that activity. It is precisely thus that one [should see].

One should know that even when there is no external action—that is, when there is non-performance of ritual acts—if an action is performed internally through the mind, that person alone among men becomes wise and discerning. A person who remains silent after perceiving with the eyes and other senses [the objects] is the individual soul (jīva) residing within the bodies of women and men; by its own nature, it does nothing at all.
If one perceives that even what is called "action performed" is indeed non-action, then he is reckoned as wise.

Even when an action is carried out by the senses through their natural proximity to the self, he who does not even mentally recall it as "performed by me"—he alone is considered truly intelligent. Thus, if he [regards] everything...
If one were to actually renounce action, then the mind of that person, being immersed in the contemplation of the very action renounced,
would remain perpetually occupied with it. Only he who renounces the sense of agency even while performing action possesses a mind [free from attachment] even during the performance of action.

He also understands the activity of karma; such a living being is celebrated as one endowed with wisdom (*prajñāśālī*). He alone is considered a *śivayogin*, being joined with the *prāṇaliṅga* manifest within the heart.
He alone becomes the performer of all actions and the accomplisher of every duty. By him, in a certain...
By attaining even now that very fruit which is obtained through all actions performed in their entirety, one becomes that same practitioner of action (karmayogin).

Now, one might object: "If action is being performed, the perception of the absence of action is indeed a contradiction; therefore, all of this must be based on delusion. Anticipating this doubt, the Supreme Self teaches the essential nature and the distinction between action and inaction, demonstrating that no mutual contradiction exists between the two.
Thus he says:
"Those wise ones call him a sage whose every undertaking is free from desire and volition, and whose actions have been consumed by knowledge. (19)

That person whose all undertakings—meaning activities—are devoid of desire and resolve; that is, they are free from desire (icchā) and the resolves (saṅkalpa) caused by it; who performs actions solely with the sense of duty, without such things as the resolve for results—he, being one who possesses the knowledge of Śiva—[is liberated].
They say that they cultivate [this]. And in that state, there is the aforementioned knowledge—the vision of action as non-action—which is itself the fire;
by that fire, the karma characterized as auspicious and inauspicious is burnt, even when one is possessed of it.

Thus, while performing action, these living beings remain untainted, untouched by modification, and are regarded as disciplined by the wise. These practitioners of *karmayoga* are distinguished from other mere performers of action (*karmiṇaḥ*).
While ordinary performers of action experience distress at every step, the practitioners of *karmayoga*, even after performing action, are not bound.
"Though they act repeatedly, they are thwarted by dejection; though they give repeatedly, they are thwarted by the loss of truth.

For whatever they might do or give through union with Truth, O Lord of Conjunction, they would surely be united with that very Truth. Thus the *śaraṇas*, the practitioners of action (*karmayogins*), describe their own excellence. One who perceives the absence of action within action is a wise man.

Knowing that everything, including the body and the senses, is connected to the Blessed One, one becomes eternally happy. The *Śaraṇagītā* describes his state of being as follows: "Since I perceive this body to be His, I have no other body of my own; since it is distinct from Your mind, it is certain to me that I have no mind at all."

"Since all wealth belongs to you, there is no wealth distinct from you; having realized that these three [the body, senses, and mind] belong to him in this way, how could there be any further deliberation? Thus does the *Śaraṇagītā* praise the humble life of the wise man who experiences Śiva. Such indeed is the knower (*jñānī*).
He is designated by people using such terms as "Śivayogin" and so forth.
Having abandoned attachment to the fruits of action, ever-contented and independent, even though fully engaged in action, he does nothing at all. (20)
To the question, "When action is being performed, how can it be possible to perceive therein the absence of action? he says:

having abandoned attachment to the fruits of action—that is, attachment and the sense of agency toward those actions and their results—one is therefore eternally contented because of the absence of desire for sense objects, and thus always satisfied; for this very reason, one is without dependence.
He who is devoid of any basis such as purpose or the like, even though he has engaged in action that has become mandatory due to its obligatory nature, does not perform any action at all;
because he is free from the conceit of agency (*kartṛtva-abhimāna*), although action is performed by him, it remains so in its transformation.

His mind does not engage at all with forms such as pleasure and pain; because he possesses equal vision and lacks expectation toward anything, the wise know that even while performing action, he does not act at all. For him, both doing and not doing are exactly the same; he is devoid of self-interest through his action.

He does not expect even the slightest fruit. The *Śaraṇagītā* describes the steadfastness (*niṣṭhā*) of such a practitioner of action (*karmayogin*) as follows: "The thought 'the wealth of another shall not be mine'—this indeed is the steadfastness observed in the *Śaraṇa*;
the thought 'the wife of another shall not be mine'—this indeed is the steadfastness observed in the *Śaraṇa*; [the thought] 'the injury of another..."
"I shall not act [for my own sake]"—
this indeed is observed as the ultimate goal in taking refuge; yet the marks, such as the stationary and the moving, remain undifferentiated.

Perfection is observed in taking refuge; however, one should not trust those men who act without such perfection, even if they are like Kūṭastha. In that regard, the life of a wise man who acts for the welfare of the world is praised as pure, beautiful, and endowed with sincerity. It is precisely for such a practitioner of *karmayoga* that what was stated previously applies.
The perception of non-action within action may be observed, but not elsewhere; and that [perception] is possible [only there]. 20.
With his mind and self free from desire, having renounced all possessions,
he incurs no sin while performing action that pertains solely to the body.
Regarding such a yogi, he describes the pervasion of actions: "free from desire" (nirāśīḥ), meaning devoid of expectation toward anything;
for that very reason, "with mind and self controlled" (yata-cittātma), meaning one by whom the mind (the internal organ) and the self are restrained;

and for that same reason, "having renounced all possessions" (tyakta-sarva-parigraha), meaning one who is free from all attachment to the enjoyment of sense objects and the like—[performs] bodily action (śārīraṃ karma).

Performing only those actions necessary for the mere maintenance of the body, one incurs no sin or evil; however, if there is any expectation beyond that, sin becomes unavoidable. The conduct of such a Śiva-yogin is clearly reflected in the life of Basavārya. He himself points out his own exemplary conduct as follows:

"Even a mere fragment from heaps of gold, or even a single thread of my garment—for the sake of this day, or for the sake of the next day—if I wait [for these], then may you be my refuge; likewise, may your attendants be my authority in this matter, O noble one who has met with his guru. Thus, for the protection of his body—
The intention of the Blessed One is that whatever action a yogi performs through the cultivation of the body, he exists as one who is true and pure. || 21 ||
Content with whatever comes by chance, transcending the pairs of opposites, free from envy,
and remaining equanimous in success and failure, one is not bound even after acting.

Thus, it has been stated that there is no sin for one who performs action solely for the sake of maintaining the body. In this very way, one should be content with only those materials acquired through the results of past actions. Otherwise, even for such a person, bondage would be constant;
thus he says: "Content with what comes by chance," meaning perfectly satisfied with whatever gain arrives unasked.
Contented again and again, ever higher and higher, free from expectation, transcending the pairs of opposites such as pleasure and pain,
and likewise free from envy— meaning devoid of any stinginess or similar traits toward anything— he is thus neither elated by success nor dejected by failure in his undertakings.

He is not bound; he does not become subject to bondage at all. Such is the conduct of the yogin: as long as he has not yet become devoted to courtesy toward his own kin, he remains opposed to the world. This one, having found refuge, fears nothing whatsoever. Merged into the mass of your very splendor, he perceives the entire universe as consisting of light alone. Thus...
He who dwells always free from fear, through contentment and tranquility, does not take pride even while performing action therein;
for one who is free from attachment, liberated, whose mind is established in knowledge, and who acts for the sake of sacrifice, his entire action is dissolved away. (23)

To the question of where the action performed by such a knower goes, he says: for one who is free from attachment— that is, whose attachment has ceased in every respect— and therefore liberated— that is, whose bondage caused by the performance of action has ceased—
whose mind is established in knowledge, meaning established in that reality-knowledge (tattvajñāna) which has been explained thus far.

The meaning is that such a Śiva-yogin is one whose mind and intellect remain established through systematic discipline (*vyavasthā*), possessing firm conviction in the knowledge of the truth (*tattva*) as it has been taught. By this, every action being performed proceeds solely for the sake of pleasing the Lord, with Him alone as its objective. Therefore, [it is] for sacrifice (*yajñāya*).

For a living being who performs action solely with the purpose of worshipping the Blessed Lord alone, that action is entirely and completely dissolved—that is, it perishes—because the fruit of action performed by a knower is solely the pleasure of the Blessed Lord; therefore, his action certainly does not produce bondage. He [is established] among the virtuous.
Acting with an equal vision toward all, even toward the wicked, he perceives only the radiance of the Supreme Self.

The entire universe becomes for him a field for the playful sport (*līlā-vinoda*) of Paraśiva. Delighting the world through his three organs of action, he sports with a mind ever contented. The *Śaraṇagītā* describes his life in this way:

"For the mortal world is a house constructed for the playful diversion of the Supreme Lord. Those who are fit here are indeed fit for union there, O noble one; but those men who were not worthy here are not capable of being worthy there. Thus [he spoke]. In this manner...
The meaning is that by practicing appropriately, the yogi shall not only be esteemed in this world, but also in the hereafter, remaining eternally happy and beloved of Śiva. || 23 ||
The offering is Brahman, the oblation is Brahman, poured by Brahman into the fire of Brahman;
by him who is absorbed in the yoga of Brahman-action, Brahman alone is to be attained. (24)

It was stated previously that when an action is performed in the form of worship of the Blessed One, that action does not lead to bondage. To explain how this is possible, he says: for one who performs an action in the very form of worship of the Blessed One solely with the realization that it is a duty (*kartavya*), even the offering of such an action to the Blessed One—

One becomes Brahman itself. Thus, even the sacrificial offering—the substance that serves as the means of worship—should be contemplated as being of the very nature of Brahman. In this way, the offering is made by the individual soul (jīva), which is a portion of Brahman, into the fire that is indeed Brahman itself. Therefore, for the knower, everything—including the agent, the action, the instrument, and the ritual act—is [Brahman].

He becomes Śiva himself. Therefore, for that knower who possesses the contemplation that his own action, through the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) upon Brahman, is a means to realize Paraśiva, Paraśiva alone is to be known;
such action does not yield for him any results such as merit or demerit.
This is the meaning: "It would be so. This very intention was already revealed by the venerable Reṇukācārya.

They speak thus: "The enjoyer, the object of enjoyment, and the impeller—all this, including the moving and the unmoving, when one contemplates as being the form of Śiva, becomes Śiva in reality. All ritual action is the worship of Śambhu; his word is [the authority]."
"For one who constantly contemplates in this way, 'How could there be bondage through karma?', such a contemplation shall bring about the highest good. (24)
Some yogis worship sacrifice as the divine alone;
others offer sacrifice by means of sacrifice itself into the fire of Brahman.

Having thus explained that the action to be performed by the knower consists in the form of Śiva-worship, [the text] now sets forth the various divisions of such activity: other yogins— those who possess the aforementioned knowledge of reality— perform only that sacrifice which is directed toward the divine,
namely, the very act of propitiating the deity in the form of Mahādeva, the Supreme Śiva.

They attend upon [the Lord] and perform [service]. Others, certain wise ones (jñānins), perform such a sacrifice as external worship individually. For these wise ones, the act of offering (homakarma) consists precisely in the devoted surrender of all sensory pleasures into the fire of Paraśiva at that very moment. || 25 ||
Others offer the senses, such as hearing and the rest, into the fires of self-restraint;
others offer the objects of the senses, such as sound and the rest, into the fires of the senses. (26)
But others, who possess knowledge, [offer] the five organs of perception, such as hearing and so forth, and the five organs of action into the fires of restraint (*saṃyama*).
Restraint is the withdrawal of the senses from their objects; it is into the fires consisting of that [restraint] that they offer them.

They offer oblations; that is to say, they exert themselves in the conquest of the senses. Others, however, [offer] the five objects of sense—sound and so forth—as well as the actions of speech and so on, into the fires of the senses, which are the very forms of those respective senses, shining forth as the fire of the conduct-marked guru.

Even for those experiencing the enjoyment of sense objects, because they act in accordance with the restraint prescribed in the scriptures, that restraint is also called "oblation" (*homa*). This very intention was previously clarified by the venerable Reṇukācārya to the great sage Agastya: "Offering all sense objects into the light of the Self, which is of the nature of consciousness and awakened by the vital breath (*prāṇavāyu*)."

"By contemplating [the enjoyment of objects] as being an integral part of the worship of Śiva, one shall attain liberation. Thus, the venerable teachers instruct everyone to contemplate the enjoyment of sense-objects as an auxiliary limb of the worship of Śiva. (26)
Others offer all the functions of the senses and the functions of the vital breaths as oblations into the fire of self-restraint, kindled by knowledge.

Furthermore, other yogins [perceive] all the functions of the senses— all the activities of the eyes and other sense organs such as seeing— and even the functions of the vital breath, such as inhalation and exhalation, as being kindled by the knowledge of Śiva, blazing with the light of wisdom.
When the fire of self-restraint-yoga has been kindled— that fire which is one's own self-restraint in the form of turning away from sense objects—
they perform oblations therein to the Supreme Lord, offering all the activities of the senses and the activities of the vital breaths.
The meaning is that some exist offering [these things] and utilizing them as a form of his grace. || 27 ||
Some perform sacrifices with material offerings, some with austerity, and others with yoga;
likewise, there are ascetics of rigid vows who offer sacrifice through self-study and knowledge.
Other yogins are performers of material sacrifices (*dravyayajña*); having procured material goods, they engage in the form of distributing them to worthy recipients.
And others are ascetics (*yatayaḥ*) who are diligent in effort, possessing vows that are strictly observed and vows that are rigorous.

Those whose sacrifice is the study of scripture and knowledge: "study" (svādhyāya) is the recitation of one's own Vedic branch; "knowledge" (jñāna) is the contemplation of its meaning. They are devoted to such sacrifices as these. For all of them, all of this constitutes a sacrifice because it takes the form of worship of the Divine.
Others offer the prāṇa into the apāna, and likewise the apāna into the prāṇa;
having restrained the movements of both prāṇa and apāna, they are devoted to prāṇāyāma.

Others cause the *prāṇa*—the activity of the vital air known as inhalation (*pūraka*)—to merge into the *apāna*, the function of exhalation (*recaka*). Likewise, others fill the *apāna* with the *prāṇa*, that is, they perform exhalation during inhalation. Still others, however, are devoted to *prāṇāyāma*, being intent on the practice of breath control.

Having blocked the movements of the prāṇa and apāna, and having restrained both inhalation (pūraka) and exhalation (recaka), they perform breath control (prāṇāyāma) by means of retention (kuṃbhaka). || 29 ||
Others, restricted in their food, offer the life-breaths into the life-breaths;
all these are knowers of sacrifice, whose taints have been destroyed by sacrifice. (30)
But others, restricted in their food— those by whom food has been regulated and fixed according to specific rules of dietary discipline—
all of them are knowers of sacrifice; they possess true knowledge of every sacrifice mentioned here, which consists of the worship of the Supreme Self,
and their impurities have been destroyed by the performance of such sacrifices.

Those by whom the stain of sin has been destroyed become such [as described]. By the performance of any one of the sacrifices mentioned, there is indeed the destruction of sin. Through one's own practice, the nature of this Śiva-sacrifice, which consists of the integration of all these [sacrifices], [is realized].
The Lord of All, the preeminent among mobile beings, explains this;

and it is described thus in the *Śaraṇagītā*. He said: "Having made one's own body a garden and having dug into it with the spade of the mind, having uprooted delusion from the heart and having skillfully shattered the clod of worldly existence,"
Having planted the seed of the Supreme Self within my own heart— the reservoir known as the thousand-spoked lotus—

I thoroughly nourished it by pouring water from the mechanism called *prāṇa* through the *suṣumṇā*. Reflecting with devotion that "the five senses shall not cause its destruction here," I cultivated the faculty known as equanimity and forgiveness.
O Lord of the Cave, by applying my attention there, I caused that very crop to flourish through your grace, for everything is indeed your play.

Thus, through its practice, the practitioner is able to perfectly experience the complete pervasion of Paraśiva within the body. This Śivayoga is capable of removing the bonds of impurity (malapāśa) existing in the body by means of the unfolding of Śiva’s power. And those who perform this sacrifice to Śiva (śivayajña)—
They become completely liberated from the snare of impurity.
Those who eat the nectar of the remnants of sacrifice go to the eternal Brahman.
This world does not belong to one who does not sacrifice; how then could another world belong to him, O best of the Kurus? (31)

He states that for those who perform various kinds of sacrifices, the exhaustion of karma leads even to the attainment of Paraśiva. By the verse, "By this [sacrifice], first nourishing the gods, may those gods nourish you," it is established that the attainment of the highest good for a human being occurs through the propitiation of the gods alone. But those sinful ones eat their own sin... [who... (Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly; the translation reflects the portion available.)
By the phrase "cooking for their own sake," the censure of those who do not perform worship of the gods and other such duties has been expressed. Therefore,

those humans who eat the nectar remaining from sacrifice— that is, the nectar which is the remnant of the sacrifice consisting of the previously mentioned propitiation of the gods, and which takes the form of a divine favor— enjoy that which is eternal, devoid of beginning and end.

They go to—that is, they attain—the Supreme Śiva-Brahman alone, which is eternally present. "The Great Lord is always the single Liṅga. Thus, those living beings who enjoy the grace of the feet of Hara’s Guru, seeing Śiva everywhere, experience Him alone even within their own selves. When the grace of Śambhu has been accomplished...

"In the cause of supreme bliss, the entire universe is seen as consisting of Śiva; there is no doubt in this matter. Thus, the venerable feet of the illustrious Reṇuka, being gracious, have thoroughly explained the greatness of grace and the vision of Śiva. Therefore, the sacrifice (yajña) should be performed by all who desire spiritual progress. For one who does not perform the sacrifice—

For one who does not perform such a sacrifice consisting of the propitiation of Maheśvara, how could this world—namely, the results pertaining to this life—be possible? O best of the Kurus, Arjuna, listen for a moment.
Thus, various kinds of sacrifices have been spread forth at the mouth of Brahman;
know them all to be born of action, and by knowing this, you shall be liberated.
Thus he concludes the investigation into the nature of the sacrifices that have been introduced: "In this manner,
according to the previously stated method, having created various kinds of numerous offspring through many types of sacrifices dedicated to Hara, Guru, and Jaṅgama, Prajāpati spoke to them first."
(130) "By this you shall procreate; let this be your cow of plenty that grants desired objects"—this was stated previously.
The sense is that those [actions] thus described are of the nature of *karmayoga*. Having understood them to be such, [one understands] this kind of *karmayoga*.

Knowing that it is also a means for attaining the Supreme Self, you shall be liberated—that is, freed—from bondage by its performance. Therefore, the sense is that you must indeed engage in battle with faith.
"O scorcher of foes, the sacrifice of knowledge is superior to the sacrifice consisting of material substances."
O Pārtha, every action in its entirety culminates in knowledge.

Having thus taught the yoga of action (*karmayoga*), He establishes the superiority of the yoga of knowledge (*jñānayoga*) in comparison to it: the sacrifice of knowledge—the sacrifice consisting of knowledge—is superior, that is, more excellent, than the sacrifice consisting of material things, which is the aforementioned yoga of action performed as a form of worship. O scorcher of foes, Arjuna, [it is] the entirety...
Every action, without exception, culminates and finds its ultimate completion in knowledge through the yoga of knowledge alone.

Since knowledge itself is the direct means to liberation, all the aforementioned yoga of action becomes a means to liberation only by way of generating such knowledge; thus, in comparison to the yoga of action—

It has been stated that the yoga of knowledge (*jñānayoga*) is supreme. This very practitioner of knowledge (*jñānayogin*) is described in the context of the conduct of knowledge (*jñānācāra*) by the venerable Reṇukācārya as follows: "One who, through knowledge, unites everything with the supreme, partless abode named Śiva, which is free from conceptual construction, is proclaimed a practitioner of the conduct of knowledge. All of his previous [actions], too—

Karma, once burnt by the fire of knowledge, shall not sprout again; nevertheless, for the welfare of the world, he practices his own duty (*svadharma*). Non-violence, truthfulness, non-stealing, celibacy, compassion, forbearance, charity, worship, recitation, and meditation—this is the compendium of his dharma. Thus is his dharma.
It has been established by the teachers, the disciples of Reṇukā; practicing in this manner, the yogin of knowledge excels all.
Know that through prostration, inquiry, and service;
the wise who perceive reality will instruct you in that knowledge. 34.

He provides the answer to the question, "What is the nature of the knowledge that serves as the means to liberation? He says: "Know—that is, learn from the presence of the Guru—the essential nature of the knowledge of Śiva which is the means to liberation, by prostration, by service to the Guru and the *jaṅgamas*, and by attending upon the Guru and the *jaṅgamas* through such acts as service; but not otherwise."

Because it is a secret, it cannot be stated explicitly. In response to the doubt as to from whom that [secret] should be asked, he says: "They will instruct," referring to those who perceive reality (*tattvadarśinaḥ*).

When you have asked your question preceded by prostrations and other marks of reverence, those wise ones who have directly realized the reality as it truly is— the nature of the Supreme Self— will instruct you in that knowledge, the knowledge of Paraśiva which is the means to liberation.
The sense is that they should impart that secret to him. "O my Lord, command me to remember Your pair of feet; for I have begun to beg from You, O God, having spread out the hem of Your garment.
Thus did Basavarya, with single-minded devotion, [approach] the supreme guru Saṅgamārya for the instruction of the knowledge of reality.
He entreats. || 34 ||
Knowing which, O Pāṇḍava, you will not again fall into such delusion,
by which you shall see all beings without exception in yourself and then in me.
He offers praise for such knowledge of reality alone: having known and realized that very secret which is the means to liberation,

you shall no longer fall into, nor attain, delusion— the kind of delusion consisting of thoughts such as, "How might I destroy these [afflictions]?"— once such knowledge of reality has arisen within you.

Such delusion as this will simply not arise. Furthermore, O Pāṇḍava Arjuna, by means of that kind of knowledge, you will see—and directly realize—all beings, the entire multitude of living creatures, without exception and in their entirety, within yourself alone; and thereafter, even within me, the Supreme Self.
"You shall directly realize all of that. Wherever you direct your gaze, there you shall behold him;
and whatever comes before your eyes, all of that is indeed your very own form. Thus, the *Śaraṇagītā* describes the vision of Śiva everywhere for the wise one, when there is the grace of Śiva.
"For one who possesses yoga, everything shines as being of the nature of Śiva. Thus, the venerable Renukācārya, a yogi of Śiva, establishes that all things are of the nature of Śiva.
Even if you are the most sinful of all sinners,
you shall cross over all evil by the boat of knowledge alone.
In this context, praise is bestowed upon him alone:

even if you are the most sinful of all evil-doers, the greatest sinner among all those existing in the world who possess sinful natures, you can still cross over the entire ocean of worldly existence (*saṃsāra*)— which is full of affliction— by means of the boat of knowledge, namely, the knowledge obtained through the aforementioned instruction of the Guru.
By the very means of practice (*sādhana*), you shall cross over completely; having transcended it, you proceed.

If it is possible for even such great sinners to have all their sins destroyed through the knowledge of Śiva, what need is there to speak regarding those who possess true devotion? Or even one who is an outcaste (*caṇḍāla*)—

The Śruti declares: "If one should utter the word 'Śiva,' he too shall surely be liberated from bondage. Whether situated in the womb, being born, already born, or even a Brāhmaṇa or an outcaste, one shall be liberated when His grace is present.

In the *Śāṅkara*: thus the venerable Reṇuka Bhagavatpāda reveals his own intention with great magnanimity—that even those of the most lowly birth may attain the knowledge of Śiva. Is this distinction of space real merely because of the difference between the exterior and interior of a village? Even in water, there is non-difference.

In this world, the realization of the true nature of the Self is clearly perceived through purity and the ritual sipping of water (ācamana). However, for those in whose family that realization exists, there is no longer any perception of duality. Indeed, the fruit obtainable through the knowledge of the six systems of philosophy is not seen as a second [distinct] result;
for one by whom the form of the Supreme Lord has been seen, there is no further goal to be reached.

"Accompanied by the True": thus, having abandoned the perception of duality within their inner selves, the Śaraṇas urge all practitioners to behold the world through the contemplation of the universal auspiciousness (sarvaśivabhāvanā). Basavārya generates a sense of true devotion among the people by means of his own example: "O Lord, listen!"

"All castes, from Brahmins down to Śūdras, who are devoted solely to Śiva—if they are possessed of devotion, I consider them all equal. Thus, beholding the world with such a broad vision, he impels that very same divine vision into others as well. In this way, for the sake of the knowledge of Śiva, who is one's own self, by everyone—
The Blessed One reveals here his noble intention that one should strive with a mind full of heedfulness:
"Just as a kindled fire reduces fuel to ashes, O Arjuna, so does the fire of knowledge reduce all actions to ashes. (36–37)
O Arjuna, just as a well-kindled and thoroughly ignited fire reduces even a great many pieces of wood to ashes,
in that very same manner, the fire of knowledge— the fire in the form of the wisdom of Śiva— reduces all actions, that is, all sins, to ashes.

It reduces to ashes, that is, it completely destroys. Just as when wood is destroyed by fire, even though there is an abundance of wood, the fire is not diminished but rather increases, in the same way, knowledge too shall completely destroy the snare of impurities; the intention is that it shall not itself be diminished.

Ignorance is destroyed by the power of knowledge, just as darkness is dispelled by the strength of light; untruth is overcome by the power of truth, and likewise iron is subdued by the power of fire. O Lord, my very existence has been destroyed through association with you, who are of great majesty and a refuge for all.
Thus, the *Śaraṇagītā* demonstrates, in a manner that touches the heart, how for the wise man the bonds of worldly existence are destroyed through non-attachment.
Indeed, there is nothing in this world as purifying as knowledge;
one who is perfected through yoga finds that very knowledge within oneself in due course of time. 38.
To the question of how such power of knowledge can possibly exist, he provides the following resolution:

"In this world, there exists no other purifying substance equal to—that is, comparable with—the aforementioned Śiva-knowledge that removes the defects of impurity; indeed, such [other substance] does not exist at all. And that knowledge—

One who is perfected in yoga—possessing full qualification through the practice of the previously mentioned *karmayoga*—attains [this state] within oneself after a long period of time; therefore, this is to be accomplished through long-term practice.
The man of faith, intent upon it and with senses restrained, attains knowledge;
having attained knowledge, he reaches supreme peace without delay. (39)
Regarding how such knowledge is attained, he says: according to the principle that "this person consists of faith;
whatever one's faith is, that he is," only the living self who possesses faith is capable of attaining such knowledge, and not one devoid of faith. Even when there is faith...

Since the knowledge of Śiva would not be obtained in the absence of effort and other means conducive to it, he says "intent upon that" (*tatpara*); the meaning is that the living being who is devoted to that—being inclined toward the sole means for such knowledge—obtains it. Furthermore, even if one is intent upon that, if the living being is fickle regarding sense-objects, he does not obtain it; therefore, it is said "with senses restrained" (*saṃyatendriya*).

The meaning is that its accomplishment occurs only for one who is turned away from worldly objects. Having attained such knowledge, the practitioner who has conquered the senses and possesses faith reaches—attains—supreme peace, which is liberation in the form of perfect tranquility, very soon, that is, quickly. || 39 ||
The ignorant, the faithless, and the doubting soul perish;
for the doubting soul, there is neither this world, nor the next, nor happiness. 40.

He says that for one who lacks faith in the meaning He has spoken, or for one who is possessed by doubt, only a miserable state can result: "The ignorant one," who exists without knowing the spoken meaning; "he who knows but does not have faith," who exists devoid of faith;
or "he whose nature is doubt," who is skeptical regarding the spoken meaning—all these indeed perish. They...

For they would not be able to accomplish their own welfare. Furthermore, compared to those who are ignorant and faithless, the loss for one whose mind is full of doubt is even greater; thus he says, "Neither this world... Those who are ignorant and faithless, having abandoned this inquiry, wander either on the worldly path or [seek] worldly happiness.
One whose nature is doubt,
being of a skeptical disposition, shall experience this world— this worldly existence— by the maxim of "falling from here and falling from there" (p. 134).

It will not come to pass; he shall find no happiness anywhere by means of violence. The *Śaraṇagītā* fully explains the miserable state of a living being who lacks faith: "For one devoid of faith, there is no guru, no moving being, nor indeed the grace of those two;
and that man finds no peace. And likewise:

One never attains the *liṅga*. When one who is full of faith again runs toward doubt, he then becomes a *sūtakī* (one defiled by birth or death). At that very moment, the Lord abandons such a person; separated from the Divine, he is considered dead. There is no attainment of prosperity or the like for him, nor for one whose soul is characterized by doubt.
"He enjoys happiness on earth"—this very sequence of calamities arising for a living being who lacks faith and possesses a doubting mind is exceedingly treacherous and terrifying;
this is established by the experience of all. In the field of spiritual science (*adhyātmakṣetra*), the noble Basava attained unsurpassed bliss.
Observing people devoid of faith, he declares his own intention thus: "People simply do not trust the Lord;

nevertheless, they constantly invoke him. Being unable to place their trust, the dull-witted still wander about out of delusion. If one were to invoke him preceded by faith, then why would he not respond?"
The Lord said: "If one devoid of faith should invoke the Divine, he would immediately fall, restrained by the goad of that [act].
Thus, it is true that only one possessed of faith, by conducting himself appropriately in this world and the next, shall attain the name of "Sādhu" (the virtuous) and become beloved of Śiva. || 40 ||
O Dhanañjaya, actions do not bind one who has renounced action through yoga, whose doubts have been severed by knowledge, and who possesses self-mastery.

Therefore, how should one conduct oneself? To the question of how a human being may dwell here with dignity while remaining free from bondage, He says: O Dhanañjaya Arjuna, [behold] one for whom all actions have been renounced through yoga—that is, through the yoga of action previously described, which is dear to Śiva—[actions] that have been renounced, meaning dedicated to Śiva.
Those actions which are performed by such a person—

by means of a stainless individual soul (*jīva*) purified by the initiation of Śiva (*śivadīkṣā*), named "the Unattached" (*asaṅgin*), and having abandoned both the desire for fruits and the sense of personal agency according to the previously stated method— become offerings unto Śiva once they have been performed.

They do not bind him. In the same way, one whose doubts have been severed by knowledge—that is, he by whom doubt has been severed and destroyed through knowledge, namely the knowledge of reality (tattvajñāna)—is such a person. For this very reason, [they do not bind] the self-possessed one—
One who is heedless yet always acts with wakefulness— performing duties prescribed for his caste, such as battle and so forth—
does not incur the bondage of *saṃsāra* through those actions because of the absence of expectation regarding the fruits of those actions.

That which bestows eternal happiness is truly called by the sacred name "Kāyaka. From this perspective, if one's duties are performed accordingly, then life itself becomes free from affliction. Conduct attains the state of being *kāyaka* only when it is supported by true devotion. When [one relies] upon the gurus...

"If one performs service solely for the sake of serving those who move on feet and those that move on their own [the immobile], having oppressed both body and mind and extracted something from dharma itself—may he who practices such service be a supreme devotee;
may his feet rest upon my head. Thus says Basavārya in the *Śaraṇagītā*.
One designates every activity performed by true devotees as "kāyaka.
If the greatness of kāyaka were thus accepted by all, then calamities would simply not arise.
Men and women devoted to kāyaka would always possess contented minds. Always...

"For those whose minds are contented, there is prosperity at every step; for those whose minds are ever discontented, there is calamity at every step"—thus say those who have experienced this. In the same way, the "view of the body as a wound," which wards off all diseases, should be practiced by all who desire progress. This alone is the supreme medicine that destroys the disease of worldly existence (*saṃsāra*).
Therefore, having cut asunder with the sword of self-knowledge this doubt born of ignorance that resides in your heart, take recourse to yoga; arise, O Bhārata! (42)

Therefore, O Bhārata, sever with the sword of knowledge— knowledge which is within my inner self— this doubt of yours concerning the Self, which resides in your heart, born of ignorance and arisen from a lack of discrimination, in the form of such uncertainty as, "How can I engage in this battle? and so forth.

The sword—that is, the blade—is precisely that knowledge of reality which consists in the realization: "It is the Supreme Lord alone, dwelling as the director, who causes His servant to act; I have no connection with sin here.
Because it is the means of cutting, knowledge is called a sword. Having cut through—that is, having destroyed—the "yoga" (bondage) that is dear to Śiva...
In order to engage him in his duty by first stating the objective, Kṛṣṇa employs the word "Arise" here (p.
[in] the fifth chapter.

Thus, although the nature of the yoga of action has been explained by the Blessed One, because he subsequently stated the excellence of the yoga of knowledge— saying, "O scorcher of foes, the sacrifice of knowledge is superior to the sacrifice consisting of material objects"—
and yet finally said, "Having abandoned this doubt, take recourse in yoga" and "engage in battle," [there arises a question].
Again, overcome by doubt, Arjuna said:
"O Kṛṣṇa, you praise the renunciation of actions and then again the yoga of action.
Tell me with certainty which one of these two is the better. (1)

At one time You praised the renunciation of actions (*karma-saṃnyāsa*) in the form of offering them to the Lord—that is, the yoga of knowledge—with such words as, "The sacrifice consisting of material objects is inferior to this," and so forth; yet at another time You also praised the yoga of action (*karma-yoga*) with such words as, "This world does not exist for one who does not sacrifice. Between these two, [which is] the one that is most firmly determined?
Tell me, having determined it, that which is the means for attaining the highest good; tell me what I must do now. Only through the removal of such doubts does certain knowledge arise within me.
Both renunciation of action and the yoga of action lead to the supreme good;
however, of these two, the yoga of action is superior to the renunciation of action.

Thus questioned, the Blessed One said: "Renunciation (saṃnyāsa) is the abandonment of actions; yoga, on the other hand, is the performance of action while relinquishing the sense of being its own agent. Both of these indeed lead to the supreme good (niḥśreyasa);
they both accomplish the supreme good and are both causes of liberation. However, between the two..."

Compared to the renunciation of action (*karmasaṃnyāsa*)— which consists of surrendering the fruits of action to the Blessed One— and to the yoga of knowledge (*jñānayoga*), it is precisely the yoga of action (*karmayoga*)—
consisting of the performance of action without egoism, viewed as a duty to be performed with faith— that [is superior],
by way of constantly producing purity of mind.
Experiencers say that one is distinguished as superior because of manifesting a nature of contentment.
He should be known as a perpetual renunciant who neither hates nor desires;
for one free from the pairs of opposites, O mighty-armed one, is easily liberated from bondage.

He states the reason for the superiority of karma-yoga: "He alone is a perpetual renunciant (nitya-saṃnyāsī) who does not hate—that is, he harbors no hatred toward anything—and who does not desire—that is, he does not seek even the slightest worldly fruit.

The meaning is this: he who performs action free from desire and aversion, and without regard for results and the like, is indeed a perpetual renunciant (*nityasaṃnyāsī*). O mighty-armed Arjuna, he who is free from the pairs of opposites (*nirdvandva*), devoid of desire and aversion, and possesses an equanimous disposition toward pleasure and pain, is easily liberated from bondage—that is, from the snare of saṃsāra.

He is liberated; he becomes free. For him, everywhere only the Supreme Self is perceived. Everything performed by him becomes nothing but the worship of Śiva. The *Śaraṇagītā* describes his conduct as follows: "The mortal world is indeed a house constructed for the playful diversion of the Supreme Lord."
Those who are fit here today are indeed fit for union there, O Noble One;

however, those men who were unworthy here are not capable of being worthy there. It is not at all true that the world of humans is entirely distinct from the world of the gods; for whatever merit or demerit is observed in this world [is likewise found there].

For all that is indeed born of the mental constructs of the mind. It is generally established that there is no merit or demerit in this world other than what has been described. Thus, one whose character is habituated to such right conduct should engage in the practice of knowledge only after becoming fit for [the performance of] action.
The ignorant, not the wise, speak of Sāṃkhya and Yoga as distinct;
one who is properly established in even one of the two attains the fruit of both.

Sāṃkhya and Yoga—namely, the yoga of knowledge and the yoga of action—are both entirely distinct from one another; yet those who are truly wise, who experience reality and know the truth as it is, understand this. For what one attains through even one of these two, the practitioner of action attains that very same thing. Thus, whatever fruit is obtained by the practitioner of action, that same [fruit] is obtained by the other as well.

One who is fit for knowledge also attains [the goal], because both are means to liberation; liberation is obtained through the practice of either one alone. Thus, because of the existence of their mutual relationship and because one is integrated into the other, the wise do not conceive of a difference between the two. In the yoga of action (karmayoga), it is solely for the sake of pleasing the Lord...

The performance of ritual action is necessary; likewise, because Mahādeva—who is all-pervading—manifests through portions of His own power for the sake of achieving human welfare, He is regarded with an impartial vision by the wise. (4)
The state which is attained by the followers of Sāṃkhya is reached by the followers of Yoga as well;
he who sees Sāṃkhya and Yoga as one truly sees.

To the question, "How can the fruit of both [paths] be attained by means of only one?", he says: "By the Sāṃkhyas, liberation is attained through knowledge; by the Yogins, it is attained through yoga. There is indeed no difference in liberation, which is the fruit of both. The atomic impurity (*aṇavamala*), consisting of the contraction of power, would be experienced [and removed]; in this regard, there is no difference whatsoever. Thus, because the fruit of both is identical, [the goal of] both is achieved by means of only one.

The meaning is that the practitioner attains the fruit. Thus, because they have a single fruit, he who sees—that is, knows—that Sāṃkhya, which is the yoga of knowledge (jñānayoga), and Yoga, which is the yoga of action (karmayoga), are one and the same due to the unity of their fruit—he alone sees correctly; he truly understands reality. He who perceives a difference in the fruit of the two [does not].

One who possesses the vision of duality cannot truly be a knower; only one with the vision of unity becomes a knower. But the one with the vision of duality, having become an agent of action, becomes a partaker of suffering. || 5 ||
But renunciation, O mighty-armed one, is difficult to attain without yoga;
the sage liberated through yoga attains Brahman before long.

Thus, since these two are one, how was it stated that the excellence of *karmayoga* lies in the fact that "the yoga of action is superior to the renunciation of action"? To this, He says: O Mādhava, true renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) consists essentially in the form of renouncing actions—that is, the yoga of knowledge—whereas [the other] is not a yoga because of the non-performance of *karmayoga*.

Indeed, only when purity of mind has arisen can practitioners obtain the qualification for the yoga of knowledge; the yoga of knowledge is not accomplished merely by the renunciation of actions. A human being does not become stainless through knowledge alone [if one thinks] that actions are performed by the Supreme Self; rather, all those [actions must be performed] with a tranquil mind.

Having performed them, the fruits thereof should be offered to the Supreme Self; this indeed is *karmayoga*. Its connection with *jñānayoga* also certainly exists. Thus, a sage who is disciplined in yoga and joined with *karmayoga*—which consists of the offering of the fruits to the Supreme Lord—is a practitioner of *karmayoga* who, before long, that is, very quickly, [attains] Brahman.
One attains, that is, reaches, the Supreme Self; therefore, the yoga of action (karmayoga) is superior to the renunciation of action (karmasaṃnyāsa).
One who is disciplined in yoga, whose self is purified, who has mastered the self and conquered the senses,
whose self has become the self of all beings— even while acting, such a person is not tainted. (7)

Praising the excellence of the individual soul (jīva) who is steadfast in the yoga of action, He says: "One who is disciplined in yoga" means one who is steadfast in the aforementioned yoga of action; by that, "one whose self is purified" means one whose internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) is purified; by that, "one who has conquered the self" means one who has conquered the internal organ; "one who has conquered the senses" means one who has conquered the external senses; and "the self of all beings" refers to [the self] of all...

He whose self is the conscious Self—the Self that has become the essence of all beings from Brahmā down to a blade of grass—is one who sees with equanimity everywhere. Such a yogi, even while performing action, is not tainted;
he does not become touched by the fruits of action, but rather attains the Supreme Śiva-Brahman itself. He is always...

Being solely intent upon the welfare of others, one becomes eternally happy. The greatness of such a practitioner of *karmayoga* is described in the *Śaraṇagītā* as follows: "Having oppressed the mind and destroyed the home, is this not a stain upon the triple-streamed [Ganges]? Therefore, he who does not oppress the mind of another and does not destroy his home [is truly pure].
"O Siddha Kapila, he alone is blessed and pure on this earth who possesses this yoga of yours.
Thus, a practitioner of Karma-yoga never causes injury to another; rather, always pleasing everyone by viewing them as oneself, he accomplishes only the welfare of all people. Therefore:
One who is fit for action is indeed superior with respect to one who is fit for knowledge. || 7 ||
The one who knows reality should remain composed, thinking, "I do nothing at all," even while seeing, hearing, touching, smelling, eating, moving, breathing, or sleeping.
Speaking, releasing, grasping, opening, and even closing the eyes—
one should maintain the awareness that it is the senses alone that operate among the objects of the senses.
He who performs actions by dedicating them to Brahman, having abandoned attachment, is not tainted by sin, just as a lotus leaf is not wetted by water. 10.
He explains the method here so that, even after performing an action, there may be no "smearing" (attachment) to it:
a person who is disciplined, whose mind is concentrated, and who knows reality—that is, who knows the true nature of the self—[thinks], "I am doing nothing at all.

"I do nothing at all because I have no desire for anything; rather, it is only the senses that act. Thus, while seeing, hearing, smelling, eating, grasping, or even opening and closing the eyes—performing such various activities—he [acts] through the senses, such as the eyes, with respect to their objects.

He who performs actions— performing them while maintaining the firm conviction that they "operate," meaning they become active, within form and other such respective objects; having placed all actions upon Brahman, the Supreme Lord who is omnipresent throughout the body, and having abandoned attachment to the fruit produced by those actions— he thus performs his duties.

He is not bound by sin—which consists of the fruits of action—any more than a lotus leaf is touched by water. Having abandoned attachment to the fruits of action, the performance of all deeds solely for the sake of pleasing the Lord is described in the *Śaraṇagītā* as follows: "O friend, at the very moment a man utters the word 'ayi'..."
For right there is the world of no-sky; for the person who calls out with the word "re," at that very moment and in that very place, indeed, is Kālasūtra.

Thus, for the practitioner of karma-yoga who carries out all actions with faith through the contemplation of worshipping the Lord, the disposition of offering the fruits [of action] arises spontaneously. In this way, a life purified by pleasing all [beings] is conducted by the practitioner of karma-yoga. Therefore, the practitioner of karma-yoga is a true devotee of the Lord of karma-yoga.
Having become dear to the Supreme Self, he attains the state of Maheśvara. || 10 ||
With body, mind, intellect, and even with the senses alone,
yogis perform action, having abandoned attachment, for the sake of self-purification.

Thus, for one engaged in action, actions performed with a view toward the welfare of all people and with the understanding of non-attachment— even by means of the senses such as sight and so forth, which are entirely devoid of the sense of "mine"— and even by the body alone, remaining like a burnt cloth, by means of that alone. (The word "alone" [kevala] is to be connected with the other terms as well.)

With an unattached mind, with pure intellect, with a thought free from the notions of "I" and "mine" in all circumstances, and with an unchanging disposition— the yogi, that is, the practitioner of action, having abandoned attachment, performs action solely for the purification of the self, for the sake of achieving the self's stainlessness, and not otherwise.
Out of a desire to attain physical pleasure, they become engaged in action. || 11 ||
The disciplined one, having abandoned the fruit of action, attains peace that is final;
the undisciplined one, impelled by desire and attached to the fruit, becomes bound. (12)

Thus, he states that liberation is certain through the gradual practice of *karmayoga*, whereas bondage is certain through its non-performance: "Therefore... [he] attains"—that is, reaches—"the steadfast peace," which is liberation.
But the unsteady person, not knowing such a secret called *karmayoga*, acts according to his own desires.

Acting according to one's own will, one who is attached—that is, clinging—to the fruit, which is the respective result of that action, becomes bound, falling under the power of bondage. One who performs action while attached to its fruit is designated as a "karmī" (an agent of action). However, all actions performed with faith for the sake of pleasing the Lord, without any intention for their fruit, [are not so].

The practitioner of action (karmayogin) becomes a partaker of suffering, whereas one who is eternally contented always dwells in happiness. Thus, the Blessed One expects that all human beings, having understood the secret of karmayoga, should become practitioners of action.
Having renounced all actions with the mind, the self-controlled embodied being dwells happily in the city of nine gates, neither acting nor causing action to be done.

But he who is a practitioner of action (karmayogin) who perceives reality, having mentally renounced all actions while remaining in the city of the physical body— distinguished by its nine gates such as the mouth, eyes, nostrils, ears, and the organs of excretion and generation—
that embodied soul, the master of the body, the self-controlled one who has conquered his senses, does not himself perform anything whatsoever with a view toward any result.

Without performing even the slightest action himself, nor causing others to do so—neither directly nor indirectly through another—he remains at ease, free from the affliction of dualities such as pleasure and pain due to his state of non-attachment; he dwells in peace and tranquility. Such a one...

For the living being, there shall never be a disruption of peace, nor is the loss of happiness possible; those who possess direct experience declare that this alone is the union with eternal bliss. (13)
The Lord creates neither agency nor actions for the world, nor the connection with the fruits of action; rather, it is inherent nature that operates.

He explains this very point by saying, "neither acting nor causing to act": the Lord, who has become the king of this city with nine gates— the Self— does not create the agency of the world, that is, of the class of living beings, nor the actions being performed by them.
Or rather, it does not create the connection with the fruit of action, nor does it create the attainment of the fruit born of action;
for in reality, this self is pure, all-pervading, stainless, and the Supreme Self, belonging to no one.

[The world] becomes an instrument. If this is so, then in response to the doubt as to what might be the cause of every category of effect proceeding in the world, the resolution is stated here: "It is nature (svabhāva) that proceeds.
Nature is indeed primordial matter (prakṛti), the power residing in the Supreme Self, designated as Māyā.

By the proximity of the Supreme Self, She accomplishes every task. As previously stated in the verse, "All actions performed in every way by the qualities of Prakṛti, the self deluded by egoism thinks, 'I am the doer,'" it has been shown that the Self possesses no agency whatsoever of its own.

The meaning is that the qualities of *prakṛti*, such as *sattva* and the rest, accomplish every effect in accordance with the will of the Blessed Lord. Although the Supreme Self resides within the body, He remains indifferent as a mere witness of the activity of *prakṛti*; the individual soul (*jīvātman*), however, being bound by *prakṛti*, [experiences] everything for itself.

It conceives of itself as the agent. This very attachment to material nature binds the individual soul (jīva) through its lack of discernment regarding the true nature of reality. This bondage, rooted in non-discrimination, is the source of all misfortune. 14.
The omnipresent Lord does not take upon Himself the sin or even the merit of anyone;
it is by ignorance that knowledge is shrouded, and thereby living beings are deluded. 15.

This all-pervading Supreme Self does not take upon itself—that is, does not appropriate—the sin committed through the egoistic conceit of any particular individual soul (jīva), even though that soul is a portion of Himself, yet appears distinct due to its innate connection with primordial nature (prakṛti). It is specified as "of any [soul]" because souls are infinite in number. He does not accept the sin produced by that [soul's] false identification.

Abiding everywhere as a witness through sheer neutrality, He indeed exists within all the senses along with the individual soul (jīva). Nevertheless, by His very nature, He does not appropriate even the slightest fruit of the jīva’s actions.
To the question, "If so, what is the basis for all the worldly activity that is observed? he says: "By ignorance" (ajñānena).

Knowledge (*jñāna*) is the realization that the Supreme Lord exists within one's own body as the inner controller (*antaryāmin*); this is discernment (*viveka*). It remains obscured and covered by ignorance (*ajñāna*), which is rooted in the false identification with the ego (*ahaṅkāra*) produced by *prakṛti*. In this context, the very notion "I am the body" constitutes ignorance. [The Self is] of the nature of consciousness and bliss (*cidānanda-svarūpa*).

The individual soul (jīva) considers itself to consist of the three qualities (guṇas). Therefore, living beings, intent on wandering within the wheel of saṃsāra, become deluded; they fall under the sway of ignorance, thinking in such forms as "I do," "I cause to be done," "I shall enjoy," "I cause to be enjoyed," "I give," and "I cause to be given. [They think: "This work was performed by me here."
By reflecting thus, one indeed attains the supreme state of Śiva. Whatever is offered to the Liṅga must not be spoken of;
if it is increased and established [in the temple], Saṅgameśa will surely grant the desired fruit to the disciplined seeker who is devoted to the Self.

And it impels them to offer the fruit of their actions with devotion through a heart-touching manner. Thus, the wise, having abandoned the sense of agency and cultivated the thought of union with the Supreme Self in their minds, become adept at acting in a skillful way for His pleasure. For such people, [the grace of] Śiva—
Having understood this, the Blessed One expects that those who act accordingly will become happy. || 15 ||
But for those whose ignorance regarding the Self has been destroyed by knowledge,
that knowledge reveals the Supreme, like the sun.

For those beings and living entities, the ignorance regarding themselves— their own innermost Supreme Lord— and the lack of acquaintance with the relationship between their distinct natures, which consists of the identification of the body with the self,
becomes destroyed and removed through knowledge, preceded by the experience of the distinction between those two.

For them, that knowledge is the supreme reality, the very nature of the Supreme Self shining within the body. Like the sun—the sun which illuminates all worldly objects—it illuminates [the truth] and brings about an acquaintance with the supreme reality. "This Self is not attained by instruction..."

"He is not to be gained by intellect nor by much hearing; he whom this [Self] chooses, by him alone is He gained; to him this one reveals His own form. Thus it is heard in the Kaṭha Upaniṣad. No person whatsoever is able to attain self-knowledge through mere force or lack of discrimination; rather, [He is attained] by one who possesses a pure mind.
With a tranquil intellect and a stainless heart, through the grace of the Guru, one seeks Him;

then the Supreme Self reveals His own true nature to that seeker. He who knows both himself and his own Controller rejoices through his own direct experience. Without such experience, the fool merely rejoices in the Brahman in vain.

By this statement of Abhinavagupta, it is established that only he who, having obtained knowledge through the grace of the Guru, enters his own heart by himself, attains the favor of the Lord; he alone finds the fruit, and at that very moment— (p.

The practitioner must correctly understand the ultimate reality as it has been described; otherwise, being deluded regarding the knowledge of this world and the next, he will fall away from everything. Therefore, the practitioner must first eliminate ignorance, which consists of the fetters of impurity that serve as his own obscuration.
For that very purpose, he must seek out a certain guru who has realized the Self;
without his instruction, no living being is capable of knowing the Supreme Reality within the body. || 16 ||
With their intellects fixed on That, with That as their very self, established in That, and having That as their supreme goal, they—
whose impurities have been washed away by knowledge— go to the state from which there is no return.

Here, he praises the very knowledge of one's own and others' [nature]. "Those whose intellect is fixed on that" means those whose intellect exists solely in that aforementioned knowledge of reality (*tattva-jñāna*). "Those whose self is that" means those whose internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*)—the self—is situated in that very knowledge of reality. For this very reason, they are "established in that," meaning their steadfastness and faith reside in that alone.
Those for whom [the Lord] is thus their sole refuge and who are exclusively devoted to Him have their impurities shaken off by knowledge;

that is, all their sins have been destroyed by the aforementioned knowledge of reality, and thus they are stainless. As it is said: "O Arjuna, the fire of knowledge reduces all actions to ashes," because the knowledge of Śiva destroys all bonds consisting of impurity.

Such wise ones attain [this state] right here in this body of grace, within the heart endowed with a pure mind and intellect, and experience the light of the Self. For those who possess such discernment between *prakṛti* and *puruṣa*, the cessation of rebirth becomes easily attained; otherwise, having conceived of the body alone as the Self—

Those who, through egoism, imagine the pleasure of the body alone to be the goal of life and conduct themselves accordingly in the world, continue to wander again and again in the wheel of saṃsāra, which consists of birth and death. Therefore, the Blessed One clarifies the intention that both women and men must strive with faith to attain discernment (viveka). || 17 ||
The wise look with an equal eye upon a Brahmin endowed with learning and humility, a cow, an elephant, a dog, and even an outcaste. 18.

Here he describes the manner of abiding for those who know the Self: the wise—those possessing the aforementioned discrimination—regard the individual souls (jīvas) residing within the bodies of women and men as equal to a preeminent Brāhmaṇa endowed with learning and humility, a knower of Brahman; to a cow, which is supremely pure; and to an elephant.

Those who possess the vision of the Supreme Self— which is impartial, all-pervading, and identical to all— regard a mighty elephant, a dog, an extremely lowly creature, or even a meat-eating outcaste as equal.

[The distinctions] exist; for although the distinction between the individual soul (*jīva*) and [the Supreme] is innate, being produced by *prakṛti*, the wise attain the vision of the Supreme Self alone, because He abides everywhere with an equal gaze. Even in the most lowly and the most exalted living beings, the Supreme Lord exists as the very measure of a thumb.

He dwells with an equal vision toward both the virtuous and the wicked; he himself says, "There is none hateful to me, nor any dear. Those who thus perceive the Supreme Śiva everywhere through an even-minded disposition are called the wise. In them, the vision of self-similarity (*ātmaupamya*) shines forth spontaneously. Thus, one who in the world...
He engages in worldly affairs while remaining entirely untainted. For him, the manifestation of the Supreme Self within his own body is thus perceived.

The fivefold group of objects, consisting of both the conscious and the unconscious, exists in all things; in all those five, the radiance of the Supreme Self is perfectly integrated. It is solely through its proximity that all of them [function].

They are engaged in their respective functions. Within them, the Supreme Self alone shines forth, eternally untainted and unmanifest. Just as a multitude of gems on a single thread, those five are joined together within that one alone. It is the experience of the Supreme Self existing in such a manner that is present here.

"Equal vision" is thus indicated by Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Self. Here, the fourfold internal organ and the individual soul (jīva) are designated: by the word "brāhmaṇa," the intellect (buddhi); by the word "cow," the mind (citta); by the word "elephant," the ego (ahaṅkāra); by the word "dog," the mind-organ (manaḥ); and by the word "outcaste," the individual soul (jīva). Among these—

By perceiving the Supreme Self, which exists as the underlying thread through all things, the man of knowledge is liberated from the bonds of worldly existence. Kṛṣṇa’s intention is that if this very spiritual vision were cultivated by people in their daily lives, then life would become healthy and beautiful.

He who perceives the Supreme Self (Paramātman) in his own body likewise perceives Him in others as well. He who does not achieve an acquaintance with the Supreme Self within himself will not find Him anywhere else. As it is heard elsewhere in the scriptures: "If one has known [the Truth] here, that is the reality; if one has not known it here, there is great ruin. Therefore...

Thus, it appears entirely consistent that whatever is observed by the Supreme Soul, Śrī Kṛṣṇa, regarding how human beings should conduct themselves through the discrimination between the body and the self, is indeed correct. || 18 ||
Even here in this world, creation has been conquered by those whose minds are established in equanimity;
for Brahman is indeed faultless and equal, and therefore they are established in Brahman. (19)

Those wise ones whose minds are established in equanimity—that is, in the cultivation of equality as described above—have conquered *sarga*, the cycle of worldly existence, in this very life; for them, rebirth simply does not exist. This is because Brahman—the reality of the Self—is present everywhere, flawless, and self-existent.

Being free from all kinds of defects, it is therefore equal—that is, the same—everywhere. Consequently, those who possess the aforementioned vision of equality are established in Brahman; they become fixed in Brahman. And it is well known that for those fixed in Brahman, there is no rebirth. || 19 ||

One who has known Brahman and is established in Brahman—steadfast in intellect and undeluded—should neither rejoice upon obtaining what is pleasant nor be agitated upon obtaining what is unpleasant. (20)

He describes the nature of one who is thus established in Brahman: The knower of Brahman—one who, according to the manner described, knows the reality of the Supreme Self and experiences the essential nature of Paraśiva—being indeed established in Brahman, that is, in Paraśiva-Brahman, remains steady-minded and should not rejoice (*prahṛṣyet*), nor should he feel elation. In the same way, he should likewise remain unmoved by what is unpleasant, undesirable, or painful.

Having attained [this state], one should not be agitated nor should one fall into despondency. For such a person, the entire range of dualities—praise and blame, pleasure and pain, and so forth—is equally meaningful and appears as beautiful. In the *Śaraṇagītā*, the equanimity of Basavārya is beautifully described; he expresses his own realization as follows:
He reports: "I consider even a reviler to be a kinsman; I consider even one who causes pain to be a protector.

I consider a censurer to be my mother and father; I consider even one who has been protected by me to be my guardian. Indeed, I consider even one who defiles me to be a birth-relative; O King, I consider even one who casts me upon a golden stake to be my praiser."

"Listen to this, O Saṅgameśa! Thus, those who possess direct experience maintain that he in whom an equal vision toward both enemy and friend, as well as praise and blame, is observed, is alone a knower of Brahman.
However, Basavārya, having become a seeker of refuge under his guru Saṅgamārya, was [further] graced by him...

By worshipping with faith his own chosen *liṅga*, which is the very form of his life-breath, he thus proclaims his own attained state of peace: "If one is slain here, one is indeed slain; if one is censured here, one is indeed censurable. One need not reflect upon the deeds of a previous birth, for likewise, present enjoyment is already in one's hand."

"The fruit of Kūḍalasaṅgameśa is obtained in one's very hand through the worship of you. Thus, by means of the propitiation of the Lord, a sense of equality arises spontaneously within a human being. Even when forgotten, He does not forget us; whatever is to be given to us, He surely gives all of that.
147) Even its familiarity is understood by us solely from the satisfaction of those who have experienced it.
This [satisfaction] might exist in some cases; however, no sign of fading or forgetfulness is observed, nor is there any lack of fruit.
