There is no fruit without the propitiation of the mobile [deity]; however, through the satisfaction of the mobile [deity], the *liṅga* becomes moist and likewise soft—O Lord of Devas, such is my firm conviction regarding union. Thus, without the complete gratification of the conscious being, who is the very life-force of the *liṅga* and whose nature is great light...

The worship of the *liṅga* alone would not be fruitful. In this very way, Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Soul, instructs that all practitioners (*sādhakas*) should, while simultaneously worshipping the Lord with an even gaze, also remain devoted to the worship of the Lord’s devotees. Such practitioners alone [are truly successful] regarding what is pleasant and unpleasant.
The meaning is that they attain an even vision. || 20 ||
The self that is powerless regarding external objects of touch finds that happiness which is within itself;
he whose self is joined in yoga with Brahman enjoys imperishable happiness.
In the same way, one whose self is unattached to external objects such as touch, form, taste, smell, and so forth— being unattached,

free from the connection characterized by the meeting of attachment— and being one whose mind (ātman) is joined with that very [state] and rejoicing therein, attains imperishable, indestructible, and eternal happiness.

One attains or reaches liberation (*mokṣa*). Since external objects such as form, taste, and so forth are perishable, the happiness dependent upon them is likewise perishable. However, because the Self (*ātman*) is eternal and consists of bliss (*ānandamaya*), the happiness produced by the experience of it is also eternal; this is the meaning. And that [Self] is the individual soul (*jīva*) whose nature is the Self.

Only [the Self] is able to experience this. Indeed, the body, being insentient by nature, cannot experience the bliss of the Self. Even the individual soul (jīva), because it is a portion of the Supreme Self who is of the nature of consciousness, is capable—though distinct from the Supreme Self—of abandoning the perception of duality and experiencing the bliss of non-duality. For the body is not connected with the Self.
One may experience the bliss of the Self even by providing a support for the Self; therefore, the Blessed One teaches that the conscious living being (jīva),
through acquaintance with its own fundamental reality, casts off the covering of impurity consisting of ignorance and indeed becomes composed of bliss (ānandamaya).
For those enjoyments born of contact are indeed sources of suffering;
they have a beginning and an end, O son of Kuntī, and the wise man does not delight in them. 22.
(p. 148) It is pointed out that he who, abandoning the bliss of the Self, delights in external pleasure, does not indeed obtain eternal happiness;
for those enjoyments born of contact—that is, produced by the conjunction of the sense objects and the senses—[are impermanent].

The meaning is that sensual pleasures are indeed sources of suffering; they are the producers of suffering, they are of the nature of suffering, they are rooted in suffering, and they culminate in suffering. Not only that, but all those parts, having a beginning and an end, are entirely impermanent. Their arising occurs exactly as follows: [text continues]
Even when that [pleasure] has ceased, suffering arises once again.

Thus, regarding worldly pleasure which exists mixed with suffering, only the undiscriminating person delights in it and becomes attached to it; the discriminating person, however, does not—meaning one who has attained the discrimination between the body and the Self, a man of knowledge. || 22 ||
He who is able here, even before the release from the body, to endure the impulse arising from desire and anger—he is disciplined, he is a happy man. (23)

Thus, one who regards his own welfare should first strive for mastery over the senses; for otherwise, a great calamity may arise. He says: the wise person, while still living here, remaining in this very body, acting and experiencing enjoyments, even before the release from the body—that is, prior to the abandonment of this body—[should achieve this].

He is able—that is, he becomes capable—of remaining such that no agitation or some kind of loss occurs within himself due to the impulse arising from desire and anger; "desire" (kāma) is the longing for sense objects, and "anger" (krodha) is the mental state rooted therein. He who endures the onset of desire and anger shall alone become eternally happy; he alone is liberated.

He ought to become a yogi; he alone would be a wise man. Otherwise, his wandering through the cycle of existence (saṃsāra) in another birth would be unavoidable. One who is possessed by desire and anger finds happiness not only in this world but even in the next; even the worship of the gods performed by him [is rendered fruitless].

It would indeed be in vain. If one who is habituated to virtuous conduct should worship the Lord, then that very worship will be accepted by the Lord. However, if one should worship the Lord while harboring anger and hatred in the mind, then by the Lord's own resolve, he shall become eternally miserable. Thus did Basavārya [describe] the worship of the sinful.
He defiles [the deity]. Overcome by anger, he causes the Lord of Ambikā to be bathed, and that bath takes the form of a stream of blood.

If a sinful soul offers an oblation of flower garlands, it becomes a wound from the edge of a sword. Thus, one who—lacking virtuous conduct—performs worship and the like merely for the sake of fame and gain...

Whoever practices such [deceit] will surely fall from this state and then fall from that as well. What can you possibly gain by immersing yourselves in the water of such hypocrites? Likewise, one should keep another’s wife at a distance, as well as wealth.
"And having abandoned one [practice], that purification would surely come through immersion in water; this is not true at all.
Seeing such hypocritical devotees and feeling distress in his heart, what Basavarya said at that time still awakens everyone today: "Every day, for the sake of beholding the Lord..."

Even now, it is observed that many people, having gone to a temple and standing before the deity, practice the remembrance (*smaraṇa*) of the two sandals (*pādukā*) that were left outside. The *Śaraṇagītā* points out such devotees in this way, generating a true realization (*satsphūrti*) within them: "All men are immersed in the worship and consecration of the *liṅga*."

Listen to my words: having cast off his sandals outside, he enters the temple and offers salutation; yet, being under the sway of constant meditation upon his own sandals, he meditates on them and not on his own Lord. Therefore, O men, do not hoard wealth; for if it is hoarded, rebirth becomes unavoidable. And as for wealth...
"Everything that has been prepared must be offered to the devotees of the Lord.
Thus, in order to make his devotees virtuous in conduct and free from desire and anger, the noble Basava proclaims his intention with most powerful speech. || 23 ||
He who is happy within, who rejoices within, and who likewise has light only within—
that yogi, having become Brahman, attains the extinction in Brahman.
He who has inner happiness— one whose happiness is within the inner self alone and not in the senses— and for that very reason is one whose delight is internal—

one whose pleasure, play, and recreation are in the self alone; likewise, he whose light is internal— one whose illumination is within the self— such a yogi, sporting while attached to the self alone, becomes Brahman.

Being of the very nature of Paraśiva-Brahman, he experiences the bliss of liberation (*kaivalyānanda*), which is the extinction into Brahman (*brahmanirvāṇa*), even in the midst of suffering. Saṃsāra itself is the root of suffering. Immersed in such a mire of impurity, the bound soul (*paśujīva*) must uplift himself by taking refuge in the Supreme Self alone; [for] it is from the Supreme Self alone...
Because the essential reality abides here, this saṃsāra becomes meaningful.
The *Śaraṇagītā* thus points out the path of self-purification for Basavārya, the preeminent Śiva-yogi:
"For an animal submerged in mud, no other way of escape is seen here than by striking its feet; I am lost."
O Śambhu, O Lord of the Mountain, I am lost; lift me up and place me within Your heart. I am a beast, and You are the sovereign of the beast; therefore, have compassion for me, Your own self.
"O Compassionate One, as long as these men perceive me as a predator and seize and kill me, O Lord, look upon me so that I may not bring reproach upon You. Thus,
for the sake of lifting up those submerged in the ocean of saṃsāra, the Supreme Self alone is the primary cause."

It is called "sādhana" because it is cultivated by those who possess direct experience. For this very reason, having known the Supreme Self as consisting of bliss, may all human beings become absorbed in union with It; thus the Blessed Lord employs His own bliss as the medicine for the disease of worldly existence. || 25 ||
The sages, whose taints are exhausted, who have severed all doubts, who have restrained their selves, and who delight in the welfare of all beings, attain the Brahman-nirvāṇa.

With their impurities exhausted—meaning all sins destroyed by the knowledge of the truth as it has been taught—and with their dualities severed, meaning their doubts completely cut away; with their selves controlled, meaning their senses restrained; and devoted to the welfare of all beings—meaning they are attached to the well-being of all creatures without regard for caste, opinion, family, lineage, sacred thread, or the like—they are intent on the benefit of everyone whatsoever.

The meaning is that they do not commit violence against living beings. Such sages attain *brahmanirvāṇa*—the liberation known as Paramaśiva, the state of formlessness—and experience it right here in this very body of grace (*prasādakāya*). Even other human beings, while remaining in the body and engaged in worldly affairs, [attain the same] through the knowledge of Śiva.
The Blessed One reveals his intention that they should become unstained. || 25 ||
For those ascetics who are free from desire and anger, whose minds are restrained,
and who have realized the Self, the extinction of Brahman exists on every side.

He says that for such as these, liberation is accomplished right here [in this very life]: for those who are free from desire and anger—meaning, liberated from desire and anger in this very birth according to the manner described—and whose minds are controlled, meaning whose internal organs (antaḥkaraṇa) are restrained—for them, the extinction in Brahman (*brahmanirvāṇa*), which is liberation in the form of identity with Supreme Śiva, exists everywhere; it is possible at all times.

The Lord conveys the intention that it is not merely after death, but even now they experience the bliss of Śiva right here; thus, the experience of Brahman is possible for those engaged in the yoga of action (karmayogins) everywhere and at all times. || 26 ||
Having thus described the power of the yogins, [the author] will teach the method of yoga in detail in the following chapter:
"Having placed the external objects of touch outside, and the eyes between the eyebrows... (p. 151).
Having made the prāṇa and apāna breaths equal, moving within the nostrils; || 27 ||
The sage who has restrained his senses, mind, and intellect, who is devoted solely to liberation, and from whom desire, fear, and anger have departed—he is indeed always liberated. (28)
Having cast out external contacts— external objects such as sound, touch, and so forth— from within them,

and having made even the prāṇa and apāna breaths, which move internally through the two nostrils (the two internal passages of the nose), equal; with senses, mind, and intellect restrained— that is, with the senses controlled.

He whose [faculties] are the eyes and so forth, the mind, and the intellect— he, employing the senses through discernment and a well-established method, being truly devoted to liberation alone, having become stainless through the release from bonds and desiring to attain the unfolding of power; he for whom desire, fear, and anger have departed— desire having departed...
He for whom desire, fear— which arises from the sight of the undesirable— and anger—
which arises from the frustration of one's wishes— do not exist, is one whose mind is always equanimous;
such a sage, practitioner, or ascetic is liberated at all times, both here and in the hereafter.

Thus, having attained oneness with the Great God (Mahādeva), who is of the nature of great light within this very heart, the yogi becomes far removed from the fear of death and experiences eternal bliss even while in the body. Content with whatever he obtains,
that yogi gladdens all beings through the contemplation of Śiva and brings about only their welfare.

Even while remaining in this saṃsāra, which is a mine of suffering, one becomes one who has accomplished all that was to be done by beholding the Lord, who consists of bliss and is most substantial. He in whose heart such spiritual contemplation (*adhyātmabhāvanā*) shines forth, though dwelling in the world with a mind always composed, shines as one beyond worldly phenomena (*alokadharma*), because he has understood the true nature of the world.
Having understood both her attachment and detachment, and having set them aside, he carries out his own duty with a vigilant mind;
dwelling like one who is innocent, untouched by worldly ways, such yogis— whose lives are purifying and exemplary— Śaraṇā rejoices in with sincere love.

Having observed the world, they teach thus: "If one builds a house on a mountain that is the refuge of deer, why indeed should this person fear the deer? If one builds a shelter on the shore of the ocean, why indeed should one fear its waves? Living in a marketplace, how could a person in this world of living beings not fear the resulting calamity?"
O wise one, even after being born in the world and encountering the duality of praise and blame, do not give way to anger in your mind; remain always composed and listen to this.

Mallikārjuna: Thus, with heartfelt expectation that those people living in the world who are deeply immersed in the bliss of the supreme self—such as the Great Goddess Akka—may remain with their minds in meditative absorption, she sought refuge in her chosen deity, the Guru, and the Śaṅkara lineage for that purpose.
Those born of noble family who are devoted to these true devotees are proclaimed as *kulajas*. It is thus [that she sought] only such true devotees.
By contemplating the welfare of all people and by his exemplary conduct, Śrī Basavārya, the crest-jewel of devotees, nurtures those born of noble lineage.
Knowing Me as the enjoyer of sacrifices and austerities, the Great Lord of all worlds, and the friend of all beings, one attains peace. 29.
Thus, by living in the world with total forbearance and a composed mind, finding happiness amidst suffering,
and being approved by both friends and enemies— if a person knows how to dwell here in such a manner,
only then does their birth become meaningful. Having become so, that person shines within his own inner self.

For the resolution of all problems, devotion to the Lord residing within one's own heart alone must be the divine elixir; for although the Supreme Lord dwells secretly in the heart as the very form of light,
if a human being realizes that his own enjoyment is offered by Him alone— then [he shall be liberated].

When one offers to Him with devotion, He accepts it with satisfaction and partakes of it; therefore, He alone becomes the enjoyer and the acceptor of all the aforementioned sacrifices and austerities. Whatever is offered with devotion, having consumed all of that, He gives the remainder to the devotee who made the offering.

He bestows grace in the form of *prasāda*. Through the enjoyment of this *prasāda*, the destruction of all the sufferings of the human being occurs. Those who have experienced it say that the enjoyment of *prasāda* itself is the medicine that wards off all diseases.
Thus, the Supreme Lord, who dwells within the hearts of all like one who is indifferent, [accepts] what is offered through devotion.
Having accepted even leaves, flowers, and the like, He bestows upon them worldly or otherworldly happiness that exceeds even those offerings.

Therefore, those who possess direct experience maintain that He alone is the most worthy of worship by all. For this very reason, He is the Great Lord of All Worlds (Sarvalokamaheśvara), the Lord even of the lords existing in all the worlds.
He is reckoned as the "Niyāmaka" (the Ordainer). The Śruti indicates that He is the supreme cause even of the three forms who establish the order of the world.

Not only is he the enjoyer of all fruits and the controller of all, but those who possess direct experience contemplate that he alone is the friend of all living beings. Thus, because he protects the welfare of the entire world, the Supreme Self is heard of as Śiva; and because he is the illuminator and the refuge of all, he alone is called Deva.
That very God is the friend of all at all times; there is no contradiction here for anyone.
This is a matter universally accepted. This intention is correctly expressed by Basavārya:
"Just as the moon rises and waxes with its appearance, yet wanes at the time of its setting, so too does the sage when he drinks water."

"Has the moon come from the ocean to assist the sea? For when Rāhu swallows the moon, does the ocean indeed go into the midst [of the fray]? O Lord, no one else provides protection; you alone are the giver, the sole kinsman of the world. Thus, for all the world, the Supreme Self alone is the true kinsman—so [it is said by] all.
The experienced ones say: he who knows that I, who am thus always the benefactor, am not merely a human being,
but am the Supreme Self itself dissolved in a state of equal flavor (samarasatā) with the Supreme Self—
he, impelled by such knowledge, performing the activity consisting of true devotion, [attains the goal] even here in this very life as a result thereof.

He attains *śānti*, which is liberation (*mokṣa*) whose very nature is eternal bliss. Thus it is established that the root of everything is indeed the grace of the Blessed Lord. Furthermore, although that Blessed Lord is all-pervading, he dwells in the heart because he is devoted to compassion for all living beings; therefore, he who practices his service right here [attains the goal].

Experiencing supreme bliss, he continues to experience that very same state eternally even after the dissolution of the body. In this context, the designation of the Supreme Self as the enjoyer of the sacrifice is fitting, as it is true to its meaning. The sacrifice consisting of the propitiation of the Guru and the *jaṅgama* (living deity), performed by the stainless individual soul (*jīva*), is for the sake of the one residing in the heart.

It has already been stated that if something is offered with devotion to the Supreme Lord, He certainly accepts it and bestows His grace. How does He accept the fruit of the sacrifice offered with devotion? Where and how does He reside within the body? What is the nature of sacrifice? And how is its fruit [attained]?

What is to be offered? These points are to be considered here: whatever is performed as worship and offering toward the Lord in His embodied form with the contemplation of Him as formless, all of that is indeed a sacrifice (*yajña*).
This includes bathing with water, the sixteen-fold ritual service (*ṣoḍaśopacāra-pūjā*), and the external presentation of fruits and other offerings—all of this is likewise [a sacrifice].

It is indeed sacrifice: the offering of food, drink, and so forth to the Śrī Gurus in their embodied forms, and the giving of meals, clothing, and other necessities to those residing in one’s home, such as kinsmen, sisters, and others.

The Lord alone shines resplendent among all—teachers, living beings, mendicants, and kinsmen alike. He dwells even within our enemies; therefore, abandoning enmity toward them as well, viewing them with a gaze of love is itself the worship of the Blessed One. Only those who perform such adoration [attain the goal].

It is designated by the word "sacrifice" (yajña). Here, Kṛṣṇa reveals the underlying intention that the Supreme Lord enjoys the fruit of austerity performed in this very manner, which takes the form of sacrifice. Within the body, among the five sense organs that are to be offered in the sacrifice, there are five objects: smell, taste, form, touch, and sound.
They exist. To accept them, even the Supreme Self manifests within the body in five ways.

It is logical for the Supreme Lord—who is of the nature of consciousness and has brought the power of *māyā* under his control—to abide simultaneously in many places through infinite forms. Along with him, the individual soul (*jīva*), who is a portion of Him, [manifests] for the purpose of offering those respective objects.

He dwells in that very place; because he is the locus for the supreme Self’s diversion, he is called an *aṅga*. Only one who exists as well-refined by initiation (*dīkṣā*) becomes denoted by the word *aṅga*. This [being] named *aṅga* is a pure soul (*śuddhajīva*), and because of his renunciation of the objects of enjoyment to the supreme Self, he is the "limb of renunciation" (*tyāgāṅga*).

Because it consists of the enjoyment of the remnants of what has been enjoyed by Him, it is designated as the "limb of enjoyment" (*bhogāṅga*). Through this perspective of the integration of renunciation and enjoyment, the individual soul (*jīva*) abandons all forms of ego-inflation;
thus, the supremely pure *jīva*, through union with the Lord (*īśvara*), is called the "limb of yoga" (*yogāṅga*) by virtue of the limb of renunciation.

It is said by the experienced practitioners that at the time of accepting an object offered, it is called the *iṣṭaliṅga*; for the acceptance of what is offered as an auxiliary to enjoyment (*bhoga*), it is called the *prāṇaliṅga*; and for the acceptance of what is offered as an auxiliary to yoga (*yoga*), it is called the *bhāvaliṇga*. Thus, that which is termed the "auxiliary to renunciation" (*tyāgāṅga*)— [The text continues: ...is established as the supreme means for attaining liberation. Therefore, one should always offer all things to the Lord with devotion, according to the prescribed rules, whether they be external objects or internal states. By this, the mind becomes purified, and through the grace of the Guru, one attains the state of being a true *liṅgin*. Thus ends the chapter on the offering of the self. *Note: This passage describes the three types of *liṅgas* (the *iṣṭaliṅga*, *prāṇaliṅga*, and *bhāvaliṅga*) corresponding to the three aims of life (*dharma*, *artha*, and *mokṣa*) in the Trika tradition.*

The *jīva* residing in the nose is called *bhakta*, while the one residing in the *rasanā* (tongue) is called *māheśvara*. It has already been stated previously that since the *jīva* is a portion of the consciousness of the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*), it is capable of abiding everywhere. Likewise, the *jīva* named *bhogāṅga* resides in the two eyes.

He is called *prāṇaliṅgin*. Likewise, the individual soul (*jīva*) named *bhogāṅga*, residing in the two eyes, is called *prasādī* while dwelling everywhere upon the skin that envelops the body; he is also called *prāṇaliṅgin*. Similarly, the individual soul named *yogāṅga*, residing in the two ears, is [called] *śaraṇa* by virtue of [the power] shining upon the head.

It is also called "oneness" (*aikya*) because of the unification with the sign of existence (*bhāvaliṅga*). Likewise, the Lord (*īśvara*), residing in the nose, is the "sign of conduct" (*ācāraliṅga*); residing in the tongue, he is the "sign of the guru" (*guruliṅga*); and [residing] in the eyes—

Dwellers in the heart perceive it as the *prasādaliṅga*, while those possessed of direct experience perceive it as the *mahāliṅga*. Because it impels the activity of inhalation and exhalation, the Lord residing in the nose is called the *ācāraliṅga*; and because the individual soul (*jīva*) performs that same activity, the names "Lord" (*Īśvara*) and "devotee" (*bhakta*) are both meaningful. Through the channel of the tongue...

Because the Lord residing therein is fit to instruct the devotee, He is called the *guruliṅga*, and since the individual soul (*jīva*) remains right there with Him as one fit to receive instruction, the name *māheśvara* is likewise meaningful.
Similarly, the Lord residing in the two eyes is the *śivaliṅga* because He illuminates all objects; thus it is in that very place.

Because it abides by beholding all things as being of the nature of clarity (*prasāda*), the living soul (*jīva*)—possessing a tranquil mind and a stainless heart—is called *prasādī*. Because it exists everywhere, pervading like a skin, yet remains untainted, the Lord (*īśvara*) is called *caraliṅga*; for in that very state, through the contemplation of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) is present everywhere.

Having grasped the sound, He favors the individual soul (jīva) by way of grace; for this very reason, He is called the "liṅga of grace. It is that very same soul who, having sought refuge in the Lord with exclusive devotion for the sake of receiving grace, is designated as "refuge" (śaraṇa). Thus, the soul who has sought refuge remains within the heart.

Experiencing oneness with the resplendent Great Liṅga (mahāliṅga), it is designated as "oneness" (aikya). The names "the Great Liṅga of the Lord" for the Lord and "oneness" for the individual soul (jīva) are significant in their literal meaning. In this sequence, if the devotee, being a Māheśvara, offers fragrance to the Ācāra-liṅga and flavor to the Guru-liṅga, then—

Whatever collection of objects is to be enjoyed by the individual soul (jīva), all of that should be offered to the Lord (Īśvara). If it is offered in this manner, then the Lord alone accepts and enjoys it all. This very intention is revealed in the verse beginning with "the enjoyer of sacrifice and austerity" (*bhoktāraṃ yajñatapasām*). Thus, [liberation] occurs precisely through the enjoyment of the remnants of grace (*śeṣaprasāda*).

The devotee who enjoys the experience of the *liṅga* is so described by those who have realized the truth. This sequence of accepting divine grace (*prasāda*) is considered the tradition of the six stations (*ṣaṭsthala-sampradāya*).

This subject has been explained in detail in the second part of the *Śaktiviśiṣṭādvaita-darśana*. During the period of worldly activity, [the soul] remains eternally as a pure individual soul (*śuddha-jīva*).

Experiencing the enjoyment of the phenomenal world while acting with detachment is described by experienced practitioners through various terms such as "living in grace," "the state of equilibrium between the *liṅga* and the *aṅga*," and "the blossoming of power.

Through this very realization, a human being perceives their own nature—composed of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*—as *saccidānanda*. This arises in that person solely through the grace of the Guru and the living master (*jaṅgamaguru*). Indeed, the Guru, by means of the instruction of the ultimate reality (*tattva*), kindles the unmanifest light of Śiva within the individual soul (*jīva*). "Arise! Awake! Having received the supreme boon, understand!"

By such instruction as this, he awakens the dormant devotion within living beings. In order to strengthen the contemplation of the formless Śiva, he causes the consciousness in the form of light— which resides precisely within his inner core—
to enter the well-consecrated *liṅga* the size of a thumb, so that it may be worshipped externally.

He establishes it. Because that very *liṅga* is as dear as life itself, it should be regarded by the devotee as the *prāṇaliṅga* (the life-force *liṅga*) and the *iṣṭaliṅga* (the chosen *liṅga*). When devotion is thus awakened by the Guru, the *jaṅgama* (the mobile form) enters therein in order to stabilize it through its blossoming. Although it moves everywhere, [it remains there].
Being devoid of worldly pride, he is called "the stainless one" (*nirañjana*) and "the supportless one" (*nirābhārī*).

Merely by the sight of him, a detachment known as "non-attachment" (*nirlepana*) is firmly established in the heart of the devotee. Thus, from the Guru one receives majesty, and from the Embodied One (*jaṅgama*), detachment.

One attains [this]. For all those who are striving for growth, both internal grandeur and external detachment are equally necessary. Through the cultivation of acquaintance with the formless Śiva, this phenomenal world—composed entirely of Gurus and Jaṅgamas—exists solely to offer His grace. That which is offered...
Kṛṣṇa’s intention is that Śiva alone, assuming that very form, enjoys all of that; for this very reason, through the contemplation of identity with Śiva, he designates himself as "me. || 29 ||
The Sixth Chapter:

In order to explain in detail the Yoga of Śiva, which was introduced at the end of the previous chapter with the words "having placed external objects outside" (*sparśān kṛtvā bahirbāhyān*), this chapter first establishes the performance of ritual action preceded by the renunciation of attachment to its fruits as a preliminary foundation for that [Yoga].

He who performs the necessary action without depending on the fruit of action is both a renunciant and a yogi; he is not one who merely lacks a sacrificial fire, nor one who merely abstains from action.
(157) One who performs— that is, brings about— action without depending upon, that is, without looking toward, the fruit of action (the result of the deed),
he alone is a *yati*, one who is diligent, a renunciant (*saṃnyāsī*), acting for the sake of the Lord residing within his own body.

One who is capable of offering the fruits of action through the previously mentioned path of worship at the six sites is designated as a *saṃnyāsī*; he alone is called a *karmayogī*. However, a person who has abandoned Vedic rites such as the *agnihotra* by ceasing to maintain the sacred fires cannot be considered a *saṃnyāsī*. Likewise, one who has not maintained the fires— [is not a *saṃnyāsī*].

It is not appropriate [to remain inactive]. Therefore, even by the man of knowledge (*jñānin*), every action must necessarily be performed as a form of worship of the Lord. Likewise, a person who does not perform actions such as offering (*arpaṇa*) would not be a yogi.
Here, by the word "person" (*puruṣa*), the individual soul (*jīva*)—who is fit to dwell within the city (*pura*) consisting of the bodies of women and men—is indicated. Thus...

The Lord clearly teaches here that both men and women, by means of a vision consisting of the integration of knowledge and action, may experience eternal bliss even in the midst of suffering, because they carry out every worldly transaction as a form of worship of Śiva. || 1 ||
That which they call renunciation, know that to be yoga, O Pāṇḍava;
for no one becomes a yogi without having renounced all purposeful intent.

He states the reason for the statement "he is both a renunciant and a yogi": because both are equal— namely, the yoga of knowledge, which consists of the renunciation of the fruits of action as described above, and the yoga of action, which consists of the performance of duty with the sense of obligation— it is precisely that which the experienced ones call "renunciation," namely, the surrender of the fruit.
Know—that is, understand—*karmayoga*. Even at the time of performing action, there is skill (*cāturya*) consisting in the renunciation of one's own interest;

for one who has not renounced *saṅkalpa*—that is, one by whom *saṅkalpa*, the mental resolve directed toward results, has not been abandoned—cannot become a *yogin*, a practitioner of *karmayoga*. Therefore, that which they call *saṃnyāsa* is indeed *yoga*.
Those who possess direct experience have said [this]. || 2 ||
For the sage who desires to ascend to yoga, action is said to be the means;
for that same person once ascended to yoga, tranquility is said to be the means.
p.

158) Having thus praised the yoga of action (karmayoga), he now shows that the yoga of action is a means for the yoga of meditation (dhyānayoga): "For the sage who desires to ascend—meaning, who wishes to mount—the yoga, [the yoga of meditation], [action is the means]."

The reason is stated: because it is impossible to practice the yoga of meditation (*dhyānayoga*) without purity of mind, the performance of action is necessary for that person; this is the meaning. However, for one who has indeed ascended to yoga—that is, for one established in the yoga of meditation—tranquility (*śama*), peace, which is the very withdrawal from all outward activities, is said to be the cause.
The meaning is that one who is intent on external activity is indeed unable to practice the yoga of meditation. || 3 ||
For when one no longer clings to the objects of the senses nor to actions,
having renounced all volitions, then one is said to have ascended to yoga.

Now he states the characteristic of one who has ascended to yoga: when a person does not become attached— that is, does not form an attachment— to the objects of the senses (the sense organs being the eyes and so forth, and their objects being sound, touch, form, taste, and smell), nor to the activities directed toward those objects.
Then, having renounced all volitions and abandoned every desire for fruits pertaining both to this world and the next,

he is said to be "one who has ascended to yoga. He alone is one who has ascended to yoga who, not engaging at all in actions that yield fruits of this world or the next, does not even mentally desire such things of small fruit.
This is the meaning. || 4 ||
One should uplift oneself by means of oneself; one should not allow oneself to sink into degradation. For the self alone is the friend of the self, and the self alone is the enemy of the self.

Having stated the characteristics of one who has ascended to yoga, the author here declares his duty: "He should protect himself from worldly existence and thereby attain the highest good. The reality of the Supreme Self, which shines within oneself in a hidden manner, is not realized by practitioners through mere knowledge alone or through mere action alone. [That which is] within oneself...

Having learned of the abiding of the Supreme Self from the presence of a living Guru, one employs the mind, senses, and so forth with faith for His service; only such a person is able to experience the Supreme Reality. Therefore, for the sake of knowing the Supreme Self, self-protection is essential. Consequently, one should not [neglect] oneself...
He should never let it reach the bottom nor cause it to fall; for both the uplifting of oneself and the destruction of oneself are within one's own hands.
The meaning is that [the self] exists [in this way]. He explains that very point with the words "the self alone" (ātmaiva).
For indeed, because the self alone is the friend of the self, other friends are merely related to the body and cannot truly be friends of the self.
In the same way, the self alone is its own enemy—that which is adverse to it. This is so if the self [does not recognize] the Supreme Self as its own true friend.

Only when one knows [the Self] will that very knowledge bring about one's own welfare; when one does not know the Self by oneself, then that very ignorance becomes adverse to oneself. Therefore, only he who reflects upon himself and strives according to the method taught by the Guru will be able to experience his own bliss. (5)
The self is the kinsman of that person by whom the self alone has been conquered by the self;
but for one who has not conquered the self, the self itself would behave as an enemy, like an actual foe.
The previously mentioned point is now explained: his own self (*ātman*) becomes a friend—that is, favorable—to himself.

When one employs the mind, senses, and so forth for the service of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) residing within them, then all those instruments become composed solely of the Supreme Self. Thus, through steadfastness in the inner self (*adhyātma*), there arises the happiness of the self.

That which one accomplishes becomes favorable to oneself; however, for one who is not the Self—that is, for one who does not personally practice self-restraint and so forth—the Self itself would behave like an enemy, as if toward an external foe, remaining in a state of enmity. Therefore, the meaning is that self-restraint is necessary for everyone. || 6 ||
For one who has conquered the self and is tranquil, the Supreme Self is fully composed amidst cold and heat, pleasure and pain, as well as honor and dishonor.

Here, the one who possesses self-restraint is described. In the stainless heart of the individual soul (jīva)—who has conquered the self, meaning whose internal organ (antaḥkaraṇa) is under its own control, and who is therefore tranquil and serene in mind—the Supreme Self (paramātman) is established and remains well-settled. The meaning is that the Supreme Self is experienced only by one whose heart is tranquil.

Alternatively, the construction may be: "The self (ātman) of the living being (jīva), whose nature (prakṛti) is under its own control, would become supremely (param) and exceedingly (atyantam) composed (samāhita) and well-established. The meaning is that his self is such a person (puruṣa). He would certainly not be subject to the transformations (vikāra) of cold and heat. When the embodied one (dehī), having purified the body, [remains] right there...
Then, with a stainless mind, one should dwell experiencing the bliss of the Self;
even upon perceiving the dualities of pleasure and pain, one should remain entirely free from modification. Such is the purity of the embodied soul.

The *Śaraṇagītā* describes life in this way: "If a row of snake fangs were torn out, a person would rejoice because of that very act; likewise, by the removal of the poison of sin, the embodied soul may dwell here without affliction."

If even a mother possessed by a demonic state does not protect her own child in this world, so too, a physical corruption that has arisen will not protect the life-force; this is the truth. O Guru Mallikārjuna, he alone who is graced by you within the body is truly blessed. Thus spoke the Blessed Goddess Akka Mahādevī regarding the purification of the body.

He establishes, through most powerful speech, the necessity of equanimity toward all beings so that all humans may attain liberation right here in this world— liberation that is dear to Śiva, purifying, and life-giving.
Through the perfect transformation of one's own nature, all practitioners shall likewise achieve spiritual progress.
All philosophers reveal this intention:

without spiritual development, no worldly person can attain peace. And that development must arise from within oneself. For one who experiences happiness and suffering every day, within just a few days—

A sense of equanimity toward these two indeed arises. For this very reason, even while dwelling in the midst of suffering, he—having attained discernment through the observation of suffering—spontaneously finds fortitude and clarity.
Thus, all those who possess experience declare that observing the defects of suffering in life is essential.
Rejoicing in that very intention, Kṛṣṇa here establishes the superiority of one who possesses equal-mindedness. || 7 ||
One whose self is satisfied with knowledge and realization, who is steadfast, whose senses are conquered,
and for whom a clod of earth, a stone, and gold are the same— he is called a yogi who is disciplined.

One whose self—the internal organ—is satisfied by both knowledge (*jñāna*) and realized wisdom (*vijñāna*); where "knowledge" is that produced from the scriptures, namely the knowledge of the Supreme Self and the knowledge of the phenomenal world which is its transformation, and "realized wisdom" is the bringing of those things known through scripture into the range of one's own direct experience; such is the person.

A human being who has attained discrimination through the knowledge of Śiva and through acquaintance with the phenomenal world (prapañca) composed of both consciousness (cit) and unconsciousness (acit), remains full of bliss even while immersed in suffering. Therefore, he is one who has conquered the senses—that is, one who has mastered all the senses—and does not pursue the objects of the senses. For this very reason, he is immovable (kūṭastha), unshakable, and free from modification.

He should dwell [thus]: regarding a clod of earth, a stone, and gold as equal; he who, perceiving clods, stones, and gold as the same, remains disciplined and concentrated—he alone is called a Śiva-yogin. (8)
One who possesses an equal mind toward friends, allies, enemies, neutrals, mediators, the hateful, and kinsmen— and even toward the virtuous and the sinful— is preeminent. (9)

A friend (*suhṛd*) is one who benefits others without regard for any return favor; a companion (*mitra*) is one with whom there is affection; an enemy (*ari*) is a foe; a neutral person (*udāsīna*) is one who is neither a friend nor an enemy; a mediator (*madhyastha*) is one who desires the welfare of both sides; a hateful person (*dveṣya*) is one who behaves disagreeably toward oneself; and a kinsman (*bandhu*) is one who is related by blood. And among these—

It has already been stated previously: "The wise look with an equal eye upon the virtuous who perform the actions prescribed by the scriptures and are habituated to good conduct, and even upon the sinful who disregard the scriptures—whether it be a learned scholar or an outcaste dog-cooker. Having perceived such pairs of opposites, such as pleasure and pain, which arise in accordance with one's past actions, [the wise remain equanimous].

Having understood the cause of diversity and remaining therein with a state free from modification, a person who perceives only the one uniform Supreme Self would exist as entirely distinct from all else. His very state is described in the world by the words, "I am a being in the worlds, yet I am not subject to worldly attributes. Such indeed is his abiding here.
This is the ultimate goal of human life; this alone is declared by the Blessed One to be the great fruition of yoga. || 9 ||
The yogi, staying in solitude, alone, with mind and self controlled, free from expectations and possessions, should constantly discipline the self. 10.

Having thus offered praise to one who has ascended to yoga, he now explains the method of yoga in detail: the yogi, performing the yoga of meditation, stays in a secluded place; even there, he remains alone and without companion, not requiring the assistance of others, with his mind and self restrained.

One whose mind, internal organ, self, and body are such [as described]; that is to say, one who employs the body, senses, and so forth according to their proper function; free from desire (*nirāśīḥ*), being devoid of thirst for external objects;

without possessions (*aparigrahaḥ*), being without the paraphernalia for comfort such as beds and seats; not seeking excessive pleasure, but content with whatever comes by chance (*yadṛcchā-lābha-santuṣṭaḥ*).
Having become thus, one should constantly engage oneself—that is, one should apply oneself to meditation (*dhyāna*) consisting of contemplation of the Lord dwelling within the inner self;
[one should contemplate] the abiding of the Supreme Self in the heart and direct the mind toward that very place.
If one conducts worldly affairs with that [the Lord] as witness, one's mind will not wander toward what is improper.

If the heart were to become turbid, then even though the Lord of Life resides therein, He would not be perceived at all. Therefore, those who possess direct experience declare that purity of heart must always be diligently guarded. With the heart...
The scripture, "He is fashioned by the mind with wisdom" (*maṇiṣā manasābhikḷptaḥ*), also teaches that the Supreme Self is to be known by one whose heart is stainless.
For this very reason, the Lord has prescribed here for all those who are thus striving: "Having established a firm seat for oneself in a clean place accessible to all... (*sthiram āsanam ātmanaḥ*).
Neither too high nor too low, covered with cloth, an antelope skin, and kusha grass.
Having made the mind one-pointed there, with the activities of the mind and senses restrained, one should sit upon a seat and practice yoga for the purification of the self. 12.

In a solitary place, in a clean and pure location, one should prepare for oneself a firm and immovable seat— neither too high nor excessively elevated, neither too low nor excessively sunken— covered with cloth, an antelope skin, and *kuśa* grass; "cloth" (*cela*) means a garment, "antelope skin" (*ajina*) means a black antelope hide, and "*kuśa*" refers to *darbha* grass.
After that, having had it prepared, consecrated, and established by them in due order, and having sat down upon that seat,

he should withdraw his mind from all objects of the senses and make it intent on that alone; thus, he whose activities of the mind and senses are restrained— meaning, whose functions of the mind and the senses are controlled and disciplined.

Such a person should practice yoga— that is, perform it— for the purification of the self, meaning for the sake of purifying the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*). Thus, having prepared a suitable seat in a solitary place, the practitioner, sitting there with a concentrated mind, [should focus] upon his own *prāṇaliṅga* all the sense organs and the mind.

Having entered into the various states of consciousness (*vṛtti*), the practitioner, purified by the initiation of Śiva (*śivadīkṣā*), should experience the Lord of Prāṇa through the observation of their characteristic signs. Having received his own Light from the Guru for external worship,
he should, by means of constant worship preceded by that observation, realize his own internal Light.
This is to be understood; this intention has been revealed in the passage, "of those who are constantly engaged [in practice].
Without external worship, the light residing within the heart would not be known. Without ritual action, [the fire] from wood...
Holding the body, head, and neck erect and motionless, remaining steady, gazing at the tip of his own nose and not looking toward the quarters; 13.
With a tranquil self, free from fear, established in the vow of celibacy,
having restrained the mind and fixing it on Me, let him sit disciplined, intent on Me as the Supreme Goal.

Regarding the question of how a yogi seated for the purpose of Śiva-pūjā should sit or what he should do—this method [is as follows]: here, because it is a compound of parts of a living being (*prāṇyaṅga*), the rule *dvandvaśca prāṇitūryasenāṅgānām* applies, resulting in the singular form. Having made them "even" (*samam*), meaning of one form, such that the body, head, and neck are in a state of equilibrium.
Having established [the body] in that manner, they should remain; likewise, holding it immovably and free from trembling,

the practitioner, becoming steady, should gaze at the tip of his own nose— having fixed his vision between the eyebrows— and place upon the palm of his hand his own chosen deity received through the grace of the Guru.
One should gaze with the eyes. Such observation of the *liṅga* alone is proclaimed as Śiva-yoga.

A practitioner of this Śiva-yoga, for the sake of facilitating practice, should at first—whenever opportunity permits—sit in a secluded place and, by gazing at the midpoint between the eyebrows, [should fix] the mind and the vital breath (*prāṇavāyu*) which follows it upon the gaze.

Through the immersion into the state of the living soul (*jīvabhāva*), the practitioner attains steadiness of mind. When this steady mind is absorbed into one's own chosen *liṅga*—which shines before the eyes upon the palm of the hand—then a great light is perceived within that *liṅga*, and it becomes one with the light residing in the heart. At that time:

Not perceiving the distinction between the internal and the external, the practitioner attains an intimate acquaintance with the Great Light in the form of the vital breath (prāṇa) through the touch of his own chosen *liṅga* throughout the body. This very experience of the *prāṇaliṅga* shines forth constantly in one who has ascended to yoga; however, by practitioners—

This experience is to be attained gradually through repeated practice. Their vision should be such that it does not wander elsewhere; thus, one should practice the worship of the *prāṇaliṅga*—which is the very form of one's own life-force, the size of a thumb, and situated right at one's own palm—in accordance with the *brahmasūtra*.

And it is prescribed in the Śruti: by means of this practice, the seeker, not looking here and there at the directions and not seeing them, becomes one whose inner organ (ātman) is thoroughly tranquil—that is, one whose internal faculty is intensely stilled. His mind—

(164) Through the grace of Śiva, he becomes serene. In this state, the practitioner— free from fear, devoid of dread, and having no cause for apprehension— remains established in the vow of a celibate student (*brahmacārin*), which is the vow of those who practice celibacy.

Abiding in the discipline of practicing alms-gathering and so forth, having restrained the mind— that is, having turned the mind away from other objects— one should be "mindful of Me" (*maccitta*), fixing the consciousness upon Me alone, who am present within as the supreme form of light in the *prāṇaliṅga*; and one should be "intent on Me" (*matpara*), regarding Me alone— the *prāṇaliṅga* itself— as the supreme goal to be attained.

One who is disciplined and established in such Śiva-yoga should remain thus. With the functions of his sight and mind concentrated in this way, and with a steady mind, he should experience the radiance of consciousness shining within himself at the very moment of gazing upon the *liṅga*. This method of worshipping Śiva is described in the Śaṅkarasaṃhitā as follows:

It is thus described by the great seer Vyāsa: "O dear one, he who, having placed his own chosen *liṅga* upon the seat of his hand, extends his mind and heart toward it, and whose soul is indifferent to the bustle of external activities—he is a Vīraśaiva. That practitioner who, upon the seat of his hand—[thinking] "This is my hand; this is the Blessed One"— (Note: The provided text fragment ends abruptly. The translation reflects the available portion.)

In the *Rudrādhyāya*, the term "Bhagavattara" (the most venerable) is heard; this usage of the word "Bhagavat" is intended to indicate that even the hand is worthy of worship because it is the locus of the *liṅga*. Upon such a hand-throne (*hastapīṭha*), one should install one's own chosen *liṅga*—one's own *prāṇaliṅga*, which is non-different from oneself—and [worship it] by constantly gazing upon it.

With his mental fluctuations stilled and remaining unattached to external activities, the practitioner, worshipping that beloved *iṣṭaliṅga* with faith and enthusiasm as if it were his own life-breath, shall behold his own inner light (*prakāśa*). Therefore, having placed this *iṣṭaliṅga*, which is graced by the Guru, in his hand for the purpose of worship—

Because it always protects the self from impurities and karma through constant reflection, it is conceived by those who possess direct experience as the *pāṇimantra* (the mantra held in the hand), and as the *pāvana* (the purifier) because it constantly purifies the practitioner. 13.
Thus, the yogi of restrained mind, ever-yoking the self in this manner...
He attains peace, which culminates in Nirvana and abides in Me. || 15 ||

Here, the fruit of the previously mentioned Śiva-yoga is revealed: the yogi, with a restrained mind and senses controlled, becomes absorbed through the *prāṇaliṅga* which shines as the nature of bliss; and he dissolves in a state of aesthetic oneness (*samarasatā*) through the *bhāvaliṅga*, which is the nature of existence (*sad-rūpa*) shining within the beloved [deity] situated between the eyebrows. This indeed is yoga here.

Thus it was indicated by the Supreme Soul, Kṛṣṇa. For such yoga, a human body is extremely difficult to obtain; indeed, this very body has been bestowed upon us by the Blessed Lord. Thus, for one established in yoga, that which stands before him— (p. 165) [is as follows].

The individual soul attains peace—which consists of the cessation of all [activity], which culminates in *nirvāṇa*, and which is *kaivalya* (isolation) consisting of union with Śiva; that is, such peace for which *kaivalya* is the ultimate goal. This kind of peace, which resides in Me, the Supreme Self—

"Existing" means being under one's own control; "he attains" that [state], meaning he reaches it. In this life, those practitioners would be able to live without contact with the bonds consisting of the three qualities (guṇas) when they, having abandoned the perception of internal and external duality, worship the external chosen *liṅga* through the contemplation of the vital breath (*prāṇa*).
A living being who has received the purificatory rite of Śiva-initiation (śivadīkṣā) prescribed for such worship,
and who proceeds with faith and devotion toward the worship of the Liṅga by means of the vision of offering everything to the Lord after first renouncing his own self-interest,
is considered a "devotee" (bhakta) by those who possess direct experience. It is precisely this devotee who, through the expansion of devotion...

Having attained a state free from conceit and having become one who is proximate to and beloved by the Lord residing in the heart, he is designated as a *māheśvara*. This very *māheśvara*, contemplating the entire phenomenal world as consisting of Śiva and becoming serene-minded through the vision of Śiva (*śivadṛṣṭi*), is called a *prasādī*. It is this same person who is the *prasādī*.

Sitting in a secluded place, having made one’s chosen *liṅga*—which is unmanifest in the space between the eyebrows and manifest upon the palm of the hand—one-pointed through the experience of it both externally and internally, one is called a *prāṇaliṅgin*.
It is this very *prāṇaliṅgin*, established in yoga (*yogārūḍha*), who is indicated here by the Blessed One. And thus:

The *prāṇaliṅgin*, having abandoned identification with the body and dwelling in a state of detachment, is able to experience the bliss of absolute liberation (*kaivalya*) within his very own body. Such an experience is to be accomplished through practice on the path of yoga alone; this indeed is the path ordained for the journey. Thus...
Apart from this path, the heart cannot be abandoned; apart from this, the experience of Śiva cannot be attained.

Apart from this sequence, peace cannot be obtained in any other way. Without peace, happiness cannot be experienced amidst suffering. By this very sequence, living beings [overcome] their own ignorance and doubt.
And they would be able to abandon the cultivation of perverted views.
Yoga is not for him who eats too much, nor for him who does not eat at all;
nor for him who is addicted to excessive sleep, nor for him who is ever wakeful, O Arjuna. (16)

In this context, he states the observances (*niyamas*) to be practiced by one devoted to *śivayoga*: "O Arjuna, for one who eats too much—that is, one who consumes excessively—yoga does not exist; it is not accomplished. Likewise, [for one who eats] too little...

Yoga is not accomplished even for one who does not eat; likewise, yoga does not take place for one whose habit is excessive sleep, even if he sleeps constantly. In the same way, even for a person who is always awake, if he exerts himself with an attentive mind while having abandoned the Lord residing in the heart, his Śivayoga is not accomplished. Only he [attains it].
The meaning is that one who is unable to endure restrictive observances (niyama) should practice yoga. || 16 ||
For one who is disciplined in diet and conduct, disciplined in actions,
and disciplined in sleep and wakefulness, yoga becomes the destroyer of suffering.

Regarding the question of what kind of person is capable of practicing yoga, he says: "of one who is regulated in diet and conduct. The meaning is that his [yoga] is "regulated," which is to say fixed or established. Such a person is one whose diet (*āhāra*)—meaning food—and conduct (*vihāra*)—meaning activities such as moving and stretching—are thus regulated. [This refers to] diet, conduct, and so forth.

The practitioner, employing [the means] according to the established rule, should practice Śiva-yoga; even while performing actions, he should be one whose efforts are disciplined and whose activities are limited—the meaning being that he does not cause affliction to the body.
For one who performs actions that cause excessive exertion, however, Śiva-yoga [is hindered] by physical fatigue.
It becomes fruitless. Therefore, even worldly activities (*vyavahāra*) should be carried out according to one's capacity.
For one who possesses proper understanding of sleep and wakefulness, and who observes fixed measures for both sleeping and waking, there is yoga;
he becomes a destroyer of suffering (*duḥkhahā*), meaning he destroys all sufferings and becomes the annihilator of all pain.

And thus, only he who has regulated his food and conduct, as well as his sleep and wakefulness, is capable of following the path of yoga by means of the vision that unifies renunciation and enjoyment.
This applies equally to one who is excessively sleepy or excessively wakeful, to one who is an excessive enjoyer or a non-enjoyer, and likewise to one who is excessively active in worldly affairs.
One is not capable of practicing yoga. || 17 ||
When the disciplined mind abides in the Self alone, free from longing for all desires, then one is said to be "yoked" (in yoga). 18.

When the mind is thus specifically restrained, controlled, and established in such a manner— free from the onset of agitation and fixed in its own natural state— and when it becomes favorable to the Self, then it becomes detached from all desires pertaining to this world and the next; the mind [becomes one] with the Supreme Self.

The contracted power consisting of the three *guṇas*, which is the very Supreme Power (*parā-śakti*) of the consciousness-power (*cit-śakti*) whose nature is *prāṇa* at the stage of culmination (*niṣṭhā*), is indeed this [power].
Consciousness-power (*cic-chakti*) is of the nature of sentience and consists of *sattva*, *cit*, and *ānanda*; however, the mental power (*citta-śakti*) is insentient by nature.

It consists of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*. This alone is the distinction between the two. If the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) is characterized by the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*), then the individual self (*jīvātman*), as its part, exists as characterized by the power of the mind (*cittaśakti*). Through the continuous contemplation, concentration, and worship of the Supreme Self, this very power of the mind of the individual self becomes, by way of being *sat-cit-ānanda* (existence-consciousness-bliss).

It undergoes transformation. This very expansion of power (*śaktivikāsa*) is to be accomplished through practice; it is only then that the individual soul (*jīva*) is called a true devotee (*sad-bhakta*). He who was distinct from Śiva during the state of the contraction of power becomes non-different from Śiva through the expansion of power. This alone is *śivayoga*, which is [to be pursued] by all.

This must necessarily be accomplished by practitioners through the continuous establishment of union with Śiva; otherwise, even though the individual soul (*jīva*) is a portion of Śiva, it remains distinct from Śiva and, falling under the sway of the power of the mind (*citta-śakti*), undergoes universal wandering within the cycle of birth and death. Therefore, all practitioners, in conjunction with the body and the senses...

The Blessed One expects that people should strive to attain union with Paramaśiva, who shines within their own inner self; for no happiness greater than the bliss of the Self is to be found anywhere. It is the intention of the Blessed One that all worldly activity is undertaken solely for the sake of attaining the bliss of the Self. This is understood by everyone.
It should be understood. || 17 ||
As a lamp standing in a windless place does not flicker—this is the simile taught for the yogi of restrained mind who practices the yoga of the Self. 19.

He provides an illustration of such a Śiva-yogin: just as a lamp situated in a windless place— that is, existing in a region devoid of wind— does not flicker or move, so too is that radiance of the Self for one who practices yoga with Śiva,
achieving identity with Him, and whose mind is restrained, meaning whose internal organ is fully controlled.

The simile for the Śiva-yogin is recorded as follows: just as a lamp shines when it is motionless, so too the yogin devoted to the meditation on Śiva makes his gaze motionless, merged in a state of equanimity (*samarasa*) upon the chosen *liṅga* located between the eyebrows, and likewise upon the chosen *liṅga* in the palm of the hand which is in the form of that [inner *liṅga*]. He who always [meditates] through the contemplation of Śiva...

By cultivating equanimity toward pleasure and pain, and by considering every worldly activity as his own duty from the perspective of the body, he carries them out; his mind, through its innate nature, becomes established in its own divine essence.
The remembrance of Śiva alone is the cause for the restraint of the mind; indeed, it is the restraint of the mind itself.
p.
168) The practice of Śiva-yoga—all of this is accomplished by the individual soul through association with the virtuous.
Where the mind, restrained through the practice of yoga, comes to rest;
and where, beholding the Self by means of the self, one finds satisfaction within the Self. (20)
That absolute bliss which is perceivable by the intellect and beyond the senses—he who knows it, and being established therein, does not deviate from reality; || 21 ||
Having obtained which, one considers no other gain to be superior to it;
established in which, one is not shaken even by heavy suffering. (22)
One should know that to be the severance of the union with suffering, designated as yoga.
That yoga must be practiced with determination by one whose mind is free from despondency. 23.
He states the essential nature of the attainment of such Śiva-yoga:

by the practice of yoga—that is, through the cultivation of Śiva-yoga and the constant contemplation of Śiva—the internal organ (citta) becomes restrained, having turned away from sense objects; when it reaches that state in which it comes to rest, attaining cessation.

And in that state, seeing the Self by means of the self— that is, by the internal organ— the yogi experiences the divine light of Śiva, who is of the nature of consciousness; he finds contentment and attains satisfaction within the Self alone,
which is graspable by the intellect through the intellect itself, when it is stainless and tranquil.

It is to be grasped solely by the intellect and not by the senses; therefore, it is beyond the senses (*atīndriya*). It is absolute bliss, whose very nature is limitless happiness. In that state, established in which the yogi knows—realizes—the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), who is the true essence of reality from which this yogi, remaining therein, [knows] in truth.

The meaning is that once this has been experienced, one never wavers nor ever falls away, and one never again encounters instability. Having attained and experienced this vision of the Self, one considers no other gain to be superior to it; one knows that there is nothing else to be obtained beyond it.

One should know that state of separation from the conjunction with suffering—which is designated by the term "yoga"—to be that reality of the Self (ātmatattva) established in which the yogi is not shaken, nor does he waver, even by great pain characterized by the falling of weapons and the like. Here, "conjunction with suffering" refers to the experience of suffering; "separation from that" is what is called by the name "yoga."
One should know this: such a Śivayoga must necessarily be practiced and performed with a mind characterized by *nirveda*—
that is,
with a mind accompanied by world-weariness— even for the duration of a single moment, so that the fruit may be attained.

Śiva-yoga is to be practiced; however, it is achievable only through uninterrupted practice. Even an ant that moves toward Mount Meru may eventually succeed in accomplishing its own welfare. He alone who attains union with Śiva, who shines resplendent within the heart, becomes blessed, happy, wise, and proficient.

If he were not [to possess it], all his unsurpassed worldly glory would become as useless as flowers in a cremation ground. Therefore, without allowing any room for world-weariness (*nirveda*), the practitioner should remain ever-yoked even in all worldly activities—whether walking, standing, eating, or sleeping; such is the teaching of the Blessed One.
Regarding the disposition (*āśaya*): to achieve that, not only continuity is necessary, but also certainty regarding the Self (*ātman*) is essential.

Only the living being (*jīva*), having become one with the Self, is capable of accomplishing and experiencing union with the Supreme Self (*paramātman*). Indeed, that which is not the Self cannot attain the experience of the Supreme Self. However, he who...

He experiences the bliss of the Self; even non-self entities such as the body and so forth, through the proximity of the Self, he perceives as being exactly like the Self. To him, everything appears as the Self alone.
That light of the heart is experienced by that yogi at all times and in all states.

If the Śiva-yogin perceives gross, external form, which belongs to the realm of phenomenal expansion (prapañca), he perceives only the subtle, internal light of consciousness (citprakāśa). This alone is the distinction between the two. Thus has the nature of meditative yoga (dhyānayoga) been described by the Blessed One. 23.
Having abandoned all desires born of mental construction without exception, and having restrained the entire collection of senses on all sides by the mind alone, [one should dwell in solitude]. (24)
Gradually, by means of the intellect held with firmness, one should bring the mind to rest within the Self and not think of anything at all. (25)

Furthermore, instruction is given once more out of an exceeding regard for that very Śiva-yoga: having abandoned entirely—that is, completely—all those things arising from volition, such as the desire for sense-objects produced by volition, which is mental action (mānasaṃ karma); thus, not thinking of any external object of enjoyment even in the slightest degree with the mind. In this way, of the mind—

When it has been established that [the mind] is devoid of activity, by means of that very mind one should thoroughly restrain— that is, completely suppress— the collection of senses, such as the eyes and other organs, through *dhṛti*, which is to say, through fortitude held fast by resolve.

By means of the reasoning grasped by the intellect and with firm resolve, one should gradually and step by step attain cessation—that is, bring about stillness. Furthermore, having made the mind—the internal organ—established in the Self, meaning focused solely on the Self as its object, one should not think of anything else whatsoever. Thus the practitioner.

Having made the intellect serene through mental resolve, being content with whatever is obtained, and having completely restrained delusion regarding sense objects through the power of association with the virtuous, one should gradually attain cessation. Having become tranquil, self-controlled, ceased from worldly activity, patient, and concentrated, one should contemplate the Self within the self.

Thus indeed the Blessed Śruti also speaks. In this way, the intention of the Blessed One—that cessation must necessarily be accomplished—is to be constantly remembered by those who desire spiritual growth. || 25 ||
From whatever cause the restless and unsteady mind wanders away, from that very cause one should restrain it and bring it under control within the Self alone. 26.
The mind is restless by its very nature, fickle, and unstable; it does not remain anywhere by its innate disposition.

From whatever cause, from whichever object, it issues forth and goes outward, and thus does not come under control—from each and every such cause, one should restrain this mind, arrest it through the power of discrimination, and bring it under the sway of the Self alone.

Just as the mind should contemplate the nature of the Supreme Self alone, so should it bring about its own conformity to that [Self]. Only through the assistance of the mind can the union between the individual self (jīvātman) and the Supreme Self (paramātman) be perfectly accomplished.
Therefore, the Lord teaches here the restraint of the mind, which is free from the defects of impurity.
For supreme happiness comes to this yogi whose mind is tranquil, whose passion has been stilled, who has become one with Brahman, and who is free from blemish. (27)

Here, the fruit of the previously mentioned Śiva-yoga is indicated: the yogin whose mind is tranquil, who is pacified—meaning one in whom the qualities of *rajas* (passion) and *tamas* (darkness) have subsided—and who is thus stainless, has become Brahman, having attained oneness with Supreme Śiva; such a one is supreme, unsurpassed, and unlike anything experienced elsewhere in the world.
One attains and reaches supreme bliss (*paramānanda*). There is no reality anywhere superior to the bliss of union with Śiva.
Only the most excellent practitioners obtain such bliss within their own pure hearts through a stainless mind. || 27 ||
Thus constantly disciplining the self, the yogi, freed from all taint, easily attains the infinite bliss that consists in contact with Brahman. (28)
It is stated here that even within such bliss there is a gradation corresponding to the degree of practice;

thus, the yogi, constantly and uninterruptedly practicing yoga by uniting the self in the manner described, becomes free from stain— that is, free from all evil in the form of the fetters of impurity— and attains bliss without effort.

He enjoys—that is, he attains—the bliss of liberation, which is the supreme happiness consisting in the experience of Paraśiva-Brahman; it is the touch of Brahman, producing a state of aesthetic oneness (sāmarasya) with Brahman. || 28 ||
One whose self is disciplined by yoga sees the Self abiding in all beings and all beings in the Self; he perceives the same everywhere with equal vision. || 29 ||
Here, the fruit of such maturation of yoga is pointed out: one who is disciplined in yoga perceives the Self— which exists within all beings,
residing in all creatures by remaining untainted and unmanifest— as being in the Self, that is, within oneself, as well as all beings, the entire multitude of living creatures, within the Self.

One whose mind—the internal organ—is thus engaged in yoga, which consists of the state of *sāmarasya* (essential identity) with Śiva, and who likewise possesses equal vision toward all beings mentioned everywhere—that is, seeing the oneness of Brahman and the Self everywhere—is a Śiva-yogin. All knowers of Śiva likewise perceive only the radiance of Śiva everywhere; therefore—
The proclamation by those great seers, the Śiva-yogins, that through a single consciousness all consciousness is realized, shines forth.

He who first perceives the Supreme Self shining within his own heart through the practice of yoga, perceives that very Great Light everywhere. [This occurs] when the impurities of karma and *mala* have been destroyed.
The knower of the Self always remains devoted solely to the vision of the Self. The Blessed One observes that through such yoga, all people in the world should abide [in this manner]. || 29 ||
He who sees Me everywhere and sees everything in Me—for him I am not lost, and he is not lost to Me. (30)
Today, He points out the fruit of such a vision of the oneness of the Self: that aforementioned yogi who perceives Me,
the Supreme Self, everywhere, and likewise perceives the entire universe within Me alone, the Supreme Self.

I never bring about the state of invisibility—that sense of being beyond perception rooted in the meaning of the verbal root *naś* (to disappear/not seeing)—for that Śiva-yogin who perceives such oneness with Myself, thinking "I shall never perish. Likewise, he too does not perish; indeed, he does not become invisible. He...

He always beholds me, and I also always behold him. He who gratifies all for my sake shall never meet with destruction. To the wise, the various objects existing in the world—such as women, gold, and the like—even when perceived, appear as nothing but the single radiance of the Supreme Self.
They see it everywhere. The *Śaraṇagītā* describes the holy life of Basavārya as follows:

"Whatever I behold, that alone my mind constantly remembers"—this is his thought. "O Kūḍalasaṅgamārya, let there be no pride in you or in your attendants regarding my conduct; [let there be no pride] regarding other women."
"It is my firm conviction that they are the very forms of Śarva’s consort.
This certainty within themselves even now awakens us moderns to the vision of the inner self (*adhyātma-darśana*):
"He who, established in unity, worships Me as abiding in all beings..."
In every way, even while acting, that yogin abides in me.

That yogi, possessing the experience of Śiva and perfected in the yoga of Śiva, established in oneness with Śiva and knowing correctly Me— the Supreme Self— exists within all beings among the multitude of living creatures; that yogi worships and serves Me, the Supreme Self, existing in all beings, regardless of his mode of conduct in every respect.

Even while remaining in this very world, he dwells in the Supreme Self alone; his mind is perpetually immersed in the Supreme Self. Regarding his state of equanimity toward all things and his vision of the self as the sole reality, the *Śaraṇagītā* describes it thus:
"In the midst of the village, only one ground is seen—the dwelling of Śiva and the dwelling of the outcaste."

"The land of the twice-born is outside the village, and the land of the outcaste is likewise; does such a distinction exist for a person who has seen you everywhere? Indeed, there is only a difference in names arising from a difference in concealment;
at the time of its destruction, there is no distinction between the internal and the external—thus should one contemplate everywhere."

"Behold Your glory! Thus, perceiving the Supreme Self alone—which exists in reality as untainted within all categories of things, whether pure or impure—the seekers (śaraṇāḥ) develop that very same vision even toward human beings. Such great souls and women [behave in this manner].

Born solely for the welfare of the world, always beholding the Lord of the World everywhere in the world and dwelling in constant peace, they seek to perceive the Supreme Self alone as the universal commonality even within ordinary living beings.
They awaken.
He who, by comparison with himself, sees equality everywhere—whether it be happiness or suffering, O Arjuna—that yogi is considered the highest. 32.

This establishes the supreme excellence of such a yogi alone. Thus, because the contemplation of the oneness of the Self exists everywhere, for the Śiva-yogi, by way of analogy with oneself— that is, through self-similarity—
there is both happiness and likewise suffering in all beings everywhere.

He who sees and knows the happiness of all as his own happiness, and the suffering of all as his own suffering— at that very moment, O Arjuna, that yogi alone is considered and esteemed as the supreme, the most excellent among all. This applies to those who cultivate a vision of equality toward all human beings.

The life of Śiva-yogins is thus described in the *Śaraṇagītā* as being like a mirror: "Without the union of the *bindu*, there is no [union] of passion; and just as water droplets fall alike, so too are objects such as hope and meat alike. What fruit could come from merely hearing or reading [the scriptures]? The body is composed of the seven constituent elements (*dhātu*)."
What is the purpose of the castes (varṇas) born from improper origins, produced from the self and the life-principle?

By heating iron himself, one becomes known as an iron-smith; by washing clothes, a washerman; and by weaving thread, a weaver. But by reciting the Veda, one becomes a twice-born (dvija). Who here is truly "born from the ear"?

For it is established that in this world all things are born from a source (yoni). Only he who recognizes the *liṅga* shining brilliantly within the body is truly fortunate. Thus, through the principle of vast realization, those who have taken refuge perceive only Śiva everywhere in the world, even among us who possess diverse natures.

They generate that very same perspective of self-identification (*ātmaupamya*). People say that among all visible objects in the world, it is the beautiful woman alone who causes delusion for everyone because of her lovely form. Discerning the true nature of such a woman, the Śaraṇas [correctly] [view] all human beings as well.

They awaken [the world]. Their practice of equanimity regarding women serves as a guide for all modern people. If their immortal speech were to shine forever within the minds of the youth, then this earth would become heaven. Their divine voice shines thus: "Himself..."

"In former times, that woman, having ascended and remained upon the head of the Self-born (Brahmā), likewise approached his creation and formerly sported within the heart of Hari as Lakṣmī. Therefore, she is not merely a woman, nor even a Rākṣasī, but rather his supreme Śakti. Thus it is said regarding a woman who is patient by nature.

The contemplation of the Supreme Power (parāśakti) is conducive to the highest good and brings happiness specifically to the class of human beings. Thus, among those [powers] pervading the universe...

The Blessed One instructs, with words of even greater vigor, that everyone should practice the vision of self-similarity (ātmaupamya-dṛṣṭi), so that the mind may not become attached to land, gold, women, and the like, and instead remain toward those very things with equanimity, becoming colored only by the light of the Supreme Self. 32.

Although such Śiva-yoga possesses an excellent fruit, Arjuna, considering it impossible to perform, asks with the intention of [inquiring] what the means therein might be, since there would be no benefit from being instructed in a reality that is impossible to achieve: [Arjuna said: "O mighty-armed one, this yoga which You have spoken of as so difficult to master—by what means, O Keśava, can one attain perfection in it?
