(Gītā 12.5) The meaning is as follows: "O mighty-armed one, this yoga which You have described as so difficult to master—that is, as exceedingly hard to accomplish—even by those who strive for it—by what means, O Keśava, can one attain perfection in it? By what means does one succeed in it? Thus he asks. (Gītā-bhāṣya 12.5) Alternatively, the meaning is: "By what means, O Keśava, can one attain perfection in it? That is to say, by what means does one succeed in it? Thus he asks. (Gītā-bhāṣya-vivaraṇa 12.5) Or again, the meaning is: "By what means, O Keśava, can one attain perfection in it? That is to say, by what means does one succeed in it? Thus he asks. (Gītā-bhāṣya-ṭīkā 12.5) Or yet again, the meaning is: "By what means, O Keśava, can one attain perfection in it? That is to say, by what means does one succeed in it? Thus he asks. (Gītā-bhāṣya-ṭippaṇī 12.5) Or further, the meaning is: "By what means, O Keśava, can one attain perfection in it? That is to say, by what means does one succeed in it? Thus he asks. (Gītā-bhāṣya-ṭīkā-saṃgraha 12.5) Or finally, the meaning is: "By what means, O Keśava, can one attain perfection in it? That is to say, by what means does one succeed in it? Thus he asks. (Gītā-bhāṣya-ṭīkā-vivaraṇa 12.5) Thus, having considered that even though such Śiva-yoga has an excellent fruit, it is impossible to perform, and fearing that there would be no gain from an instruction on a reality that cannot be accomplished, he asks: "What is the means in that regard? (Śiva-yoga-prakaraṇa-vivaraṇa)
O Madhusūdana, regarding this yoga of equanimity which has been taught by you, I do not perceive its steady persistence because of the mind's restlessness. (33)

Arjuna said: O Madhusūdana Kṛṣṇa, regarding this yoga characterized by equanimity—that state of mental poise toward all—which has now been proclaimed and taught by you, I do not perceive its attainment due to the instability of the mind. Indeed, it is the mind alone that is unsteady for me.

I am not capable of knowing or practicing yoga; such a wretched state has come upon me because of the mind's inherent restlessness. I do not see a steady, unmoving state for this trivial mind of mine. If this mind were stable, then...
"This instruction of yours will surely bear fruit. In this way, Arjuna, like an ordinary man, makes clear his own weakness. || 33 ||
For the mind, O Kṛṣṇa, is restless, turbulent, powerful, and obstinate;
I consider its restraint to be as difficult as that of the wind. (34)

Here too, [the Lord] further elucidates the restlessness of the mind: "O Kṛṣṇa, my mind—indeed, it is well known that the mind is by its very nature restless and fickle. However, my mind is not only restless by nature, but moreover, it is *pramāthin*, meaning it is habitually turbulent, having overwhelmed the senses such as the eyes."

And it is capable of bringing others under its own control; it is able to subjugate the powerful group of senses and bring them under its own authority. This mind of mine, being thus powerful, cannot be easily restrained. Not only is it powerful, but it is also firm, like an elephant bound by a lotus fiber.
It is possible to bind it; however, I consider the restraint or suppression of such a being to be as extremely difficult and exceedingly hard to accomplish as [the binding] of the wind. Therefore, p.

"Who is capable of practicing the yoga taught by you? Or rather, what means exists for the restraint of the mind? If such a means exists, may you instruct me in it," thus Arjuna entreated Kṛṣṇa. || 34 ||
Without doubt, O mighty-armed one, the mind is restless and difficult to restrain;
yet, O son of Kuntī, it is brought under control through practice and dispassion. (35)

Having thus accepted what was said by Arjuna, the Blessed One spoke this reply to him: "O mighty-armed Arjuna, there is indeed no doubt regarding the matter you have stated. It is true that the mind is restless, fickle, and difficult to restrain—that is, impossible to subdue. In this regard, there is no disagreement among anyone."

This subject is accepted by all; however, O Kaunteya, O Arjuna, this mind is restrained and bound through practice and dispassion. And thus, as long as there remains a longing for sense objects within the mind, the conquest of the mind is simply impossible. Of the mind—

The state of being objectless must now be established. When one contemplates that even worldly objects are to be employed for the sake of pleasing the Supreme Self, then the mind becomes attached solely to the Supreme Self, which is the Great Object. The Supreme Self, however, is formless and consists of existence, consciousness, and bliss (*saccidānanda*).
When the mind, though attached to that [world], delights in abiding in the formless state, it becomes composed of existence, consciousness, and bliss (*saccidānanda*).

Whatever object the mind contemplates incessantly, it attains a form corresponding to that very thing. Through contemplation of worldly objects, it becomes mundane; through contemplation of the Lord, it becomes divine.
It becomes ultimate. For this very reason, the wise represent the mind as both a cuckoo and a parrot. The *Śaraṇagītā* thus describes the method for those seeking refuge to restrain the mind:
"O noble one who has attained the company of the venerable Guru, listen to this cry of distress from the parrot that is the mind; it is being tormented."

"Afflicted by the disease of existence and suffering, he wanders here and there due to deluded vision. Having confined him within the cage of devotion to Śiva, feed him divine nectar out of a fatherly disposition. Act with compassion in such a way that he may now utter the word 'Śiva. Thus, those who have taken refuge [should place him] within the cage of devotion to Śiva."

Restraining this mind and employing it for the service of this world which is composed of Śiva, they place before them a divine ideal for the welfare of the world with a gentle heart, so that all people, both renunciants and worldly ones alike, might act in the same way. || 35 ||
(176) Yoga is difficult to attain by one whose self is uncontrolled; this is my conviction.
But by one whose self is controlled and who strives, it can be attained through the proper means. 36.
For one whose self is uncontrolled—that is, for one who has not conquered the mind through practice and dispassion—the yoga described is difficult to attain;

indeed, it is impossible to achieve, according to my opinion and final conclusion. But by one whose self is controlled—that is, by one who has conquered the mind—through effort, meaning by exerting oneself by means of the methods such as dispassion already mentioned, yoga can be attained.

By conquering the mind alone, the practitioner shall attain progress in the field of the inner self (*adhyātma*). For those who have realized Śiva declare that the mind is the primary support for *māyā-śakti*, which creates all forms. While many consider women, gold, and the like to be *māyā*, the *śaraṇas* [hold a different view].

They imagine the very hope of the mind to be an illusion; therefore, the learned say that if the mind should find delight in Mahādeva, the Great Object, then it would become Mahādeva himself. The Śaraṇas proclaim an easy means for conquering this illusory mind. Basavārya, the foremost among the Śaraṇas, speaks thus:

O noble Gurukūḍala, your māyā envelops the entire world on all sides; likewise, it spreads around you. Yet, this mind of mine is struck with wonder here: if you, O Lord, are indeed the master of the universe, then I am here merely as your plaything. Just as an elephant dissolves into a mirror, so too do you [dissolve] today.

"You dwell within me. Having thus clarified the abiding of the Supreme Self (Paramātman) in the mind of Basavārya, he points out that contemplation of that very Self is the cause for conquering the mind. All philosophers maintain that the constant remembrance of the Supreme Self residing in the heart is the sole means for warding off all maladies.

The formless mind is never satisfied by the remembrance of that which possesses form; rather, it is through the contemplation of the formless Lord alone, and by the experience of oneness with Him, that the mind finds contentment. The wise declare that the Supreme Lord Himself—who is reckoned as the most excellent in all the world—enters the stainless heart of the true devotee.
The *Śaraṇagītā* thus describes the greatness of the true devotee who has become the dwelling place of the Supreme Self:
"Is it a cloud? No, for it is dissolved upon the earth.
Is the earth a cloud? That is not possible, for it rests upon the head of a serpent. [The serpent...]"

Is the cloud dense? That is not fitting, for does the Naga indeed support Umā? Is Umā dense? That too is not fitting, for she is seated upon the portion intended for Śiva. Is Śiva dense? That cannot be, for he remains in union with Āryā.
"Indeed,
for one who is solely devoted to you, the light of your majesty resides within the region of the heart. Thus, in the company of true devotees.

The Blessed One teaches that the perfection of yoga is possible only for the practitioner who has conquered the mind, with the intention that if the seeker, remaining steady, contemplates true reality in his mind at every step by listening to the teachings on the True Object, then the restraint of the mind will become easy to achieve. 36.

When the Blessed One has thus established that the conquest of the mind is exceedingly difficult to achieve through effort, Arjuna asks: what would be the fate of someone who, having set out to practice yoga, should at some point fall away from it due to such instability of the mind?
One who possesses faith and is intent on the future, but whose mind wavers from yoga—failing to attain perfection in yoga, O Kṛṣṇa, what goal does he go to? (37)

Arjuna said: O Kṛṣṇa, although it is taught that yoga is to be accomplished through faith, even a person endowed with faith who lacks self-restraint—due to mental unsteadiness and the failure to perform practice and the like—is unable to exert the appropriate effort; being thus lacking in the power to practice, he is unable to attain the perfection of yoga, which is the fruit of yoga.
Not attaining such [a state], what destination does the practitioner reach while failing to attain it? What is his subsequent destination? This is the purport of Arjuna’s question. || 37 ||
O mighty-armed one, I fear that he who is without support and bewildered on the path of Brahman might perish like a scattered cloud, having fallen away from both.

He himself explains the intent of his own question: "O mighty-armed Kṛṣṇa, that deluded person—characterized by confusion regarding sense objects—is without support, being devoid of a firm foundation on the path of Brahman at the time of attaining union with Supreme Śiva due to having fallen from yoga; yet, through the grace of the Supreme Self, he does not fall into a miserable state in this world."

Like a fragment of cloud in the sky, does he not perish? Does he not meet with destruction? If a person established in yoga should ever fall from yoga, then even though he has fallen away from the yoga of Śiva, would he also have fallen away from the path of action conducive to the enjoyment of sense-objects in this world? [He has not fallen] from yoga.

Indeed, many always remain clinging solely to the path of worldly enjoyment; regarding them, there is nothing at all to be said. But as for those who are devoted to the path of yoga, even if they should fall away from yoga—
"Would they not always resort even to the path of enjoyment in another birth?
Arjuna became curious to know whether one who has fallen from yoga would be fallen from both. || 38 ||
O Kṛṣṇa, you ought to sever this doubt of mine completely;
for no one other than you is capable of being the dispeller of this doubt. (39)
O Kṛṣṇa, you ought to sever—that is, resolve—this doubt of mine entirely and completely;
for there can be no one other than you, distinct from you, who is capable of being the seizer or resolver of this great doubt. Who else is there, another like you, who possesses such knowledge?
There is truly no one else who brings me greater benefit than you; therefore, this doubt of mine must be dispelled by you alone.
O Pārtha, neither in this world nor in the next does destruction exist for him;
for no one who performs good deeds, my dear, ever goes to a miserable state. 40.

Thus questioned, the Blessed Lord said: "O Pārtha Arjuna, for such a person whose mind has been shaken from yoga—even for one fallen from yoga—there is no destruction (vināśa), as you have described it, either in this world or in the next world; destruction, that is to say,"

Even for one currently existing in a high birth, the attainment of a low birth might occur; yet even that shall not happen for him. Why? To this he says: "Not indeed," O Tāta Arjuna. No person whatsoever who performs auspicious deeds—that is, one who performs virtuous actions—goes to a miserable state or a low condition; such a one is never destined to attain it.
Those who experience both [good and bad] fruits maintain that the very effort made for the sake of attaining one's own welfare is itself a virtuous deed (*śubhakarma*).

Even if one engaged in such a virtuous deed should at some point become a victim of the crooked gaze of *māyā* and fall away from that virtuous deed, he will still certainly not experience an inauspicious fruit.
One shall obtain [it]. || 40 ||
Having attained the worlds of those who perform meritorious deeds and having dwelt there for countless years, he who has fallen from yoga is born again in the home of the pure and the prosperous.

To the question, "What will become of one who has fallen from yoga? he says: One who has fallen from yoga—that is, one who has strayed from the yoga of Śiva—having reached the worlds of the doers of meritorious deeds, such as the great men who perform great merits like the Aśvamedha sacrifice, namely the heavens and so forth, and having dwelt there for many eternal years—that is, many years—he [returns]. Dwelling...
Immediately after performing [the rite],
he should [place it] in the house of those who are pure, whose souls are completely purified, who are illustrious, and distinguished by unsurpassed sovereignty.
"In the family" means in the lineage. "He is born" means he obtains rebirth.
And thus, when worldly or otherworldly happiness is to be attained, only excellence is seen for him; it is said that only the attainment of superior results is possible for him. || 41 ||
Or else, one is born into a family of wise yogis;
for such a birth as this is indeed more difficult to obtain in the world.

He states that for those who have fallen from yoga, even the attainment of a superior birth may occur compared to merely attaining birth in a family of the illustrious (*śrīmat*). Alternatively, even if he is not born into a family of the illustrious— that is, into a family filled with prosperity— he is born into the family of the wise (*dhīmat*), of discerning yogis, as one who has fallen from yoga.

Such a birth occurs only in the family of those perfected in yoga; this is exceedingly rare in the world, even more difficult to attain than anything else. Even for one who has fallen from yoga, an excellent birth is possible. Therefore, human beings should be solely devoted to yoga. Those who rely on the path of enjoyment are always intent upon their own self-interest.

Through the vision of delusion, they forget their own fundamental Self, the Supreme Soul; for them, a downward descent is inevitable. Those devoted to the path of Yoga, however, being exceedingly dear to the Supreme Lord, the foremost of Yogis, have attained the designation of *Māheśvara* and [attain] the supreme bliss and peace of *Haha*.

For them, happiness shall indeed be found both in this world and the next. Thus, the Lord commands that all practitioners, having become auspicious in nature, should strive with all their power and according to their intelligence for union with Śiva. 42.
There he regains that same mental disposition belonging to his previous body;
from that point, O descendant of Kuru, he strives even more for perfection.
He describes the distinction regarding the birth of one who has fallen from yoga in such an exalted family:

"O Pārtha, descendant of Kuru, in that family, that one who has fallen from yoga obtains such a connection with intelligence— that is, the state of possessing correct understanding— which was acquired in a previous body, belonging to his former life."

One attains [this] precisely through the power of co-residence (*sahavāsa*). And thus, even for one who has fallen from yoga, the yoga previously performed continues to exist in the form of a latent impression (*saṃskāra*). By means of that impression— (p.

He attains a distinguished birth in another life; in that birth, the latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) from his previous life become awakened. For that reason, he strives once again for perfection—that is, he indeed makes an effort for the sake of the attainment of yoga. Thus, there is no loss of the auspicious yoga performed even once.
The meaning is that it might possibly occur at some time. || 43 ||
By that very same previous practice, he is indeed carried forward even against his will;
even one who merely desires to know yoga transcends the Word-Brahman (Śabdabrahman).
That one who has fallen from yoga, having been born into a family of yogis, by that very same practice of his former birth becomes a yogi once again.
Even he who has fallen from yoga, though merely desiring to know yoga— that is, wishing to understand the true nature of yoga—
by virtue of his past impressions transcends the Śabdabrahman, the entire collection of ritual acts prescribed in the Vedas.
He remains on the very path of Śiva-yoga; by that alone, his yoga becomes easily accomplished—this is the meaning. || 44 ||
But the yogi who strives with effort, having his impurities completely cleansed and perfected through many births, thereafter attains the supreme goal. (45)
If yoga were easily attainable even for one who merely desires it, then a yogi—

who exerts effort and applies intense endeavor toward the practice of yoga— would become purified; that yogi, through the accumulation of latent impressions (*saṃskāra*) born from some slight practice over many lifetimes, would have attained perfection in the yoga of Śiva.
As the fruit of that, one attains the supreme goal, which is liberation in the form of union with Śiva. || 45 ||
The yogi is superior to the ascetics, and he is considered superior even to the men of knowledge;
the yogi is also superior to the performers of ritual action. Therefore, O Arjuna, become a yogi.

This establishes the superiority of the Śiva-yogin over all others. Even compared to ascetics (tapasvin) who are devoted to austerity, the yogin devoted to Śiva-yoga is superior and more excellent. Even compared to those possessed of knowledge—that is, those possessing the scholarly erudition born of the scriptures—the yogin is considered and recognized as superior and more excellent.

O Arjuna, compared to those performers of rituals— those who perform rites such as the Agnihotra while remaining ignorant of the true nature of Śiva and being devoted solely to ritual action— the yogi who has attained identity-in-essence (*sāmarasya*) with Śiva possesses a superior and more excellent perfection of yoga.

Therefore, for that reason, you too, O yogi, become established in yoga. In this way, under the pretext of addressing Arjuna, [the Lord instructs] all worldly people to dwell in the world only by uniting themselves with the Lord who shines within their own inner self.

In the same way, the Blessed Lord impels one to realize the nature of Īśvara. For in the Brahma-sūtra, "The two who have entered the cave, because of the vision of Him," the abiding of the two selves is clearly indicated. Having attained lordship over the body, the individual self [seeks] its own Master.

Having forgotten the Supreme Self and acting out of egoism, although afflicted by a succession of miseries, one perceives that very state as happiness and becomes deluded therein. The Supreme Self, however, remains untainted and untouched by pleasure or pain; if the individual soul (jīva) were united with Him, [it would likewise remain so].

They attain the Supreme Self, whose very nature is bliss. Being separated from that, one experiences suffering through worldly activity. Furthermore, that separation increases the soul's suffering by nourishing egoism and self-conceit. Yoga, however, stabilizes the blissful nature through the expansion of power by Śiva.

The meaning of the word "yoga" here is precisely the experience of *sāmarasya* (perfect equilibrium). This alone is designated as *śivayoga*, which is to be accomplished through practice. In this way, the Lord teaches the indispensability of yoga; the intention is that in the absence of yoga, human birth itself would be in vain. And thus, by Śiva, one who has attained perfection in *śivayoga*—
The Śivayogins maintain that if one, having become a beloved of Śiva while living there, should dwell here for even a single day, he thereby achieves the true purpose of his birth.
Of all yogis as well, he who worships Me with his inner self absorbed in Me, full of faith—he is deemed by Me to be the most disciplined. (47)
Among all yogis— even those devoted to meditating on other deities such as Āditya, Caturmukha, and others— he who,

possessing faith, being single-mindedly intent, and full of devotion, worships and serves Me alone as the *prāṇaliṅga* shining within their hearts with his entire inner organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), he alone is the most disciplined among all yogis.

Kṛṣṇa instructs through the contemplation of identity with Śiva; thus, yoga is indicated here as being primary. Yoga, it should be noted, means *sāmarasya* (harmony). Harmony is not possible between two things that are entirely distinct, nor does the necessity for demonstrating harmony even arise between two things that are already identical.

In reality, union is possible only between two things that are non-different and of a single nature; therefore, since the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Supreme (*parama*) are in fact of one kind by virtue of their conscious nature (*cidrūpa*), [their union occurs] through contact with *prakṛti* as an innate [state].

In this context, the union (*yoga*) of two distinct entities is taught by the Blessed One. If the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Supreme Self (*para-brahman*) were entirely distinct like sesame seeds and rice grains, their union would not be possible.

However, for those who are of one essence yet immersed in different states, union occurs naturally through devotion (*bhakti*), which consists of the integration of knowledge and action. Thus, in this system, union occurs only between two things of the same nature.

It is possible for two things that possess distinct powers, but not for two things of different species. Although the individual soul (*jīva*) and the supreme self (*paramātman*) belong to the same species—namely, consciousness—they exist as distinct due to their specific qualities of power (*śakti-vaiśiṣṭya*). Therefore, in their bound state (*baddhāvasthā*), they possess an innate difference arising from the distinction of their powers; whereas in their enlightened state (*buddhāvasthā*), they possess non-difference in the form of the unity of consciousness.

In reality, the individual soul (jīva), its sovereignty eclipsed by māyā, exists with diminished power due to the contraction of its own energy; it is small and limited. The Supreme Self (paramātman), however, possesses full power and is immeasurable and indivisible. The power of will (icchā-śakti) residing in Him is vast.

That power, residing in the individual soul (*jīva*), exists as all-pervasive, undivided, and infinite; yet, when directed solely toward its own objects, it becomes limited. In the same way, the power of knowledge (*jñāna-śakti*) residing in the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) shines forth as unimpeded, unrestrained, and all-pervading. [The power] residing in the individual soul, however, belongs to the person...

Power residing in the individual soul is extremely limited, its scope is narrow, and it is preceded by false pride; likewise, the power of action grounded in the Supreme Self shines forth as more vigorous, unrivaled, limitless, wonderful, and indivisible. However, that same power when grounded in the individual soul is restricted and serves only its own self-interest.

It exists with limitations of space, time, and so forth. Thus, although the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Supreme (*parama*) are of the same nature as consciousness (*cidrūpa*), their natural distinction manifests through the contraction and expansion of power (*śakti*). Therefore, they are not entirely non-different; however, both are indeed qualified by power (*śaktiviśiṣṭa*). The power of one [the Supreme] is immeasurable.

But for the other [the individual soul], it is limited. As has already been stated, if the Supreme Self (paramātman) is characterized by the power of consciousness (cicchakti), the individual soul (jīvātman) exists as characterized by the power of the mind (cittaśakti).

And thus, here there is non-duality (advaita) and aesthetic integration (sāmarasya) between the individual soul, characterized by the power of the mind, and Śiva, characterized by the power of consciousness.

This is taught by the Supreme Soul, Kṛṣṇa. Such non-duality (advaita) must certainly be realized. Fundamentally, two things that are non-distinct become distinct through the possession of power (śakti), and non-duality is achieved through the unfolding of that very power. Such a yoga is attained through practice.

The Blessed One teaches that [liberation] is to be attained through uninterrupted practice. Like a river and the ocean, although the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Lord (*īśvara*) are fundamentally non-different, they exist as distinct by virtue of their innate nature. Their discernment, contemplation, and cultivation are each entirely separate. Of the individual soul...

(183) Discernment rooted in one's own self-interest is heard [in scripture] to be all-pervading, yet that of the Supreme Self is dependent upon the welfare of the world. Likewise, the reflection of the individual soul (jīva) brings benefit to oneself and to those related to oneself.

It is well known that the Supreme Self is intent on the welfare of the world; likewise, the constitution of the individual soul (jīva) is directed solely toward its own self-interest, filling its own belly, whereas the nature of the Supreme Self is universal, sincere, and spontaneous. Thus, these two, though distinct by nature, are both composed of consciousness (cidātmaka).

Through mutual knowledge and the activity prompted by it, a state of aesthetic integration (*sāmarasya*) arises; likewise, in their union, no contradiction whatsoever manifests. Although a river originates from the ocean, it is nevertheless conventionally designated as a "river" and not as an "ocean. When the river enters the ocean, then—

From the dissolution of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), the conventional designation "the ocean" alone becomes possible. In this way, although the individual soul (*jīva*) is a portion of the consciousness of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), it remains distinct due to its natural state of constant contact with the impurity called the power of the mind (*citta-śakti*). This is so as long as the mind consists of the qualities of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*.

When the mind transforms through constant contemplation of Śiva into the nature of Truth, Knowledge, and Bliss, then the individual soul (jīva) shall indeed be united with the Supreme Self (paramātman). Thus, Kṛṣṇa’s intention is that yoga is to be accomplished by means of the transformation of the mind. This occurs when the human nature is transformed into a divine nature.

At that very moment of transformation, the union of the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Supreme (*parama*) must be brought about. Thus, Yoga— as taught by the Supreme Lord Kṛṣṇa as the doctrine of non-duality qualified by power (*śaktiviśiṣṭādvaita*)—
properly accords with the individual soul and the Supreme Soul, which are non-different in their nature as consciousness (*cidrūpa*) yet distinct through their qualification by power.

And thus, such a yoga alone is the means for warding off all suffering. A living being endowed with such yoga, whatever he performs, appears as something that accomplishes the welfare of the world. Indeed, the experience of those who have realized the truth is this: "May a person of virtuous nature, beloved of Śiva, dwell in this world even for a single day."

In the *Gītā*, it is stated that the support of life (*jīvanādhāra*) here consists of internal cultivation (*adhyātmabhāvanāmaya*) which produces equanimity (*sāmarasya*). Furthermore, it is well known that it is not appropriate to contemplate the individual soul (*jīva*) as being directly the Supreme Brahman; for the *Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad* states, "He grieves, deluded by his lack of sovereignty," indicating the soul's incapacity caused by its own powerlessness.

He points out grief and delusion: "In this way, no one [recognizes] the individual soul—seized by fear, afflicted by grief and delusion, and shrouded in impurity—to be the manifest Brahman itself during the state of worldly existence, that is, while in a bound condition.

He would say: thus, in order to remove the sense of individuality from the soul that is indeed [perceived as] separate, and to produce a yoga consisting of *sāmarasya* (perfect equilibrium) within Śiva, who is its very foundation, the venerable Lord Kṛṣṇa would have initiated the Yogaśāstra. Only between two things that are inherently distinct can a union truly occur. Thus...

In the state of worldly existence (*saṃsāra*), the distinction between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) exists as something inherent. At that time, the non-difference (*abheda*) consisting of the unity of consciousness, which was exceedingly subtle and unmanifest, becomes manifest in the stage of awakening through the power of devotion (*bhakti*), which is a transformation of the power of consciousness (*cicchakti*).

It blossoms both externally and internally. The individual soul (*jīva*), having entered into worldly activity through *śakti*, attains cessation through *bhakti* and, becoming Supreme Śiva by means of the all-pervading expansion of power known as self-perfection, accomplishes the welfare of the world. Therefore, although all individual souls are distinct due to their association with the mind, [they are ultimately one].

The Blessed One observes that by gaining an intimate acquaintance with the one Supreme Self who abides within all, they may attain supreme peace and conduct themselves toward one another with a spirit of love; thus, because it teaches the yoga of those who are naturally distinct, the Gītā scripture does not have the doctrine of absolute non-duality (*kevalādvaita*) as its ultimate purport.

Those who possess discernment should reflect upon this. Since yoga is intent upon the expansion of power (*śakti*), practitioners of realization maintain that this Yoga scripture accords with the Śaktiviśiṣṭādvaita doctrine according to its literal sense.
Furthermore, this contemplation appears to be rooted in scripture, reasoning, and direct experience; thus, everything is perfectly clear. || 47 ||
The Seventh Chapter.
At the end of the previous chapter, it was stated that among all yogis, only one who is steadfast in Śiva-yoga is the most excellent.
In this chapter, the reason for that is indicated in detail:
O Pārtha, with your mind attached to Me, practicing yoga and taking refuge in Me, listen to how you shall know Me in My entirety and without doubt. 1.

The Blessed Lord said: O Pārtha Arjuna! With your mind attached to me—the Supreme Lord whose qualities will be described hereafter—being such that your mind is thus absorbed, and with me alone as your refuge and support, you should practice yoga, performing yoga.
Without doubt—
and without even a trace of doubt— [he perceives] me standing before him, assuming a divine form, as the Supreme Self.

Listen now to the manner in which you shall understand it entirely and completely: how a human being, by regarding Kṛṣṇa— the teacher of reality— who though assuming a mortal form is the Supreme Self,
with the realization that He is the Supreme Self, should honor and place Him before him, and how the reality of the Supreme Self may be known through Him.
The Blessed One begins the instruction on reality not only for Arjuna, but for the entire world:
"I shall declare to you in its entirety this knowledge along with realized wisdom (vijñāna), by knowing which nothing further remains here to be known. (1.2)
I shall declare to you, in its entirety— that is, completely— this knowledge which is about to be spoken, along with realization (savijñāna), meaning accompanied by direct experience;
and having known that which I shall speak, there remains nothing further to be known here in this world.

I shall declare that knowledge of the principle of Śiva (śivatattva), which is such that no means for achieving the goals of human life remains [unfulfilled]. (2) Among thousands of men, scarcely one strives for perfection; and among those who strive and attain perfection, scarcely one knows Me in truth. (3)
Regarding the question "What is the distinction? concerning the knowledge that is about to be described, [the Lord] demonstrates that it is likewise extremely difficult to attain:
"Among men, only one strives for perfection—that is, for the attainment of the knowledge about to be described. Even among those who strive in this manner...

Even among those who are striving for perfection and have attained it, only some rare individual knows Me as I truly am—that is, knows Me correctly. Those who exert effort for the sake of attaining the knowledge to be described hereafter are indeed rare; yet even among those who strive, those who know the reality in its entirety are even rarer.
The meaning is that they are even rarer than those. || 3 ||
Earth, water, fire, air, ether, mind, intellect, and ego—thus is my nature divided eightfold. (4)

Having thus praised the knowledge of reality concerning one's own true nature which is about to be described, he now begins to instruct upon that very subject: Earth is the element of solidity; water is the element of fluidity; fire is the element of heat; air is well known; space is the element of ether; and the three principles of mind, intellect, and ego constitute the triad of mental faculties. Altogether—
"In this manner, 'eightfold' (p. 186), my nature is divided into eight parts; and thus [it belongs] to the Supreme Self."
The meaning is that Prakṛti, which is insentient and of the nature of acid (the primordial cause), exists in eight forms, serving as the locus for the body. || 4 ||
O mighty-armed one, know that this other nature of Mine is distinct from this [lower one]; it is the life-force by which this entire world is sustained. (5)
Having thus described the eightfold division of the insentient *prakṛti*, he then defines the sentient *prakṛti*:

"This aforementioned *prakṛti* is called 'inferior' (*aparā*), meaning it is perceived as having the nature of bondage within *saṃsāra*. Beyond this, there is another *prakṛti* which is 'superior' (*parā*), pure, and excellent—the *prakṛti* that constitutes the living being (*jīvabhūtā*), whose very nature is the individual soul (*jīva*)."

Know that she who stands in the place of His wife, the object of His love, is that very Prakṛti in the form of the individual soul (jīva) by whom this entire world— composed of the five elements and insentient in nature— is sustained and held together. And thus,
it is indeed through contact with the power of the individual soul (jīva-śakti), which is of the same nature as the Supreme Self and related to Him, that the world exists.
The meaning is that stability arises. || 5 ||
Understand that all beings have this as their source;
I am the origin and likewise the dissolution of the entire universe.

In this context, it is established that these two very natures (*prakṛti*) are the cause of all things. "Having these as their source" (*etadyonīni*): understand and know that all beings—that is, the entire class of living creatures—have these two aforementioned natures, the higher and the lower, which stand in the place of a body, as their *yoni*, meaning their cause. However, [the Lord says:]...
By this much, he demonstrates today that one should not be deluded into thinking that these two possess the status of being the cause of everything independently;

rather, through these two natures (*prakṛti*), I alone am the source— that is, the cause of origin— of the entire world, and likewise, at the end, during the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*), the dissolution of everything occurs in Me alone.

And dissolution also occurs. Thus, since the Supreme Self alone is possible as the cause of both origination and dissolution, it is likewise possible for the Supreme Self alone to be the cause of preservation. For this very reason, although the individual soul (*jīva*) is the cause of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) composed of the five elements, it is not possible for it to be its cause independently. This is because [the world] has that [Supreme Self] as its root.

The individual soul (jīva) exists engaged in worldly activity with the five elements solely through the volition of the Supreme Self (paramātman), in accordance with His will, and in conformity with His impulsion. Thus, although the jīva may indeed be an agent because of its nature as consciousness, it remains dependent upon the Supreme Self.

Agency alone follows upon that [intellect]. And thus, the individual soul (*jīva*) would not, by its own nature, engage in any activity whatsoever through the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*), nor would it ever desist from such a state of indifference and detachment. For him...

Both engagement and withdrawal depend upon the Supreme Self; therefore, since everything is performed by the Supreme Self alone as the universal cause, He should not maintain indifference. Likewise, He should not Himself fail to engage, while imagining Himself to be the sole agent of everything. Neither of these two [extremes] is appropriate for Him.

The Supreme Self alone is the primary cause of both its engagement and its withdrawal. Thus, the individual soul (jīva), always directing the mind—which is his internal nature—toward contemplation of the Supreme Self, should employ his external nature, the body, for the sake of his own conscious kinsmen. It is exactly thus.

If he were to survive, he would attain the fulfillment of his birth at that very moment; otherwise, a great calamity would descend upon him. If he were to give even a moment’s space in his mind to thoughts of his brothers and sisters, setting aside his father as the Supreme Self, his mental derangement would be certain. Therefore, the individual soul—

Having become related to the Supreme Self, and while constantly contemplating that very Supreme Self— who is one's own cause and protector— within the mind through the cooperation of the five elements, if one should strive for the sake of satisfying one's circle of kinsmen by removing their suffering in accordance with His will, then he...

One should become a vessel for the grace of the Supreme Self. Thus, the exceedingly heavy burden consisting of the welfare of the world, which has been entrusted by the Supreme Self to the individual soul (jīva) who is of the same nature as Himself through the form of consciousness, must be borne by the soul in such a way that satisfaction arises for the Supreme Self. 6.
There is nothing whatsoever else higher than Me, O Dhanañjaya;
all this is strung upon Me like clusters of gems on a thread.

There is no other cause whatsoever superior to Me, the Supreme Lord, the cause of all. O Dhanañjaya Arjuna, this entire world is strung upon Me— the Supreme Lord in My embodied form who stands as its locus— just as clusters of gems, that is, collections of jewels, are strung upon a thread.

"Entwined" (grathita) means that I alone am the substratum of everything. Although Kṛṣṇa employs the word "we" (asmatpada) in several places through the contemplation of identity with Śiva— the formless cause of all— there is no mutual contradiction therein, as has been explained at length right from the beginning.
It has been explained. The application of the word "me" (mām) refers exclusively to the formless Supreme Self, because [the Self] is the substratum of all things.
What is described by the realized ones as "the abode of the Supreme Self" appears entirely consistent; for this very reason,

because He is the locus for the dissolution of all beings and the entire class of living creatures, that Supreme Self— who is indivisible consciousness— is designated by such names as Rudra, Viṣṇu, and so forth, and belongs to everyone.

The wise should reflect that he shines forth, making his sovereignty and lordship meaningful by granting space upon the earth. This very same formless Supreme Self assumes the divine, embodied, and gentle form of Viṣṇu for the protection of the world, and the form of Kālarudra for the dissolution of the universe.

He assumes a terrifying form. Thus, there is no difference between the causal form—the fundamental Supreme Self—and the three forms (trimūrtis) which are divine manifestations that have entered into the category of effects.
If Vaiṣṇavas and Śaivas were to imagine a mutual distinction and consider the Supreme Self as an enemy within their own kin...

It is the Lord’s intention that humans should always reflect: "We are parts of the Supreme Self; we have not come here for the sake of mutual dispute, but rather we have received this holy body solely for the purpose of spreading mutual love and friendship. || 7 ||
I am the taste in the waters, O son of Kuntī; I am the radiance in the moon and the sun; I am the sacred syllable Om in all the Vedas; I am the sound in space; and I am the virility in men.

He provides several illustrations regarding the form in which the Supreme Self dwells among all existing things in the world, like a thread through a cluster of gems. O Kaunteya, I am the *rasa*—the essence—in the waters; for *rasa* alone is the primary quality of water. And likewise, in the moon and the sun...

I alone am the radiance and the beauty of the sun and the moon. Among all the Vedas, I alone am the *praṇava*, which is the most preeminent. In the sky (*kha*), I am sound; for sound is the unique quality of space, and it is said that the definition of space is that which has sound as its quality.

By the Naiyāyikas [it is said]: "In this very way, among human beings—living souls who have assumed male forms—that which is seen as manliness or prowess is also I alone. Thus, whatever excellence exists in all things, residing in the place of their unique attributes (*asādhāraṇadharma*), all that should be understood as the power of the Supreme Self alone. Where...
The conclusion is that whatever excellence manifests therein is entirely the grace of the Blessed One alone. || 8 ||
I am the pure fragrance in the earth and the radiance in the fire;
I am the life-force in all beings and the austerity in ascetics. (9)

Whatever holy fragrance exists on the earth, that is indeed I; whatever luster or brilliance is in the fire, that is indeed I; and whatever life—meaning the principle that supports the body—is in all beings, among all living creatures, that too is indeed I; and in ascetics, I am austerity, existing in the form of penance. Thus, whatever there may be in any place...

The meaning is that the wise person, having contemplated that all excellence exists as the very nature of the Blessed One, should please the multitude of living beings—who are distinguished by that [excellence]—as if they were their own; by conducting oneself in this way alone, the grace of the Blessed One is obtained. || 9 ||
Know Me, O Pārtha, as the eternal seed of all beings;
I am the intellect of the intelligent and the splendor of the splendid. (10)

O Pārtha, know that I alone am the eternal seed of all beings—that is, of all living creatures—operating from the beginning of time. Of the intelligent, those endowed with wisdom, I am their very intelligence. And of the radiant, that which is their splendor, their boldness, that too is I alone.

Precisely because of this nature, due to my abiding within all living beings, whatever particular distinction manifests in each one— whatever specific quality exists that is capable of distinguishing one soul from another— I am all of that. Therefore, when living beings perceive mutual differences [among themselves], [they do so only through these limiting adjuncts].

The Blessed One instructs that one should not defile the heart with hatred, envy, and the like. He who hates his own brother with a sense of otherness actually hates himself; for although living beings are diverse according to their own karma, they are of a single nature insofar as they are governed by the Inner Controller, and thus [one should act] for the sake of His pleasure.

The intention of the Blessed One is that they should find mutual delight in one another. Nevertheless, for one who hates out of a lack of discrimination, self-destruction is inevitable; whereas he who delights other living beings by viewing them with the perspective of the Supreme Self becomes eternally happy through the grace of the Supreme Self—this is the underlying meaning. || 10 ||
Of powers, I am the power of those who possess strength, devoid of desire and attachment;
O bull among the Bharatas, I am the desire in beings that is not contrary to dharma. 11.

O bull of the Bharatas, Arjuna, among those who are powerful and possessed of strength, I alone am that strength which is free from desire and attachment—desire being longing, and attachment being the clinging to fortune once it has been attained.

That strength which manifests effortlessly and spontaneously within the most powerful beings—even without the need for effort, desire, or the like—that is indeed I myself. Therefore, the person of discrimination, contemplating that all innate strength in all beings belongs to Me, attains My grace. Among living beings, that which is not opposed to *dharma*—the *dharma* established by the scriptures—is [to be understood as such].
He too is indeed myself. Thus, even the experience of the enjoyments of *saṃsāra* is in accordance with *dharma*.

O Rāmanātha, if this devotion to the Blessed One—which consists of the identity of being (*bhāvaikya*)—is desired by Śiva, then such devotion is not [mere] non-identity. The portion concerning how one may become dear to the Supreme Lord has been correctly expounded by them. This...

Basavarya describes in an appropriate manner how desire, rooted in the unity of being, may become the dispeller of all diseases: "If the bride and groom attain a state of single flavor within their minds toward one another, declare that marriage to be auspicious; do not speak otherwise."

"Since there exist the strength of Tārā and Candra, as well as debts, frauds, and the signs (rāśi) and so forth—let this be established. This Dhasra [star] is superior to the day; when it is said that such is for the sake of the construction of the world, it will certainly be the fruit of the worship of Saṅgameśa. Thus is its greatness described.

Since desire that is not contrary to the Dharma has been envisioned by the wise as a refuge, the Blessed One’s intention is that worldly people should always apply their minds to the acquisition of wealth and pleasure solely in accordance with the Dharma.
Whatever states of being there are—whether characterized by goodness (sāttvika), passion (rājasa), or darkness (tāmasa)—know them to proceed from Me alone; yet I am not in them, but they are in Me.

What need is there to speak further regarding my presence in all things? He explains that this is the summary here: those who are *sāttvika*, rooted in the quality of *sattva*, and those who are *rājasa*, rooted in the quality of *rajas*—they are born from me alone; nevertheless, I am not the Lord of any fruit therein.
Thus, he now clarifies this intention: although I abide within them, I am not dependent upon them;
rather, they themselves abide in me. All of them are always entirely dependent upon me. Their...

Whatever object anyone gives to me with devotion, I accept it with satisfaction and consume it at that time. Only that which is offered with devotion is accepted by me; otherwise, I remain indifferent toward their life, and none of that bears fruit for them. Whatever fruit is to be attained by them, that alone I bestow upon them.
Whatever he might desire, I am not able to give all of that to him. Whatever he gave to me—the inner controller of all—in his previous birth, that very same thing I give to him today.
For the sake of my pleasure, he gave with joy at that very moment to everyone who came to his house.

All that was given [to me] belonged to Him alone; that very same thing is now being given to me by Him. In this way, all living beings exist as dependent upon Me alone; I am not dependent upon them. Therefore, I am the Lord and the Master of all. || 12 ||
Deluded by these three states consisting of the qualities, this entire world does not recognize Me, who am beyond them and imperishable.

Anticipating the objection—"If you are such the cause of the entire world, why then does the world not know you?"—he says [the following] to resolve it: "Deluded and bound by these three states consisting of the qualities (*guṇas*)—namely *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*—in the form of fetters consisting of passion, hatred, delusion, and so forth; for this very reason..."

This entire world, brought about by lack of discrimination, does not recognize Me as being beyond and distinct from these aforementioned bonds of material nature. Because they are dominated by such qualities, people are unable to know Me, who am beyond the modes (*guṇātīta*). Bound by these fetters, living beings who resemble tethered animals [do not perceive] within their own inner self...

People do not know how to place their trust in the Supreme Self, who shines forth in a state of stainless detachment. In the absence of faith, knowledge of Him is utterly cast away. In the absence of such knowledge, there is no possibility of engaging in His service.
Yet, even though people do not believe in God, they nevertheless constantly invoke Him and [seek to] act [for His sake].

Nevertheless, the dull-witted wander about out of delusion, unable to attain faith. If one were to invoke the Lord with faith, why would He not respond? If one devoid of faith should invoke the Lord, he would immediately fall, struck by the goad of His punishment. Thus ends the *Śaraṇagītā* concerning the living being bound by the noose.
It describes the poverty of trust. All of this is the harsh consequence of the snare that takes the form of bondage. Therefore, (p.
People, having forgotten the Supreme Self, spend their time merely in filling their own bellies. || 13 ||
For this divine illusion of Mine, consisting of the three qualities, is indeed difficult to overcome.
Those who take refuge in Me alone cross over this illusion.

The Supreme Self Himself teaches the means for the destruction of such delusion: "This divine power of Mine—the Goddess who belongs to Me, the Supreme Lord—is composed of the three qualities (guṇas), known as Māyā; she causes universal delusion, is capable of attracting all, and is difficult to overcome. With difficulty...

That which has transgression or overstepping is "atyaya. Thus, even though that Māyā is mine, it cannot easily be conquered by people, for they are but portions of My own self; this indeed is the wonder here. Living beings (*jīvas*) are also mine, yet they are portions of My consciousness (*cetanā*). In the same way, the Māyā that causes their delusion is also mine, but—
The portion of My consciousness, when joined with the portion of My power,
has its conscious power eclipsed by that [power] and, forgetting Me, functions everywhere through its own egoism.
Thus, having become a slave to Māyā, it is drawn toward the objects of form, taste, smell, and so forth, which constitute her attraction.
This point has been correctly established by Śaraṇa: "O Lord, never spread out before me the objects of enjoyment such as form and the rest;
for at that time, would this beast surely not abandon its desire for grass?
Acting in that very way, one should indeed look upon a servant who is deprived of sense-objects with wonder."

"O Lord Kūḍalasaṅgamārya," Basavārya thus entreated him: "By Your glance, feed me constantly with Your own grass-like [simple] devotion according to my desire; likewise, water me with the rain of excellent wisdom. By the grace of the Lord, he [bestowed upon him] the objects of enjoyment that had been produced by the power of Māyā.

Having offered them as a form of His grace and having enjoyed them, the Lord Himself, through devotion, requests that the body alone may experience eternal bliss. In this very way, the Blessed Lord Kṛṣṇa also acts for the sake of favoring Māyā;
therefore, those who take refuge in Me—the Great Lord (Maheśvara), the master of such Māyā—[attain their goal].
It is they alone who go toward this *māyā* and are able to cross it;

thus, for the sake of attaining what is obtainable through *māyā*, those with experience contemplate that the very root of the clamor of *māyā* is the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) itself. Otherwise, the pursuit of *māyā* would be nothing but weeping in the wilderness.
There is no other means for victory over illusion than taking refuge in the Supreme Self;
this intention has been clarified by Basavārya himself through the authority of his own experience.

O noble Gurukūḍala, your Māyā envelops the entire universe on all sides; likewise, it spreads around you. Yet, this mind of mine is struck with wonder at this. O Lord, if you are indeed the Master of the world, then I am here as your playground for diversion; just as an elephant dissolves into a mirror, so too do you [dissolve] into me today.
"You hide within me"— it is to restrain such crooked course of *māyā* that the grace of the Lord alone,

along with divine teachers such as Anukā and others, instructs practitioners in the yoga of steady devotion connected to the Supreme Self for the sake of quelling the playful manifestations of *māyā’s* power. For:

This Māyā has come forth from the Supreme Self alone and remains here testing us; therefore, without Him, we cannot become distant from the crooked course of Māyā by any other means. Thus, for victory over Māyā, the Lord of Māyā alone must be taken as our refuge. || 14 ||
The evil-doers, the deluded, the lowest of men, do not seek refuge in me;
their wisdom carried away by illusion, they have taken recourse to a demonic nature.

If it is only through Your grace that *māyā* is to be restrained, then why do all who have taken refuge in You not obtain liberation from the snare of *māyā*? To this he replies: "The evildoers" (*duṣkṛtinaḥ*) are those of sinful deeds;
for that very reason they are "deluded" (*mūḍhāḥ*), lacking discrimination, and "the lowest of men" (*narādhamāḥ*), the most base among persons. By *māyā*, [is meant] the aforementioned...

The sense is that only those endowed with a divine nature (*daivī-prakṛti*) serve Me; and this very point He will state later: "But the high-souled ones, O Pārtha, having taken refuge in the divine nature, worship Me with undistracted mind, knowing Me as the imperishable source of all beings. Thus, those whose conduct is virtuous and who possess purity of heart—

Thus, they place their trust in the Supreme Self and take refuge in Him; for others, however, even the inclination toward that path does not arise. But those who have sought shelter in Māyā and are deeply immersed in the enjoyment of sense-objects remain forever bound by fetters and do not attain contact with the Supreme Self. Their miserable condition—

The *Śaraṇagītā* describes it thus: "Just as a deer caught in the jaws of a tiger, or just as a frog stuck in the mouth of a serpent, so too, seeing the snares of the illusory deer, I am terrified and take refuge [in You]. Therefore, O Lord who art unbroken, it is right for You alone to protect me; today, bestow Your compassion."

Thus, one should always remember what those who have taken refuge say through their own direct experience: that the favor of Māyā is to be secured solely by taking refuge in the Supreme Self. (p. 194) || 15 ||
Four kinds of virtuous people worship Me, O Arjuna:
the distressed, the seeker of knowledge, the seeker of wealth, and the man of wisdom, O bull of the Bharatas. (16)

Thus, He says that even among those who worship the Supreme Self, there is a gradation: "O Arjuna, the virtuous"—those who stand as the opposite of the 'doers of evil' mentioned in the previous verse, those of meritorious deeds—worship Me in four ways; O bull of the Bharatas, O Arjuna, and among them..."

The distressed (ārta), afflicted by internal and external diseases, fallen into calamity—this is one. The seeker (jijñāsu), desiring to know and wishing to attain the knowledge of reality—this is another. The seeker of wealth (arthārthī), possessing a longing for power and the like—this is yet another. And the man of knowledge (jñānī), who knows the reality of the Supreme Self—this is the fourth. Thus, these four kinds of people worship Me. [In times of] distress...

They take refuge in me for the attainment of knowledge; however, those who have attained the knowledge of reality—the wise—worship me solely to experience the bliss of identity with me. Since all living beings are portions of me, everyone ought to strive to attain union with me alone; nevertheless, only a few do so.

Practitioners who are liberated from the defects of impurity and are dear to the Supreme Self, being united with Him alone, desire to experience eternal bliss; yet all of this depends upon the power of *māyā*. To the extent that they are abandoned by *māyā*, to that same extent are they honored by the Supreme Self.
Therefore, everyone must also strive for the cessation of Māyā. || 16 ||
Among them, the one who possesses knowledge, who is constantly disciplined and devoted to the One alone, is preeminent;
for I am exceedingly dear to the man of knowledge, and he is dear to Me.

Among those four, the one who is "constantly disciplined" (*nityayukta*) is one who is always, at all times, attached solely to the Supreme Self; the meaning is that he is established in That. For this very reason, he is "single-mindedly devoted" (*ekabhakti*), meaning one whose devotion is directed toward Me alone, the formless Supreme Lord. Because there is nothing else for him to attain, he looks to the Supreme Lord alone.

This is the meaning. Such a knower is distinguished; that is, he excels in comparison with the other three. For, on account of this, I alone am exceedingly—meaning absolutely—dear to him, being the object of his love. Likewise, he alone is dear to me because his mind is fixed solely upon Me. Therefore, the sense is that he alone is the best of all. Thus...
The Lord establishes the greatness of the man of knowledge by stating that he alone is the supreme devotee; for the man of knowledge is always... (p. 195)
Abiding in a state free from egoism, relying solely upon the grace of the Blessed Lord as the instrumental cause, one desists from worldly activity.

The *Śaraṇagītā* describes the conduct of a human being regarding the Supreme Self in this way: "O man, does your prowess shine before a lion? Reflect on this: what is the play of a bird in the presence of the cosmic fire at the end of an aeon?"

"O God of gods, how can the dancing of a worm take place before the sun? O Lord, how could our play befitful at Your feet? Thus, those who have taken refuge contemplate that for the conquest of *māyā*, there is no other path than seeking refuge through devotion and humility toward the Supreme Self. [They contemplate] such a knower.
The Supreme Self tests His devotee through many deceptions for the sake of His own satisfaction;

this method of testing is clarified in the *Śaraṇagītā*. However, Hara may employ His devotee in dancing—He might crush him again like a stalk of sugarcane—but Rāmanātha will take by the hand that one who never becomes afraid.
Thus, the Blessed One extends His compassion only toward that practitioner who is not deceived by all such forms of testing.
Because he has been thus tested, the man of knowledge becomes exceedingly dear to the Supreme Self; he alone dwells in the place of His very life-breath. || 17 ||
All these are indeed noble; yet it is my opinion that the man of knowledge alone is truly My very Self, for he, being disciplined in mind, is established in Me alone as the unsurpassed goal.
Now, having thus established the superiority of the man of knowledge (jñānin), the Lord speaks regarding the status of the other three:

"All these three are indeed noble (udāra), meaning excellent; because they are devotees of the Supreme Self as compared to those who worship other deities, they are all indeed excellent. However (tu), the man of knowledge is My very Self."
"It is my considered opinion that he is indeed equal to My own life-breath. To explain why this is so, He says "established," and so forth.
For that wise man, whose self is disciplined and whose mind is concentrated, has attained Me alone—the Supreme Self—who am unsurpassed and the highest goal;
since there is no higher state than the Supreme Self to be reached, he is such.
The sense is that [the devotee] is the very life-breath of my Supreme Self. In this way, the Blessed One points out the supreme excellence of the man of knowledge. || 18 ||
At the end of many births, the man of knowledge attains Me, realizing "Vāsudeva is everything. Such a great soul is very rare to find. 19.

196) He speaks of the extreme rarity of such a knower: "at the end of many births," meaning solely due to a specific refinement (*saṃskāra*) accomplished over many lifetimes in meditative absorption (*samādhi*). [Such a person is] Vāsudeva.

He who possesses the knowledge that "this entire world is Vāsudeva"—just as in the passages "all this is indeed Brahman" and so forth—that very one, being of the nature of the Supreme Self (paramātman) and the vital breath (prāṇa), is the Supreme Power (parāśakti) in the form of the Person (puruṣa);
he approaches and worships me. In the statement "Rudra is indeed everything," the word *rudra* fundamentally denotes the Person (puruṣa).

In this way, the term Vāsudeva should be understood as denoting primordial nature (prakṛti). Likewise, it should be understood that the entire multitude of existing things is indeed Vāsudeva alone. The sense is that only one possessing such knowledge attains me, the formless Supreme Śiva. Such a great soul is extremely rare and exceedingly difficult to find. || 19 ||
Those whose knowledge has been carried away by various desires resort to other deities,
adhering to their respective rules of conduct, constrained by their own innate natures.

Having stated that "all these [devotees] are indeed noble" thus declaring the excellence of His own devotees, He now speaks of those whose knowledge has been stolen away— whose discrimination has been taken by desires in the form of other deities, sons, cattle, heaven, fame, and so forth— and who,
being constrained and bound by their own innate nature as established at birth, follow various specific observances for the sake of attaining those respective fruits.

Adhering to and practicing the injunctions being proclaimed, they take refuge in other deities— namely, minor deities distinct from the Supreme Self— and serve them; those who, setting aside the Supreme Self,
conceive of other deities and worship them for the sake of attaining worldly fruits, [abandon] the contemplation of oneness with the Self.

They do not attain it. Seeing such lay devotees (upāsakas), the Śaraṇas instruct them as follows: "Indeed, there is but one God; for a devoted wife, the husband alone is her [God]. If she should desire another, then that husband would cut off her ears and likewise her life-breath here. Having abandoned the God she should worship, she turns to another."

"If one worships [the deity] while fallen, he shall not become so; but tell me yourself, O Lord, what do the learned say of one who eats what has been abandoned by many gods? Thus, one who worships all the gods should not be single-mindedly devoted to any one, except through the worship of the one Supreme Self who consists of all the deities.
The meaning is that for one engaged in the propitiation of different deities, no fixed rule whatsoever would be observed.
Whatever form of deity a devotee desires to worship with faith,
I make that very faith of his steadfast.

He says that even when worshipping other deities, they do not know the reality as it truly is: "Whosoever, being a devotee desiring such-and-such a small fruit, is a devotee of this or that deity—whatever form [of that deity] he worships... (p. 197).

Even for one who worships various deities out of a desire for their respective fruits, it is I alone who ordain that very same firm and unwavering faith, which is in accordance with each [deity]. Abiding within the forms of those various deities as well, it is I alone who nourish their faith, grant them the corresponding fruit, and [fulfill] their [desire].

I nourish devotion to the Deity. And in this way, even by those who worship other deities, the worship of the one Supreme Self alone is accomplished; for it is that very Supreme Self, existing there as the inner controller (*antaryāmin*), who certainly generates such a realization. Such a realization must be conceived at that time by all worshippers alike.

The scripture, which is the authority for verbal testimony, teaches this: it is the intention of the Blessed One that this very principle of viewing others as oneself must be practiced by all practitioners. || 21 ||
Endowed with that faith, he strives for the propitiation of that [deity];
and from that, he obtains his desires, which are indeed ordained by Me alone.

Endowed with that faith which has been graced by Me, he strives—that is, performs—the propitiation of that very deity; and for that reason, he obtains and attains those very desires and their respective fruits ordained and granted by Me alone, the Supreme Self, who possesses form. And thus, even for those of small intellect—

For the sake of nourishing faith, I myself, abiding in an incorporeal form within all the divine forms worshipped by human beings, generate in them the specific faith appropriate to each and grant them their respective desired fruits. A devotee, through devotion, [worships] his chosen deity by means of his own preferred name and form.

If one should perform worship, then I alone accept that worship; I alone cause such worship to be performed, and I alone shall bestow the appropriate fruit of that worship. Wherever a devotee performs worship, if they engage in it everywhere with the contemplation of the Supreme Self alone—

Then that worship would become dear to the Supreme Self. Since the one God alone assumes many forms and names, if a devotee proceeds everywhere with the single-minded conception [of Him as one], then peace will arise in his mind. This very point the Blessed One will state: "For I am the enjoyer and the Lord of all sacrifices..."
"He is both the enjoyer and the lord, yet they do not know Me in truth. || 22 ||
But for those of small intelligence, their fruit is finite;
the worshippers of the gods go to the gods, but my devotees come to me as well. (23)

He says that the fruit given by the gods propitiated through other forms of meditation is impermanent and meager. Those whose minds are set on the supreme goal of human life are indeed called "great-minded" and "high-souled. On the contrary, the base and small-minded obtain only a meager result despite great exertion. [The goal] is the Supreme Self alone.

He is reckoned as "Great. For one who worships with the contemplation of Him as the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), a truly great fruit is attained. However, for one in whom such a contemplation does not exist, only a small fruit is obtained through such worship. That fruit of theirs is acquired only with great exertion.

Even that fruit being accomplished is finite and indeed perishable. Those who sacrifice to the gods—those who worship the perishable deities other than the Supreme Self—go to and attain such perishable gods alone. But My devotees, those who worship Me, attain even Me; they reach Me alone.
Those who worship with the contemplation of the Supreme Self go to the Supreme Self alone.

Even in such a state, the Lord grieves thus: "Alas, even after having worshipped Me, fools do not attain the eternal fruit. And He will say: "O Arjuna, all worlds, up to the realm of Brahmā, are subject to return."
"But having come to Me, O son of Kuntī, rebirth does not exist. (23)
The unintelligent, not knowing my supreme, imperishable, and unsurpassed nature, think of me—the unmanifest—as having attained manifestation. (24)
To the question, "Why do they all not take refuge in the Supreme Self? he says: because they are *abuddhayaḥ*, devoid of wisdom;

they do not recognize my supreme state (*paramaṃ bhāvam*), which is mine, imperishable (*avyayam*)—meaning free from decay and eternally present even during the state of incarnation—and unsurpassed (*anuttamam*), meaning that there is nothing superior to it.

Not knowing and not comprehending my nature as the Supreme Self—though I am by nature unmanifest and birthless—they perceive me as having attained manifestation and birth only at this very moment, as something newly come into being; they regard even me just like any other ordinary person. Therefore, all of them do not recognize me as formless.
By relying on the Great, they attain the great fruit;
whereas those who are small, having obtained only a small fruit, are born again and again and dissolve away. Such is this [state].
Enveloped by my yoga-māyā, I am not manifest to everyone;
deluded, this world does not recognize me, the unborn and imperishable.
To the question, "Why are all practitioners unable to know you?", he says:

It has already been stated previously that "my Māyā consists of the qualities" (*guṇamayī*). Enveloped or concealed by that [Māyā], I, the Supreme Self, am not manifest—that is, not fit to be known—by ordinary people in general. However, those who...

They take refuge in Me alone; for them, let Me be known as the Light. For this very reason, this world, deluded by Māyā and ignorant, does not recognize—that is, does not understand—Me as unborn, who am in reality devoid of birth, and undecaying, who am devoid of death. Thus, having correctly understood the all-pervasiveness of the Supreme Self...
The meaning is that he who worships becomes a recipient of love for the Supreme Self and thereby attains union (sāmarasya) with the Supreme Self. || 25 ||
I know all beings that have passed away, those that are present, O Arjuna, and those yet to come; but no one knows Me.

He says that while illusion (māyā), which produces all afflictions, can never delude the Supreme Self: "O Arjuna, I know—through direct perception—all beings of the past, those of the present, and those of the future; I know the states of existence and movement of all. But, however...

"No one whatsoever has known, nor does anyone know, Me as such. The meaning is that only My devotee—who is established in Me, who has Me as his supreme goal, and who worships Me—can truly know Me. || 26 ||
O Bhārata, O scorcher of foes, at the time of creation all beings fall into delusion through the confusion of dualities arising from desire and aversion.

Now, He describes the manner in which Māyā deludes: O Bhārata, O scion of the Bharata lineage, O scorcher of foes Arjuna, all beings are deluded by the delusion of duality arising from desire and aversion— that is, by the delusion consisting of the pairs of opposites such as pleasure and pain, gain and loss.

At the time of creation (*sarga*), at the moment of birth, all living beings (*sarvaprāṇinaḥ*) fall into delusion (*saṃmoha*), that is, they attain a state of bewilderment or ignorance (*ajñatā*). When there is birth...

At that time, because the connection with *prakṛti* is inevitable, people, deluded by passion, hatred, and so forth rooted therein, do not know Me, the Supreme Self. Therefore, a human being should first remain in the company of the virtuous (*satsaṅga*) and abandon passion, hatred, and the like. For the abandonment of passion and hatred, both knowledge and action are required.
Practice through the vision of pervasive unity is essential. For one who has correctly understood the pervasion of the Supreme Self and,

having realized its abiding within his own body through the instruction of the virtuous, performs worship and other rites according to the prescribed method, the manifestation of the Supreme Self alone remains ever awake in his mind.
This point is indicated in the *Śaraṇagītā* as follows: "In this matter, a mind devoid of action is not accepted;

without the body, the maintenance of the vital breath is impossible. Without the vital breath, there is no body, and without action, the self does not attain knowledge. Without knowledge, conduct is not beautiful."

"The mark (liṅga) [of the body] is devoid of the radiance of knowledge and action; therefore, in this world, let a mortal be endowed with knowledge and action. Having understood this, he who acts is alone capable of experiencing the Great Light within his own heart; otherwise, he is not.
One obtains even some small measure of the supreme fruit.
The *Śaraṇagītā* describes the worship of those who lack such a vision of integration (*samanvaya*) as follows:
"Is the cessation of hunger seen here by merely tying provisions to the upper part of the belly? In the same way..."

What can be gained today merely by holding a linga to the upper part of the heart? Does anything placed within a bamboo ever attain the nature of a linga? Likewise, would a devotee not become a bamboo, and a guru a stone, simply through being cast aside? Seeing such things, I am filled with shame.

"O Lord of Guha, truly great wonder arises! Thus, for a practitioner who does not know the identity of the two—the light of the Supreme Self shining both internally and externally—then even the external wearing of the marks of the Self (*liṅga*) for the sake of achieving constant union with the Supreme Self would be utterly futile. Therefore...

The light that shines inherently within the heart, having emerged externally through the grace of the Guru and further increased by the favor of the moving [deity], is what those who meditate upon their chosen *liṅga* (sveṣṭaliṅga) truly perceive as the one who bears the Vow of the Hero (*vīravratadhārī*) and is a true Śaiva; otherwise, his downfall is certain. Therefore:
Human beings should resort to the path of the integration of knowledge and action. || 27 ||
But those people of meritorious deeds whose evil has come to an end, being freed from the delusion of dualities, worship Me with firm resolve. (28)
p.
201) Since *māyā* is thus so difficult to transcend, one might ask: when will liberation from its delusion occur? To this he says:
for those people who possess merit—those whose sinful karma has reached its end (*antya-gata*)—[liberation occurs].

"Attained destruction" means that which has reached its end, being almost exhausted. Those who are "freed from the delusion of the pairs"—that is, freed from the delusion in the form of the pairs previously mentioned—and who are "steadfast in their vows," meaning they are distinguished by a firm resolve of the nature: "The Supreme Self alone is my goal to be attained, and nothing else," [they reach] Me.

They worship and serve the Supreme Self. Thus, the meaning is that only those who are free from the delusion of duality and possessed of faith are capable of becoming one with the Supreme Self. || 28 ||
Those who strive for liberation from old age and death by taking refuge in Me—they know that Brahman, the whole of the inner self (adhyātma), and all action in its entirety. (29)

Under the guise of answering the question, "For what purpose do practitioners worship me?", the Teacher provides the following instruction: for the sake of liberation— such that there may be no further rebirth— those who strive by taking refuge in and relying upon Me, the Supreme Self with form, attain that Formless Brahman, the Supreme Brahman.

They know the whole— everything pertaining to the inner self (adhyātma)— and they also know the entirety of action and the nature of action itself. The sense is that, by striving for liberation while taking refuge in Me, they shall come to know all this mystery by themselves.
Therefore, for the sake of experiencing the formless Supreme Śiva-Brahman, all practitioners must rely upon a manifested form; thus it exists. || 29 ||
Those who know Me as the presiding deity of the elements, the presiding deity of the divine, and the presiding deity of sacrifice—
even at the time of departure— they, with disciplined minds, know Me.
Those practitioners mentioned previously, together with the *adhibhūta* and the *adhidaiva*—
where *adhibhūta* refers to objects related to the elements and *adhidaiva* refers to objects related to the deities;
while the subject matter related to the *adhyātma* was already stated in the preceding verse— they [attain] that which is distinguished by the *adhibhūta* and the *adhidaiva*.

Thus, those who know Me as being present in the sacrifice (*adhiyajña*)—that is, as related to the sacrifice—and as distinguished by that [sacrifice], they, being of disciplined mind and concentrated heart, know Me even at the time of departure, at the final moment; they shall never forget Me. (30)
Chapter Eight:
Those who worship me in my divine embodied form know me as the formless Brahman.

"They know me as distinguished by the internal, the elemental, and the divine; they also know me as distinguished by the sacrifice. At the end of the previous chapter, it was stated in brief that "they know me even at the time of departure, at the moment of casting off the body.
Desiring to know this in detail, Arjuna said:

What is that Brahman? What is the inner self (adhyātma)? What is action (karma), O Supreme Person? What is declared to be the objective world (adhibhūta), and what is called the divine realm (adhidaiva)? (1)
Who is the Lord of Sacrifice here in this body, O Madhusūdana?
And how are You to be known at the time of death by those of self-restraint?

O Kṛṣṇa, Supreme Person, that Brahman which was previously spoken of by you—what is it, and what is its essential nature? And what is meant by "the field of material elements" (adhibhūta)? And what is expressed here by the term "the field of the gods" (adhidaiva)? O Madhusūdana, who is designated here by the word "the field of sacrifice" (adhiyajña), and how does he abide?
