"In this body" or "in another"—this is the ellipsis. Thus, by those of self-restraint with concentrated minds, how are You to be known at the time of departure, that is, at the final moment? Arjuna awaits the answer to these questions.
The supreme Brahman is the Imperishable; its inherent nature is called the Adhyātma (the internal self).
The creative emission that brings about the origin of the existence of beings is designated as Karma (action). || 3 ||

The Blessed Lord spoke the answers to these questions in due order: That which is supreme, the most excellent, the imperishable—that which does not decay—and the undecaying reality, that alone is Brahman, expressed by the word "Brahman. Its own nature: that which is the very nature of the aforementioned Supreme Brahman is itself...

It is called "internal" (adhyātma). That which brings about the manifestation of the state of beings—that is, the cause of the arising of the nature (bhāva), which is the inherent essence (svabhāva) of all beings or living creatures—is the emission (visarga) consisting of the renunciation of substances for the sake of a deity; that alone is designated as "action" (karman). Sacrifice (yajña) also becomes denoted by the word "action."

Whatever is performed as a form of worship for the sake of satisfying those who know Paraśiva-Brahman, that too becomes a sacrifice; likewise, whatever is done for the sake of removing the suffering of living beings afflicted by distress,
that too [is a sacrifice].

It is indeed sacrifice. From such sacrifice and the like, the origin of all beings is possible through the sequence beginning with rain. Therefore, that alone becomes what is designated by the term "action" (karman).
The perishable state is the object of the physical world (adhibhūta), and the Puruṣa is the presiding deity (adhidaivata);
and I alone am the sacrifice (adhiyajña) here in this body, O best among the embodied beings.

O best among those who bear bodies, O foremost of men, O Arjuna: that which is perishable—that is, subject to destruction—is *adhibhūta*, designated by the term *adhibhūta*. And the *puruṣa* (the individual self) is indeed *adhidaivata*, designated by the word *adhidaivata*. And *adhiyajña* is the deity who presides over all sacrifices.
She also dwells in this body; for it is said, "I am indeed the enjoyer and the Lord of all sacrifices. The *Śaraṇagītā* clearly establishes the omnipresent state of the Supreme Self:
"If one contemplates, 'I worship You,' then there is no body of Yours separate from mine. You...
"If it is perceived that 'I am thinking,' yet there is no mind of yours separate from mine;

O unbroken God, dwelling thus within my body, I am like a glowing camphor. Thus, the Supreme Self alone, remaining in the body, carries out all activities through its servants while remaining entirely unattached.
Having experienced the fruits of their actions, He bestows those very same fruits upon His servants as a mark of grace.
Nevertheless, all of this is known only by those who have direct experience, and not by those who identify with the body.
Those engaged in ritual action are not capable of knowing the Supreme Śiva, whose nature is the Adhiyajña; such is this secret.
The intention of the Blessed One is that, having realized this, a human being, by constantly meditating upon the Lord within his own body, may experience eternal bliss. || 4 ||
And whoever, at the time of death, departs casting off the body while remembering Me alone, attains My state; there is no doubt about this.
He who, always remembering Me alone— the Supreme Self— who dwells within the body for the sake of protecting the individual soul (jīva),
conducts himself in the world with detachment, goes forth at the time of death,
even at the final moment, abandoning the physical body; such a devotee attains My own state.

My own state attains—that is, reaches—the formless condition. Regarding this point, there is no doubt at all. On this matter, the *Śaraṇagītā* intends as follows: "I know that [the world] is Your own body;
therefore, I have no other body whatsoever. For there is no mind distinct from Your mind."

(204) This is my firm conviction: since all wealth belongs to you alone, there is no wealth whatsoever that is separate from you. Having understood these three things of yours to be thus, how indeed could there be any further deliberation? Thus says Basavārya.

He declares his state of total self-surrender to the Supreme Self: "It is indeed the truth that for one who, while remaining in the body, knows the Supreme Self as the sovereign of the body and merges into Him, no other thought remains.
His abiding in the formless state is certain both here and hereafter; whatever state is experienced here is that very same [state]."
And it manifests elsewhere through its eternal nature. || 5 ||
Whatever state of being one remembers when leaving the body at the end,
to that very state one goes, O son of Kuntī, having been constantly absorbed in that state.

To the question "How is this so?", he states that this is the general principle: O Kaunteya Arjuna, whatever state of being— whatever particular object— a person remembers at the end, at the time of death, when they cast off the body,
that very same state they shall attain, for they have been constantly permeated by that state throughout all time.

Being manifested by that very state, he attains it; therefore, there is no doubt that whoever remembers Me at the time of death goes to My very nature. If, at the moment of departure, there were thoughts of a beloved woman or gold, for that reason alone the living being would surely be born again. Whoever, at the time of separation from the body—
He who contemplates the Supreme Self alone becomes that very Supreme Self. || 6 ||
Therefore, at all times, remember Me and fight;
with mind and intellect dedicated to Me, you shall come to Me alone, without doubt.

Thus, recollection of me at the final moment is not easily achieved, but must be accomplished through constant practice. Therefore, O Arjuna, the Blessed Lord instructs what is beneficial: "Think of me not only during the time of worship, but always, even during the time of worldly activity. For that reason, from this very moment onward, remember me at all times.

Reflect on this constantly. While thus remembering Me, engage in battle; and perform the battle that has presented itself as your duty according to My word. In this way, with mind and intellect surrendered to Me alone—by whom the mind and intellect have been cast and deposited—you shall attain Me alone; of this there is no doubt.
There is no possibility whatsoever for doubt. || 7 ||
With a mind disciplined by the yoga of practice and not wandering elsewhere, O Pārtha, one goes to the supreme, divine Person by constantly meditating upon Him. (8)

Having stated the fruit of final recollection, the remainder of the chapter explains that very point because of its supreme importance: "O Pārtha, O Arjuna, with a mind— meaning a mental faculty— that is disciplined by the yoga of practice (wherein practice itself is the yoga), which is not wandering elsewhere but is focused on nothing but That, [one beholds] the divine, which is non-material."

Contemplating, recollecting, and meditating upon the Supreme Person, the Supreme Self, the practitioner attains—that is, reaches—that very same formless Śiva, who is the nature of the supreme light. || 8 ||
One should meditate upon the Poet, the Ancient, the Ruler, subtler than the subtle, the Sustainer of all, whose form is inconceivable, who is resplendent like the sun, beyond darkness. 9.
He explains this very point—namely, what kind of Supreme Self one who is constantly devoted to the yoga of meditation attains—as follows:

[he is] the Seer (*kavi*), whose vision is beautiful; the Ancient (*purāṇa*), meaning eternal; the Instructor (*anuśāsitāra*), the regulator of the entire universe; subtler than the subtle (*aṇoraṇīyāṃsaṃ*), more minute even than the most minute; and the Inner Controller of all.

One who would remember the Supreme Lord, who is formless, the sustainer and creator of the entire world, whose nature is inconceivable— meaning his form cannot even be imagined— endowed with a splendor like that of the sun, and who exists beyond darkness, that is, transcending the darkness of ignorance.
"He goes to such a supreme Person"—this is the connection with what precedes.
At the time of departure, with a steady mind, endowed with devotion and the power of yoga,
having properly fixed the vital breath between the eyebrows, he attains that supreme, divine Person.

An explanation of what was previously stated is provided here: at the time of departure, that is, at the time of the body's end, one who is endowed with a steady and firm mind as well as devotion (*bhakti*), and likewise endowed with the power of yoga— the strength of yoga—
and having properly fixed the vital breath (*prāṇa*) in the space between the eyebrows with vigilance.
The yogin who remains established [in this way] attains—that is, reaches—that aforementioned divine, supreme Person.
That which those who know the Vedas call the Imperishable, that which the ascetics free from passion enter,
and desiring which they lead a life of celibacy— that goal I shall declare to you in brief.
Furthermore, he describes another state of the yogi:

that which the knowers of the Vedas and the knowers of Brahman declare to be the imperishable, immutable, universal support, the form of the indivisible Liṅga— the Supreme Śiva-Brahman— having realized it.

They describe its true nature: that divine, formless state which those ascetics and renunciants—who are free from passion, whose character is dispassion, and who are practitioners desiring to attain all things—practice and perform through celibacy consisting of dwelling in the teacher's house and so forth; that state I shall proclaim to you in brief, in summary.
I shall describe its true nature. || 11 ||
Restraining all the gates [of the senses] and confining the mind within the heart,
placing his own life-breath in the head, he remained established in the practice of yoga-concentration.
Uttering the single-syllable Brahman "Om" and remembering Me, he who departs, casting off the body, attains the supreme goal. (13)
All the doors—the senses, which are the means for the attainment of knowledge—are denoted by the word "doors";

that is, all the sense organs. Having restrained them—that is, having withdrawn them from their objects—and having fixed the mind within the heart, having controlled it, one should place one's own life-breath (prāṇa) in the head, specifically in the *bhāvaliṅga* located there.
Having cast aside the practice of yoga and established himself in the steady holding of yoga— firmly rooted in yoga—

he utters and recites the single syllable "Om," which is the form of the Praṇava, indestructible, non-dual, and the Supreme Brahman known as Paraśiva, the indivisible Liṅga; and he [recites] me, who am its signified meaning, the formless.

Remembering Me with his mind and meditating on Me while abandoning the body—the physical frame—he who departs, going forth from the body, attains the supreme goal, reaching the most excellent state. || 12-13 ||
For that yogi who is constantly and eternally mindful of Me with an undivided mind, O Pārtha, I am easily attained, being ever-disciplined. 14.

Having spoken of the state at the final hour, He now declares the superiority of His own devotee compared to those devoted to other deities. "With a mind fixed on no other" (*ananya-cetāḥ*) means one whose mind or heart is not directed toward anything else, being single-mindedly intent on Me alone. O Pārtha, O Arjuna, for such a person who remembers—that is, meditates upon—Me, the Supreme Self, constantly and always, and who is ever-disciplined (*nitya-yuktasya*):
For that yogi who is constantly absorbed in meditative concentration, I am indeed easily attained; I am accessible with ease.
Having come to Me, these great-souled ones do not undergo rebirth, which is transient and an abode of suffering; they have attained the supreme perfection.

Thus, those great-souled ones— great persons whose minds are fixed elsewhere [in worldly objects] but who have become solely devoted to the Supreme Self, having attained the final perfection which is the fruit of yoga, reach and attain Me, the Supreme Self.

They do not undergo this rebirth, which is an abode of suffering, the substratum of all miseries, impermanent, and transitory; indeed, for them, further attachment to saṃsāra is no longer possible. || 15 ||
All worlds, O Arjuna, up to the realm of Brahmā, are subject to return;
but having attained Me, O son of Kuntī, there is no rebirth. 16.

But for others, however, return is indeed unavoidable; thus he says: "O Arjuna, from the world of Brahmā"—the world of the four-faced Brahmā—up to that limit, all those worlds are *punarāvartinaḥ*, meaning they are of the very nature of returning again. This applies even to those who have reached as far as the world of Brahmā.

The meaning is that for yogins who have not attained oneness with Paraśiva-Brahman, there is indeed rebirth. But, O son of Kuntī, having approached—that is, having attained—Me, the Supreme Self, rebirth does not exist; for them, there is no return at all, just as water poured into water [becomes one]. 16.
Those people who know that the day of Brahmā extends for a thousand yugas,
and that his night likewise ends after a thousand yugas— they are the ones who truly understand day and night.

By stating that even the four-faced Brahmā is impermanent, he establishes the impermanence of the world of Brahmā as well. That period of time which has a thousand yugas as its limit—that is, whose end or conclusion consists of a thousand yugas—is the measure of a day for Brahmā; so say those who know the divisions of day and night.

Those who know the measure of day and night, the experienced ones, understand that the night likewise lasts for a thousand yugas and ends with a thousand yugas. Therefore, the meaning is that even the world of the four-faced Brahmā is indeed limited by time:
"At the arrival of the day, all manifest beings emerge from the unmanifest."
At the arrival of night, they dissolve right there in that which is designated as the unmanifest.

Regarding what occurs on such a day and night, he says: at the arrival of the day, when the time of the sun has come, all manifestations—whether stationary or moving, and so forth—originate from, or manifest from, the unmanifest Pradhāna, the support of all, the formless Supreme Self. In the same way, at the arrival of night, during the time of night...

When that very state designated as the Unmanifest (avyakta) has arrived, they dissolve—that is, they undergo re-absorption—into the Supreme Self (pramātman). Thus, the meaning is that for the four-faced one (Brahmā), the creation of the world occurs during the day, while its dissolution occurs at night. || 18 ||
This very collection of beings, having come into existence again and again, dissolves helplessly at the arrival of night, O Pārtha; it comes forth again at the arrival of day. (19)

If a complete dissolution (pralaya) of all things occurs, then at the time of renewed creation, it must be stated that only entirely new living beings are created. If this were the case, one might ask: "What accounts for the mutual gradations among them? To address this doubt, it follows from the mere acceptance of a complete dissolution that even individual souls (jīvas) are destroyed without exception.
However, they may exist then in an unmanifest state; indeed, at that time, all of them abide within the formless Supreme Self alone.

And at the time of creation, it is these very same beings that become manifest. Thus, since even during the dissolution (pralaya) the individual souls (jīvas) remain in a subtle and unmanifest state, they—endowed precisely with the latent impressions (saṃskāras) of their diverse karmas—reappear at the time of renewed creation.

With the intention that there is no fault whatsoever in the view that this gradation is rooted precisely in such diverse karma from the very beginning of creation, he says: "O Pārtha, that very same host of beings— that collection of living entities which exists even now— having come into being again and again at various times, and having arisen, becomes that very same [host] once more upon the arrival of night."

When the time of night arrives for the aforementioned four-faced one, he dissolves involuntarily and by himself at the time of dissolution; likewise, upon the arrival of day, when the time of daylight has come for the aforementioned four-faced one, he comes forth and is born again.
Therefore, the meaning is that there is no complete destruction of living beings. || 19 ||
But beyond that unmanifested state, there is another eternal unmanifested being, which does not perish even when all beings perish. (20)

Having thus stated that even individual souls (jīvas) are indeed perishable because they are subject to birth and dissolution, he declares that the Supreme Self, which is distinct from them, is eternally of the nature of the Imperishable (akṣara). Therefore, there is another entity— a supreme reality— that excels even the aforementioned unmanifest (avyakta), which has attained a state of unmanifestness at the time of dissolution.

The eternal one, existing always in a single form, unmanifest, and indeed forever of an unmanifest nature, is the formless Supreme Self; He does not perish even when all beings perish at the time of the aforementioned dissolution. || 20 ||
He is called the unmanifest and the imperishable; they say he is the supreme goal, attaining which they do not return—that is my supreme abode.

For this very reason, that unmanifest Supreme Self is said to be the imperishable and indestructible. They declare that very imperishable, formless Paraśiva to be the supreme goal and the ultimate attainment for all people.
[This is] for those who experience Śiva. Why is this so? To this he says "yam" and so forth. Having reached that imperishable state, they do not return;

they do not return again—being liberated from bonds, stainless, and perfected. That supreme abode, that most excellent place, belongs to me alone; thus the Blessed One teaches. Therefore, He alone is [the goal] of all.
To be attained through valid cognition. || 21 ||
That Supreme Person, O Pārtha, is attainable through unswerving devotion alone—He within whom all beings dwell and by whom all this is pervaded. (22)

He states the means for attaining Paraśiva-Brahman: "O Pārtha, He—the Supreme Person (paraḥ puruṣaḥ), the Highest Person (paramapuruṣaḥ), the Supreme Self (paramātmā)—is I. Therefore, it will be stated that the Supreme Self is the "Supreme Person" (puruṣottama) in the verse: "Thus I am celebrated in the world and in the Veda as Puruṣottama. [This is attained] by means of undiverted (ananyayā) devotion—that is, by devotion whose object is none other than Me, having Me alone as its sole object.

He is to be attained and reached through devotion alone— that Supreme Self (paramātman) within whom all beings exist and who is dependent upon Him alone; and by that Supreme Self this entire universe is pervaded— He is the Supreme Person (puruṣa), the Supreme Self whose nature consists of both the formed and the formless.
I shall describe that time, O bull of the Bharatas, at which yogis who have departed go either to non-return or to return. (23)

By the statements, "All worlds up to the realm of Brahmā are subject to return," and "Having attained that, they do not return— that is My supreme abode," it is established that for those who attain the Supreme Self there is no return, whereas for others there is return. Now, for such [beings], the path corresponding to each respective state is also distinct.

To state this, he first makes a formal proposition: "O bull among the Bharatas, Arjuna, I shall declare that time— at which specific occasion and in what manner yogis, having departed and died, go to either return (āvṛtti), that is, come back again, or not return (anāvṛtti), that is, do not come back again."
Listen. || 23 ||
Fire, light, day, the bright fortnight, and the six months of the northern solstice—departing during these, those people who know Brahman go to Brahman. (24)

Agni is the deity presiding over Time; Jyotis is the deity presiding over that [Light]. In this manner, Day, the bright fortnight, the light half of the month, and the six months reckoned as the northern course (uttarāyaṇa)—(p.

Those knowers of Brahman who depart and die during such an auspicious time within those six months do not wander in the wheel of saṃsāra; only the meritorious cast off their bodies at that time. || 24 ||
Smoke, night, as well as the dark fortnight and the six months of the sun’s southern course—having attained the lunar light there, the yogin returns. (25)

In the case of "smoke" and so forth, as before, the deities presiding over each respective element are the meaning. Likewise, night, the dark fortnight, the six months of the southern solstice— that is,
the six months constituting the southern course— and during such a time, the yogi [attains] the lunar light, which is the radiance associated with the moon.
The yogin who is attached to deities other than the Supreme Self, having reached those respective worlds, returns from them; he returns again to take birth here in this world of mortals. (25)
These two paths of the world, the bright and the dark, are considered eternal.
By one a man goes to non-return, by the other he returns again. (26)

For these two paths—the white and the black—are the two eternal and constant ways of the world; there can never be a reversal of this established order of paths. Of these, one who proceeds by the white path attains non-return, that is, no further rebirth; by the other [the black path], he returns.
But the practitioner who has departed by the dark path returns;
he undergoes rebirth and experiences wandering through the wheel of saṃsāra. || 26 ||
Knowing these two paths, O Pārtha, no yogin whatsoever is deluded.
Therefore, at all times, be disciplined in yoga, O Arjuna.
He states the purpose of this instruction on the two paths: O Pārtha, knowing these two paths—this pair of ways—no yogi is deluded; that is, he does not fall under the sway of delusion.
For those who travel by the white path, there is no return; for those who travel by the black path, there is a return.
And the meaning is: how could that yogi who knows this desire for the path of rebirth? For that reason, O Arjuna, remain ever-yoked in yoga at all times;
do not be unyoked from yoga, which is the cause of rebirth conducive to attaining Me.
p.
211) Do not, however, become engaged in the yoga of another deity that is conducive to rebirth;
rather, let the practitioner be devoted to any form whatsoever desired by himself through the contemplation of it as the Supreme Self alone.
He attains only the white path. He who, having realized his own self to be a portion of the Supreme Self,

seeks to experience that Supreme Self dwelling within him, and by means of the contemplation of the vital breath (prāṇa) worships Him externally, thereby attaining constant yoga— he too, proceeding by the white path alone, reaches that very same [Self] previously experienced.

He follows the yoga of Śiva. He who does not know nor practice such a yoga in this very world is one of unsettled mind; for the sake of satisfying his own body, he adopts some deity whatsoever according to the requirements of that particular time, yet he does not contemplate the Supreme Self, who is the soul of all, within that [deity]. He [failing to see] the Self residing in himself...

Not knowing the formless God and being attached only to external pleasures, one goes as far as the world of the moon at the time of the body's end by means of the dark path (*kṛṣṇagati*), and then returns right back here again. Having thus understood the difference between the bright and dark paths, the man of discrimination desires the attainment of the bright path.

One should rely solely on the path that unites knowledge and action (*jñāna-kriyā-samanvaya-mārga*). Those who declare, "No happiness whatsoever is obtained from external worship, nor is any fruit attained through its transformation," are the *śaraṇas*;
they censure external worship which is devoid of the yoga of Śiva within one's own heart. For one [in whom this is so], even at the very time of external worship—

Through the expansion of the heart, the worship of Guheśvara shall proceed perpetually as mere play; he alone, dwelling here in eternal bliss, at the time of separation from the body, taking recourse to the path of *śukra*, experiences the bliss of oneness with Śiva everywhere. He who perceives the phenomenal world through the expansion of the heart [perceives it] everywhere and at all times.
One experiences only the light of the Supreme Self. Its worship is thus described in the *Śaraṇagītā*.
The eight kinds of flowers belonging to it are exceedingly dear to the Supreme Self. Among all living beings, the first flower is the act of pleasing them without any violence.

The restraint of the entire collection of the senses is indeed the second flower to be placed within the heart. Abandoning notions such as "I" and "mine," conduct characterized by tranquility constitutes the third flower. Discarding ill-will that brings unbearable suffering, the union with the true state of being among those of virtuous mind is the fifth flower. One who has enjoyed [the fruits] yet remains fasting.
If one established in Śiva-yoga remains steady, that is the sixth flower;
truthful speech alone, due to its separation from falsehood, is considered the seventh flower;
and the contemplation of Śiva within the entire phenomenal world is proclaimed as the eighth flower itself—in such [a state]...
Having performed a thousand-fold worship with the flower known as the eight-petaled lotus in this world, those who take refuge [in you],

O Kūḍalacannasaṅga, dwell eternally in the state of your own image. Those by whom such worship of the Śaraṇas is thus performed and resorted to, they will certainly become steadfast in the yoga of Śiva.
They attain only the white course. The Blessed One teaches that for the sake of achieving such a supreme fruit, practitioners must always be devoted to Śiva-yoga.
Whatever fruit of merit is declared to come from the Vedas, sacrifices, austerities, and gifts—all that he transcends by knowing this; the yogi attains the supreme, primordial state. (28)

The Blessed One praises those who are steadfast in such yoga of the Supreme Self: "Whatever great fruit of merit— whatever result in the form of merit— is produced when the Vedas have been studied, when sacrifices such as the Agnihotra have been performed, when austerities have been practiced, and likewise when gifts and great donations have been made."

Having understood all that which is prescribed and taught in the scriptures—including all such results—and having known this secret that has been spoken, the yogi, the Śiva-yogi, transcends it; he goes beyond it.
He goes to a station superior even to all of this. He states that very station: "The primordial..."

Such a Śiva-yogin attains—that is, reaches—the supreme and most excellent state, which is Brahman in form and the cause of all, immediately after the separation from the body. He who experiences the bliss of Śiva within this very body of grace (prasādakāya) alone finds that formless happiness consisting of union with Śiva. Thus...
The meaning is that the state attainable by those devoted to Śiva-yoga is indeed superior to all others.
Chapter Nine.
Having thus stated the superiority of the Śiva-yogin over all other types of yogis, now—

Desiring to teach the subject matter useful for Śiva-yoga, the Blessed Lord first spoke as follows to indicate its supreme secrecy and other special qualities: "But this most secret [knowledge] I shall declare to you, who are free from malice."
This knowledge, together with realized wisdom—having known which, you shall be liberated from evil. (1)

But this which is about to be spoken— most secret and to be strictly concealed— I shall declare and tell to you, who are free from malice (*anasūya*) and possessed of good qualities. It is that knowledge which is about to be declared, accompanied by *vijñāna*— that is, distinguished knowledge in the form of direct experience.

Having known and attained [this], you will be liberated from the impure cycle of existence; you will become free. And thus, the knowledge of Śiva alone is that which releases one from the bonds of saṃsāra.

Success is achieved. At that very moment, the living being (jīva), having abandoned its own sense of "I" and "mine" (ahaṅkāra-mamakāra) and so forth, becomes free from worldly desire and free from possessiveness. || 1 ||
This is the king of sciences, the king of secrets, this supreme purifier;
it is directly perceivable, in accordance with dharma, very easy to perform, and imperishable.

The royal science among sciences, the king, the best; for He will say that it is the "science of the supreme self among sciences. The royal secret among secrets, the king, the most hidden; this reality is not easily known by all. This is the highest purifier, the supreme sanctifier even among purifiers.
"Directly perceivable" means that its comprehension is through direct perception; it is capable of being experienced through direct perception.

"In accordance with dharma" means consistent with righteousness. "Easy to perform" means easily accessible. "Imperishable" means, like the act of worshipping the Lord and so forth, it is free from destruction—the word "knowledge" is to be understood as the subject. Thus...

Although knowledge is extremely profound, both the object of knowledge and its practice exist; indeed, the playful manifestation of the Lord residing within the body is known by practitioners with pure hearts. The Lord’s teaching—that for them, such knowledge is a matter of direct perception—is worthy of respect by all.
It should be understood that this is for the purpose of accomplishing the purity of the heart. || 2 ||
O scorcher of foes, those men who lack faith in this dharma do not reach Me, but sink down on the path of the mortal cycle of rebirth.

The Blessed One spoke out of sorrow, thinking that people do not listen to such knowledge, even though it is so easily attained. O scorcher of the foe, Arjuna, those persons who lack faith (*aśraddadhānāḥ*) regarding this aforementioned supreme dharma, failing to reach Me, the Supreme Self—

Not having attained [liberation] on the path of death-bound saṃsāra, they turn back; they revolve again and again, for they do not obtain non-return. Alas! Not attaining the bliss of union with Śiva—the pervasive Lord of the universe—they fall under the power of death, sharing in the suffering of this world and the next.
Such beings, devoid of knowledge, are like animals in their existence. || 3 ||
By me, whose form is unmanifest, all this world is pervaded;
all beings dwell in Me, yet I do not dwell in them.

Having thus praised that which is about to be spoken, he now states the portion that is to be said: by me, the Supreme Self, who am of unmanifest form— that is, by me whose form is not manifest, whose nature is unmanifest— this...

The entire world is spread out and pervaded by Him; therefore, all beings—even all created entities—are situated in Me, being entirely dependent on Me. Nevertheless, I do not abide within those beings, nor am I subject to them.
Even though I exist everywhere, I do not remain under the control of anything—such is the statement of the Blessed Lord regarding the formless Śiva.
It indicates abiding everywhere in a state of non-attachment. || 4 ||
And yet, beings do not dwell in Me; behold My divine yoga!
My Self, the source of all beings, sustains beings but does not dwell within them.

Thus, by abiding in His own singular way, He declares His state of being untainted. "In this manner, I remain untainted"—this indeed is my power related to the Lord. This wonderful and most majestic [Lord], though the sustainer of beings (*bhūtabhṛt*)—even while supporting all beings and being the support of all—is not situated in beings; He does not abide in beings alone.
I abide. This Self of mine is the *svarūpa*, the creator of beings—the progenitor of all creatures. The sense is that Śiva is not only the support of all, but is also the originator of all. || 5 ||
Just as the great wind, moving everywhere, is eternally situated in space,
even so, understand that all beings abide in Me.

He states the aforementioned point with an illustration: Just as the great wind, which is all-pervading and exists everywhere, eternally abides in space— that is, it remains within space— even so, all beings dwell in Me alone, who am of the nature of the subtle body (liṅga), and not elsewhere, like a jar or other objects on the ground.

Understand and ascertain this. Thus, the Lord Mahādeva’s status as the substratum of all has been established through a well-ordered argument. For this very reason, it is appropriate to designate him by the name "Sthala" (the Support). || 6 ||
O son of Kuntī, at the end of a kalpa all beings go to my own nature;
again, at the beginning of a kalpa, I send them forth.

O Kaunteya Arjuna, at the end of the eon, at the time of dissolution, all beings go to— that is, they reach— my own nature, which consists of the three qualities and is my *māyā*; there they become dissolved.
At the beginning of the aeon, at the commencement of creation, I alone again emit those beings born of life;

I produce them. At the time of dissolution, the multitude of things that exist within Māyā in an unmanifest state are manifested externally in a manifest form at the time of creation. Thus, because I am the substratum of the creation and dissolution of all things—

The sense is that the formless Supreme Self (paramātman), whose nature is the indivisible Liṅga, exists everywhere. Thus, having deceived Paraśiva, who is the witness of all, it is not possible for human beings to create anything at all as something new; everything they do is [already contained within] the all-pervading Paraśiva.

It is dependent solely upon His will; therefore, knowing that the entire activity of the universe proceeds only in accordance with His desire, the wise, engaging in worldly affairs as mere instruments, clearly perceive the power of the Divine Self hidden by its own qualities. Everywhere in the world, His...

The *Śaraṇagītā* teaches the vision of the Supreme Self (*paramātma-saṃdarśana*) as follows: Śiva alone, shining forth with detachment within all things, is perceived by them. The conduct of those who have sought refuge in Him is described therein as follows: "You alone are the mother and you alone are the father; you alone are the kinsman; you alone are [all]."

In the same way, [you are] my friend. O venerable Sangāryadeva, listen to my words: there is no one else for me but you. Act as you see fit—either milk me or cast me into water. Thus did those who had sought refuge place the heavy burden of their own welfare and security upon him who shines both within and without.

They surrender unto the Supreme Lord alone. Such unwavering faith must necessarily be cultivated and increased at every moment by those who are striving for progress. One devoid of faith never finds happiness nor attains peace. Thus, it is precisely to generate self-confidence within all practitioners that [this is taught].
Although the Blessed One possesses a physical body, he teaches his own all-pervasiveness with illustrative examples while remaining in his own formless state. (7)
Taking hold of my own nature,
I send forth again and again this entire multitude of beings, which is powerless under the sway of nature.

He elucidates the very same intention stated previously: having taken hold of— meaning having brought under control and pervaded— my own *prakṛti*, this entire multitude of beings (*bhūtagrāma*), which is helpless and dependent on *prakṛti*, [I project] again and again solely by the power of *prakṛti* and its dependence upon that.

I emit [the world] according to the sequence of each preceding karma; I create only those things that are under the supreme control of *prakṛti*. The Supreme Self creates every object solely in accordance with its respective *prakṛti*.

Objects composed of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas* are created precisely as distinguished by their respective qualities. If the association with these qualities is abandoned by living beings through the power of Śiva-yoga, then their rebirth is indeed obstructed.
As long as the connection with the qualities persists, for that long all living beings [remain bound].
They indeed wander in the wheel of birth and death; all things manifest themselves solely in accordance with their respective natures.
And those actions do not bind me, O Dhanañjaya,
because I sit as if indifferent, unattached to those actions.

Thus, because I am the cause of creation in accordance with each respective karma, He says that I have no attachment therein: "O Dhanañjaya (Arjuna), [behold] Me existing (*āsīnam*) among those activities of the world such as creation and so forth, like one who is indifferent (*udāsīnavat*), like a spectator, unattached (*asaktam*) and free from clinging (*saṅgarahitam*). Those actions...

The activities of creation and so forth do not bind, nor indeed do they cause one to be bound. Bondage accrues only to one who is attached to action; for me, however, who am unattached, no taint of action is possible. Thus, all human beings [should perform] their own activities without self-interest.

If they should act out of a sense of duty in accordance with the Lord’s impulsion, then they would never experience suffering; it is this very arrangement for eternal happiness that the Lord reveals here through His noble intention. Attachment to the fruit alone binds everyone to action.

Engaging in worldly affairs with the vision of duty makes those who engage in them eternally happy. Just as the Blessed Lord remains untainted even while carrying out everything, so too should we, as His portions, strive to act with detachment; such is the intention of the Blessed One. 9.
Under my supervision, Nature produces the world of the moving and the unmoving;
by this cause, O son of Kuntī, the universe revolves.

In response to the doubt that the statement "I create" appears to be mutually contradictory with the description [of Me] as "sitting like one indifferent," the following resolution is stated: O Kaunteya, by Me acting as the presiding authority (adhyakṣeṇa), Nature (prakṛti) brings forth—produces—the entire world, including all things moving and unmoving; for it is only when presided over by the Supreme Self (paramātma-adhiṣṭhitā) that it acts.
The meaning is that primordial nature (prakṛti) becomes the cause of the world. For this reason—that is, solely by virtue of being presided over by Me—the world revolves.

It transforms into various forms. Indeed, in the absence of the Supreme Self’s presiding presence, primordial nature (*prakṛti*) would not create the world at all. Thus, there is no contradiction in the sense that, although I am the cause in one respect, I am also indifferent in another respect. However, because of the independence of the Supreme Self, both states are established within Him; He alone [is the ultimate agent].

Because it transforms into the form of the born, because it accomplishes all effects by its own presence through its inherent nature, and because it remains indifferent toward those very things already created, everything indeed becomes established in it. || 10 ||
Fools disregard me when I have assumed a human form, being ignorant of my supreme nature as the Great Lord of all beings. 11.

Foolish people, lacking discrimination, do not know my supreme, most excellent state— the previously mentioned formless nature— and thus fail to recognize me as the Great Lord of beings who, for the sake of the world's welfare alone,
has assumed a human body connected with the human race.

They disregard me— the formless Supreme Self, the Lord of even those lords and controllers such as Indra who exist— and treat me with contempt, regarding me with the notion that I am an ordinary man. || 11 ||
Futile in hope, futile in action, and futile in knowledge, they are devoid of discernment;
they have taken refuge in a delusive nature that is both demonic and asuric.
And he says that this is the nature of the dull-witted, who are of the character of Asuras and Rākṣasas and are of a *tāmasa* disposition:

"Their hopes are vain. Those whose hopes (*āśā*) are vain—that is, fruitless—for them, even though they know [the truth], their hope will never at all bear fruit. Like Hiraṇyakaśipu, Rāvaṇa, and others, even though they set out to conquer the three worlds itself...

In the end, they will certainly not remain; their destruction is inevitable. For this very reason, they are of futile actions—all the deeds performed by them are indeed fruitless. Likewise, they are of futile knowledge—even their knowledge of the scriptures and so forth becomes entirely useless. Rāvaṇa, too—

It is well known that he had reached the further shore of the knowledge of the four Vedas; for this very reason, they were bewildered, their minds dissolved, lacking discrimination. Moreover, they resorted to and were possessed by a demonic and Rākṣasa nature that causes delusion. Such people, perceiving me as a mere mortal and failing to know me according to reality—

They disregard me; having reflected according to their own nature, they meditate accordingly. They must inevitably experience the fruit of that action. Because they have not attained familiarity with divine nature, such conduct is pleasing to them.
But the high-souled ones, O Pārtha, having taken refuge in my divine nature, worship me with undivided minds, knowing me as the imperishable source of all beings. (13)

He here points out the true disposition of the high-souled ones who are distinguished by their divine nature: "O Pārtha Arjuna, the high-souled ones who have taken refuge in the divine nature perceive Me— the origin of beings, the cause of all beings, the imperishable, who exists everywhere due to My changelessness— with minds focused on no other."

Those of meager intellect resort to and serve [the former]. Those filled with divine nature (daivī-saṃpad) know Me as I truly am, honor Me, and indeed receive My grace; however, those filled with demoniac nature (āsurī-saṃpad), being unable to know or honor Me in this way, do not even attain My favor. For those of evil desires—

In their lives, however, peace is not seen; for it will be explained in detail later that "the divine endowment is considered to lead to liberation, while the demonic leads to bondage. This is the nature of these dispositions.
Constantly glorifying me, striving with firm vows, and bowing down to me with devotion, they worship me, ever-disciplined. (14)

To explain how those endowed with divine nature worship the Supreme Self, He says: "Worshipping Me as the Supreme Lord, engaged in self-restraint, austerity, and charity, and practicing the conquest of the senses and so forth; firm in their vows, steady in their resolve, and established in mind;
and bowing down to Me, offering salutations—thus ever-disciplined, they are always possessed of concentrated minds."
They worship me with devotion. Their way of life is perfectly described in the *Śaraṇagītā*:

"Neither by day nor by night, neither by day nor by night, I know not what I am doing; 'whatever is mine'—having completely forgotten my body and composed my mind, I have united myself in yoga with Your lotus feet. Thus...
But those who have chosen the divine nature always delight in the Lord alone; therefore, for them, worldly existence shines as being endowed with substantial reality. (14)
Others also, sacrificing with the sacrifice of knowledge, worship me as one,
as distinct, and manifoldly as the one whose face is everywhere.

In this very context, the different modes are stated: "But others, the worshippers, worship Me even by means of the sacrifice of knowledge—some as one, some as distinct, and some in many ways; some [worship] the one Supreme Brahman alone as all-pervading, while others worship the one Brahman itself as distinct [deities] such as Indra, Candra, and so forth."
(219) Others, however, say that the Supreme Brahman exists in many ways as the infinite form; because it has attained a manifold state,
I am "facing all directions," all-pervading, existing as one, as distinct, and in many ways.
Having known [this], they worship; that is, they perform worship. || 15 ||

To explain that because He Himself faces all directions, any form of worship whatsoever is appropriate for Him with the thought "I alone am everything," He declares His own nature as the Self of all through four verses:
"I am the sacrifice; I am the oblation; I am the ancestral offering; I am the medicinal herb."
I am the mantra, I alone am the clarified butter, I am the fire, and I am the oblation.

The *kratu*, such as the *agnihotra* and other Vedic rituals, is indeed myself; all ritual action performed by those following the Vedas is also myself. Likewise, even sacrifice (*yajña*) in the form of the worship of the Guru, the *liṅga*, and the *jaṅgama* is the Supreme Brahman itself. The meaning is that even rites such as the ancestral offerings (*śrāddha*) are of the very nature of the Blessed Lord. Medicine is the remedy for disease.

The very nature of the Lord is [the fire]. Although the fire is the substratum for the oblation, it is indeed the very nature of the Lord. Whatever act of offering (*havana*) is performed as an oblation therein, that too is myself alone. At that very time, the Guru and the *Jaṅgama*, who are of the nature of fire, are also to be worshipped through the contemplation (*bhāvanā*) of them as the Supreme Brahman. Whatever is offered with satisfaction for their gratification, that too—
It should be contemplated as being of the very nature of the Supreme Brahman. || 16 ||
He is the grandfather of the world, the mother, the creator, and the great-grandfather; he is that which is to be known, the purifier, the syllable Om, and indeed the Rig, Sāman, and Yajur Vedas.

I alone am the father, the progenitor, of this world; I am the mother, the progenitress; I am the sustainer, the ordainer of the fruits of actions; I am the grandfather, the father of the father; I am that which is to be known, the object of knowledge, the purifier, the sanctifying syllable *Oṃ*; I am the *Ṛg*, the *Sāman*, and the *Yajus*—all three Vedas, indeed, am I alone. Thus it should be understood: I am everything that is expounded by all the Vedas.

The fool, not realizing that "I am indeed the Supreme Reality," conceives of me as a mere human being; consequently, he does not place his trust in my words, which are for the benefit of all people. For him, total ruin is certain to occur—ruin not only for me, but for everyone, because he disregards that which truly exists everywhere as a portion of the Divine.
p.

220) He alone becomes filled with bliss (*ānandamaya*). Therefore, having realized the all-pervasiveness of the Blessed One and acting accordingly, a human being shall accomplish his own welfare. || 17 ||
He is the goal, the sustainer, the lord, the witness, the abode, the refuge, the friend, the source of origin, the dissolution, the station, the treasure-store, and the imperishable seed. (18)
He is the goal, the fruit of karma, the sustainer, the nourisher, the lord, the master capable of protecting all,
the witness who observes both dharma and adharma, the abode which is the ground fit for all to dwell upon,
the refuge and protector of the distressed, the friend who benefits everyone, the source from which all originate, and the dissolution.

Abode, stability, treasure—meaning that which is to be enjoyed at a later time—the deposit of living beings in the form of jewels and so forth, and the imperishable seed existing through the three periods of time which is the cause of sprouting—all this is indeed I alone. The formless Supreme Śiva, the support of all, transforms Himself into infinite forms in order to carry out the activities of the universe; He alone is [all this].
The seed becomes the sprout, the tree, and the fruit; such is its transformation, a manifestation of its perfection and sovereignty. Therefore, it remains the attractor of all:
"I burn, I withhold rain, and I release it."
I am both immortality and death, O Arjuna; I am being and non-being. (19)

O Arjuna, I heat the world through the sun and dry it up; I withhold the rain, and I alone send it forth. I alone am the creator of rain and the withdrawer of rain. I am both the nectar of the gods and the death of mortals. That which is related to this "Being" (sat) is indeed "Being."

Both of these—the unrelated and the unreal—are indeed myself alone. However, here the word "unreal" (*asat*) does not refer to something entirely non-existent; rather, even that which is devoid of knowledge (*avidyā*) and every object is the very nature of the Blessed Lord. It should be contemplated that both that which is of the nature of nectar, such as happiness, and that which is of the nature of death, such as suffering, are the very nature of the Supreme Brahman. For this very reason, for those who possess knowledge of reality (*tattvajñānin*),...

Having become possessed of equal vision toward the world, they conduct themselves with peace. Those who desire spiritual growth must certainly practice the vision of equality in order to carry out worldly affairs that are inherently uneven in form. Otherwise, as with the experience of praise and pleasure, men must likewise master the experience of blame and suffering; such was the intention of the Blessed One.
He clarifies [this]. || 29 ||

(221) Thus, with two verses he says that those who worship only this or that particular form, while neglecting the Reality which exists as all forms, obtain only that which corresponds to it— namely, something perishable.
The knowers of the three Vedas, drinkers of Soma, purified of sin, having worshipped Me with sacrifices, pray for the way to heaven;
reaching the holy world of the lords of men, they enjoy divine pleasures in heaven like the gods. (20)

The *traividyāḥ* are those who know the three Vedas—the *Ṛg*, *Yajur*, and *Sāma*—and are solely devoted to the ritual section (*karmakāṇḍa*). They are *somapāḥ*, meaning "drinkers of Soma. By that drinking of Soma, they have their sins purified and are rendered completely cleansed. Having worshipped me through sacrifices such as the Soma sacrifice, they pray for, or desire, the goal of heaven—that is, the fruit consisting of the heavenly realm. And they...
Having reached and attained that merit— the world of the Lord of Gods, the world of the Sovereign of Devas, the heaven— which is the fruit of that merit,

they enjoy and experience in that celestial realm of the gods the divine enjoyments of the gods, those pleasures which belong to the gods. If action is performed with a view solely toward enjoyment, setting aside contact with the Supreme Self, then in this case—

Although it is possible to experience happiness in heaven, even so, that happiness will not be long-lasting. The practitioner shall enjoy only as much happiness as lasts for the duration of the fruit of his karma; beyond that, he shall never obtain further happiness.
Having enjoyed that vast heavenly world, they enter the world of mortals when their merit is exhausted.
Thus, following the dharma of the three Vedas and desiring objects of desire, they obtain the state of coming and going.

And those men, having enjoyed that vast and extensive heavenly world and its pleasures, enter— that is, reach— this mortal world again once the merit that was the cause for experiencing them has been exhausted. Thus, they have followed and resorted to the *trayī-dharma*, the dharma of sacrifice and so forth as declared in the Vedas.

People who desire objects of pleasure, longing only for those desires and not desiring the Self, obtain the state of going and returning— that is, coming and going— and do not attain the state of non-return. Thus,
performing sacrifices and other rites out of a longing for enjoyment, they obtain only such a meager fruit.
Having obtained [objects of enjoyment] and experiencing them, they are born again and again for that very purpose;

their wandering in the wheel of saṃsāra is thus inevitable. Therefore, those possessed of discernment should abandon the path of worldly enjoyment and, by regarding such enjoyment as a grace from the Lord, employ it toward the attainment of their own spiritual welfare. 21
For those people who worship Me, thinking of no other,
and who are ever-devoted, I provide for their acquisition and preservation.

But regarding those who do not desire objects of desire in this way, but instead take refuge in Me alone, He says that for them there is no fear whatsoever: "Those people who are *ananya*— that is, devoid of any other purpose— who are practitioners [of yoga], [take refuge] in Me alone..."
Thinking of Me alone, they worship Me, attending upon Me from every side—both within and without.

For those who are constantly devoted, eternally intent on Me, and bound to Me on all sides, I provide their *yogakṣema*: *yoga* is the attainment of what has not been attained, and *kṣema* is the preservation of that which has been attained.

I carry and sustain both of those. Here, the term *nityābhiyukta* (constantly engaged) illuminates Śiva’s eternal engagement (*nityābhiyoga*). Therefore, this constant engagement indicates that the Supreme Self, who exists in the form of the *liṅga*, is maintained within the body precisely in the form of the *liṅga*. For the Supreme Self resides in the heart.

It is indeed heard that [the Lord] shines forth, measured by the size of a thumb. If contact with Him alone is conceived even externally, then and only then will constant application toward Him arise in the devotee. Such application is not possible without wearing the *liṅga* on the body. Only for those endowed with such constant application...
The Blessed One promises here: "I shall carry the acquisition and preservation (yogakṣema) of true devotees.
By such holding alone, the practitioner attains eternal contact with the Supreme Self.
Through such contact, the body of the practitioner becomes purifying as it consists of mantra. It is only one who possesses such a body [who...]

The devotee shall become a recipient of the Lord's grace; indeed, no thought of sin shall arise in him. Thus, through constant application to the Supreme Self, the practitioner’s right understanding and right contemplation are made firm.
Such constant application is preserved word-for-word and meaning-for-meaning by Vīraśaivism, whereas for others—

Even in the absence of external dhāraṇā, the constant recollection of the names of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), when practiced perpetually, brings about perpetual application (*nityābhiyoga*). Therefore, it is the intention of the Blessed One that all practitioners must always perform the recollection of the Supreme Self with a living faith. Although this applies to all...

The Blessed Lord alone is the bestower of all fruits; nevertheless, for those who seek specific fruits, He acts as their protector only in accordance with their respective actions, and not directly. However, for those who do not expect the fruit of their own actions, because they lack any connection between action and fruit, the Blessed Lord Paraśiva is their protector directly.
This indeed is the distinction conceived by the Blessed One among devotees who offer with desire and those who offer without desire.

Now, one might object: even those devotees who worship other deities for the sake of specific fruits actually worship the formless Supreme Śiva alone, since it is heard in the scriptures, recorded in the traditional texts, and experienced that He alone exists in every form.

Nevertheless, even they would be worshippers of the Blessed One alone. Therefore, what is the distinction between those who worship the Supreme Self and those who worship other deities? To this he says: "Even those who are devotees of other deities and worship them, endowed with faith..."
They too, O son of Kuntī, sacrifice to me alone, though not according to the prescribed rules.
O Kaunteya, even those who are devotees of other deities— those who worship other gods— if they are endowed with faith and disciplined, they worship Me alone, the formless Śiva; however,
they do so according to improper rites (avidhipūrvakam), due to the absence of the knowledge that the formless Śiva alone is the inner controller of all and is to be worshipped everywhere.

It is precisely because they lack the ritual procedure corresponding to that [formless reality] that they worship me, Śiva, as formless. And thus, according to the maxim that "what is performed without the prescribed rule is as if not performed at all," such worship of a material form conducted without the proper rite does not, in reality, constitute the worship of the formless.

Therefore, their fruit also becomes exactly in accordance with that; this alone is the distinction between those who are devotees of the formless Śiva and those who worship other embodied forms. Even those who worship the physical form are indeed worshippers of the formless one residing within it.
Furthermore, those who worship the sign of Prāṇa known as the formless (amūrta) indeed merge into Prāṇa and experience eternal bliss.

Those who worship the formed (mūrta), however, experience momentary worldly pleasures and subsequently become partakers of suffering. But those who desire eternal happiness, even at the time of worshipping the formed, [should focus on the formless].
The intention of the Blessed One is that if they were to conceive of the formless state alone, then they would have accomplished all that was to be done. || 23 ||
For I alone am the enjoyer and also the Lord of all sacrifices;
yet they do not recognize Me in truth, and therefore they fall.

He explains this very point—that they sacrifice without following the prescribed rules—by stating: "I alone am the Lord of all sacrifices, including those prescribed by the Śruti and Smṛti; I am indeed the protector and the regulator of them all. However, those persons who perform actions out of a desire for results, seeking worldly fruits, [worship] Me as such."
They do not recognize [it] in its true essence as a reality; therefore, they fall away and do not attain that fruit. || 24 ||
Those devoted to the gods go to the gods; those devoted to the ancestors go to the ancestors; those who worship the spirits go to the spirits; and those who sacrifice to me go to me as well. (25)

Those who worship other deities do not obtain the fruit of worshipping the Formless; rather, they certainly obtain the fruit of those respective actions. This is stated as follows: "Devoted to the gods" (*devavratāḥ*) means those whose vows (*vratāni*) are connected to various specific deities.
Such devotees go to—that is, attain—those very gods as the result [of their worship]. Thus...

Those who are devoted to the ancestors (*pitṛvrata*) and worship the ancestors as their deities go to the ancestors. Likewise, those who worship the spirits (*bhūta*), such as Vināyaka, Subrahmaṇya, and other hosts of spirits, go to those very spirits.
But those who sacrifice to me—those who worship me, the Supreme Self, whose nature consists of both the manifest and the unmanifest—they [attain me].
They go to me alone, the formless Supreme Self; as was previously stated: "The worshippers of the gods go to the gods, but my devotees come to me as well. (25)
Whoever offers Me with devotion a leaf, a flower, a fruit, or water— that offering made with devotion by one of purified soul, I accept.

He further states that my worship as the Supreme Self is exceedingly easy compared to the worship of other deities: "I do not expect any greater gain from my devotees; I am satisfied simply by whatever is offered to me with devotion—be it a leaf, a flower, a fruit, or at the very least, water."

Or, whoever with devotion and affection gives or offers [something] to me—one who is self-restrained and pure of heart—I accept and take that very thing offered through devotion with contentment. The sense is this: devotion alone is required by me, and no other collection of material objects. || 26 ||
Whatever you do, whatever you eat, whatever you offer in sacrifice, whatever you give, and whatever austerity you practice, O Kaunteya, perform that as an offering unto Me. 27.

For this very reason, Kṛṣṇa teaches here not only to Arjuna, but to all practitioners, the state of total surrender: "O Kaunteya! Whatever action you perform, whatever food you eat from time immemorial, whatever oblation such as clarified butter you offer in sacrifice, and whatever you give to those who have come to your home—"
Whatever you perform, such as acts of charity and the like, and whatever austerity you practice—that entire austerity, offer it as an offering unto Me;
surrender it to Me alone, the formless Supreme Self who dwells within your own inner heart. The Supreme Self is to be sought by devotees within their own hearts alone. [The body...]
p.

225) Thus it is reckoned as a temple by those who possess direct experience. Therein, the Lord dwelling in an unmanifest state is to be experienced by practitioners through the state of total self-surrender (*sarvārpaṇa*). [This is from] the *Śaraṇagītā* of the devotee.
Thus he describes the state of total self-surrender: "Make my body a drumstick, and likewise my head a gourd; fashion my veins into strings and my fingers into wooden blocks;
striking my chest, produce within yourself the victorious sound of your own voice."

O noble Saṅgama! Thus, only by dedicating all the instruments of the body and so forth to the Supreme Self with devotion do human beings become partakers of His grace. Without the renunciation that takes the form of offering, the bliss of yoga cannot be attained by anyone. Therefore, all people engaged in worldly affairs [should offer everything] to Him whose nature consists of both the manifest and the unmanifest.

The Blessed One observes that by surrendering their own happiness for the sake of their own kingdom, and by establishing a sense of brotherhood with all those residing there, they should dwell with contentment and respect, so that at the time of departure they may experience peace. 27.

Thus, through the bonds of action consisting of the fruits of both the auspicious and the inauspicious, you—whose self is disciplined by the yoga of renunciation—being liberated, shall come unto Me. (28)

Thus, he states the fruit of this entire surrender to the Blessed One: when such surrender has been performed, you will be liberated from the bonds of auspicious and inauspicious karma—that is, from the means of bondage consisting of the form of action. Therefore, with your self united through the yoga of renunciation, [offer yourself] to Me, who am of formless nature and who shine both externally and internally.

Surrender to the Supreme Lord—that is, offering oneself—is itself yoga; he whose self (the mind) is endowed with that [yoga] is such a person. Being thus liberated, you shall be freed from saṃsāra itself and attain Me, the Supreme Self.
[Objection: In that case, it must be said that You are partial, since You bestow grace only upon Your own devotees.
"You exercise restraint toward those who are not devoted; thus, since these [actions] are rooted in passion and hatred, you too must surely have enemies, friends, and so forth. To this, He says:
"I am equal toward all beings; there is none hateful to Me, nor any dear."
But those who worship me with devotion, they are in me, and I am also in them.
I, the Blessed One, dwell with perfect equanimity toward all beings and living creatures, viewing them all with an equal eye.
I have no partiality toward anyone; therefore, to me, neither an enemy nor a foe is hateful, nor is a friend dear.

There is no one who is not my friend in this world; all are indeed mine. Nevertheless, those who hate me experience the fruit of hatred, and those who please me likewise experience the fruit of pleasing me—and I am present within them as well. Thus, there is no distinction between me and my devotee, for my devotee is indeed myself.

The Beloved [says]: "Thus, devotion alone is the root of my sense of 'belonging' toward those who abide as devotees; it is not that I am showing partiality toward them. In this way, the Blessed One clarifies his own intention. The *Śaraṇagītā* perfectly demonstrates the sense of belonging that exists within the Supreme Self toward the devotee, because—

"Indeed, nothing belongs to me; you alone are everything, O Noble One, through union with the Guru. Having understood the Veda which conveys the meaning that there is no difference between the devotee and the Lord, and having touched the Lord dwelling within the heart, one attains non-difference even in this very world. Thus [is described] devotion, which is a constituent part of consciousness.
By this power, a human being, having meditated upon Śiva within his own body and worshipped him, becomes Śiva himself and is able to experience His unbroken bliss. || 29 ||
But even if one of very wicked conduct worships Me with undivided devotion,
he must be regarded as righteous indeed, for he has rightly resolved.

Even if one is of very bad conduct, even if he is possessed of extremely contemptible behavior, if he is an exclusive devotee (*ananyabhāk*)— meaning he possesses exclusive devotion— and worships me, he is to be regarded, that is, known, as a saintly person (*sādhu*) alone, whose nature is virtuous conduct; for (*hi*),
because he is one whose resolve is perfect (*samyagvyavasitaḥ*), being endowed with right determination, therefore he shall indeed become a saintly person.

It is known by those who have experienced it: even though the Supreme Self is thus extremely easy to attain for all, He merely observes their inclination toward renunciation. Even a person who has committed a great sin attains self-purification by experiencing remorse for his own sinful deeds; and thereafter—
Through the grace of the Supreme Self, he becomes one who conducts himself rightly; all of this is considered to be the true fruition of heartfelt repentance.
He quickly becomes righteous in soul and attains eternal peace;
O son of Kuntī, declare this with certainty: my devotee never perishes.
Even though he is possessed of evil conduct, by means of devotion, he very quickly—indeed, immediately—becomes a righteous soul, firmly established in dharma.

By that power, he attains and reaches eternal, perpetual peace. O Kaunteya, my devotee—one endowed with devotion to Me—never perishes; he never meets with destruction. This is the meaning: "Understand this. Thus, through self-confidence alone, a human being finds happiness. 31.
For even those who may be of low birth—women, vaiśyas, and likewise śūdras—even they, O Pārtha, attain the supreme goal by taking refuge in me. (32)
How much more so, O meritorious brahmins, and likewise royal sages devoted to me! Having reached this world which is impermanent and full of suffering, worship me. (33)
O Pārtha, for indeed, by taking refuge in me— the Supreme Self— whosoever they may be, even those of sinful birth, such as women, Vaiśyas, or Śūdras,
they too attain the supreme goal, which is the highest liberation. This being so, what need is there to mention those of virtuous birth?

If even Brahmins, devoted ones, and royal sages such as Janaka and others go to the Supreme Self alone and become dissolved therein through the state of equanimity (samarasatā), what more need be said? Therefore, you too, having reached this human world which is impermanent, momentary, and devoid of happiness, [should strive for the Supreme].

Having attained such supreme human status in the world of men, recognize Me—the formless Supreme Self—residing right within your own heart; and having thus conceived of Me, worship and take refuge in Me with devotion. (32-33)
Fix your mind on Me, be devoted to Me, sacrifice to Me, and bow down to Me.
Thus, with your self disciplined and making Me your supreme goal, you shall come to Me alone. 34.

He now describes the very method for worshipping the Supreme Self: "Be one whose mind is fixed on Me (*manmanā bhava*)," meaning become such that your mind is directed toward Me; likewise, "be My devotee" (*madbhaktaś ca bhava*); furthermore, "be My sacrificer" (*madyājī*), meaning a worshipper of Me;
and likewise, "bow down to Me alone" (*mām eva namaskuru*). Having thus united and joined yourself with the Self in this way, be one who has Me as your supreme goal (*matparāyaṇaḥ*).
Thinking that Me alone is the supreme goal to be attained, you shall come— that is, you shall reach—
Me alone. In this way, the Blessed One spoke without guile in order to make all practitioners fix their minds on the Supreme Self.
In the tenth chapter,

beginning with the words "But this most secret thing I shall declare to you," the Blessed One teaches His own essential nature and points out that devotion to Him alone is the means to liberation. In that very [chapter]:
In order to teach in detail, in this chapter, the subjects that must necessarily be known regarding the true nature of the Blessed Lord,
the Blessed One said: "O mighty-armed one, listen to My supreme word, which is indeed the truth."
That which I shall speak to you, who are pleased with me, out of a desire for your welfare.

O mighty-armed Arjuna! Listen once again to my supreme and most excellent word; that speech which, out of a desire for your welfare and wishing your benefit, I shall speak to you who take pleasure in Me and show affection toward My subject, and not out of self-praise. (1)
Neither the hosts of gods nor the great seers know my origin;
for I am the source of the gods and the great seers in every respect.
Even the hosts of gods, including the divine assembly headed by Brahmā, did not know—did not understand—my power and majesty;
nor did the great sages, such as Bhṛgu and others, know it. To the question "Why do they not know?
he says: "I... and so forth; for [it is because] of the gods beginning with Brahmā and of the great sages beginning with Bhṛgu...
I alone am the primordial source and the root cause in every respect and in every way; therefore, how could they know me? || 2 ||
He who knows Me as unborn and beginningless, the Great Lord of the worlds—
he, undeluded among mortals, is liberated from all sins.

Among mortals—among human beings—he who knows Me as the unborn, devoid of origin, and the Great Lord of the worlds—the supreme, unsurpassed Sovereign of the worlds—and who, being undeluded, free from delusion, and possessed of discernment, knows this, is liberated from all sins;
that is, he is completely released even from all kinds of sins. Thus...
The Blessed One teaches that through the knowledge of the Supreme Self alone, all impurities are destroyed. || 3 ||
Intellect, knowledge, delusion, forgiveness, truth, self-restraint, tranquility, pleasure, pain, birth, death, fear, and even fearlessness; || 4 ||
Non-violence, equanimity, contentment, austerity, charity, fame, and infamy—these various states of beings arise from Me alone. (5)

Buddhi is the capacity of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*). Jñāna is the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*). Asaṃmoha is correct discernment (*viveka*). Kṣamā is the state of an unagitated mind. Satya is the speaking of things exactly as they have been perceived. Dama is...

Victory over the external senses; tranquility is victory over the internal organ; pleasure is bliss; pain is distress; existence is the arising of things; non-existence is their destruction; fear is terror;
fearlessness is the state of being free from terror; non-violence is the non-affliction of living beings; equanimity is even-mindedness; contentment is satisfaction.

Contentment; austerity, such as bodily mortification and the like; charity, which is renunciation; fame, which is renown; infamy, which is ill-repute—such various and manifold states of beings, that is, the mental dispositions of living creatures, arise and originate from Me alone, having Me as their sole cause. (4–5)
The seven great sages of old and likewise the four Manus—possessing my own nature, they were born from my mind; from them these creatures in this world have descended.
The seven great sages, Bhṛgu and the others, as well as the four past Manus, were of My nature— distinguished by their state of being absorbed in Me—
and were born from My mind, produced by Me through the mind alone. From these Manus, whose progeny remain in this world, such Manus were born from Me alone.
He who knows this glory and this yoga of Mine in their true essence is united with unwavering yoga; of this there is no doubt.

He who knows— truly and as it is— this majesty (*vibhūti*) spoken by Me, this divine sovereignty (*aiśvara vaibhava*), and that Yoga which is the capacity for its manifestation, he is joined with an unshakable, very firm, and well-established Yoga— that is, he attains such a Yoga, namely Śiva-yoga; this is the meaning.
In this matter, there is no doubt. || 7 ||
"I am the source of all; from me everything proceeds.
Thinking thus, the wise, filled with devotion, worship me. (8)

Here he points out the manner of his own vessel: I alone am the source—the cause of origin—of the entire world. Therefore, it is from me alone that everything, including creation, maintenance, and dissolution, proceeds.
Having understood and known this with such a conviction, the wise, the possessors of knowledge, endowed with true contemplation, [realize it].

(230) They worship and serve me. The *Śaraṇagītā* describes this very process of the wise worshipping the Supreme Self as follows: having filled [the mouth] with the nectar of His name through speech, and having completely filled the eyes with His form, [one should place Him] in the mind.

"O noble one who has attained the company of the Guru, having filled my ears with the remembrance of Him and having filled them with His glory, I am thus a bee submerged in the nectar of Your lotus feet. In this way, even regarding all the senses,
the wise dwell finding their delight and ultimate rest solely in the contact with the Supreme Self, conceiving it as such.
With their minds fixed on me and their lives surrendered to me, awakening one another and constantly speaking of me, they are both satisfied and delighted.
"With minds fixed on Me"—those whose consciousness is centered solely on Me, who are absorbed in meditation upon Me;

"with life-breaths gone to Me"—those whose very vital energies have entered into Me. Such as these, mutually awakening one another, making known My glory, and speaking of Me in accordance with that, [should engage] only in discourse concerning Me.

Performing these [acts], they are satisfied; being contented, they dwell within this very body, and in that Supreme Self alone, they find delight. The *Śaraṇagītā* thus describes the bliss of true devotees: "Having become satisfied by hearing the accounts of Śambhu, and likewise having performed the glorification of Śiva, and having reflected in that same way, even without..."

Performing service to Him with such diligent effort, and expanding worship according to the prescribed method toward the independent *mūrti*, the *guru-siddha-liṅga*, and Śiva— the worthy refuge— one should constantly contemplate Him. Having devotedly offered His belongings and those belonging to His retinue, being solely intent on Bhava, one becomes Śiva Himself.

"He is a devotee right here. Thus, by hearing news of Śiva, by chanting the praises of Śiva, by meditating on Śiva, by worshipping Śiva, and by offering objects related to Śiva to the devotees of Śiva, a human being who conducts himself with single-minded devotion to Śiva shall become Śiva himself; it cannot be otherwise. This is certain.
Those who have sought refuge manifest trust. || 9 ||
To those who are constantly devoted and worship Me with love,
I give that yoga of discernment by which they come to Me.

To those who are constantly disciplined, who are ever-yoked to Me, and who worship and serve Me with love— I grant that same yoga of intellect, the yoga of knowledge. This applies to those who are perpetually immersed in contemplation of the Supreme Self, who perform worldly activities with faith, and who engage in the worship of Śiva.

He indeed bestows the grace of attaining His own vision; by means of that yoga of knowledge (*jñānayoga*), they approach— that is, attain— Me, the formless Supreme Self, and I grant such a yoga of knowledge.

"I myself shall bestow grace," thus the Supreme Self Himself promises. This reassurance of His inspires the true devotion of practitioners. Encouraged by this very divine radiance, may all practitioners place their trust firmly within their own hearts—so says the Lord.
The disposition. || 10 ||
Out of compassion for them alone, I, dwelling within their very self, destroy the darkness born of ignorance with the radiant lamp of knowledge.

He points out the fruit of such yoga of knowledge: "For the sake of compassion— that is, for the purpose of mercy— toward those very ones who worship Me alone, I, abiding within their own state of being— that is, existing within the disposition (āśaya) of their inner organ (antaḥkaraṇa)— by means of the shining, luminous lamp of knowledge," [I dispel their darkness].

By means of the lamp called knowledge, I destroy—that is, I dispel—the darkness born of ignorance, which originates from ignorance. And thus, the knowers who have destroyed that darkness attain me, the formless Supreme Śiva. || 11 ||

When the Blessed One had thus spoken of His own power, Arjuna— endowed with a divine nature and his devotion to the Blessed One further increased— desiring once more to hear in detail the preeminent majesty of the Blessed One, praised the Blessed One with extreme humility and asked:
You are the supreme Brahman, the supreme abode, the highest purity;
you are the eternal, divine Puruṣa, the primordial God, unborn and all-pervading.
All the ṛṣis, as well as the celestial sage Nārada, Asita, Devala, and Vyāsa, have said this to you; and you yourself are telling it to me.

O Kṛṣṇa, you alone are the Supreme Brahman, having become the Supreme Brahman; likewise, you are the supreme abode and the supreme splendor; you are the supreme purity and the purifier. All the sages, such as Vasiṣṭha and others, as well as the celestial sage Nārada, Asita, and Devala—all of these [regard] you alone as the Puruṣa, the Supreme Puruṣa.

Due to the state of *sāmarasya* (essential identity) between Vāsudeva— who is the Supreme Nature (*parā-prakṛti*) and possesses the form of the Puruṣa— and Paraśiva, who is designated as the Puruṣa, it is appropriate here to refer to Kṛṣṇa, the son of Vasudeva, also by the term "Puruṣa. Likewise, [he is] the eternal, constant, divine, non-material, supreme light, whose nature is that of the primordial God (*ādideva*).
They say that even among all the gods, there is a god who exists from the very beginning— the unborn (*aja*),
