devoid of origin (*utpattirahita*), and all-pervading (*vibhu*, *sarvavyāpaka*). And this is exactly how it is for me as well.
You speak of your own true nature; therefore, you are indeed the Supreme Self in person. 13.
I consider all this that you tell me to be true, O Keśava;
for neither the gods nor the demons, O Blessed One, know your manifestation.

O Keśava, I consider all this that has been spoken by the sages and by you to be entirely right and true—just as you yourself say to me. O Blessed One, even the gods, Indra and the others, do not know your manifestation (*vyakti*), nor do the Dānavas or Asuras; for you are all-pervading and formless.
The meaning is that the form of the Supreme Self is unknowable even to gods and demons. || 14 ||
O Supreme Person, O Creator of beings, O Lord of beings, O God of gods, O Master of the world, you alone know yourself by yourself. 15.

O Puruṣottama Kṛṣṇa; O Bhūtabhāvana—one who brings all beings into existence, generating them; O creator of the world and performer of such incomparable great deeds; O Bhūteśa—ruler and controller of all living creatures; O Devadeva—God of gods; O Jagatpate—Lord of the universe!
O Lord of the worlds, You alone know Yourself by Yourself; who else could know You,
who possess a form both manifest and unmanifest, who abide in the world like one indifferent, yet remain beyond worldly attributes, and are distinguished by extraordinary powers?
You should describe in their entirety Your divine self-manifestations,
by which manifestations You abide pervading these worlds.

O Lord, You ought to describe Your majesty in its entirety and fullness; for, O Master, Your own manifestations are divine, non-material, and indeed unique. Therefore, You ought to speak of those manifestations by which You pervade all these worlds with Your glories.
You abide. Your various powers, which pervade the world, are indeed all your manifestations.

Endowed with such wonderful powers, although you are formless, through the play of bestowing grace upon your devotees, you possess a divine form that is eternally beautiful and captivating to all. Therefore, of you—
(233) "The supreme greatness of others cannot be known; you alone, by teaching me of your own majesty, deliver me, your devotee, from the well of doubt. Thus spoke Arjuna.
Having prostrated before Śrī Kṛṣṇa with devotion, he made this request.
O Yogin, how may I know you by constantly reflecting upon you? In which various states, O Blessed One, are you to be meditated upon by me? (17)

O Lord of all yogas, how may I know You, the Knower, while constantly and at all times contemplating and meditating upon You? O Blessed One, in what various states and objects am I to contemplate and meditate upon You? Since You abide everywhere in an unmanifest form, where is Your [manifestation]?

How may I know You? You dwell everywhere in concealment; although You exist within this phenomenal world in the form of the expansion of the five elements, You are not perceived by anyone through external vision. Therefore, how may I know You? In what state and in what form?
"Should I worship you?"—such questions and others are asked by Arjuna. || 17 ||
O Janārdana, tell me again in detail of your own yoga and your divine manifestations; for there is no satiety for me as I drink this nectar.

O Janārdana, O Kṛṣṇa, tell me once again in detail Your own yoga—the yoga of Your divine sovereignty—and Your vibhūti, Your majesty; for as I listen to the nectar of Your words, there is no satiety, no contentment, and no sense of having had enough. Even after hearing it again and again...
I wish to hear this; therefore, tell me once more of the excellence of your splendor.
Come, I shall declare to you my divine self-manifestations in their principal forms, O best of the Kurus; for there is no end to my full extent.

"Hanta" is used here to express joy, compassion, or the commencement of a statement. O best of the Kurus, Arjuna, I shall describe to you the divine manifestations of My own self—the specific powers of splendor—predominantly and primarily, since this power and majesty of Mine is infinite and boundless; for it is from Me that they proceed.

There is no end whatsoever to his manifestation, his expansion, or his vastness. This particular power has arisen as the support of life for all, pervading this entire world from every side, by which all are drawn [toward him].

In this world, people conduct their affairs through mutual trust. Among all things that are objects of affection, it is indeed the majesty of the Supreme Self’s power alone. His power, having transformed itself into the form of the universe, remains hidden within it and attracts everyone. It is only through the knowledge of the application of this power that—

Therefore, knowledge of the Supreme Self, who is the inner controller and possesses power, becomes easily attainable; thus, Arjuna, being a person of the highest qualification, is indeed capable of understanding this yoga of power. || 19 ||
I am the Self, O Guḍākeśa, seated in the heart of all beings;
I am the beginning, the middle, and indeed the end of all beings.

In this regard, the Blessed One begins by declaring, "First of all, hear this essential yoga of My power," in order to describe His majesty: "O Guḍākeśa"— O Arjuna, conqueror of sleep, whose nature is ever-awake— "residing in the heart" (āśaya) of all beings, that is, in the hearts of all creatures.

The existing Self, the inner controller Self, is indeed I myself. As the Lord Himself will declare: "O Arjuna, the Lord dwells in the heart-region of all beings; I am seated within the heart of all. Of all beings, I alone am the beginning, the root cause, and the middle during the intermediate period.
Likewise, I am the cause of maintenance and the cause of internal dissolution; thus, the meaning is that I alone am the cause of the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of all things. || 20 ||
Among the Ādityas I am Viṣṇu; among luminaries, the radiant Sun;
among the Maruts I am Marīci; and among the stars, I am the Moon.
Among the Ādityas—the twelve Ādityas—I am the one named Viṣṇu. Among luminaries—those who illuminate—I am the thousand-rayed Sun, Ravi.
Among the Maruts—the deities of the wind—I am Marīci. Among the constellations, I am the Moon, Śaśin.
And thus, in the world, wherever there is an excellence of power, all of that is indeed the Supreme Self; in this way, the Blessed One reveals his noble intention. 21.
Among the Vedas, I am the Sāmaveda; among beings, I am Vāsava;
among the senses, I am the mind; and among living entities, I am consciousness. 22.
Among the four Vedas, I am the Sāmaveda; among the gods, I am Vāsava, Indra;
among the senses, I am the mind that impels them; and among sentient beings—those possessed of consciousness—I am [the intellect].
The consciousness and sentience of living beings are indeed myself.
Among the Rudras, I am Śaṅkara; among the Yakṣas and Rākṣasas, I am the Lord of Wealth (Kubera);
among the Vasus, I am Pāvaka; and among the peaked mountains, I am Meru.
Among the eleven Rudras, I alone am Śaṅkara Kālarudra;
among the Yakṣas and Rākṣasas, I alone am Vitteśa Kubera; among the eight Vasus, I alone am Pāvaka Agni; and among the peaked mountains, I alone am Meru, the mountain Meru.
I alone. || 23 ||
And know me, O Pārtha, to be Bṛhaspati, the chief among domestic priests;
among army commanders I am Skanda, and among bodies of water I am the ocean. (24)

O Pārtha, know me to be Bṛhaspati, the foremost and most excellent among the household priests (purodhasaḥ) and domestic chaplains (purohitāḥ), the priest of the gods; among commanders of armies (senānīnām), I am Skanda, the commander of the divine host, known as Subrahmaṇya; and among all bodies of water (sarasām), I am the ocean (sāgaraḥ). || 24 ||
Among the great seers, I am Bhṛgu; among words, I am the single syllable Om.
Among sacrifices, I am the sacrifice of silent recitation (japayajña); among immovable things, I am the Himalaya.

Among the great sages who possess knowledge, I alone am Bhṛgu. Among the words and syllables, I alone am the single syllable in the form of the Praṇava. Among sacrifices, I alone am the sacrifice of recitation (japayajña), which consists of the recitation of Śiva’s mantra. Among immobile things—that is, among stable objects—
Even there, in the midst of the immovable mountains, I myself am the sovereign of mountains named Himālaya. || 25 ||
The Aśvattha among all trees, Nārada among the divine sages, Citraratha among the Gandharvas, and the sage Kapila among the Siddhas. || 26 ||
Among all trees, I alone am the one known as the *aśvattha*, the famous tree;
among the divine seers (*devarṣi*), I am Nārada; among the Gandharvas, I alone am the Gandharva named Citraratha; and among the perfected ones (*siddha*), I alone am the sage Kapila. (26)
Know me as Uccaiḥśravas among horses, born from the nectar;
as Airāvata among lordly elephants, and as the king among men. (27)

Know me to be Uccaiḥśravas, born from the nectar— that which arose at the time of churning the ocean of nectar— standing among horses; and know me as Airāvata, the celestial elephant among the lordly elephants,
and as the king among men.
Know this: whatever object exists in the world that is most excellent, all that is indeed myself. 27.
Of weapons I am the thunderbolt; of cows I am the wish-fulfilling cow Kāmadhuk; I am Kandarpa, the progenitor; and of serpents I am Vāsuki. || 28 ||

Among weapons, I alone am the thunderbolt; among cows, I alone am the wish-fulfilling cow, Kāmadhenu; I alone am Kandarpa, the god of love, the progenitor who impels the world and draws it toward himself;
and among serpents, I alone am Vāsuki. (28)
Among the Nāgas I am Ananta; among the aquatic creatures I am Varuṇa;
among the ancestors I am Aryaman; and among those who exercise restraint, I am Yama. (29)

Among the Nāgas, I am the Nāga named Ananta; among the Yādasa, the water-deities, I alone am Varuṇa; among the Pitṛs, I alone am the king of the Pitṛs named Aryaman; and among those who exercise restraint, the restrainers—the Yogins—I alone am Yama, the Restrainer. 29.
Among the Daityas I am Prahlāda; among those who reckon time, I am Time; among beasts I am the king of beasts, and among birds I am Vainateya. (30)
Among the Daityas and Asuras, I alone am Prahlāda. Among those who reckon—that is, among those performing calculation—I am Kāla, the well-known observer and calculator of all.
Among wild beasts, I alone am the lion. Among birds, I am Vainateya.
I am Garuḍa.
Of purifiers I am the wind; of weapon-bearers I am Rāma;
of aquatic creatures I am the makara; and of rivers I am the Ganges.
Among those who purify, I alone am the Purifier, the wind that removes the impurities and defects of all. Among the wielders of weapons, I am Rāma.
I am indeed Rāma, the son of Daśaratha; among fish (jhaṣa), I am the Makara, a specific species of fish; and among streams (srotas), I am the Jāhnavī, the divine Gaṅgā who purifies all. 31.
I am the beginning, the end, and also the middle of all creations, O Arjuna;
among sciences, I am the science of the Self (adhyātmavidyā), and I am the debate of those who debate.

O Arjuna, I alone am the beginning, the end, and the middle of all creations; I alone am the discourse of those who debate among themselves regarding the creation, maintenance, and dissolution of the world.
Among letters I am the letter 'A', and among compounds I am the copulative (dvandva).
I alone am inexhaustible Time; I am the Ordainer whose face is turned everywhere.

Among letters and phonemes, I am the letter *a* and the vowel *a*. Among all compound formations, I am the *dvandva* compound. The letter *a* is connected as the underlying thread (*anusyūta*) throughout all phonemes; therefore, it is contemplated as being the very nature of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*). Furthermore, regarding both members employed in a *dvandva* compound—
Because the two words possess equal primacy, that [compound] is contemplated by the experienced ones as being the very nature of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*).

In other compounds, however, because of the primacy of either the first member, the second member, or another element, there is no equality of primacy between the two. Śiva-yogis understand that the state of Brahman (*brahmabhāva*) is known to consist precisely in abiding as the primary reality in all cases.

In a copulative compound (dvandva), such usage is appropriate because of the equal predominance of both members; likewise, time—which is inexhaustible and devoid of decay—is indeed of the very nature of Brahman. In this same way, I alone am the all-facing Ordainer, the dispenser of the fruits of actions.
I am death, the destroyer of all, and the source of those who are yet to be;
among women, I am fame, fortune, speech, memory, intelligence, fortitude, and forgiveness.

I alone am the destroyer of all and the annihilator of all; I am the source of the arising of all future things destined for auspiciousness. Among women, whatever excellence is naturally perceived in women is the very nature of the Supreme Self. In that regard as well—
Fame, prosperity, speech, memory,
intelligence, fortitude, and forbearance— such praiseworthy qualities exist in women as individual traits.
They are seen. One should reflect that every such excellence is indeed a portion of the Lord's splendor (*tejoṃśa*).

Here, the Lord indicates that whatever excellence is observed in any individual must necessarily be considered a portion of a deity (*devāṃśa*) and should be honored accordingly. For this very reason, [the speech] of women is sweet, pleasing, and profound.
The wise consider that speech is indeed the unique manifestation of the power of the Divine Self. 34.
Likewise, among the Sāmans I am the Bṛhat-sāman; among the meters (chandas) I am the Gāyatrī;
among the months I am Mārgaśīrṣa; and among the seasons I am Kusumākara (the spring). || 35 ||
Among the *sāmans*, I alone am the preeminent *sāman*, the *Bṛhat-sāman*. Among the meters (*chandas*), I alone am the *Gāyatrī* meter. Among the months, I am Mārgaśīrṣa;
it was during that very month, on the field of battle, that this yoga of action was taught to Arjuna, specifically because the teaching of the *Gītā* took place there on the eleventh lunar day.

Discerning persons consider that [Ekādaśī] to be preeminent. Since every moment of time brings about the abiding in immortality, it is connected to the Supreme Self by virtue of being dear to Him. Because such instruction regarding immortality manifested on the eleventh day (Ekādaśī) of the month of Mārgaśīrṣa, its status as a portion of the Blessed Lord is contemplated. Likewise...

The Bṛhat Sāman is exceedingly dear to the Supreme Self; likewise, the Gāyatrī meter is proclaimed to be completely filled with divine prosperity. Similarly, among the seasons, I alone am Vasanta, the maker of flowers. || 35 ||
I am the gambling of the deceitful, and I am the splendor of the splendid;
I am victory, I am resolve, and I am the courage of the courageous.

Of those who move forward and employ their shields, I alone am the game of dice and the science of the dice. Of the radiant, I alone am that radiance. Of victors, I alone am the victory attained through the nature of being victorious.
Of worldly people in their transactions, whatever profit they obtain—all that is I.

Only he who honors that which is to be regarded as the very nature of the Blessed One receives the grace of the Blessed One. He who does not know this truth experiences envy, malice, and other such states for the sake of gaining something else.
Therefore, the discerning, with a concentrated mind, rejoice upon seeing the prosperity of others. It is just so.
I alone am the courage of the courageous.

Thus, that which was taught by the great sage Upamanyu to the Blessed Lord Kṛṣṇa— that pleasing others, favoring others, and assisting others is nothing other than the worship of Śiva— appears entirely consistent and correct.
Among the Vṛṣṇis I am Vāsudeva; among the Pāṇḍavas, Dhanañjaya.
Among the sages I am Vyāsa; among the poets, the poet Uśanas. (37)
Among the Vṛṣṇis—those born of the Vṛṣṇi lineage—I am this Vāsudeva, the son of Vasudeva;
I alone am the formless Supreme Self. Likewise, among the five Pāṇḍavas, you are Dhanañjaya, Arjuna; I alone am you, for you are indeed the very nature of the Blessed Lord.

The Blessed One teaches this to Arjuna. Even among sages, Vyāsa—the possessor of great knowledge and the establisher of the Nigamas and Āgamas—is declared by the Blessed One himself to be of the very nature of the Lord; thus he shines as the one who bestows inspiration upon all. Likewise, among poets and knowers, Uśanas Śukra [is preeminent].
"One who possesses divine vision" is thus cultivated. || 37 ||
I am the rod for those who seek to subdue, and I am statesmanship for those who desire victory;
I am silence among secrets, and I am knowledge for the wise. (38)

For those practicing self-restraint, I alone am the rod that serves as the means for that restraint; for those desiring victory, I alone am the policy or justice to be followed; for yogis, I alone am the silence that serves as their model for what is to be kept secret; and for the wise, I alone am their knowledge.
Moreover, O Arjuna, I am the seed of all beings;
there exists no being, whether moving or unmoving, that can exist without me. (39)

O Arjuna, I alone am that which is the seed and the cause of growth for all beings. Without me—that is, apart from me—whatever being has arisen or exists, whether moving or unmoving, no such entity could have come into existence at all. Everything has originated from me alone and is indeed inseparable from me. In this world...
Although all things exist, the presence of the Supreme Self shines forth as innate;

thus, though dwelling within, He is not perceived by worldly people because He is concealed by His own qualities, but is experienced only by yogis with inward vision. "He is seen indeed by the highest, subtle intellect."
By the scriptural statement "by those who see the subtle," it is promised that its vision would be easily attainable only for those with subtle insight.
There is no end to my divine manifestations, O scorcher of the foe;
this detailed expansion of my manifestations has been declared by me only in brief.

(240) O scorcher of foes, Arjuna, there is simply no end—that is, no limit—to my divine manifestations. This much should be known: as the saying of those who are proficient goes, "The time available is short and obstacles are many," [this is the extent of what can be understood] regarding the Supreme Self.

It does not exist. Even when such effort is made, obstacles that are beyond remedy can arise; this is the intention of the author of the *Amūrta-bhāṣya*. Furthermore, even the Blessed Lord does not say that the extent of His own manifestation is merely this much; rather, He indicates His divine glory only by way of general reference or partial description, and not [in its entirety].

He speaks with complete fullness: "Śiva alone knows the reality (tattva) of Śiva, as do Nandin, Viṣṇu, and Kumāra, the son of the Mountain King"—thus state the venerable Śrīpati Paṇḍitārādhya Mahodaya at the beginning of the Śrīkarabhāṣya. Likewise, the reality of the formless Śiva [is known] by Śiva who possesses a divine form.

Just as Viṣṇu knows, so too Kṛṣṇa, who is His incarnation, certainly knows it as well. Nevertheless, He teaches such a complete and majestic reality to Arjuna. Indeed, Arjuna is not able to comprehend the reality in its entirety; for even Arjuna himself is one whose sleep has been conquered.

If one cannot know the full majesty of Śiva’s power, how could other people of a tamasic nature be capable of it? Therefore, the Blessed One indicates here only a very small fraction of His own power's majesty for the purpose of providing a general direction. || 40 ||
Whatever being is possessed of majesty, or endowed with beauty, or even with power—
know each of those to be born from a mere fragment of My splendor.
Whatever being exists in the world that possesses majesty, opulence, splendor such as beauty and so forth,
or even power endowed with energy and the like— know, understand, that every such being has arisen from but a single portion of my splendor; in a mere fragment of whose power everything is contained.
Thus, the statement of the learned becomes consistent for this very reason:

even the entirety of divine majesty dissolves into but a minute fraction of the vital energy (*prāṇaśakti*), which is of the nature of His splendor. If the entire, undivided universe were contained within but a single part of the Supreme Self’s power of consciousness (*cicchakti*), then a human being would not harbor pride.
Dwelling everywhere in a state of non-attachment, the Supreme Self,
by the majesty of His own power, effortlessly and as mere sport, carries out His own cosmic activity through His own portions, the individual souls.
It proceeds. In such a state, it is indeed a cause for despondency that human beings, having forgotten the Supreme Self, engage in worldly affairs solely out of their own sense of agency.
Therefore, by those possessed of discernment, [effort must be made] for the realization of the Supreme Power, which is all-pervasive and consists of the splendor of the Lord.

One should strive according to one's capacity and according to one's intellect. Just as the Supreme Self naturally shines forth, distinguished by its power in the form of light (*tejas*), so too do all individual souls (*jīvas*), which are its constituent parts, exist as distinguished by the power of the intellect (*buddhi-śakti*) which consists of a portion of that light. In the same way, the phenomenal world (*prapañca*), composed of the five elements, is also [distinguished by it].

An entity exists only as qualified by its power (*śakti*). An object devoid of power is never perceived. There is no object anywhere in the phenomenal world that is bereft of energy (*tejas*). The power existing in the earth, which consists of the support of all things, is experienced by everyone; likewise, [the power] existing in water...

The energy in the form of nourishment is indeed well-known to all. Furthermore, that energy which exists within fire in the form of the burning of all things is also merely a portion of the Supreme Self's energy. Likewise, the energy that exists within air in the form of the removal of all impurities and defects is also merely a portion of the Lord's power. Within space...

It should be understood that even the light which exists as all-pervasive, stainless, and so forth, arises solely from a portion of the Lord’s power. And thus, the Supreme Self, the individual souls who are its portions, and the phenomenal world which is the field for His sport— all this [is of the same nature].

The Lord clarifies here that [the soul] is indeed characterized by the power of the nature of light (*tejorūpa-śakti*). Nevertheless, among individual souls (*jīva*), this power exists in a contracted state, being veiled by the three qualities (*triguṇa*) consisting of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*. And this contraction must be gradually removed by human beings through the continuous worship of the Lord. [This is] the contraction of power (*śakti-saṅkoca*).

Thus do the experienced ones declare that this is *mala*. This very *mala* manifests as threefold, through the divisions of *āṇava*, *māyeya*, and *kārmika*. Now, *āṇava-mala* is a contraction of the power of will (*icchā-śakti*);
it produces in individual souls (*jīvas*) the preoccupation with their own self-interest. Furthermore, *māyeya-mala* is also a contraction of the power of will.

It produces the vision of delusion regarding living beings. In the very same way, the impurity of karma (*kārmikamala*), which consists of the contraction of the power of action (*kriyāśakti*), produces the sense of egoism (*ahaṅkāra*) in living beings. Thus, all living beings, endowed with self-interest, delusion, and egoism, have indeed fallen into delusion through their own will by means of conceit.
Because they engage in worldly activities everywhere, they consequently undergo a succession of sufferings.
By abandoning this contraction, the expansion of power must be attained through the firmness of practice;
the means for attaining this is discussed elsewhere. || 41 ||
Or rather, what is the use of this extensive knowledge of yours, O Arjuna?
Sustaining this entire universe with but a single fraction of Myself, I remain as the world. (42)

Concluding the description of the majesty of His power, the Blessed One said: "O Arjuna, what is the fruit of speaking at length? If more were spoken, you would not understand it. Or rather, even if you were to know my infinite majesty of splendor in its many forms, what fruit would that bring you? For however much might be known, it would still be but a small portion."

It would indeed remain with something left over. If it is stated according to its essence (*sārataḥ*), [it means] that I stand pervading and supporting even this entire universe by a single part—that is, by a mere portion of my power. As the *Puruṣasūkta* states: "All beings are but one foot of Him; His three feet are the immortal in heaven," thus [the world exists] by a single part of the Supreme Self.
The universal pervasiveness is thus described; therefore, no one is able to know the limit of His majesty.
In this way, the Blessed One briefly teaches His yoga of manifestations for the welfare of the world. 42.
The Eleventh Chapter. When the Blessed One had thus described His own majesty, Arjuna, his devotion further increased and desiring to behold such a Blessed One face to face, said:
By those words which you have spoken for my benefit— the supreme secret known as the inner self— this delusion of mine has vanished.
Out of compassion alone, for the sake of favoring me—that is, for the purpose of bestowing grace upon me—you have explained this supreme secret concerning the inner self (*adhyātma*).

This delusion of mine—the ignorance existing within me—has departed; it has been destroyed. Through the grace of the Blessed One, he whose heart was purified was thoroughly sprinkled with the nectar of instruction.
Having become personally stainless through the removal of his own doubts, and having completely abandoned all former lack of discernment,
delusion regarding kinsmen, and his own sense of agency, he pervaded everything everywhere.

Arjuna, having resolved to personally follow the divine example of the Supreme Self— who brings about all the actions of the world without any desire for fruits, but through steadfastness in duty and the wish for the welfare of the world— [spoke as follows].

Through the Vinaya, he became one who had taken refuge in that [Dharma]. Today, Arjuna has truly understood the reality that his own duty consists merely in acting as an instrument when the Supreme Self performs the great battle for the welfare of the world. Previously, during his state of non-discrimination, this truth remained clinging within his heart.

Now, this doubt has been destroyed by itself through the instruction of the Blessed One. In this very way, those who have sought refuge express through their own experience the supreme and virtuous transformation brought about by the divine speech of the Great-Souled Ones—like a stream of milk filled with molasses-paste, yet distinguished by pure sugar-sand. And so it is.

"Even though there exists well-spoken divine speech endowed with fragments of foam, the destiny of one who digs another well and drinks its salty, undrinkable water will be such [as described]. Thus, the speech of the great-souled ones is indeed possessed of divine power; having heard it with faith, [one should act accordingly].
With all our doubts severed and our minds purified, if we fulfill our own duty and become recipients of the Lord’s grace, then our birth will surely be meaningful.
Having observed Arjuna’s state, may we all, with great inspiration, live a life that is simple and free from ostentation.

Engaging in worldly discourse, may we attain the fulfillment of our birth. May we be possessed of present awareness so that this sacred body, obtained through the grace of the Blessed One, does not become misused through the wasting of time in vain deliberation.
The doubt experienced by Arjuna purifies the daily lives of us all;
it is suggested here that we must remain vigilant so that no such doubt may find a place within our hearts.
For the origin and dissolution of beings have been heard by me in detail from you,
O lotus-petal-eyed one, as well as your imperishable majesty.

With all his doubts dispelled, Arjuna reveals his own intention: "O lotus-eyed one, O Puṇḍarīkākṣa, O Kṛṣṇa, I have heard from you in detail about the origin and dissolution—both birth and destruction—of all beings; as well as the Imperishable, which is devoid of decay, all-pervading by virtue of being changeless."
Your majesty, full of splendor, and your purifying life—these too have been heard by me correctly from you alone. || 2 ||
It is even so as you have said; O Supreme Lord, O Supreme Person, I desire to see your sovereign form, your very self.
p.

244) O Supreme Lord, you have grasped all that you say regarding yourself—namely, the manner in which you describe yourself; nevertheless, it is well known by me that you possess a divine body. Therefore, of you—

"A desire to see Your divine form has arisen within me in particular; this longing of my heart, too, must be fulfilled by You alone through Your compassion. Thus did Arjuna reveal the intention of his own heart. (3)
If you think it is possible for me to see that, O Lord,
then, O Master of Yoga, show me your imperishable self.
"O Lord, O Master of Yoga, O Sovereign of all, O Regulator of all yogas,
please show me Your imperishable Self, which is the very nature of Your own being"— with these words of devotion, Arjuna prayed to the Supreme Self. (4)
Behold, O Pārtha, my forms by the hundreds and thousands—
divine, of various kinds, and of diverse colors and shapes.
With sincere affection, the Blessed One fulfilled Arjuna’s noble resolve: "O Pārtha, O Arjuna,
behold hundreds and thousands of various kinds, of diverse colors and forms— many-colored and many-formed Adityas, Vasus, Rudras, the two Aśvins, and likewise the Maruts."
Behold, O Bhārata, many wonders never seen before!

O Bhārata Arjuna, behold the Ādityas, Vasus, Rudras, as well as the two Aśvins and the Maruts, shining within me. What more need be said? Behold many wonders within me, the likes of which have never been seen before by anyone during all this time. 6.
Behold today, O Guḍākeśa, the entire universe with its moving and non-moving beings gathered here in one place within my body, as well as whatever else you wish to see.
Behold today the entire world, including all that moves and is immobile, situated here within me alone;
see it acting within me, who am the support of all, the place of rest for all, and whose form is the undivided universe.
Behold the entire multitude of living beings! O Guḍākeśa, you who have conquered sleep and are habituated to vigilance, behold today within my body whatever else you wish to see as well. || 7 ||
But you cannot see Me with these very eyes of yours;
I shall give you divine vision; behold My sovereign yoga-power.
Although you are worthy to behold my divine majesty due to the excellence of your devotion,
nevertheless, you are unable to see me with these eyes of yours— the physical eyes. Therefore,
I grant and bestow upon you a divine eye, endowed with divine power, which enables the vision of Me.

Behold with divine vision my sovereign yoga— the power of conjunction and so forth pertaining to the Supreme Self. Whoever dissolves through the state of flavor-identity (*samarasatā*) within the Supreme Lord residing in the heart,
such a person, in every respect, attains divine power through the yoga of the Supreme Lord.

If such a yoga were possible even for an ordinary person, then what need is there to speak of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, who is the very embodiment of supreme power, in his union with Śiva-yoga? Although Kṛṣṇa is in reality divine light, by assuming a human form he joined that very yoga within a divine state.
He establishes that the connection with the Lord exists not only in Arjuna, but in all of us as well.
In this way, through the very contemplation of identity (*tādātmya-bhāvanā*), the yoga of Śiva will be perfected and bear fruit.
Otherwise, due to the weakness of his own power, a man is himself ruined and ruins others as well; he [is] himself...

By its own power alone, it is not able to accomplish any action whatsoever. In the same way, only when the eye situated in the body is joined with the light of the sun can objects present before it be seen by people.
Likewise, if the individual soul-power (jīva-śakti) were to be joined with the power of the Supreme Self (paramātma-śakti), then the individual soul [could likewise fulfill its purpose].
One would be able to attain the expansion of the powers of will, knowledge, and action. A living being whose sovereignty has been stolen by *māyā* is not the Supreme Self;

rather, the Lord teaches the yoga of Śiva to all living beings. By the power of this very yoga of Śiva, a human being becomes Śiva himself and, through the expansion of the powers of will, knowledge, and action, brings about the welfare of the world.
He is able to accomplish it. || 8 ||
Having spoken thus, O King, Hari, the great lord of yoga,
then revealed his supreme sovereign form to Pārtha.

246) In accordance with Arjuna’s request, Sañjaya reported to Dhṛtarāṣṭra the sequence of the Lord’s own teaching on Yoga as it was graciously bestowed upon him: "O King Dhṛtarāṣṭra, the Great Lord of Yoga..."

He who is both Great and the Lord of Yoga— that Hari, Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the remover of all sins— thereupon revealed to Pārtha, Arjuna, His own supreme and most excellent divine form, pertaining to the Lord. || 9 ||
He possessed many mouths and eyes, displaying many wonders;
he was adorned with many divine ornaments and held many uplifted divine weapons.
Wearing divine garlands and garments, anointed with divine perfumes and unguents,
the god was composed of every wonder— Ananta, whose faces are turned in every direction.

The description of such a form is now being provided: it has many faces and eyes—that is, one in which there are many, indeed innumerable, faces and eyes; it possesses many wonderful appearances—distinguished by various kinds of marvelous sights; it is adorned with many divine ornaments—that great form of such a kind.

Wherein [were] such weapons; wearing divine garlands and garments—divine garlands being flowers and garments being clothes; anointed with divine perfumes—anointing of divine fragrance—the Lord, the God whose face is on all sides, Arjuna beheld him. This is the ellipsis. (10–11)
If the light of a thousand suns were to rise simultaneously in the sky,
that might resemble the radiance of that Great-Souled One.

If the radiance of a thousand suns were to arise simultaneously—that is, at one and the same time—in the sky, in the atmosphere; since such a thing is impossible, the expression "if it were" (*yadi syāt*) is used. That radiance would be equal to, or similar to, the light of that Great-Souled One, the Supreme Self, who is the Great Illumination. Sañjaya.
He described to Dhṛtarāṣṭra the excellence of the manifestation of the Supreme Self. || 12 ||
There, the son of Pāṇḍu likewise beheld the entire universe, divided into many parts, situated within the body of the God of gods.
There, upon the body of the God of gods, Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the Pāṇḍava Arjuna then beheld the entire universe— divided in many ways, in manifold forms— standing as one, situated in a single place.

Indeed, Arjuna beheld this entire world, consisting of both the moving and the unmoving, as distinct from one another within the Universal Form revealed by Śrī Kṛṣṇa; at that time, all living beings were seen within that divine body—which was of the nature of the indivisible universe, in the form of the Liṅga, unlimited, and all-pervading. Such is the worldly convention regarding the universe.

Just as people perceive according to their diverse mental impressions (*saṃskāra*), so too was the divine form of the Supreme Self beheld by Arjuna. Previously, Arjuna had been seeing the material, five-elemental form of the phenomenal world with his physical eyes;
now, however, through the divine eye bestowed by the grace of the Blessed One, he saw that very same [Self].

He beheld a manifestation distinguished by divine splendor. Previously, that divine splendor residing within all bodies had remained unmanifest and was not seen by Arjuna; for this very reason, his vision of delusion increased, and by its power alone, his mind became seized by doubt. Now, with his divine eye—

With all his doubts completely dispelled, he obtained a divine vision of the Supreme Lord who was manifesting for the fulfillment of His purpose. Previously, although the Supreme Lord was present there, He had not been seen by him in the manner that He was now perceived within the phenomenal world. Thus, whether the Lord was seen or unseen—
He is indeed always engaged in activity everywhere; however, practitioners must first attain divine vision through practice on the path of yoga in order to perceive him. || 13 ||
Then Dhananjaya, filled with wonder and his hair standing on end,
bowed his head to the God and spoke with palms joined in reverence.

Thereupon, immediately after that, overcome with wonder— that is, filled with amazement— and with his hair standing on end, that Dhananjaya Arjuna, having bowed his head in salutation to the Lord, the Blessed Śrī Kṛṣṇa, spoke with palms joined in reverence.

Having beheld the divine majesty of the Supreme Self, Arjuna, with his inner being satisfied, bowed down with devotion to that very Great Light, Mahādeva, and made this request; thus Sañjaya spoke to Dhṛtarāṣṭra. (14)
O God, I see all the gods within Your body, as well as the various hosts of beings, Brahmā seated upon his lotus throne, all the ṛṣis, and the divine serpents. (15)

(248) Satisfied by obtaining the divine vision of the Supreme Self, Arjuna, bowing low in devotion, reported everything that he had seen within that very Universal Form: "O God, O Blessed One, [I see] all [beings] within Your body..."

I see the gods; likewise, I see the hosts of various classes of beings, the Lord and Controller of living beings, Kālarudra—who is included within the Trinity and presides over the dissolution—as well as the divine sages, the Uragas, and the serpents. He himself—

Because he is an incarnation of Viṣṇu, he is indeed seen as having the form of Viṣṇu. In this way, the three deities (trimūrtis) were also seen by Arjuna shining within the universal form (viśvarūpa) of the Lord, the formless Supreme Lord who possesses a divine form. Viṣṇu, too, within that all-pervading form, is the very same formless Supreme Lord.

He who dwells in Vaikuṇṭha and bears a divine, auspicious form is considered to be that very Viṣṇu who is included within the Trimūrti; for this reason, those who possess direct experience do not count as a distinction between the formless Supreme Śiva and the three deities in their divine embodied forms. 15.
I behold You with many arms, bellies, mouths, and eyes, possessing infinite forms on all sides;
O Lord of the Universe, O Universal Form, I see neither Your end, nor Your middle, nor again Your beginning.

I behold you with many arms, bellies, mouths, and eyes—that is, one in whom there are many arms, bellies, mouths, and eyes; everywhere and in every way, I see you as having infinite forms, that is, innumerable forms. O Lord of the Universe, O Ruler of the World, O Universal Form, I do not see your end.
I do not see a middle; likewise, I do not see a beginning. Thus, having assumed a human form, you conduct yourself in the world through a beginning, a middle, and an end.

I behold You wearing a crown, bearing a mace, and holding a discus—a mass of splendor blazing on all sides, difficult to look upon, possessing the immeasurable radiance of a flaming fire and the sun in every direction. 17.

Wearing a crown, possessing a diadem; wielding a mace, possessing a club; radiant everywhere, shining on all sides as a mass of splendor, the very nature of the supreme light; possessing a luster like that of blazing fire and the sun in every direction—blazing fire (*anala*) and the sun (*arka*), having a brilliance like theirs.
"I behold you, who are immeasurable—incapable of being measured—and difficult to perceive—incapable of being seen.
Thus Arjuna beheld the God who is the soul of all. 17.
You are the supreme imperishable to be known; you are the ultimate refuge of this universe.
You are the undecaying protector of the eternal dharma; I consider you to be the ancient Puruṣa. 18.

You alone are to be known as the supreme, the most excellent, the imperishable, the transcendent Brahman. You are the ultimate repository and the supreme refuge of this entire universe. You are the undecaying, devoid of destruction, eternal, and the protector of the eternal dharma—that which is the perpetual and constant Indian way of life.
You are the protector and guardian of that Dharma which consists of universal forbearance and equanimity;
you are considered and intended by me to be the eternal Puruṣa, the ancient Puruṣa. || 18 ||
I behold You, who are without beginning, middle, or end, possessed of infinite vigor and infinite arms, with eyes like the moon and the sun;
I see You with Your mouth like a blazing fire, scorching this entire universe with Your own splendor.

The Lord who is without beginning, middle, or end, devoid of beginning, middle, and end; whose vigor is infinite—such that there is no limit or measure to His vigor—who possesses infinite arms, endowed with countless arms; whose eyes are the moon and the sun, having the moon and the sun themselves as His eyes; and whose mouth is the blazing fire.
I behold you with a face like a blazing fire, heating this entire universe with your own splendor and radiance. 19.
For this space between heaven and earth, as well as all the directions, is pervaded by you alone;
O Great-Souled One, seeing this wondrous and fierce form of yours, the three worlds are trembling with fear.

O Great-Souled One, O Supreme Self, that which is the interval— the intermediate space— between heaven and earth, or the sky and the earth, as well as all the directions, have been pervaded by You alone. Having seen this wondrous and marvelous, fierce and terrifying form of Yours...
The three worlds—the triad of worlds—have become utterly distressed, being exceedingly terrified. || 20 ||
And these hosts of gods and Siddhas enter into you; some, filled with fear, praise you with palms joined in reverence.
Having cried "Hail!", the assemblies of great seers and Siddhas extol you with abundant hymns of praise.

For these hosts of gods, those humans who have become portions of the deities, have come for battle; with palms joined in reverence, they praise and extol Dharma. Thus, all of them are fully prepared for war.

Arjuna saw the warriors [of his own army] within the Blessed One’s universal form (viśvarūpa). Likewise, hosts of great seers (maharṣi) and perfected beings (siddha), saying "May there be well-being for the world! May there be well-being! offered abundant and magnificent hymns of praise.

With hymns they praise You; they perform a song of praise. Thus Arjuna saw the great seers praising with eulogies that very one who is the soul of all, the Supreme Self whose form is the universe. 21.
The Rudras, Ādityas, Vasus, and those who are Sādhyas; the Viśvedevas, the two Aśvins, the Maruts, and the Uṣmapās;
the hosts of Gandharvas, Yakṣas, Asuras, and Siddhas—all of them gaze upon you, utterly amazed.

There were eleven Rudras and twelve Ādityas; likewise the Vasus, the Sādhyas, the Viśvedevas, the two Aśvin gods, the host of Maruts, the Pitṛs who drink the steam, and the Gandharvas, Yakṣas, and Asuras.
In this way, Arjuna beheld all these, including the Gandharvas and others, filled with wonder within the divine body of the Blessed One.

O mighty-armed one, having seen Your form as vast, with many mouths and eyes, many arms, thighs, and feet, many bellies, and terrifying with many tusks, the worlds are struck with terror, and so am I.

O mighty-armed one, O you who possess the strength of arms, O Mahādeva, [I see you] with many mouths and eyes—one who has many such faces; with many arms, thighs, and feet—one who has many such arms, thighs, and feet; with many bellies—one who has many such stomachs; and with many formidable fangs.
Having seen this great form of yours— terrible with many fangs, fearsome—
all the worlds are deeply distressed and remain in fear; likewise, I too am greatly distressed and exceedingly afraid of you,
who touch the sky, who are blazing, multicolored, with gaping mouths and glowing, wide eyes.
For upon seeing you, O Viṣṇu, my inner self is deeply agitated; I find neither steadfastness nor peace.

O Viṣṇu, having seen you—touching the sky, reaching into the atmosphere; blazing, shining; possessing many colors, endowed with manifold hues; with wide-gaping mouth, with open jaws; and with blazing, vast eyes, such as you are—having seen you...
With my inner self deeply distressed and my mind terrified, I find no steadfastness or fortitude, nor do I attain peace or tranquility. || 24 ||

Having merely seen your mouths, terrible with tusks and resembling the fire of cosmic destruction, I no longer know the directions nor do I find peace; be gracious, O Lord of Gods, Abode of the World! (25)

With fangs formidable, terrifying with their fangs, resembling the fire of cosmic destruction at the time of universal dissolution—since that very moment, I have not known even the directions; I find no peace, nor do I obtain any happiness. O Lord of gods, O Sovereign of the gods, O Abode of the universe, O Support of the worlds, be merciful to me!
Be gracious; be pleased. || 25 ||
And here are all these sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra together with the hosts of kings, as well as Bhīṣma, Droṇa, and that son of a charioteer (Karna), along with our own preeminent warriors. (26)
Hurrying, they enter your mouths, which are terrifying with their formidable tusks;
some are seen caught between the teeth with their heads crushed to powder. (27)
Here are all the sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra, headed by Duryodhana,
together with hosts of kings and assemblies of monarchs; likewise Bhīṣma, Droṇa, and that son of a Sūta, Karṇa,
along with our own preeminent warriors and heroes on our side— all these [stand] with mouths formidable with fangs.

Hurrying and filled with haste, they enter— meaning they penetrate— your mouths and faces, which are terrifying, fearsome, and exceedingly dreadful due to your fangs. Some are caught and stuck between the teeth, their heads crushed to powder.
They are seen and perceived. || 26–27 ||
Just as the many currents of water in rivers flow toward the ocean alone, so do these heroes of the world of men enter your blazing mouths. 28.
Just as the many, endless currents of water— the rushing flows of rivers— run and go toward the ocean alone, having directed themselves toward the ocean; even so, these heroes of the world of men,
shining brightly, enter your blazing faces.
They enter. || 28 ||
Just as moths enter a blazing fire with full force for their own destruction,
even so do these worlds enter your mouths with full force for their destruction.

Just as moths— either birds or a specific kind of insect— possessing great speed, that is, endowed with extreme velocity, enter a blazing, radiant, and flaming fire for their own destruction; even so [do they enter Me].

These worlds, these people, endowed with intense momentum and possessed of extreme speed, are entering—indeed, they are currently entering—your mouths, that is, your faces, for their own destruction. || 29 ||
Licking all the worlds on every side with your roaring mouths as you devour them, you fill the entire universe with your splendors; O Viṣṇu, your fierce rays scorch everything.

With your blazing, radiant faces, you are swallowing all the worlds entirely on every side; thus, licking them with your tongue, you taste them. In this manner, the Supreme Self is seen tasting even all the worlds with such a terrifying form. These two are His bodies: the terrible and the non-terrible.

Thus, in the Śruti, two faces of the Supreme Self are heard of: the non-terrible (aghora), which is gracious, and the terrible (ghora), which is fearsome. With his non-terrible face, he bestows grace upon devotees, and with his terrible face, he restrains the wicked. Now, for the unimpeded completion of the great battle that is about to occur—

Terrified, Arjuna prays to the Blessed One for the withdrawal of that form: "O Viṣṇu, your fierce and sharp splendors—your radiances—having filled and pervaded the entire world with their energies—that is, their own effulgences—are scorching it, exerting their heat. Here, [the Lord is described] by way of the Supreme Self's nature as light.

The use of the term *viṣṇupada* is appropriate for indicating universal pervasion (*viśvavyāpti*). The term *viṣṇupada* reveals Mahādeva, who is formless, the source of all beings, the witness of everything, and whose nature is the supreme light.
By conveying its etymological meaning as "universal pervasion," the term *viṣṇupada* [applies] to Him who is included within the Trimūrti.

Just as it follows [the Lord] who is the guardian, so too does it follow, by its very nature, even the formless Supreme Self which is the support of all through its function as the witness (sākṣivṛtti). Therefore, there is no room for Śaivas to conceive of it otherwise than through the application of the term "Viṣṇu-pada. || 30 ||
Tell me, who is this Lord of such fierce form? Homage be to you, O best of gods; be gracious!
I desire to know you, the Primordial One, for I do not understand your activity.

Who are you, possessing such a fierce form and cruel appearance? Tell me, speak! O best of gods, O supreme deity, homage be to you! Be gracious toward me; show me favor. You are the primordial one, existing at the beginning of all things.

I wish to know your identity, sir; I desire to know what your former appearance was like before you assumed such a terrifying form. I do not understand why you, who possess such a gentle nature, have taken on this fearsome shape. Please tell me all of this out of compassion. Thus [he spoke] out of fear.
And with humility, Arjuna entreats the Blessed One. || 31 ||
I am Time, the destroyer of worlds, grown mighty; I have set out here to sweep away all beings.
Even without you, all these warriors stationed in the opposing armies shall cease to exist.

Thus questioned, the Blessed One said: "I am Time, grown great—having reached the height of increase—as the destroyer of the world, the agent of the dissolution of the worlds. I alone am Kālarudra, the one authorized for the dissolution. Now, here, I have set out to withdraw and destroy all the worlds, in order to lighten the burden of the earth."

Now, all these warriors who have come together in this great battle exist only under the sway of Time. All of them, dwelling and acting within me—who am Viṣṇu in form—for all this time, finally enter into me as the terrible Kālarudra. Therefore, those warriors who are heroes in these opposing armies...
All of them, even without you—even apart from you—will cease to exist; they will no longer live.

The time for their destruction has arrived. It is for that very purpose that they have gathered here. I too am present; by me alone are they now being slain. This terrible task of slaying them is mine alone.

"You are despondent under the delusion that all this is being done by you alone; such despondency is not appropriate regarding an unavoidable matter. In the affairs of the world, even a minor dissolution must be brought about on a grand scale, and that is entirely within my power; no deliberation need be made thereon."

By living beings such as you: while the Lord dwells within the heart, whatever kind of action He impels you toward, that very same action must be performed by you; you should proceed as a mere instrument with the vision that "it is only people subject to death who have come together for this battle through my impulsion."
In this regard, the Blessed Lord clarifies that the accomplishment of their welfare and security is not connected to any single individual, but rather is connected to the omniscient Lord. || 32 ||
Therefore, arise! Win glory; having conquered your enemies, enjoy a prosperous kingdom.
These have already been slain by me alone; be merely an instrument, O Savyasācin. (33)

Therefore, since death is imminent for them, arise for battle! Fulfill your duty with faith; thereby you shall surely obtain and attain glory. If you are firmly resolved upon personal honor, then engage in this battle that has come as your duty.

Carry out [this task] in accordance with the impulse of the Lord. O Savyasācin Arjuna, all these warriors assembled here have already been slain by me alone in my form as Kālarudra, even prior to their being killed by you in battle;
therefore, they have all come forth merely as living corpses. They shall never be slain by you.

Nevertheless, for the sake of fulfilling your duty as one who has become a portion of My own self, you are employed here merely as an instrument; indeed, primary agency does not reside in you. Knowing this, become a recipient of My grace by practicing the yoga of action (*karmayoga*). [Thus spoke He,] such was the divine instruction.
The Blessed One bestows grace for the welfare of humanity. || 33 ||
"Droṇa, Bhīṣma, Jayadratha, Karṇa, and likewise other heroic warriors—slay them as they have already been slain by me; do not be distressed. Fight, and you shall conquer your enemies in battle. (34)
Having taught in general, the Blessed One now speaks specifically as well: "Slay Droṇa, Bhīṣma, Jayadratha, Karṇa, and likewise other chief warriors and preeminent heroes;
do not be distressed—do not yield to affliction; fight, engage in battle; [slay] your rivals, your enemies."

"You shall be victorious; you will conquer in battle. You must never entertain doubts such as 'How shall I slay Droṇa and the others? or 'Shall we win, or shall they defeat us? You were not born for such deliberation, but rather to attain my grace through the fulfillment of your own duty.
He was born solely to attain My yoga. Thus the Blessed One taught Arjuna, out of affection, the duty that must necessarily be performed. 34.
Having heard these words of Keśava, the diadem-wearing Arjuna, trembling and with palms joined in reverence,
bowed down again and spoke to Kṛṣṇa with a faltering voice, prostrating himself in utter fear.
Having drunk the nectar of the words of Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Self, what did Arjuna do?
Regarding this point, Sañjaya said: Having heard these words of Keśava, Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the diadem-wearing Arjuna—
Trembling and shaking, with palms joined in reverence, he bowed again to Kṛṣṇa;
then, overcome with fear, his voice faltering with trepidation and bowing once more, he spoke these words that follow. || 35 ||
It is fitting, O Hṛṣīkeśa, that by the proclamation of Your glory the world rejoices and is filled with love;
the demons flee in fear to every quarter, and all the hosts of Siddhas offer their salutations.

O Hṛṣīkeśa, O Kṛṣṇa, by the proclamation of Your majesty, the entire world rejoices, attains joy, and becomes devoted, even feeling affection for You. In this very way, the Rākṣasas, being terrified, flee in all directions; and all the hosts of Siddhas offer their salutations. All of this—
It is indeed fitting; for since you possess such marvelous power, you are therefore eternally beautiful and serve as a model for all. || 36 ||
And why should they not bow down to You, O Great-Souled One, who are greater even than Brahmā, the original creator?
O Infinite Lord of Gods, Abode of the Universe, You are the Imperishable, that which is both being and non-being, and that which is beyond them.

O Great Soul, O Supreme Soul, O Primordial Creator even of Brahmā Hiraṇyagarbha—why do these hosts of Siddhas offer salutations to You? While offering worship to You, the Worthy One, these Siddhas indeed unite the class of human beings with auspicious intellect and conduct. O Infinite One, O You who have destroyed the inner darkness!

O Lord of gods, O Sovereign even of the gods, O Abode of the universe—you who are the dwelling place of all worlds—you alone are the supreme, the highest, the existent and non-existent (sadasat), meaning you are the essence of all. You alone are that which is called the Imperishable, the Supreme Brahman. Even while assuming a human body, you yourself are directly the Supreme Brahman. || 37 ||
You are the primordial God, the ancient Puruṣa; you are the supreme repository of this universe.
You are the knower and that which is to be known, and the highest abode; by you, O one of infinite forms, the entire universe is pervaded.

You alone are the primordial god, the deity who stands at the beginning of all gods. Thus, you alone are the ancient, eternal Puruṣa. You are the supreme, ultimate abode of this entire universe—*tat tvam asi*.
You alone are the supreme and most excellent abode, the radiance. O Infinite One, whose form is the universe, by you the entire world is pervaded.
You are Vāyu, Yama, Agni, Varuṇa, Śaśāṅka, Prajāpati, and the Great-Grandfather.
Salutations, salutations be unto you a thousand times; and again, yet once more, salutations, salutations unto you! (39)
In the play of bestowing grace upon devotees, You alone have assumed a physical form through the analogy of the hardness of ghee [solidified butter]—[You who are otherwise] the formless Supreme Self.

You alone are Varuṇa, Agni, Śaśāṅka (the Moon), Prajāpati such as Kaśyapa and others, and the Great-grandfather (Prapitāmaha). Because You are the progenitor even of the Grandfather, the Four-faced One (Brahmā), You are the Great-grandfather. Therefore, for You...

"Let there be salutation a thousand times," that is, many times; "and again, yet once more, salutation unto you, salutation. Thus, due to the intensity of devotion, there is a repetition of the prostration. (39)

Salutations to You from the front, and salutations to You from behind; let there be salutations to You from every side, O All! You possess infinite power and immeasurable valor; You pervade all things, and therefore You are everything.

Thus, out of the very intensity of devotion, he says: "Salutation to You in front," that is, in the eastern direction; likewise, "salutation" even from behind. What need is there for more? O All, O You whose nature is everything! "Salutation be to You from all sides," that is, in all directions as well. To the question of how the Blessed One possesses the nature of all things, he says "Ananta... and so forth. Ananta... [the rest of the verse follows].

Both of those are beyond you. Since you, possessing such wonderful power, pervade and abide within everything, you are all; you are the very nature of all. Thus, it is stated that being the pervader of all is itself the reason for being the nature of all. || 40 ||
Thinking "he is my friend," whatever was spoken by me rashly—O Kṛṣṇa, O Yādava, O friend—either through negligence or out of affection, being ignorant of this greatness of yours; || 41 ||
And whatever disrespect you have suffered from me for the sake of mockery— whether in recreation, on a bed, in a seat, or at a meal—
either alone or in the presence of others, O Acyuta, I beg forgiveness from you, the immeasurable one.

Thus, perceiving Kṛṣṇa as the nature of the Supreme Self, Arjuna— recalling everything he had done regarding Him during this time, such as contempt and the like, due to his lack of knowledge of His majesty— [remained] reflecting upon it all.
Out of fear, he begs forgiveness from Kṛṣṇa, the Supreme Soul: "Thinking that You were my friend of equal age, I—
failing to recognize this unsurpassed majesty and glory of Your divine form—
out of sheer negligence, lack of attention, or even out of intimacy and affection, have acted with force."

That which was spoken by me through forceful subjugation—“O Kṛṣṇa! O Yādava! O Friend!”—and that which was spoken for the sake of derision, for the sake of mockery, during the activities of sport, lying down, sitting, and eating; "sport" meaning play and the like, "lying down" meaning reclining, "sitting" meaning being seated, and "eating" and so forth, while these activities were underway.

Whether alone, in private, or in your presence, or before all people, you have been treated with disrespect and insulted in many ways, O Acyuta, O Blessed One; I beg forgiveness from you, who possess immeasurable and great majesty that is impossible even to describe, for all of that.
Arjuna requests with humility that all of this must indeed be forgiven by you. || 41-42 ||
You are the father of this world of the moving and the unmoving; you are its object of worship, the teacher, and the greatest of teachers.
O You of incomparable power, there is no one equal to you, nor has anyone superior been made in all the three worlds. (43)

To the question, "For what purpose do you seek forgiveness?", he says: O Mahādeva, endowed with a marvelous majesty according to the scriptural statement, "O You of incomparable power, neither one equal nor superior to You is seen," for You are indeed the father— the progenitor— of the world consisting of the moving and the unmoving, that is, of all things animate and inanimate.

Since the Supreme Brahman alone is the cause of the origin of the universe, you alone are the one worthy of worship, the one deserving of honor, the most venerable, the most excellent, and the teacher of this world; the meaning is that you alone are the teacher of the entire universe. What need is there for more?
Even throughout the three worlds, there is no one at all who is equal to you or like unto you.
How could there be anyone superior to you, or even more excellent than you? All others are indeed inferior compared to you; therefore, I pray for your forgiveness. || 43 ||
Therefore, having bowed down and prostrated my body, I seek to propitiate you, the adorable Lord;
as a father toward his son, a friend toward his friend, or a lover toward his beloved, it behooves you, O God, to endure me.
Therefore, because you are thus devoid of equal or superior, you are the Lord, the Great Lord of all worlds;

having known me as the enjoyer of sacrifices and austerities, the Great Lord, one attains peace—this has indeed been stated previously. For this very reason, having bowed down—that is, having prostrated my body—to you, who are worthy of worship and praise, I...
Having prostrated— that is, having lowered my body thoroughly— I pray, that is, I entreat you, to be gracious, to become pleased.
Having committed such offenses, how can my body become gracious through a mere request for forgiveness today?

To this he says: "Like a father," and so forth. O Lord, O Blessed One, O Kṛṣṇa: just as a father might forgive the offense of a son, or as a friend might forgive the offense of a friend, or [as a husband might forgive] that of his beloved...
Just as a beloved person might forgive an offense, so too you ought to endure me; "for the beloved" (*priyāya*) is a Vedic sandhi form for *priyāyai*. Thus, you ought to tolerate me. 44.
I am thrilled at seeing what has never been seen before, yet my mind is distressed with fear;
therefore, O God, show me that very form again. Be gracious, O Lord of Gods, O Abode of the Universe! (45)
Thus, beholding the Lord in His universal form, Arjuna, being unable to look further,
humbly entreats Him to withdraw that universal form:
"Having seen this divine form of Yours, never before seen anywhere or at any time, I am exceedingly thrilled."

I am satisfied. Moreover, my mind is intensely pained and trembling with fear—specifically, with the terror born from seeing such a fearsome form. O Lord of gods, O Sovereign even of the gods; O Abode of the universe, O Support of the world, O Master, O God!
Show me that very same former, common human form of mine; be gracious. The meaning is: having become gracious, withdraw the universal form. || 45 ||
I wish to see you likewise as one wearing a crown, holding a mace, and with a discus in hand;
in that very four-armed form, O thousand-armed one, O you whose body is the universe! 46.

This is also an elliptical expression for the conch. I desire to see you, who bear the conch and discus, in that very same way as before; therefore, by means of that very same four-armed form seen previously, become [as you were], and assume your former form once again. || 46 ||
O Arjuna, being pleased with you, I have through my own yoga shown you this supreme form—
effulgent, universal, infinite, and primordial— which has never been seen before by anyone other than you.

Thus requested by Arjuna with humility, the Blessed One said: "O Arjuna, because you are pleased with me and have been shown favor, through my own yoga— that is, by the very majesty of my Self— I shall show you this supreme, universal form, which is full of splendor, consisting of light, infinite (without end), boundless (without interior), and ancient (existing at the beginning of all things)."
The form (rūpa),
which is the nature of the Supreme Self (paramātmasvarūpa), has been shown to you; that form which is distinct from you, separate from you.
Such a form as this has never been seen by anyone before; it was never seen before, yet I have now revealed it to you. || 47 ||
Neither by Vedic sacrifices, nor by study, nor by gifts, nor by rituals, nor by fierce austerities, can I be seen in this form in the world of men by anyone other than you, O hero of the Kurus. (48)

He confirms the very point already stated: "O hero of the Kurus, I cannot be seen through the Vedas, sacrifices, and studies"—the connection is to be understood individually for each. Likewise, [I cannot be seen] through gifts, ritual acts, or even through fierce and intense austerities such as the Agnihotra and other rites; such is my nature.

"I am Viśvarūpa (the Universal Form) in the world of men, the world of humanity; I cannot be seen by anyone other than you, that is, by anyone distinct from you. Thus, the Supreme Self, being attainable through the yoga of steady devotion, bestows the grace of His own vision only upon the most excellent among true devotees. This is the purport, as stated in the *Śaraṇagītā*: "O Lord, You are not easily accessible to those who are devoid of devotion, nor to those who are merely devoted to worldly objects, nor even to those who possess knowledge. O Lord, You are attained only by those who have taken refuge at Your feet."

Śambhu is called "Vedapriya" (fond of the Vedas) by people, yet Śiva is not satisfied by the Veda alone. For instance, Brahmā, who was born with half his lifespan remaining, became headless. Therefore, Śiva is not merely devoted to the *nāda* (the primordial sound), nor is he fond of the Veda alone; rather, devotion is what truly pleases the Lord. Indeed, may I become a devotee of Bhava.

"O noble Saṅgama! Thus, those who have taken refuge [in Him] [do so] for the sake of their own welfare, through His sincere compassion toward those of humble nature, regarding the Supreme Lord as one accessible only through exclusive devotion. || 48 ||
Let there be no distress for you, nor any state of confusion, upon seeing this terrible form of mine;
with fear dispelled and a joyful mind, behold once again that very same form of mine. 49.
Then the Blessed One consoled the terrified Arjuna: "Behold once again this very same form of mine as it was before—this terrible form of such-and-such a kind. (49)
Having spoken thus to Arjuna, Vāsudeva showed him his own form once more;
and the Great-Souled One, assuming again his gentle appearance, comforted him who was terrified. (50)
Saṃjaya said: Having spoken thus to Arjuna—in this manner—the Blessed Kṛṣṇa Vāsudeva again displayed his own former form.
Furthermore, the Great-Souled One, the Supreme Self, Śrī Kṛṣṇa, having assumed a gentle body, a serene form—
He comforted and consoled the terrified Arjuna; likewise, Sañjaya reported to Dhṛtarāṣṭra the manner in which the Blessed One had consoled Arjuna.
"O Janārdana, having seen this gentle human form of yours, I have now become composed in mind and have returned to my natural state. (51)
Thus consoled by the Blessed One, Arjuna said: "O Janārdana Kṛṣṇa, having seen this gentle human form of yours, I have now regained my senses and become tranquil in mind;
I have returned to my own nature. (51)
This form of mine which you have seen is very difficult to behold;
even the gods are constantly longing for a vision of this form.

Having assumed the state of a human being, the Blessed Lord spoke again: "You have seen this form of Mine which is exceedingly difficult to behold, utterly impossible to see; even the gods, Indra and the others, are constantly desirous of seeing this form, yet they remain merely longing for its vision. By you—
Even the gods have not seen the universal form as it has been seen up to this point, nor will they ever see it again.
Neither by the Vedas, nor by austerity, nor by charity,
nor by sacrifice can I be seen in such a form as you have seen me.

To explain how the vision of the universal form is difficult to attain, he says: "In whatever manner you have seen Me, in such a way—whether through the Vedas, that is, by the study of the Rig, Yajur, and other Vedas; or through severe austerity;
or through charity; or through sacrifice, such as the performance of rituals—I cannot be seen at all. This Self..."

"By the sacred word He is to be attained, not by intellect nor by much hearing; he alone whom this [Self] chooses, by him is He attainable; to him this [Self] reveals His own form. Thus it is stated in the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad regarding the Supreme Self.

Having negated the notion that [the Supreme] is accessible solely through scriptural knowledge, it is taught that He is accessible only through right conduct (*sadvartana*). Right conduct, moreover, is nothing other than service (*sevā*) to the True Reality, which is the Supreme Self (*paramātman*). This very service is designated by the term "devotion" (*bhakti*).
The great poet Kālidāsa [describes] the Supreme Self as attainable through the yoga of steadfast devotion.

He thus points out the excellence of devotion to the Supreme Soul (Kṛṣṇa): that which is given shines forth as having auspicious results in the future. Even within this devotion, that devotion which is devoid of desire for rewards is dear to the Supreme Soul and is designated by the term "supreme" (parā). By means of this supreme devotion—

Having gratified the Supreme Power (Parāśakti) and the Supreme Self (Paramātman), human beings must indeed make their birth meaningful. Therefore, what was stated by the Lord—that He cannot be seen merely through Vedic study, austerity, and so forth—is here rendered true to its meaning. || 53 ||
But by unswerving devotion alone, O Arjuna, I who am of such a nature can be known in truth, seen in truth, and entered into, O scorcher of the foe. (54)

If one asks, "What then is the means for seeing you?", he says: O Arjuna, by *bhakti* alone—that is, by devotion whose sole purpose is nothing other than Me—such as I am, I can be seen. The fruit of *bhakti* is not merely vision; rather, he says "knowledge," and so forth, to show that *bhakti* bestows all fruits. [It enables one] to know in truth, according to reality (*tattvaśaḥ*).
To know My true nature as it is, or to enter into Me—by "entering" is meant liberation.

Just as a river [merges] into the ocean, liberation is simply the unification of the individual soul (*jīva*) with the Supreme Self (*paramātman*). Therefore, the knowledge of My true nature or the vision of Me is entirely attainable through devotion alone.
But it is accessible through other means. || 44 ||
He who performs my work, who regards me as the supreme goal, who is my devotee, who is free from attachment,
and who is without enmity toward all beings— he comes to me, O Pāṇḍava.
Therefore, O Pāṇḍava Arjuna, he who performs my work—that is, one who performs actions solely for my sake;

who has me as his supreme goal, knowing that I alone am the supreme object to be attained; who is my devotee, being devoted to me alone; and who, for that very reason, is free from attachment, devoid of clinging to anything other than me, and is without enmity toward all beings, even toward all living creatures—[he attains peace].

He becomes free from hatred and attains me; there is no doubt in this matter. Thus, by serving Paraśiva, whose nature is existence (*sadrūpa*), a human being, having abandoned the impurities and defects such as egoism (*ahaṃkāra*) and possessiveness (*mamakāra*), [attains liberation].

Abiding in the stainless state, having united with the supreme Śiva who is inherently stainless, and experiencing the bliss of Śiva while gladdening all beings through the contemplation of their Śiva-nature, he carries out every worldly transaction solely from the perspective of worshipping Śiva.
In this very way, the vision of Śiva everywhere is accomplished as if through the yoga of Śiva; therefore, everyone should likewise [act].
One should strive. || 55 ||
The Twelfth Chapter:

At the conclusion of the preceding chapter, by the words "one who performs my work" (*matkarmakṛt*) and so forth, it was stated that devotion (*bhakti*) is the cause of liberation. And since devotion is indeed meditation (*upāsana*), it follows that meditation upon the Supreme Self alone is the cause of liberation.

The worship of the Supreme Self (paramātman) is of two kinds: with attributes (sopādhika) and without attributes (nirupādhika). Worship performed through the form of a particular deity is called worship with attributes; worship of the Supreme Śiva-Brahman, from whom all attributes have been eliminated, is alone called worship without attributes.

Desiring to know which of these two modes of worship is superior, Arjuna said: "Of those devotees who, being thus constantly disciplined, worship You, and those who worship the Imperishable and Unmanifest—the latter being formless, unchanging, omnipresent, extremely subtle, and immovable; of these two groups, who are the most proficient in yoga? (1)

Those devotees and worshippers who, being constantly engaged— meaning having their minds distinguished by a continuous application to your ritual actions and so forth— worship you in this manner as the one possessing the aforementioned form of the universal manifestation;
and those others who worship the Imperishable (akṣara), which is eternally uniform in nature, unmanifest, beyond the reach of the senses, and formless (amūrta).
Among those who worship the Supreme Self, who are the best knowers of yoga—that is, who are the most distinguished practitioners of yoga?
Arjuna asks: between one who worships the embodied form associated with the Supreme Self and one who contemplates His formless state, which of the two is superior? (1)
Those who, fixing their minds on Me, worship Me with constant discipline,
endowed with supreme faith— they are considered by Me to be the most perfectly disciplined.

Thus questioned, the Blessed Lord said: "Those worshippers who, having fixed and concentrated their minds upon Me, the Blessed One who am the soul of the universe, are ever-disciplined— meaning they are constantly and perpetually joined with Me alone."

Those who have reached the culmination of yoga and are endowed with the highest, most excellent faith, regarding Me as the Self within all beings—between these two groups, they are considered and esteemed as superior; for they worship the Supreme Self alone as the very deity in each respective form, and thus they are celebrated as the best of yogis. || 2 ||
But those who worship the Imperishable, which is indefinable, unmanifest, all-pervading, unthinkable, immovable, and eternal; (3)
Having fully restrained the collection of their senses and possessing equal intelligence toward all,
those who delight in the welfare of all beings attain Me alone.

Regarding the question, "What is the destination of those who worship the Unmanifest? it is said here: Those worshippers, however, who—having restrained the entire collection of senses within the heart—possess an even mind, devoid of any sense of gradation, toward this world filled with passion and hatred; and who, for that very reason, are devoted to the welfare of all beings—that is, intent on wishing well for all living creatures—[attain] the Imperishable.

It is devoid of destruction, indescribable—meaning it is unfit to be described as "this is such"—all-pervading, immutable, immovable, omnipresent, and for that very reason inconceivable, meaning impossible to conceive; it is fixed, changeless, and immovable because of its omnipresence; it is eternal, constant, and unmanifest.

Even those who worship the reality of the Supreme Self as unmanifested and distinguished in some particular way, they too attain Me alone, the formless Supreme Self; therefore, the fruit for both types of worshippers is indeed of one and the same nature. (3-4)
The affliction of those whose minds are attached to the Unmanifest is greater;
for the goal that is unmanifest is attained with difficulty by the embodied. (5)

If that is so, why is it said that your very devotees are the most excellent? For it is heard in scripture that you possess both a formed and a formless nature. Your formed aspect alone is the undivided universe. The propitiation of the universe is itself the worship of the universe. In comparison to that, the worship of your formed aspect is indeed superior.
How is it stated by those who possess direct experience? Why is it said that those who worship the formless are indeed superior even to those who worship the formed?

He states the resolution to this: for those practitioners whose minds are attached to the unmanifest— that is, those whose minds are attached to such an unmanifest, all-pervading, formless reality— their exertion, the labor experienced by them in attaining their own fruit, is exceedingly great.

They are superior to those who worship me in the form of my physical image; therefore, it is said that my worshippers alone are the best. Wherever there is a form, those who worship it with the contemplation (*bhāvanā*) of me as being present therein are indeed worshippers of my own form.
It is understood that they alone obtain the fruit without effort; hence their superiority is established. Why? Because [it is difficult] in the worship of the unmanifest (*avyakta*).

Regarding the point that affliction (*kleśa*) is greater, he says: "For [the path] is unmanifest" (*avyaktā hi*). For this reason—because such a path consisting of the meditation upon the Unmanifest is attained by embodied beings with as much difficulty as possible; that is to say, that meditation is extremely difficult to perform. Thus, regarding the meditation on the formless...
The meaning is that, precisely because of the nature of extreme affliction, only those who worship my manifest form are proclaimed as the most excellent. || 5 ||
