But those who, having renounced all actions unto Me, are devoted to Me, and worship Me, meditating upon Me with an exclusive yoga of union; || 6 ||
I become their deliverer from the ocean of death and worldly existence,
O Pārtha, without delay, for those whose minds are absorbed in Me.
In response to the doubt as to why those who worship you would have less affliction, he says that because I myself am their protector,
the attainment of the fruit for them becomes easy; however, those who are my worshippers,
having renounced and surrendered all actions unto me, should perform whatever they do and whatever they eat.
Having surrendered [themselves] according to the manner described as "madarpaṇam," being devoted to me (matparāḥ) with their minds fixed on me alone (madekacittāḥ),

they worship me— meditating upon and contemplating me through yoga, which is single-minded (ananya), devoid of other purposes, and having me alone as its fruit; O Pārtha, for those whose consciousness is absorbed in me, the Supreme Self, and whose minds are thus concentrated.

I alone shall be their rescuer—indeed, their perfect deliverer—from the ocean of saṃsāra in the form of death, before long and with great speed. And since the responsibility for their acquisition and preservation (yogakṣema) has been accepted by Me alone, there is no possibility whatsoever of delay or failure in their attainment of the fruit. Therefore...
They are reckoned as being my devotees alone, the very best of all. || 6-7 ||
Fix your mind on Me alone; establish your intellect in Me.
Thereafter you shall dwell in Me alone; of this there is no doubt. (8)

Therefore, you too should fix and direct your mind upon me alone— the Self of all, consisting of all the gods— and likewise establish your intellect in me alone. By doing so, immediately thereafter, you shall dwell in me alone, the Supreme Self, and not elsewhere after having abandoned me.
You do not even have the opportunity to depart; regarding this, there is no doubt at all.
But if you are unable to fix your mind steadily on Me,
then seek to reach Me, O Dhanañjaya, by the yoga of practice.
Having thus taught the yoga of devotion, the Blessed One, out of compassion, also taught the various stages for those unable to practice it:

"If you are not able [to practice devotion], then seek to attain Me—that is, pray to attain Me—by means of the yoga of constant practice, which consists in the repeated fixing of the mind upon Me. If you are a devotee, fix that mind on the Supreme Self alone."

The Blessed One teaches here that if one is unable to fix [the mind] there, one should practice for the very sake of attaining it. If a devotee’s devotion is endowed with faith, they will always desire union with the Supreme Self alone;
otherwise, they will not be pleasing to the Supreme Self. Indeed, devotion devoid of steadfastness does not accomplish the happiness of this world or the next.

The *Śaraṇagītā* ruthlessly refutes the devotion of one devoid of steadfastness and the conduct of one devoid of faith. Just as no happiness ever arises from a painted image of a cow, and just as no juice flows from a sugarcane depicted on a cloth, so it is here.

"But this devotion of one devoid of steadfastness (niṣṭhā) can never lead to the satisfaction of the Lord; likewise, this worldly conduct cannot lead to aesthetic flavor (rasa) in the state of existence that liberates from saṃsāra. Thus, only when devotion is possessed of steadfastness is it capable of releasing one from the bonds of worldly existence. It is solely through its power that...
The devotee becomes united with Paraśiva, who shines within the heart, through the firmness of practice. || 9 ||
If you are unable even to practice, become intent on performing actions for Me;
by performing actions for My sake, you shall attain perfection.
p.

266) Even if you are unable—that is, if you are not capable—of such practice or performing such practice, then be one for whom My work is supreme (*matkarmaparamaḥ*): *matkarma* is work for My sake; he for whom that alone is the supreme objective.
Become such a one. Perform actions solely with Me as the objective, and not for the sake of your own self-interest.
Even while performing actions for My sake in this way, you will gradually attain perfection—the attainment of the fruit;
there is no doubt in this matter. When a person striving to practice for the attainment of the Blessed One is unable [to do so], then...

The Blessed One indicates that for the sake of attaining the Blessed One alone, the performance of all ritual actions is indeed sufficient. A practitioner should strive to carry out every worldly transaction, such as giving and receiving, solely for the pleasure of the Blessed One; even then, one is certainly able to obtain the grace of the Blessed One.
The intention of the Supreme Self. || 10 ||
But if you are unable even to do this, then, taking refuge in my yoga,
renounce the fruits of all actions with a self-controlled mind.

Furthermore, if you are unable even to perform this, being intent on your own duties yet incapable of performing those actions, and if you are likewise unable to remain [in that state], then, having resorted to my yoga— my yoga consisting of devotion—
and being self-controlled with a restrained mind, for that reason, practice the renunciation of the fruits of all actions, of all [actions whatsoever].

Renounce the fruit of your actions. Whatever you perform from morning until evening, surrender the fruit of every one of those actions to me at that very moment, in both my manifest and unmanifest forms. Through that, by means of the gradual purification of the mind and so forth, the attainment of me will surely come to pass. || 11 ||
Knowledge is indeed better than practice; meditation is distinguished as superior to knowledge;
the renunciation of the fruits of action is superior to meditation; and from renunciation, peace follows immediately.

He praises such renunciation of the fruits of all actions: through practice—that is, by the yoga of practice—and from that aforementioned [knowledge], meditation on the Supreme Self becomes distinguished; it becomes superior.
Indeed, the renunciation of the fruits of all actions, which was just mentioned, is superior even to meditation.
It is distinguished [from other means]. And immediately following renunciation, peace and the gradual concentration of the mind certainly come to pass;
this is the remainder [of the sense]. || 12 ||
Now, with the remainder of this chapter, he describes the qualities to be cultivated by devotees:
267) "One who is not a hater of any being, but is friendly and compassionate..."
Free from the sense of "mine," free from egoism, equal in pain and pleasure, and patient. || 13 ||
The yogi who is always content, self-controlled, and firm in resolve;
whose mind and intellect are dedicated to Me—he, my devotee, is dear to Me. 14.

He who is non-hostile toward all beings— that is, he who does not feel hatred for any living creature— is therefore friendly toward all, distinguished by a disposition of friendship; and being compassionate, that is, distinguished by mercy,
he remains free from the sense of "mine" (*nirmama*) and free from egoism (*nirahaṅkāra*), regarding pain and pleasure with equanimity.

Cultivating happiness through equanimity, patient and of a forgiving nature, always and ever content and never discontented, the yogi— intent on the practice of yoga, self-controlled with a restrained mind, firm in resolve,
and possessing unwavering certainty regarding his own goal directed toward Me, the Supreme Self— [attains perfection].
One whose mind and intellect are surrendered— meaning one by whom the mind and intellect have been fully offered—
is such a devotee of Mine who is dear to Me, beloved by Me; for he is attached to the Supreme Self alone,
lives solely for Its sake, experiences only Its grace, and perceives That alone everywhere throughout the entire expansion of sense-objects.
The practitioner, whose inner self is always contented and who always dwells in the Supreme Self alone, becomes exceedingly dear to Him. || 13-14 ||
He by whom the world is not agitated and who is not agitated by the world, and who is free from joy, envy, fear, and anxiety—he indeed is dear to Me. 15.
Because that devotee from whom the world does not shrink— that is, does not experience agitation— and who himself does not shrink from the world— that is,

upon seeing whom the world does not experience agitation, or who, having seen the world, does not experience agitation— for that very reason he is free from joy, resentment, fear, and agitation; "joy" being contentment, "resentment" being anger, and "fear" being well known.
He who is free from agitation and anxiety regarding all that has been experienced—that devotee is dear to me, an object of my affection. || 15 ||
He who is free from expectations, pure, skillful, impartial, free from distress, and has renounced all undertakings—he who is my devotee is dear to me. (16)

Free from expectation, being devoid of longing for the objects of the body, senses, and so forth; therefore, pure, always perfectly cleansed, and capable; indifferent, being free from the states of friendliness or enmity and the like; free from distress, with all afflictions gone;
and a renouncer of all undertakings—those things which are called "undertakings" because they are begun, yielding fruits pertaining to this world and the next.
Even one who abandons all those actions—if he is my devotee, he is dear to me. (16)
He who neither rejoices nor hates, neither grieves nor desires,
who has renounced both good and evil, and who is full of devotion— he is dear to Me. (17)

He who does not rejoice—that is, does not experience joy—even upon attaining what is desired; and likewise, who does not grieve—that is, does not feel sorrow—even upon encountering the undesired; who feels no hatred toward anyone nor harbors any aversion; and who desires nothing at all; for this very reason, he is a renouncer of both the auspicious and the inauspicious, having abandoned the discrimination between good and evil actions.

He who acts in all things solely with the vision of duty and remains devoted is dear to Me. Thus, the devotee always abandons concern for the auspicious and the inauspicious and remains immersed in contemplation of the Supreme Self alone.
Day after day, he prays to the Supreme Self alone: "Who is this? From where has He come here?"
"Do not worry at all as to who this prisoner is; think thus: 'This one is mine, this servant is mine;
this attendant is to be united with me alone. O Lord of Saṅgama, reflect in this way upon your own servant as indeed your son. Thus, the devotee [acts] for the sake of attaining identity with Śiva.

Even one who strives with the three organs of action may, at the end, when having no other recourse, entrust the burden of his own protection to Śiva alone. The *Śaraṇagītā* describes the very relationship between the Lord and the devotee in a way that touches the heart. Regarding the great soul Basavārya’s [devotion] toward the Supreme Self...
The state of total self-surrender is thus described therein: "You alone are my mother and you alone are my father;
you alone are my kinsman and likewise my friend. O Lord of the Sangha, there is no one for me other than you;
hear my words! Do as you please, whether you give me milk or [punish me]."

"Cast it into the water. Thus, the devotee who is dependent on the Supreme Lord, fearless of the world, and eternally satisfied, employs even his own body, senses, and all else for the service of the Supreme Lord, contemplating them as belonging solely to Him. His relationship with the Lord is described in the *Śaraṇagītā* as follows:

Since I understand that your body is mine, therefore I have no body other than yours; since my mind is not at all distinct from your mind, such is my firm conviction. Since all wealth is indeed yours, there is no wealth distinct from you. Having realized these three things of yours to be thus, how indeed could [separateness] exist?

This is the subsequent deliberation. Thus, dwelling as a devotee in accordance with reality—free from the sense of "mine" and free from egoistic conceit—experiencing all contemporary pleasure, pain, and so forth through the contemplation of divine grace, he becomes eternally happy. Even in the act of offering to the Lord, he abandons the perception of good and evil.
Since everything that is to be offered has been given by the Blessed One, he [the Lord] does not even entertain the discrimination that "this is to be offered" or "this is not to be offered. (p. 269)
He does not act [in this way]. This point is correctly explained in the *Śaraṇagītā*:
"The milk of a cow, the remains of food, water for a fish, and likewise the flower for a bee—how indeed could I perform your worship, O Śambhu? O Guru, how may I honor you?"
"O Noble One, having come into the presence of my Guru, it is not possible for me to wipe away this impurity today.

Indeed, that which was given by you for my sake is now being offered back to you. In this very way, the devotee, casting aside both joy and sorrow regarding the phenomenal world, offers even his own collection of objects of enjoyment to the Supreme Self.
He dwells in a state free from anxiety. || 17 ||
He is the same toward enemy and friend, as well as toward honor and dishonor;
he is the same in cold and heat, in pleasure and pain, and is free from attachment.
A man who is equal in blame and praise, silent, content with whatever comes,
homeless, steady-minded, and full of devotion— such a person is dear to Me.

Being equal toward enemy and friend, thus possessing a state of equanimity, as well as toward honor and dishonor— remaining likewise indifferent to respect and disrespect— and similarly equal amidst cold and heat, pleasure and pain, being even-minded in such pairs that produce happiness and sorrow, he is free from attachment, devoid of clinging.

Regarding praise and blame as equal, he contemplates both praise and blame with equanimity; silent and possessing the power of silence, he is satisfied with whatever little he obtains, being perfectly content and not looking for more—meaning he is fulfilled with whatever comes his way; and homeless, meaning devoid of a fixed abode, shelter, or dwelling.

Free from attachment to one's own home and possessions, steady-minded, and firm in intellect— such a devoted person who is my bhakta is dear to Me, an object of My affection. Thus, a devotee who always lives uprightly,
sustaining his life by whatever means endowed with dignity, perceives the Lord alone as the most substantial reality within this world.

Constantly reflecting upon the Supreme Self alone as abiding with equanimity even amidst all worldly objects, he passes his time solely through the experience of bliss. A certain devotee describes his own stainless state thus: "Whether it be on a snake, or on a necklace, or on a bed of flowers, or on a stone, or on a gem..."
Whether toward a clod of earth or a powerful enemy, toward a friend or a blade of grass, or even toward a woman—my days pass with an equal eye in some sacred forest. Śiva! Śiva!

"O Śiva!"—thus he cries out. In this way, the devotee, disregarding the comforts of home, gardens, and the like, dwells wherever he may be, remaining solely absorbed in contemplation of the Supreme Self. Therefore, Mahādeva, satisfied by his stainless heart, takes no account of his external dress, ostentation, or such things.
He gazes [upon the Lord]. The *Śaraṇagītā* describes his heartfelt prayer in a manner that provides inspiration to all practitioners:
he constantly prays day and night to the Supreme Self solely for the sake of abandoning the instability caused by the delusion of his own *māyā*.

The great-souled Siddharāma thus prays to Śrī Guru Mallikārjuna: "O Mallikārjuna, shatter the intoxication of *māyā*; destroy the wakefulness of the body. Constantly dispel the flickering of the mind and loosen the expansion of delusion—do you alone! Thus.

The Śaraṇas, who strive to transform their physical nature (aṅga-prakṛti) into the nature of the Liṅga through meditation on the Blessed Lord, are worthy of the respect of all. In this very manner, Basavārya describes the transformation of his own nature: "By your grace, my body itself has perished."

"By your power, my very mind has been destroyed; by your power, my karma has been destroyed. O Noble One, through association with you, I have nothing left. Having spoken thus again and again, and having displayed the jewel-ornament called devotion unto you alone, they made it truly so there by becoming agents of your grace."

"The one who causes [the Lord] to act is the enjoyer. Thus, having contemplated the dwelling of the Divine alone within the body and all the senses, the devotee, together with Him, offers even his own enjoyment of form and so forth to Him for the sake of His service through devotion;
he then contemplates himself as dwelling right there. Therefore, in that [state]...
There is simply no room for the increase of the notions of "I" and "mine. || 19 ||
But those who worship this immortal nectar of dharma as it has been described, full of faith, regarding Me as their supreme goal—those devotees are exceedingly dear to Me. (20)

Having thus described the qualities to be adopted by devotees, and having praised those possessed of such qualities, [the Lord says: "Those who attend upon this aforementioned instruction—which is not devoid of dharma and which serves as the cause for realizing the true nature of the Self—become intent on such instruction;
they conduct themselves in the arena of life according to such instruction."
Those devotees who are endowed with faith, who regard Me alone as the supreme goal, and who hold Me as their ultimate refuge—
they become exceedingly dear to Me, objects of My supreme affection. Of the devotee...
The *Śaraṇagītā* clearly sets forth the method of worshiping the Blessed One through the very words of the experience of those who have sought refuge:
"May you, the Guru, bestow upon me either virtue or vice—whatever may become an enemy to the attainment of You.
O You of incomparable nature, may I never at any time be equal to those [who oppose You]."

"O Blessed One, it is indeed through falling within the range of Your compassion that I have attained my very self-nature. This being so, understand how it is fitting for You to direct anger toward me today. Thus, the devotee, having always become a vessel for the Supreme Lord's compassion and becoming His very own, acts in accordance with His will.
Performing various actions, he remains free from the bonds of merit and demerit, experiencing the bliss of Śiva.
The *Śaraṇagītā* describes his state of ultimate, faultless steadfastness as follows:
"You are the sovereign of my body, and likewise of my mind, wealth, and so forth; my very knowledge is yours."

"O Lord, this delusion of mine is also subject to you alone; thus, since all that belongs to me comes under your dominion, if some offense should suddenly befall me, you alone shall receive its fruit. In this way, with total self-surrender and an absence of reserve toward the Supreme Self—

Having become one who has taken refuge, the devotee establishes his own innocence at the time of conducting legal proceedings. Since he lives by relying solely upon the Supreme Self in all circumstances, the Supreme Self alone fully accomplishes his *yogakṣema* (acquisition and preservation). This is the nature of devotion.

In the state of ultimate perfection, even the prior distinction between the devotee and the God vanishes. At that time, his condition is described thus: "You alone perform devotion, and likewise you alone are the devotee;
you alone are the form of the one to be served. Your feet have not been seen by me here, nor indeed have they been granted by you."
"Your state. Thus: here, you alone are the servant and you alone are the one to be served;

your state has not been seen by me, nor has my state been fashioned as yours by you. Therefore, you alone are everything—the giver, the enjoyer, the doer, and the cause of action. There is no one else for the sake of my independent activity.

There exists some such opportunity; in this state of stainless devotion, passion and hatred, as well as lust and anger, can never increase within him. Thus, all human beings, becoming true devotees and abandoning egoism and pride, should cherish their own country as their own.

"May they dwell in eternal contentment through peace"—thus does the Supreme Self, Śrī Kṛṣṇa, look upon them, maintaining an equal vision toward both enemy and friend, as well as toward praise and blame.
Wherever equanimous meditation shines forth, that very devotee experiences contentment in a state free from modification.
He always regards one who disparages Him as a kinsman to his own birth, and likewise perceives one who praises Him as an enemy to his birth.
In this very way, he does not hanker after pleasure nor does he tremble at suffering. In such a state—

When his mind, intellect, consciousness, and ego are established in a state of full maturity and are infused with the highest impressions (*saṃskāra*), it is the intention of the Supreme Self that the welfare of the world must be accomplished by devotees of such a kind. O my Lord, instruct me so that I may remember Your pair of feet; for, having spread out the hem of Your garment—

"I have come to you, O Lord, to make a request"—this very intention, revealed by the venerable Śrī Yāmunācārya, a devotee at the feet of the Supreme Self, on the occasion of his prayer to the Blessed One, shines forth as something to be remembered by all spiritual aspirants. "Never before has such a thing occurred, nor will it ever happen; indeed, I shall endure everything."

"For this suffering is indeed innate to me; however, the humiliation of those who have come to you for refuge is not befitting of you. Thus, with full confidence, those noble-minded ones reveal their intention that the burden of protecting those who have sought refuge must necessarily rest upon the Lord. This is the conviction that "He will protect us."

Only he in whom this firm [conviction] exists is truly fit to be a devotee. Such a devotee, by the grace of Mahādeva, becomes eternally happy. Thus, the Supreme Soul Śrī Kṛṣṇa, while instructing on the state of equilibrium (*sāmarasya*)—which is the nature of oneness with the Supreme Self for the purified soul within the yoga of devotion—said:
It correctly establishes the preeminence of devotion. || 20 ||
Chapter Thirteen.

In the preceding chapters, it has been stated many times that the Supreme Self is attainable through devotion alone. Now, regarding such a Self—O son of Kuntī, this body is called the "field" (kṣetra).
Those who know this declare that he who understands this is the "knower of the field" (kṣetrajña). || 1 ||
p.

273) O Kaunteya Arjuna! This body, composed of the five elements, is designated as the "field" (kṣetra) by those who know the truth. It is called a field because it protects one from injury—that is, from suffering. Indeed, this very body is the locus for meditation and worship.

Indeed, even the great poet says that the body is truly the primary instrument for achieving dharma. Alternatively, because the fruits of action—happiness and suffering—are obtained in this very thing, just as they are in a field, this body is designated as the "field" (kṣetra). He who knows this field, [perceiving] from head to foot, "This body is mine," is...
Those who know that, the knowers of reality, say—that is, they declare—that he is the "knower of the field" (kṣetrajña). || 1 ||
And know Me also as the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña) in all fields, O Bhārata;
that which is the knowledge of the Field and the Knower of the Field is, in My view, true knowledge. || 2 ||

Regarding the question, "Who is this Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña)?", He says: O Bhārata Arjuna, know that the Knower of the Field—the individual soul (jīva)—existing even in all fields, is indeed Me alone, My very own portion. This is My conviction: that the knowledge concerning the relationship between the individual soul and Brahman, and concerning the soul existing therein, is precisely what is meant here by "knowledge."
For knowledge is the means to liberation. The meaning is that this very knowledge—the knowledge of the field and the Knower of the field—is the cause of liberation;

it is my conviction that this alone is knowledge and nothing else. This point is stated in the passage beginning with "Humility, freedom from hypocrisy... and ending with "...this is declared to be knowledge; what is contrary to this is ignorance."
Thus, he will explain this in detail. || 2 ||
Listen to me in brief concerning that field— what it is, of what nature, what its modifications are, from whence it arises, who he is, and what his power is.

Thus, having briefly described the distinction in essential nature between the field (*kṣetra*) and the knower of the field (*kṣetrajña*), and having explained it in detail, [the Lord asks]: "Of what kind is it, and characterized by what attributes? What are its modifications, and what are those modifications?
From this field, what effect is produced? And who is that which has been called the knower of the field?"
"Of what power [is he], meaning endowed with what kind of power? Hear all that from me in brief, in summary. I shall tell you the essential nature and the specific qualities of both; listen. (3)
It has been sung in many ways by the seers, separately in various Vedic meters,
and also in the words of the Brahma-sūtras, which are reasoned and definitive. (4)

He praises the subject matter already stated so that it may be necessarily known: it has been sung—that is, narrated—in many ways, by many modes, by the sages such as Vasiṣṭha and others; it has been sung—that is, narrated—individually and distinctly by various kinds of meters, namely the Vedas such as the Ṛgveda and others; and it is endowed with reasons, that is, supported by logical arguments.

This very knowledge has been proclaimed and taught by the words of the Brahma-sūtras whose meanings have been ascertained and determined—by the well-known collection of Brahma-sūtras beginning with "Then, therefore, the desire to know Brahman" (athāto brahmajijñāsā). The meaning is that this alone is the subject matter expounded by all the scriptures. || 4 ||
The great elements, the ego-sense, the intellect, and the unmanifest;
the ten senses and the one [mind], and the five objects of the senses. || 5 ||
Desire, aversion, pleasure, pain, the aggregate, consciousness, and fortitude—this is declared to be the field, together with its modifications, in brief. (6)

Having thus praised both the field and the knower of the field, he first explains the field: the five great elements—earth, water, fire, air, and ether; egoism; intellect; and the unmanifested as well as primordial nature (prakṛti);
the ten senses and the one—that is, the eleven organs; and the five organs of perception.

The five organs of action and the mind constitute the eleven organs. The spheres of the senses—the objects of the five cognitive organs, namely the nose, tongue, eyes, skin, and ears—are the five: smell, taste, form, touch, and sound. All these taken together are designated by the term "field" (kṣetra).

This is the description of the nature of the field (*kṣetra*). Now, he states its effects: desire, aversion, suffering, the aggregate—the collection of the body and the senses—consciousness, which is the state of being conscious, and fortitude, which is the sustaining of these;
thus all this is the field as a state of transformation. And so, this very field is with its transformations.
It has been illustrated—that is, stated—in brief, that is, in summary, as distinguished by its own category of functions. || 5-6 ||
Humility, freedom from hypocrisy, non-violence, patience, straightforwardness, service to the teacher, purity, steadfastness, and self-restraint. (7)
Detachment from the objects of the senses, as well as the absence of egoism, and the contemplation of the defects of birth, death, old age, disease, and suffering. (8)
Non-attachment and absence of clinging toward children, wife, home, and so forth; and constant equanimity of mind amidst the occurrence of the pleasant and the unpleasant. (9)
And unswerving devotion to me through the yoga of undivided concentration;
the habit of resorting to solitary places; and a distaste for the assembly of worldly people. (10)
Constancy in the knowledge of the Self and the vision of the goal that is the knowledge of reality—this is declared to be knowledge;
what is other than this is ignorance. || 11 ||
With five verses, he teaches certain qualities that must necessarily be adopted by the discerning person: *amānitvam* (humility) is the absence of self-praise;
*adambhitvam* (freedom from hypocrisy) is the absence of ostentatious display of one's own dharma; and *ahiṃsā* (non-violence) is the non-infliction of pain upon living beings.

Forbearance (*kṣānti*) is the absence of agitation even when encountering offenses from others. Straightforwardness (*ārjava*) is the uprightness of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*). Firm resolve (*dṛḍhādhyavasāya*) is the steadfast determination of the mind. Self-restraint (*ātmavinigraha*) is the control and subduing of oneself, namely the body, senses, and so forth. Detachment (*vairāgya*) is the absence of passion regarding the five objects of the senses, such as sound and the rest.

Non-egoism (*anahaṅkāra*) is the absence of the sense of "I. Constant mindfulness is the contemplation and reflection upon birth, death, old age, disease, suffering, and defects; that is to say, the contemplation of the defects of *saṃsāra*. Non-attachment (*asakti*) is the absence of attachment even toward objects already obtained, such as children, wife, and home.
Non-attachment to external comforts such as power and the like means the absence of intimate connection with them;

that is to say, freedom from delusion. Equanimity of mind at all times, even upon the occurrence of the pleasant and the unpleasant—that is, maintaining the mind in a single mode despite the attainment of what is desired or undesired—and [equanimity] toward Me, the all-pervading one.

Devotion (*bhakti*) is that which is single-minded, uniform, and unswerving toward the Supreme Self, who possesses both embodied and unembodied forms; it is practiced through non-dual yoga, without aiming for any other purpose. Cultivating solitude is taking refuge in secluded places.
Disliking the assembly of people is having no desire for the company of common folk for the sake of fame, gain, and the like.
The absence of attachment; constant devotion to the knowledge of the inner self (*adhyātmajñānanityatva*) means always reflecting upon the inner self;

and the vision of the goal of the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñānārthadarśana*) means likewise reflecting upon that very goal, which is liberation—the fruit of the aforementioned knowledge of reality. Thus, because this alone is the means to liberation, it is called "knowledge" (*jñāna*).

Therefore, that which exists otherwise than our [view] is declared to be ignorance (*ajñāna*), consisting precisely of the absence of knowledge (*jñānābhāva*). "That is true knowledge (*vidyā*) which leads to liberation"—thus, only that knowledge which is the cause of liberation is called "knowledge.

However, knowledge concerning other objects is called "ignorance" (ajñāna) because it is a cause of saṃsāra. Therefore, those seeking liberation must first adopt these qualities, beginning with humility (amānitva). These virtues, by means of purifying the inner organ of the seeker, cause his devotion (bhakti) to blossom. And thus:

Having united with the great light shining within the stainless heart, one should follow its bliss and strive according to one's capacity. This method of internal purification is thus indicated in the *Śaraṇagītā*:
"One should never commit theft or violence, nor should untruth ever be spoken."
One should act thus: "Do not praise yourself at any time; do not be a reviler of others.
O Noble One, purity is indeed this: through association with the Guru, that very purity has been prescribed by the learned for the sake of pleasing You.
Thus, only one who possesses internal purity, through the expansion of the heart, [perceives] the Great Light within himself.

Having correctly experienced it, one directly realizes that very same light in all things. As the Blessed One himself has taught: "He who sees Me everywhere and sees everything in Me, for him I am not lost, and he is not lost to Me. Such a devotee speaks only gentle words toward everyone.

By applying oneself to virtuous conduct, one achieves fitness for this world and the next. He who is reckoned as unfit in this life due to wicked behavior will not be honored anywhere else; he alone is fit for the hereafter who is counted as worthy in this world. Thus, purity of character is the means for attaining happiness both in this life and the next.
Those who have experienced it declare that it is unavoidable. For this very reason, the Blessed One has said here for the sake of all practitioners:
"I shall proclaim that which is to be known, by knowing which one attains immortality—the beginningless Supreme Brahman, which is said to be neither being nor non-being. (12)
If it is asked, "If humility and so forth are themselves knowledge, then what is the object to be known by them? he says: "The object to be known is Brahman. [He explains:

the practitioner attains—that is, experiences—liberation (*mokṣa*), which is immortal and consists of eternal bliss. To the question "What is that?", he says: "That which is without beginning," and so forth. "Without beginning" means devoid of origination. This also implies its freedom from destruction.

Such is the supreme Brahman; that alone is to be known. And that supreme Brahman cannot be called "existent," nor can it be called "non-existent"; it transcends all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

The meaning is that it is beyond the reach of speech and mind. Experiential practitioners do not conceive of the Supreme Śiva-Brahman as being solely of the nature of existence (*sat*), nor do they conceive of it as being solely of the nature of non-existence (*asat*).
Furthermore, it is not to be contemplated as being of the nature of both existence and non-existence; for it is both immortality and death.

"O Arjuna, I am both being and non-being," thus it was taught by the Blessed One himself. That which, at the time of creation, becomes composed of both being and non-being, is this very Supreme Śiva-Brahman; at the time of dissolution, having abandoned even the state of being both being and non-being, it assumes its own natural state, which is the condition of absolute isolation (kaivalya). When that [state] prevails, there is neither darkness nor day, nor night, nor being...

And "He is indeed Śiva alone, the absolute"—thus the great seer Śvetāśvatara teaches that Paraśiva is of the nature of being, non-being, and neither. This very state is a particular condition occurring during the contraction of Śakti. That same Paraśiva, through the expansion of Śakti in the state oriented toward creation—
It transforms by way of having both existent and non-existent forms; and its state of contracted power is reckoned as its formless condition. || 12 ||
With hands and feet everywhere, with eyes, heads, and faces everywhere,
and with ears everywhere in the world, It stands encompassing all.

Today, he specifically describes the nature of this Paraśiva-Brahman, which is utterly distinct from both existence and non-existence. That supreme Brahman, known as Paraśiva, is formless (*amūrta*), stainless (*nirañjana*), and omnipresent;
it is capable of performing its respective functions everywhere. Likewise, it has eyes, heads, and faces on all sides, with sight and the other senses directed in every direction.

Even in the absence of the eye, it perceives everything; likewise, even in the absence of the sense of hearing, it hears everything. Not only that, but it remains pervading and encompassing all. Thus, the meaning is that this very Supreme Reality, abiding everywhere, is the accomplisher of all functions. || 13 ||
It appears to possess the qualities of all the senses, yet it is devoid of all senses;
it is unattached and yet the sustainer of all; it is free from qualities and yet the experiencer of qualities.
That reality known as Paraśiva manifests through the qualities and respective functions of all the senses, such as sight and the rest;
its apprehension occurs precisely through those very functions of the senses, namely, form and the other objects of perception.

Moreover, that reality exists entirely devoid of all sense organs; for it is the body alone that is the locus of the senses and so forth, and not the Supreme Brahman. In this very way, that reality is unattached, being free from attachment to anything whatsoever.
It is the sustainer of all, the supporter of everything. It is devoid of qualities (nirguṇa), lacking the qualities of sattva, rajas, and tamas. And yet—
It exists as the enjoyer of qualities and the experiencer of the fruits of such qualities. || 15 ||
It exists both outside and inside all beings; it is both the unmoving and the moving.
Because of its subtlety, it is incomprehensible; it is far away, yet it is near.

That supreme Śiva-tattva exists always externally, internally, and everywhere for all beings—that is, for all living creatures; the meaning is that it is all-pervasive. Precisely because of its pervasiveness, it is "unmoving," meaning it is devoid of motion. Nevertheless, due to its nature as the cause of various effects, it cannot be known by the senses and other such means. That supreme reality, although existing at a distance at one time, is nonetheless near.

And he is also present nearby; because of his all-pervasiveness and sovereignty, that Supreme Śiva exists even within the circle of the stars and so forth, and likewise dwells within the cave of the heart of us and all living beings. In him, however, who is perfectly full, there is the coexistence of mutually contradictory attributes in one place.

The distinctive nature of the Veda and the Āgama, which constitute the means of valid knowledge (*śabda-pramāṇa*), is correctly demonstrated through the form of their integration. Here too, following this very sequence, the Blessed One himself, in a manner that is heart-pleasing, [describes] the nature of his own formless state using only concise words.
He indicates by means of words. || 15 ||
It is undivided among beings, yet it exists as if divided;
it should be known as both the sustainer and the destroyer, as well as the devourer and the source of all.
That which exists as undivided and of one form everywhere among all living beings who appear divided,
yet which remains as if divided and as if distinct from one another—
that should be known as the sustainer of beings, the supporter of all creatures; likewise, it is the devourer at the time of dissolution.
The destroyer of all; likewise, at the time of creation, it should be known as the powerful creator of all. And so, [this applies] to the Supreme Śiva-Brahman. (p.

Precisely because they possess distinct characteristics (*vilakṣaṇatva*), there is no contradiction even when qualities that appear mutually opposed are combined within that single [consciousness] at one time; it was stated in that manner solely to express this distinctiveness. || 16 ||

That which is the light even of lights, which is said to be beyond darkness, which is knowledge, the object of knowledge, and that which is attainable through knowledge—It is seated in the heart of every being. 17.

That Supreme Brahman is the light even of lights such as the moon and the sun; by its radiance all this shines. That Imperishable is the most excellent boon of Savitṛ, and from it has issued forth the ancient wisdom—thus, the fact that the Supreme Self is the illuminator of all is well-established in the Śruti. Therefore:

The Supreme Brahman known as Mahāliṅga is beyond darkness; it is called the supreme light that transcends all darkness. In the Śruti, "the source of beings, the witness of all, beyond darkness," the transcendence of darkness by the Paramātman is clearly established. And that is the Supreme Reality.

It should be understood as being of the nature of knowledge. And thus, that supreme reality—which is accessible through knowledge, attainable solely through the knowledge of truth, and which dwells within the heart of all as the inner controller—is established there. || 17 ||
Thus, the field, as well as knowledge and the object of knowledge, have been described in brief.
My devotee, having realized this, becomes fit for my own state of being. (18)

In this manner, the field (*kṣetra*), as well as knowledge (*jñāna*) and the object of knowledge (*jñeya*), and the supreme Śiva-liṅga, have been stated in brief— that is, in summary— in accordance with the promise [made in the verse] beginning with "That field which... Having understood this, the practitioner, becoming my devotee, shall attain my state— that is, the realization of oneness with the formless Śiva.
The meaning is that, according to the scripture, such liberation—consisting of the state of essential identity (*sāmarasya*) with Paraśiva—arises from the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*).
Know that both Prakṛti and Puruṣa are indeed beginningless;
know also that the modifications and the qualities (guṇas) arise from Prakṛti.

Having explained the nature of the field and the knower of the field in the seventh chapter, [the Lord] here reflects upon the nature of *prakṛti* and *puruṣa* as previously mentioned. Know that both *prakṛti* and *puruṣa* are beginningless; both are eternal. Among them, know that the modifications (*vikāra*)—the entire collection of transformations such as the *mahat* and so forth—as well as the qualities (*guṇa*), namely *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*, arise from *prakṛti*.
The meaning is "connected. || 19 ||
(280) Nature is said to be the cause of agency with respect to the body and the instruments;
the Spirit is said to be the cause of being the experiencer of pleasures and pains. || 20 ||

The effect (*kārya*) is the body in its state of transformation; the instruments (*karaṇa*) are the sense organs and so forth. Nature (*prakṛti*) is said to be the cause for the agency of both of these—that is, the cause for the creation of both. The meaning is that *prakṛti* is the cause of the body, the senses, and so on. As for the person (*puruṣa*), however, [he is the cause] in the experience of pleasure and pain.

It is stated that [the Puruṣa] is the cause of being the experiencer. The effects, such as the body and so forth, are indeed of the nature of modifications of Prakṛti; however, the one who enjoys their fruit is called the Puruṣa. || 20 ||
For the person, situated in material nature, experiences the qualities born of that nature;
attachment to these qualities is the cause of his births in good and evil wombs. 21.

It establishes that this is indeed for the experience of the Puruṣa. This conscious Puruṣa, residing in Prakṛti, experiences—that is, undergoes—the qualities of Prakṛti, namely Sattva, Rajas, and Tamas; in other words, the fruits thereof.
For this experiencing Puruṣa, throughout births in good or evil wombs—whether it be the attainment of a good womb or the attainment of an evil womb—[this experience continues].

Experienced practitioners maintain that the cause of birth as a Brāhmaṇa or others who are appropriate [for their status], or of birth as a dog or others who are inappropriate, is indeed attachment to the *guṇas*—that is, contact with the three *guṇas*. The meaning is this: one characterized by *sattva* attains a superior birth, whereas those characterized by *rajas* and *tamas* attain an inferior birth. Therefore, of all this...
The three qualities alone are the root of this cycle of birth and death, which consists of saṃsāra. || 21 ||
The supreme Puruṣa within this body is called the witness, the consenter, the sustainer, the enjoyer, the Great Lord, and also the Supreme Self. (22)

The Supreme Person residing in this body is indeed the Supreme Self; being present near all things, He is the overseer, the beholder, the witness. In the same way, He is the consenter to actions being performed, and likewise, He is the sustainer and the protector of all.

In this very way, He becomes the enjoyer and the experiencer of all fruits. Thus, that very Maheśvara, possessed of such wonderful power, is also called the Supreme Self (Paramātman). The meaning is that He who exists everywhere and at all times—the Supreme Self alone—performs everything and experiences everything. || 22 ||
He who thus knows the Puruṣa and Prakṛti along with its qualities (guṇas), in whatever manner he may live, is not born again. (23)

He states the fruit of this discernment between *prakṛti* and *puruṣa* as follows: he who knows both *prakṛti* and *puruṣa*, along with their previously mentioned qualities, does not take birth again—that is, he does not undergo rebirth—regardless of how he conducts himself in any manner whatsoever; the meaning is that he becomes liberated through the cessation of rebirth.

The mind and the senses are designated by the term "prakṛti. These are always engaged with the guṇas. Through this attachment to the guṇas, the pairs of opposites—such as passion and aversion, pleasure and pain—that arise in the Puruṣa become bound to the self. Therefore, [this is the cause] of the connection between prakṛti and puruṣa.

The connection consisting of the conjunction with the *guṇas* is such that if it is known by the *puruṣa*, then all worldly activity proceeds spontaneously, and the true state of affairs is understood.
This very discernment (*viveka*) is reckoned as the cause of the *puruṣa*'s liberation from bondage. One who possesses such discernment—

Content with whatever he obtains from whomever, sustaining his life by any means whatsoever, he dwells pure and free from the sense of "mine. His discernment also expands in this way: that Supreme Self who is present as the unifier of himself and nature is Himself the inner controller in every instance.

The individual soul (*jīva*), which constitutes the aspect of consciousness, carries out all activity in relation to *prakṛti*, which constitutes the aspect of power. It is precisely such a distinction that is intended here. In reality, it is solely due to the proximity of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) that the individual soul, termed *puruṣa*, is able to engage with *prakṛti*.
It prevails; even primordial nature (*prakṛti*), through its mere proximity to that [Spirit], functions everywhere as if it were conscious.

Thus, he who understands the wheel of saṃsāra as functioning by way of innate connection—due to that association, the experience of objects blinds the Spirit and causes it to become dissolved in primordial nature. For this very reason, regarding the Spirit...
Experienced practitioners declare that the knowledge of the qualities of *prakṛti* is essential for the cessation of bondage.
If a person offers all these sensory pleasures with devotion to the Supreme Lord— who shines eternally within the five senses and the mind— then those very same [pleasures] become [liberation].

They attain the state of being His very grace. This alone is called the worship of the six stations (*ṣaṭsthalopāsana*). For a person, the offering of the six kinds of sensory pleasures to the Lord residing within the six senses through the sixfold modes of devotion is indeed the worship of the six stations.

It produces in the *puruṣa* an acquaintance with the *vyavahāra* (the process of manifestation). Through this acquaintance, the *puruṣa*'s association with *prakṛti* is abandoned. When the *puruṣa* realizes its relationship with the Supreme Self—

This is called the discernment between *prakṛti* and *puruṣa*. Such discernment relies upon the natural connection with the six senses of the Supreme Lord (*parameśvara*), who consists of six stations. It is the Supreme Self alone, existing within the six senses, who is called *Īśvara* through the expansion of power (*śakti*) and *jīva* through the contraction of power.

It is said: the undiscriminating individual soul (jīva) considers all sensory pleasures to be its own, and for that very reason, it experiences great suffering in order to attain them. The discriminating soul, however, accepts those very same pleasures and pains as being the grace of the Lord, and thus becomes eternally happy.

"The self, deluded by egoism, thinks 'I am the doer'"; thus the Blessed One himself points out the sense of agency in those lacking discrimination. In one who possesses discrimination, however, the very occurrence of this sense of agency does not arise.
Therefore, for all those seeking spiritual progress, [the path] consists in remaining unstained amidst the six senses, established in the Lord.
Having become [thus], by the expansion of his power, he honors this very world with the vision of Śiva and becomes the Lord (Īśvara);
for him, there is indeed no rebirth. || 23 ||
Some perceive the Self within the self by means of meditation through the self;
others by the yoga of Sāṃkhya, and still others by the yoga of action.

He points out certain methods for the vision of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*). Some practitioners, through meditation—by constant contemplation of the Supreme Self like a stream of oil—behold the Self within their own intellects by means of the self, that is, by the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) refined through meditation. Others [behold it] through the yoga of Sāṃkhya, which is knowledge.

Having abandoned [the fruits of action] through the vision of what ought to be done, they perceive the Supreme Self within themselves by means of the yoga of action known as *kāyaka*, which consists of the performance of actions solely for the sake of pleasing the Supreme Self. Thus, certain yogis, constantly contemplating the Supreme Self shining within the heart, [perceive Him] right there.

Having established the mind, intellect, and so forth [in the Self], they themselves dissolve away. This yoga of meditation (dhyānayoga) is followed in the Vīraśaiva tradition during the worship of the *prāṇaliṅgin*. The *prāṇaliṅga* is indeed the object of meditation. Some practitioners rely upon the yoga of knowledge (*jñānayoga*). The practitioner...
Indeed, that very knowledge which one possesses— that the self is related [to the Supreme] because it is a portion of the Supreme Self—
is itself *jñānayoga*. In the same way, he [the Supreme Self] alone exists both within oneself and in primordial nature (*prakṛti*).

That which is known as "dwelling for the sake of accomplishing one's own welfare" is also indeed the yoga of knowledge (*jñānayoga*). And this yoga of knowledge is the primary support for all practitioners. It concerns the pure soul (*jīva*) who, while functioning through the body and senses, dwells within itself as the inner controller (*antaryāmin*).
Furthermore, the knowledge of Mahādeva is primarily required for the expansion of one's practice in the inner self (adhyātma-sādhana).

Only when sprinkled with the nectar of such divine knowledge does the practitioner become free from the impurities of defects and arise as a devotee (bhakta). It is this very devotee who, through his own righteous conduct, [purifies] those residing within all the senses...

Having become exceedingly dear to the Supreme Lord, he becomes a Māheśvara. This very Māheśvara, gladdening the entire world shrouded by his own [ignorance] through the contemplation of Śiva’s grace, becomes one whose mind is serene and thus attains the state of a Prasādī. Such a Prasādī, being perfectly stainless...

Experiencing the form of the Great Light within his own inner self as the *prāṇaliṅga*, he becomes a *prāṇaliṅgin*. This very *prāṇaliṅgin*, not perceiving any difference between himself and his own Great Liṅga, dissolves into the bliss of the Liṅga and abandons even the external perception of duality. Through the experience of the *prāṇaliṅga*...

The practitioner, having cast off all bonds of karma, takes refuge in every way within the Supreme Self consisting of bliss; he even forgets his own individuality. Possessing the experience of the *prāṇaliṅga*, he seeks refuge in Śiva alone, and becoming dissolved in Him, he no longer perceives any difference between himself and Śiva. This is the state of the devotee (*bhakta*).

One proceeds by practicing *karmayoga* itself. Only where action is performed while relying upon knowledge does *karmayoga* truly come into being; otherwise, it should be regarded as merely worldly action. If action is performed for the sake of nourishing the belly, then it is not *karmayoga*, which is indeed for the sake of one’s own welfare and the welfare of the world.
And it is thus practiced. Through such *karmayoga*, certain practitioners perceive the Self within the self.

These three yogas, being interwoven within the path of worship at the six stages (*ṣaṭsthalopāsana*), lead the practitioner—through the state of devotion up to the state of seeking refuge—effortlessly, by means of the body and senses themselves.

By means of the contemplation of Śiva, while abiding in the state of a Māheśvara, he serves [the world]; likewise, by regarding it as his own, he pleases it while abiding in the state of one who has attained grace; contemplating that very phenomenal world as grace, he abides in the state of one whose *liṅga* is his vital breath; experiencing it as identical with Śiva both externally and internally, he abides in the state of refuge for himself, who is the form of the universe.
Even while not perceiving any distinction from the Supreme Lord, he experiences bliss; such a yogi, though engaging in worldly affairs, remains free from attachment to them.

Existing devoid of self-interest and with the welfare of the world as his sole vision, he becomes eternally happy. When that [mind] shines forth in its stainless state within the Great Lord (Mahādeva), who is his own partial manifestation, it attains a state of equal flavor (*samarasa*) through the union of fire and camphor; thus, they are able to attain the realization of the Great Lord residing within their own inner self. This very [state]—
The path of yoga, which accomplishes the welfare of humanity, has been described in detail in the Gītā from the very beginning.
But others, not knowing this, worship having heard it from others;
they too, being devoted to what they have heard, certainly cross over death.

Others, however, not knowing the nature of the Self as it has been described, worship the Self after hearing the truth from other teachers. According to the Vedic injunction, "It is to be heard, it is to be reflected upon, it is to be meditated upon," inquiry into the Self must indeed first be heard. In this very way, those devoted to the Śruti [attain] the truth—

Even those devoted solely to hearing [the teachings] are liberated from the snares of *saṃsāra* and surely attain liberation. Thus, by means of mere hearing and reflection (*śravaṇa-manana*), one realizes the principle of Śiva (*śivatattva*) within the body; herein, he teaches a method easily accessible to all practitioners through the six stages (*ṣaṭsthala*) of that [realization]. || 25 ||
Whatever being is born, whether stationary or moving, know that, O bull of the Bharatas, it arises from the union of the field and the knower of the field. 26.

Now, referring to the nature of the field (*kṣetra*) and the knower of the field (*kṣetrajña*) as stated in the opening verse, the Lord concludes the discussion by speaking on what remains: "O bull among the Bharatas, O Arjuna, whatever being (*sattva*)— whether stationary,
such as trees and the like, or moving, such as beasts and birds— is born."

"From the union of the field and the knower of the field": understand that it is precisely from the union of the aforementioned field and the knower of the field. Just as all activities occurring within the body depend upon the union of the body and the living soul (*jīva*), so too do all operations such as creation occurring in the phenomenal world depend upon [the union] of that which stands in the place of the body.
They depend upon the relationship with the Supreme Lord, the Master of Māyā, who shines forth spontaneously through the power of Māyā known as Prakṛti. And thus:

This entire phenomenal world, consisting of both the moving and the unmoving, eternally exists in constant contact with the Māyā of the Supreme Lord; it shines forth by its own nature as the very form of Reality (Sat). Through this thorough realization, the contemplation of Śiva arises spontaneously for all practitioners everywhere. There is no such thing as an object devoid of Śiva.

Because it is perceived everywhere, the very act of presenting each and every object in its true nature as being conjoined with Śiva in the form of light is designated in various ways as "the knowledge of Śiva" (śivajñāna) and "the contemplation of Śiva" (śivabhāvanā). Such is the case regarding Śiva, who is the maker of all auspiciousness, who is omnipresent, and who is present within all things.
The Blessed One teaches here that constant recollection causes worldly activity to bring happiness to practitioners at all times. || 26 ||
He who sees the Supreme Lord dwelling equally in all beings,
remaining undecaying while they perish— he truly sees.

Now, having distinguished [the soul], he shows the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña): "In all beings," beginning from insects up to humans—this is the sense that [the body] is produced by karma. In this very way, because the gradations of the physical body are produced by karma, although remaining in the body, [one perceives] the Supreme Lord himself, who is the divine portion of the formless Supreme Self, even while [the bodies] are perishing.

Even when the body and other such things have met with destruction, he who does not himself perish and perceives that which is indestructible—through uninterrupted meditation, he realizes [the Self] directly; he alone is said to "see," meaning he possesses excellent vision. Others, however, are considered as if blind, because they do not see that which is to be seen. This very one is Prāṇa.
This is the meaning. He is the witness in all the worldly transactions of living beings, and for their very upliftment, He has descended [in various forms].

Through ignorance of this, a human being—whose entire power is lost and who is deluded—though grieving for a moment, immediately becomes attached to sense-enjoyment in accordance with the perverse impulses of the senses.

Thus, the individual soul (jīva), being excessively attached to enjoyments and devoid of the discrimination between what is appropriate and inappropriate, becomes blind. The *Śaraṇagītā* points out such a person lacking discrimination by contrasting him with one who possesses it; behold this other work of mine.
p.

286) "There is no purity in speech that is otherwise than in one's resolve; if there is uniformity between word and deed, then the noble one dwells within. In that very context, at the occasion of self-purification, Basavārya [spoke] of himself:
Seeing the poverty of devotion, he grieves for its sake. This is his path of purifying truth:

when the two minds have attained a state of oneness, when no horripilation manifests upon touch, when tears do not fall from the eyes through mutual remembrance, and when no faltering voice is observed upon speaking.

"This alone is the mark of one whose devotion is genuine: that all this has not been seen by me in [the external] Śiva; therefore, I am indeed a wearer of the guise of a hypocrite. Thus, having realized Śiva as the one shining within the body, he who employs the body, mind, senses, and so forth for His sake—he alone is [devoted] to Śiva.

He becomes a vessel for compassion and grace. Having thus become one possessed of vision, seeing only auspiciousness even among the virtuous and the wicked, and conducting himself with equanimity toward all, he becomes a Śivayogin. Otherwise, by failing to perceive the Śiva who exists everywhere, he would remain truly blind.
This intention is clearly revealed in the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad: "Where fire is churned, where wind is mounted upon, and where soma overflows—there the mind is born.
Here, it is stated that the churning of fire itself is called *jñānayoga* (the yoga of knowledge), and the mounting upon the wind itself is *karmayoga* (the yoga of action).

It is explained as follows: by means of this path of the integration of knowledge and action, that which is to be attained is indeed the union of the individual soul (*jīva*) and Śiva, known as the "overflowing of the moon" (*somātirecana*). Having contemplated the presence of Śiva and having restrained the vital breaths (*prāṇa* and other winds) for the sake of that union, he who proceeds by way of the *suṣumṇā* channel will certainly [attain it].

He indeed unites with the Supreme Lord, who is distinguished by the power of Umā. At that time, his mind, having abandoned its human nature, attains a divine nature. Only a person who has reached such a state becomes truly sighted and perceives auspiciousness everywhere. Others...
The meaning is that they live in vain, like blind people being led by those who are themselves blind. || 27 ||
For seeing the Lord established equally everywhere, one does not destroy oneself by means of the self; therefore, one attains the supreme goal. 28.

He says that those who do not perceive this reality of the Self are indeed self-destroyers: "He who sees with equality the Lord established equally in all classes of living beings— this Controller of the Field—
he becomes immortal."

Then, by thus [realizing] the Self through the non-destruction of the self—that is, through the vision of the Self—he goes to, or attains, the supreme goal, the highest state, which is liberation. For one who has seen the Self, liberation is indeed already within the palm of the hand. He who—
Even while engaging in worldly affairs through the body, senses, and so forth, one who does not perceive the Self alone will certainly suffer the destruction of that Self.
He who perceives the Self also perceives the Lord residing within himself.

Because both the individual self (*ātman*) and the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) are of the nature of consciousness (*cidrūpa*), they exist as belonging to the same category; between them, there is a relationship of part and whole.

He is so designated. Through divine vision and worship of that Supreme Self who is of the same nature as him, he becomes possessed of immeasurable and wonderful power. He never perishes. Having become full of bliss (*ānandamaya*) right here, experiencing eternal happiness, he [experiences] that very happiness as something perpetual even after the abandonment of the body.
It is to be accomplished by those who are increasing [in strength]. || 28 ||
And he who sees that actions are being performed in every way by nature alone, and likewise sees the Self as the non-doer; || 29 ||

He teaches the non-agency of the Self. It has been stated in many ways that "actions performed in every way, by all means, are performed by the qualities of *prakṛti* alone," and so forth. He who perceives in this manner sees the Self as indeed a non-agent. Not at all...

"It is one who knows the truth who should think, 'I am doing something,' for this has been stated in many ways. The Supreme Lord, residing within the body, remains untainted while carrying out all worldly activities through his own senses and other faculties. This body, which is a transformation of *prakṛti*, is indeed connected to the Supreme Self. Therefore, by means of the body..."
The discerning person perceives that all actions, even as they are being performed, are carried out by the Supreme Self alone.

Contemplating that every daily activity, such as giving and receiving, has the Supreme Self as its sole agent, the knower of reality realizes his own self to be a non-doer. This occurs through the proximity of the Supreme Self.

Although the qualities of *prakṛti* are insentient, they carry out all worldly transactions as if they were endowed with consciousness. Therefore, the person of discrimination perceives himself as a non-doer in all transactions, regarding himself merely as the instrumental cause. Through the proximity of the Blessed Lord, it is *prakṛti* that carries out the execution of all worldly transactions.
In those by whom that knowledge is experienced, the sense of being its own agent does not arise at all due to its innate nature;
it is precisely because they are devoid of this [notion of agency] that humans [attain liberation].

Delighting in the notions of "I" and "mine," they have completely forgotten the Supreme Soul’s playful sport of bestowing grace upon His devotees. For this very reason, many people—both women and men—devoid of self-knowledge, fallen under the sway of *prakṛti*, and seized by fear, grief, and delusion, continue to live. The Supreme Soul, too, [perceives] everything...

While effortlessly carrying out the activities of the world by its very nature, the Lord shines forth as one filled with bliss, delighting in Himself, while contemplating His own state as a non-agent. In that same manner, why should the individual soul (jīvātman), who is a portion of Him, contemplate itself as the agent of all worldly activity? This is the point [of inquiry].

It should be cultivated with faith. How could a person who considers every task performed by another to be his own not become a practitioner of falsehood? How could such a thief ever achieve his own spiritual welfare? Therefore, the knowledge of the Self, which is beneficial to all, must necessarily be practiced.
However, he instructs not only Arjuna, but all practitioners as well. || 29 ||
When he perceives the diverse existence of beings as situated in one place,
and likewise their expansion from that very source, then he attains Brahman.
When— at which time— one perceives, that is, experiences, the separate existence of beings— the distinctness of living creatures— residing in the one alone, namely in the Self;
and when one perceives that reality described here as being undivided, yet existing as if divided among all beings.
At that time, for that very reason, the practitioner becomes—that is, attains—the state of Brahman, which is all-pervasive and expansive;

the meaning is that he becomes Paraśiva, whose nature is the indivisible *liṅga*. This is because, as previously stated in the passage, "He who sees me everywhere and sees everything in me," [the practitioner realizes] the entire phenomenal world consisting of the moving and the unmoving.
The Lord Himself has taught that [the Self] exists as the Supreme Self in the form of the *liṅga*.

He who attains such an experience merges in a state of equal flavor (*samarasa*) within the all-pervading, indivisible *liṅga*. For one for whom even space itself were a garment like leather, his pervasiveness would be infinite and immeasurable.
And it becomes so: through the dissolution of such undivided light, a human being indeed becomes possessed of undivided power and endowed with the glory of the Self.
This very sovereignty of the Self must necessarily be attained by humans through the integration of knowledge and action.

By this path, for one with whom the Supreme Self alone is pleased, there can be no acquaintance whatsoever with poverty or weakness. This very intention is described thus in the *Śaraṇagītā*: "When you are pleased, even this piece of wood flourishes, its nature becoming sprouted."
Even a barren cow brings forth a young calf before long; this is indeed established.
By your grace, nectar shall become poison, and by your grace, poison shall surely become nectar. In you—
"O noble one, through association with the Guru, all the goals of human life shall be attained when [the mind] is serene.
Thus, by this vision of the Supreme Self, not only does human life itself become composed of nectar, but it also becomes eternally beautiful and thus rendered fruitful. 30.
Because it is beginningless and devoid of qualities, this supreme Self is immutable;
O son of Kuntī, even though dwelling within the body, it neither acts nor is it tainted.

This Kaunteya is imperishable, meaning free from decay; this Supreme Self, although residing within the body, is said indeed to dwell within all living beings. Because He is inherently beginningless, devoid of birth, and free from the qualities of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*, He does nothing—that is, He performs no action whatsoever. For every action is brought about solely by the three *guṇas*.

The entire range of effects also exists as consisting solely of the three *guṇas*. Thus, since both the effect and the cause consist of the three *guṇas*, agency cannot possibly belong to the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), who is devoid of such *guṇas*.
For this very reason, the Blessed One clearly teaches that it is indeed *prakṛti*, composed of the three *guṇas*, that performs everything. Thus...

Even though the Supreme Self resides within the body, if it performs no action whatsoever, it is never tainted by the fruits of such actions; it remains entirely unattached. Only he who performs action is tainted by the fruits of action. This is the case for the Supreme Lord, who is untainted and delights only in the Self.
Because of the absence of both the performance of action and the connection between action and its fruit, changelessness is inherent. 31.
Just as space, being all-pervading, is not defiled because of its subtlety, so the Self, though residing everywhere within the body, is not defiled. || 32 ||

Even though the Supreme Self exists within the body, it does not experience the fruits of actions performed by its material nature (*prakṛti*), because it is distinct from that nature; just as space, although all-pervading and present everywhere, is not tainted by various objects due to its subtlety— that is, its extremely difficult-to-perceive subtle nature— and remains unattached to them.

In the same way, although the *ātman* and the *paramātman* abide everywhere within all bodies, they are not defiled by the karma and other factors bound to such bodies, precisely because of their extreme subtlety. (p. 290)

He becomes involved. Just as the Supreme Self is not tainted by action or its fruit, so too the individual soul (jīva), being a portion of that [Self], is by its very nature not tainted by action and its fruit—this is the intended meaning.
However, due to the lack of recognition between himself and the Supreme Self, one who is fully engaged in action becomes attached to its fruit.

Through the knowledge of self and others, a person attains the state of non-attachment. Such knowledge arises in practitioners precisely from association with the virtuous (saṅga). Therefore, all human beings, from birth until death, should remain in the company of the wise and engage in the inquiry into Vedānta.
Just as the one sun illumines this entire world, so too does the Knower of the Field illumine the entire field, O Bhārata. (33)

O Bhārata, Arjuna, although the sun is but one, it remains pervading this entire world with its own radiance and illuminates it; in the very same way, this Supreme Lord, the Knower of the Field (kṣetrajña),
illuminates this entire field— the body— with His own power of consciousness.
It abides pervading all. By its light alone this body shines. For it is heard in scripture: "Without hands or feet, he is swift and a grasper;

he sees without eyes and hears without ears. And regarding the Supreme Self, it is said: "The maker of all, the knower of all, partless, actionless, tranquil, irreproachable, and stainless. Thus [these qualities] are mutually [attributed] to the Supreme Self.
The coexistence of contradictory attributes is heard [in scripture]. In that very way, everything is possible for that independent, perfect Pradhāna-Kṣetrajña who possesses such wonderful powers.
Thus, the difference between the field (kṣetra) and the knower of the field (kṣetrajña) is seen through the eye of knowledge.
And those who know the liberation from the nature of the elements go to the Supreme.

Thus, he concludes the description of the nature of the field (*kṣetra*) and the knower of the field (*kṣetrajña*). Those living beings who have seen with the eye of knowledge— that is, with the eye called wisdom— the distinction between these two, namely the mutual difference between the field, which is the body, and the knower of the field, which is the Supreme Self, [they see] exactly thus.

And those who know the liberation from the nature of reality—that is, the manner of releasing living beings from the bondage of transmigratory existence consisting of the three qualities—and [who know] the cause.

In passages such as "Attachment to qualities leads to births in good and evil wombs," this meaning has been taught: they go to that supreme Brahman known as the Great Liṅga, which is Paraśiva; by that, they become of one form. Within the body, the Supreme Self, remaining unattached, effortlessly performs that activity through the six senses for the sake of the welfare of the world.

If a person understands that [Self] which shines forth as the underlying support, then his own nature, being established, makes him eternally happy. Therefore, for all those engaged in worldly affairs, knowledge of the Field and the Knower of the Field is indispensably required from the perspective of their welfare. This alone—

The knowledge of the field (*kṣetra*) and the knower of the field (*kṣetrajña*) is designated in the Vīraśaiva tradition as the path of the six stations (*ṣaṭsthalopāsanamārga*). By means of this path, the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Supreme (*parama*) exist within each respective sense organ, carrying out the functions of those organs while remaining untainted. The individual soul...

At that very moment, he offers the pleasures and pains arising from each respective sense organ with devotion to the Supreme Lord, who is their own source. The Supreme Lord, too, having accepted them with love, bestows grace upon him in the form of those very experiences. It has already been stated that the Lord neither acts nor enjoys anything; nevertheless, [this occurs].

Because it has been taught by Him Himself that "I eat what is offered with devotion," the Lord necessarily accepts whatever the individual soul (jīva) gives with devotion and returns that very same thing to him as a grace (prasāda).
This very play of the six stages (ṣaṭsthalalīlā) is what is taught here under the heading "the knowledge of the field and the knower of the field" (kṣetra-kṣetrajña-vijñāna).

By the very thorough understanding of this, a human being becomes a partaker of grace (*prasāda*). In this very way, the Blessed One blesses all practitioners that they should likewise live by means of grace. By this life of grace, the earth itself becomes like heaven, even poison becomes like nectar, and even suffering becomes like happiness.
This alone is called the immortal life and the unfolding of power by those who have experienced it;
the knowledge of the six planes (*ṣaṭsthala*) has been described in detail elsewhere for the faithful.
— Chapter Fourteen.

"Whatever being is produced, whether stationary or moving, know that, O bull of the Bharatas, it arises from the union of the field and the knower of the field"— thus, in the preceding chapter, the nature of the union of the field and the knower of the field belonging to Maheśvara, the wielder of *māyā*, was described.
It has been stated that contact with the power of *māyā* alone is the cause of all origination. In the same way,
it has also been stated that "the attachment to the *guṇas* is the cause for his births in good and evil wombs," meaning that the connection with the *guṇas* alone is the cause of bondage.
Thus, the meaning stated in brief is elaborated upon in this chapter.
The Blessed Lord said: "I shall again declare that supreme knowledge, the best among all forms of knowledge."
Knowing which, all the sages have attained supreme perfection from this state. || 1 ||
This is the supreme among all forms of knowledge; this is the highest knowledge that must necessarily be known, the knowledge of the ultimate secret.

I shall proclaim that knowledge, by knowing and realizing which all the sages and great seers have attained—from this bondage of the body—the supreme perfection, which is the state of ultimate liberation. || 1 ||
Having taken refuge in this knowledge, they have attained my own nature;
even at the time of creation they are not born, and at the time of dissolution they do not suffer.

He provides an explanation of this very "supreme perfection": having resorted to, that is, accomplished, this supreme knowledge, those sages attain *sādharmya*—the state of having identical attributes—with me.
This is based on such scriptural passages as, "The knower of Brahman, being stainless, attains supreme equality; he becomes Brahman itself."

They have come together, having attained union with that which possesses identical qualities. Having enjoyed the grace of the beloved Prāṇa who shines within the body, and having united with the Supreme Reality in its essential nature, there is indeed the attainment of the experience of one's own own nature as Saccidānanda. In former times, many sages [attained] such [a state].

They have attained the [final] stage. Since they have realized the state of identity (*sāmarasyam*) within the formless existential sign (*bhāvaliṅga*) residing in the body, they are celebrated as "eternally living. For this very reason, even at the time of creation (*sarge*), during the creation of the world, they are not born again;
they do not undergo rebirth. Through the cessation of rebirth, they experience immortality and do not [return].
They enter the womb of a woman; yet even at the time of dissolution (*pralaya*), they do not suffer, nor do they perish, for they are indeed one with Paraśiva.

They experience [this] and do not meet with destruction even at the time of cosmic dissolution (*pralaya*). Thus, the teaching of the Śruti—“If one has known this here, then there is truth; if one has not known this here, there is great ruin”—is rendered meaningful and beautiful. Here, if the practitioner [realizes this] within his own body alone...

Having attained oneness with Śiva by means of the path that unites knowledge and action, one should experience the bliss of Śiva; then, one experiences such bliss eternally. Making one's own body the lower friction-stick and the *praṇava* the upper friction-stick, through the practice of churning with meditation, one should behold the God as if hidden, just as oil is found within sesame seeds.

"Just as butter is [extracted] from curds, water from flowing streams, and fire from [friction], so is that Self grasped within the self by one who perceives It through truth and austerity. Thus, in the Śruti, it is clearly taught that the practitioner should attain the vision of the Supreme Self within his own body alone. For this very reason, the vision of the Self is exceedingly subtle.
