That which is profound and unmanifest is so designated by those who possess direct experience.
This realization of the Self must be accomplished precisely through the cooperation of the body.

In the processes of hearing (*śravaṇa*), reflection (*manana*), and meditative absorption (*nididhyāsana*), the body alone is the primary support. [This pertains to] the conventional level of reality (*vyavahārika*).

The Lord’s intention is that people, with great faith, might fix their gaze upon both this-worldly and other-worldly happiness within their own bodies—and therein, even more so, within the heart, which is the dwelling place of the Supreme Self. || 2 ||
My womb is the Great Brahman; therein I place the germ. From that, O Bhārata, occurs the birth of all beings.

O Bhārata, O Arjuna, that which is my own—my great, pervasive, and extensive Brahman, consisting of the three qualities (triguṇa) as a substance—is itself the *yoni* (womb); because it is the cause of the origin of the entire universe, it is called the root of everything. In that *yoni*, I place the *garbha*—the *garbha* consisting of the maintenance of the power of consciousness (*caitanya-śakti*).
I place [it]. From that very source, the birth and origin of all beings—that is, of all living creatures—comes to pass.
The meaning is that the production of the entire universe occurs precisely through the conjunction of the power of consciousness with the insentient *prakṛti*.
This alone is called the "conjunction of the field and the knower of the field" (*kṣetra-kṣetrajña-saṃyoga*) by those who possess direct experience. For this very reason, the entire world...
It is said that consciousness is mixed with the unconscious; likewise, the body also exists as a mixture of the conscious and the unconscious.

It is by depending upon the unconscious body alone that the conscious individual soul (jīva) worships the Supreme Self (paramātman), its own kinsman, for the expansion of its own power. The Supreme Self itself becomes the embodied one (śarīrī), and His unconscious [nature]...

The power of *māyā* becomes the body; the Supreme Self itself, whose nature is consciousness, becomes the individual soul (*jīva*) through the contraction of the powers of will, knowledge, and action. Thus, it is a portion of Śiva.

Through the uninterrupted meditation on Śiva, the individual soul (jīva) attains an all-pervasive expansion of its power (śakti). By means of this expansion of power, experiencing the bliss of union with Śiva even in this very life, acting with detachment, and beholding the world through the vision of Śiva, he shines forth while manifesting Śiva everywhere. In this very manner, he...
Contemplating that this body and the world consist of both conscious and unconscious elements and are pervaded by the Lord, he generates that very same contemplation in others as well. || 3 ||
O son of Kuntī, whatever forms arise in all wombs, the Great Brahman is their womb, and I am the father who provides the seed. 4.

O Kaunteya Arjuna, among all wombs— indeed, among all types of wombs such as gods, humans, and so forth— whatever forms arise, whatever forms consisting of bodily structures come into being, for those forms as well, the Great Brahman alone, which is the substance of the three qualities (*triguṇa*), becomes the womb, that is, the cause. But I, in that regard...

"I am the progenitor, the father who bestows the seed—that is, the seed which consists of the power of consciousness (*caitanya-śakti*). For all living beings (*prāṇin*), who possess embodied forms, it is *māyā*—known as *prakṛti*—which has assumed the state of a body that stands in the place of the father. Therefore, I salute the two parents of the universe, Pārvatī and Parameśvara."
The designation of them as mother and father by the great poet Kālidāsa is perfectly appropriate. || 4 ||
Sattva, rajas, and tamas— these qualities born of material nature,
O mighty-armed one, bind the imperishable embodied soul within the body.

Having thus described the sequence of the birth of living beings, He now explains the sequence of their bondage: O mighty-armed Arjuna, those born of *prakṛti*— produced from the substance of the three qualities (*guṇas*) known as *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*— these very qualities bind the embodied soul, the *jīva*, which is imperishable (devoid of birth and other states by its own nature), to this body, the physical frame.
The meaning is that the substance consisting of the three qualities (triguṇa) alone is the cause of the soul's bondage to a body. || 5 ||
In that regard, O sinless one, sattva, being pure, illuminating, and free from affliction, binds [the self] through attachment to pleasure and through attachment to knowledge.
Therein, among the three qualities (*triguṇa*), *sattva*— the quality of purity— is, because it is stainless and transparent, free from affliction (*anāmaya*) and devoid of obstacles;
it is illuminating and serves as the cause of illumination, revealing the true nature of the Self (*ātmasvarūpa*).

The meaning is that it becomes [the cause]. O sinless Arjuna, that *sattva* binds by means of attachment to pleasure—that is, by producing attachment to pleasure—and having produced an addiction to pleasure, it binds the individual soul (*jīva*) or conscious being through that medium. Wise men consider even pleasure to be indeed bondage, because it acts as an obstacle to liberation.

And thus, even though goodness (*sattva*) is a means for attaining self-knowledge, it would become a cause of bondage precisely because it generates an attachment in the individual soul (*jīva*) toward such knowledge. (6)
Know that *rajas* is of the nature of passion, arising from thirst and attachment;
it binds the embodied soul, O son of Kuntī, through attachment to action. (7)

Rajas, the quality of passion (rajo-guṇa), is also of the nature of attachment because it increases the pride that results from such attachment; know that it is indeed a bond of that very kind. Furthermore, know that it arises from the attachment to craving—that is, from the clinging to the desire for the enjoyment of sense objects. Therefore, O [Arjuna], that rajas—

O Kaunteya, the quality of *rajas* binds the embodied soul— the individual living being— at all times, by means of attachment to action, that is, by producing a connection with actions through the instigation of activities such as the pursuit of wealth and desire; thus, having produced the longing for the enjoyment of sense objects, it increases the soul's attachment to those very things.
It causes him to become especially attached specifically to the acquisition of wealth and sensual pleasure. || 7 ||
Know that *tamas* arises from ignorance and deludes all embodied beings;
it binds them, O Bhārata, through negligence, laziness, and sleep.

Know that *tamas*—which arises from ignorance (*ajñāna*) and, being born of ignorance, causes delusion for all embodied beings, that is, for all living creatures—to be the cause of delusion. O Bhārata, Arjuna, that *tamas* binds the individual soul (*jīva*) through negligence (*pramāda*), indolence (*ālasya*), and sleep (*nidrā*). Negligence is lack of attentiveness; indolence and sleep are well known. By these, it binds the soul.
It acts [thus]: the quality of darkness (tamas), having produced a deluded vision in living beings, brings about sleep, laziness, and negligence.
O Bhārata, goodness (sattva) attaches one to happiness, and passion (rajas) to action.
But Tamas, veiling knowledge, binds one to negligence.
And so, O Bhārata Arjuna, *sattva*—the quality of purity—binds the living being through attachment to happiness;
having veiled knowledge and destroyed it, it binds the living being by producing attachment to negligence, that is, lack of attentiveness. || 9 ||
Overpowering both rajas and tamas, sattva prevails, O Bhārata;
likewise, rajas overcomes sattva and tamas, and tamas overcomes sattva and rajas. (10)

O Bhārata, Arjuna, the quality of *sattva*, at its own time, having overcome and suppressed *rajas* and *tamas*—that is, the *rajo-guṇa* and the *tamo-guṇa*—becomes capable of producing its own effects. In the very same way, *rajas*, the *rajo-guṇa*, at its own time, overcomes *sattva* and *tamas* and accomplishes its own work. Likewise, *tamas* also [overcomes the others] at its own time.

Sattva, having overcome rajas, performs its own function; likewise, through emergence and suppression, these qualities accomplish their respective effects. In all cases, these qualities indeed exist in varying degrees of intensity; however, due to the predominance of one at a time, the others become subordinate.

The subordination of the other two qualities is established by universal experience. In the same way, even among human beings, because of the predominance of *sattva* in some, *rajas* in others, and *tamas* in yet others, while the remaining qualities are subordinate, a manifold diversity arises. For this very reason, individual souls (*jīvas*) are distinct and diverse in every body. || 10 ||
When light arises in all the gates of this body,
then one should know that the quality of goodness (sattva) has increased.

If it is asked, "What is the sign of the manifestation of those respective qualities? he says in response: "In this body, in all the gates—that is, in all the senses which serve as the gates of knowledge—there is light, light in the form of knowledge."
p.

297) Know—that is, understand—that when, at whatever time, *sattva*—the quality of *sattva*—arises, it is "increased," meaning it has become manifest. [This refers to] the Supreme Self, who dwells untainted within the senses and consists of the six abodes (*ṣaṭsthala*).

When knowledge, arising from hearing the instructions of the Guru, shines forth in the heart of a practitioner, then it should be understood that the quality of *sattva* has emerged therein. Furthermore, it should be understood that when the senses and other instruments of practice are absorbed into that very state, it is the Supreme Self alone who, having become all the senses, remains right there.

Abiding as the essence of volition (*cetanā*), it engages in worldly activity. It is that very same [principle] which exists as the seer in the eyes; it is that very same [principle] which exists as the hearer in the ears. In this very way, having become the nose, it becomes the smeller of odors;
likewise, having become the tongue, it exists there as the taster of flavors. In the same manner, having become the skin—

Therein, he exists as the enjoyer of the pleasure of touch; likewise, having become the mind itself, he exists there as the experiencer of the pleasure of satisfaction. Thus, when an expansion of the *sattva* quality arises in any [organ] among all the senses, Paramaśiva, who abides as their innate nature, is experienced at that time by those who experience.
It is said: || 11 ||
Greed, activity, undertaking of actions, restlessness, and longing—these arise when rajas has increased, O bull of the Bharatas. (12)
O bull of the Bharata race, O Arjuna, when *rajas*— the quality of passion— is increased, there arise greed (the lack of contentment regarding the desire for material objects),
the undertaking of actions (the commencement of activities for that purpose),
lack of tranquility (the absence of peace in the senses and so forth), and longing (desire for ever-increasing things). This is how it occurs.

The meaning is that all these are the functions of the quality of passion (rajas). When an excessive longing for the accomplishment of an object arises, and when constant activity and restlessness toward that end especially emerge—at that time, and in that state, it should be known that the quality of passion has blossomed. || 12 ||
Lack of illumination, lack of activity, negligence, and even delusion—these arise when Tamas has increased, O joy of the Kurus. (13)

O Arjuna, son of Kuru, when the quality of *tamas* has increased—that is, when it has especially attained pervasiveness—there arises non-illumination, which is a lack of discrimination; and non-activity, which is the absence of engagement even toward duties that ought to be performed.
Indifference means being averse to what ought to be done. Negligence is a lack of attentiveness;

as it is heard in the Sanatsujātīya: "I declare negligence indeed to be death. Negligence is like the death of one who is still living, and it is the very effect of darkness (tamas). From this, delusion (moha) and stupidity (mauḍhya) arise.
Undertaking actions without discriminating between what is appropriate and inappropriate, and the abandonment of duties—this is the nature of one who acts without discernment.
When the embodied soul meets its end while sattva is predominant, then it attains the stainless worlds of those who know the highest. (14)

Now, he describes the function of the qualities such as *sattva* at the time of death: when, at which time, *sattva*—the quality of *sattva*—having increased, having become predominant, the embodied soul (*jīva*) undergoes dissolution, that is, death or the state of the five elements; then that *jīva* [attains] the stainless [realms] of those who know the highest, the knowers of reality.
He attains and reaches the meritorious worlds that are free from disease. || 14 ||
Having gone to dissolution in rajas, one is born among those attached to action;
likewise, dissolved in tamas, one is born in the wombs of the deluded.
When the quality of passion (*rajas*) has increased, the embodied soul, having met its end— having undergone death—

is born among worlds attached to action, that is, among those possessed by desire for worldly activity. Those who perform ritual acts reach such a world of action— the mortal world, the earthly realm (*bhūrloka*)— again.

They die at the time of the expansion of the quality of *rajas*. In the very same way, when *tamas*—the quality of darkness—has increased, the embodied soul (*jīva*), having undergone dissolution, is born—that is, it attains birth—in deluded wombs, such as the wombs of animals and the like.
He who casts off the body during a time when *tamas* predominates attains birth among animals and similar beings. (15)
They say that the fruit of well-performed action is pure and characterized by goodness (sattva);
the fruit of passion (rajas), however, is suffering, and the fruit of ignorance (tamas) is delusion. 16.

To summarize the meaning already stated: the wise declare that the fruit of well-performed meritorious action (*puṇya-karman*) is stainless, completely pure, and characterized by *sattva*—that is, connected with the quality of *sattva*. In the same way, however, the fruit of *rajas*—the quality of *rajas*—is suffering.
They say that its fruit is ignorance; likewise, they say that the fruit of the quality of darkness (tamas) is precisely ignorance—that is, the lack of knowledge of reality. || 16 ||
From *sattva* arises knowledge, and from *rajas* indeed greed;
from *tamas* arise negligence and delusion, as well as ignorance itself. (17)

From the quality of *sattva*, knowledge arises, because knowledge is the effect of the *sattva* quality. In the same way, from the *rajas* [quality] of *rajas*, greed and evil desire (*durāśā*) arise; that evil desire has *rajas* as its cause is indeed well-known. Likewise, from the *tamas* [quality] of *tamas*, negligence and delusion arise—negligence being lack of attention, and delusion being stupidity.
In that way, ignorance and lack of discernment arise. || 17 ||
Those established in sattva go upward; those characterized by rajas remain in the middle; and those of tamas, abiding in the conduct of the lowest quality, go downward. 18.

Those established in *sattva*, devoted to the quality of *sattva*, go upwards to the higher worlds. Those characterized by *rajas*, devoted to the quality of *rajas*, remain in the middle world. But those characterized by *tamas*, devoted to *tamas*—remaining in the activity of the lowest quality—the "lowest" being that which is base.
Those who abide in the state of the quality of darkness (tamas) and are intent upon its effects go—meaning they reach—the lower world below. || 18 ||

"Sattva, rajas, and tamas—these qualities born of nature bind the immutable embodied self within the body, O mighty-armed one. Thus, the meaning already stated has been further elucidated by this much of the text. Now, the state of transcending the qualities (guṇātīta), which is the most excellent form, is described:
When the seer perceives no agent other than the qualities, and knows that which is beyond the qualities, he attains my state of being. (19)
When the perceiving individual soul (jīva), at whatever time, does not perceive any agent other than the qualities— that is,
he perceives that the qualities alone are the agents of all actions— and thus knows himself to be beyond the three qualities, distinct from them, and supreme, he attains My state (madbhāvam).
He attains—that is, reaches—liberation in the form of the state of Brahman as Paraśiva. He who knows the non-agency (akartṛtva) of both the Supreme Self and his own self becomes liberated.
From the time of deep sleep until death, the qualities of Prakṛti are active everywhere toward all [beings].
They carry out their worldly activities; however, by the very proximity of the Supreme Self (p.
300), this activity of the senses is carried out as if it were natural. In the presence of the Supreme Self, His...

The kinsman, who is a portion [of the Lord], exists even as the individual soul (jīva). One who understands that it is merely the proximity of these two that is conducive to the accomplishment of actions will not harbor the egoism of agency and so forth. For one who serves as the witness of both the senses and their activities without the notion of being an agent, there exists the very seed for attaining another birth.

He would be frustrated. Yet, during his lifetime, conducting himself with total non-attachment like a burnt cloth, he carries out every worldly transaction for the sake of the welfare of the world; he alone is designated as "immortal" and "consisting of bliss. || 19 ||
Having transcended these three qualities that arise from the body, the embodied soul,
liberated from the sufferings of birth, death, and old age, attains immortality.

Here, he explains the very state of immortality for one who is liberated: having transcended—having gone beyond—these three qualities, *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*, which are the source of the body's emergence and serve as the seeds for the production of the embodied soul (*jīvātman*), [the soul] is freed from birth, death, old age, and suffering; that is, from birth (*janana*), death (*maraṇa*), and old age (*jarā*).

Being liberated from these, one experiences the deathless state of eternal bliss. Therefore, the implication is that if the individual soul (*jīva*) does not transcend the three *guṇas*, liberation would likewise not exist. When the soul is bound by the three *guṇas* which act as fetters and remains attached to them, it is designated as a transmigrating being (*saṃsārī*).

When he realizes that the three qualities (guṇas) are the product of action and considers himself to be a non-doer, then he transcends the three qualities. Although appearing as if subject to the power of the qualities, he remains entirely untouched by them;
being independent, he dissolves in a state of equanimity within Śiva, his own essential portion who is the root of all. || 20 ||
By what marks, O Lord, does one become transcendent over these three qualities?
What is his conduct, and how does he go beyond these three qualities? (21)
Having been told thus, Arjuna spoke in order to know by what marks it can be understood that the state beyond the qualities (*guṇātītāvasthā*) has been attained.

"O Lord, O Sovereign of All, O Śrī Kṛṣṇa, by what marks or signs does the living being (*jīva*) transcend—that is, go beyond—these three qualities, beginning with *sattva*? And what is the conduct of such a person?"

What kind of conduct should he possess? And by what means and through what method should he abide having transcended these three qualities (guṇas)? What are the signs of one who has transcended the three qualities? What is his activity? And what is the means for transcending them? [These are the questions.]
Arjuna asks. || 21 ||
O Pāṇḍava, he does not hate illumination, activity, or even delusion when they have arisen, nor does he long for them when they have ceased. (22)

He does not hate— nor does he feel aversion toward— the manifestation that is the effect of *sattva*, nor the manifestation that is the effect of *rajas*; being under the influence of past karma, these have arisen and come upon him,
yet he does not suffer affliction or the like on account of them, nor does he strive for their cessation.

And for this very reason, even when those [states] such as pleasure have ceased, he does not seek them nor does he long for them; the meaning is that he experiences silently whatever has been obtained. || 22 ||
He who remains seated like one indifferent, not shaken by the qualities; who stays firm, knowing that "it is only the qualities that are acting," and does not waver—[he is a sage]. (23)

Even while sattva and the other qualities are active in their functions, he who remains as if indifferent toward them, as if himself unattached, and does not waver or fall into agitation because of them; rather, he abides thinking only that "these qualities abide in their own nature"—he is one who has transcended the qualities. He does not move, nor does he stir. He is the one who has gone beyond the gunas.

Thus it is said: he who, perceiving that the senses move among the objects of the senses, remains among them alone as a witness and as one free from modification—he is said to have transcended the three qualities (guṇas). || 23 ||
Equal in pain and pleasure, established in his own self, regarding a clod of earth, a stone, and gold as the same;
the wise man is equal toward the pleasant and the unpleasant, and equal in blame and self-praise. (24)
He who is the same in honor and dishonor, the same toward the parties of friend and foe, and who has renounced all undertakings—he is said to have transcended the qualities. 25.

He for whom pleasure and pain are the same; he who is established in himself (*svasthaḥ*), abiding in his own self (*ātmani*); he who is serene and equanimous; he for whom a clod of earth, a stone, and gold—all this is equal—such a one is called "one of equal vision" (*samadarśana*). He for whom the pleasant and the unpleasant are alike (*tulyapriyāpriyaḥ*); that which is desired is the pleasant, and that which is not desired is the unpleasant.

One for whom censure and self-praise are equal—where "censure" refers to the censure of others and "self-praise" refers to praising oneself—and such a person for whom both of these are equal [is one who remains equanimous] toward honor and dishonor.
He is equal toward honor and dishonor—both being well known—and thus possesses the cultivation of equanimity.
Likewise, he is equal toward the parties of friend and foe; that is, he is impartial toward both the side of friends and the side of enemies.
He is a renouncer of all undertakings; "all undertakings" refers to all activities directed toward results pertaining to this world or the next.
He who is such toward those who have been abandoned is said to have transcended the qualities (guṇātīta). || 24–25 ||
And he who serves Me with unswerving yoga of devotion,
having transcended these qualities, is fit for becoming Brahman.

Having thus described the signs and activities of one who has transcended the qualities (*guṇātīta*), he now provides the answer to the question of how one transcends these three: "He who serves— that is, worships— Me, the Supreme Lord, the cause of all, with unswerving devotion, having completely transcended and passed beyond even these three, attains the state of Brahman, which is the nature of Supreme Śiva."
The meaning is: the means for transcending that. || 26 ||
For I am the foundation of Brahman, of the immortal and the imperishable, of the eternal dharma, and of absolute bliss. 27.

He explains how the transcendence of the qualities (*guṇas*) may become easily attainable through devotion: for this reason, I alone am the foundation (*pratiṣṭhā*), the ultimate limit, of Brahmā, the four-faced one; I alone am the formless Supreme Śiva-Brahman, meaning that I am indeed the Supreme Śiva-Brahman. Thus, of the Imperishable...

Since I alone am the foundation—the support and the substratum—of immortality, which is free from destruction and characterized by the state of being deathless; and since I alone am the foundation of absolute happiness, unmixed with suffering;
therefore, he who serves Me with unswerving yoga of devotion transcends these three and attains the state of Brahman.

"Those who do not recognize my supreme, immutable, and unsurpassed nature as one who has assumed a human form"—by such words, my own true essence was already established repeatedly previously. In the very same way: "The wicked, the deluded, the lowest of men, do not take refuge in me; their wisdom has been carried away by illusion, they possess a demonic nature."
p.

303) The state of suffering for those who are bound has been described. And so, worldly living beings, having correctly understood the relationship between themselves and their own qualities, [engage] in the activities performed spontaneously along with them.

The Blessed One observes that they should abandon the notion of identity with the body, unite with the Supreme Lord who stands in the place of their own father, and while experiencing the bliss of Śiva, allow no room for egoism and possessiveness, nor for the attachment and aversion caused by them. || 27 ||
Fifteenth Chapter:

Thus, the attainment of liberation by the transmigrating individual soul (*jīva*) through devotion to the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) was established at the end of the preceding chapter; that very same subject is elaborated upon in this chapter. Therein, the nature of the transmigrating soul is [described].
To explain this, he first describes the nature of saṃsāra:
"They speak of the imperishable aśvattha tree as having its roots above and its branches below; the Vedas are its leaves—he who knows it is a knower of the Veda. (1)

"Rooted above. For the root of saṃsāra—which consists of birth and death—is indeed the noose of impurity composed of ignorance. And that [noose] is the seed of existence (*bhava*). Because it is the fundamental cause of saṃsāra, the branches of saṃsāra extend toward the upper portion. Of this tree of saṃsāra, however, both of these [the root and the branches]...

That this [tree] exists in a state of inversion—this alone is the wonder here. The seed of worldly existence, consisting of ignorance in the form of bonds, is attached at the top, at the head, within the body composed of the microcosm (piṇḍāṇḍa). The senses and other faculties, however, occupy the place of branches;
they exist below, pervading the lower part. Such is this Aśvattha tree.

The wise say that this tree of worldly existence is imperishable, eternal, and established from beginningless time. Of this very tree of worldly existence, the *chandāṃsi*—the Vedas such as the *Ṛgveda* and others—are the leaves. Just as a tree stands protected by depending upon its leaves, so too does this worldly existence, which is rooted in merit (*dharma*) and demerit (*adharma*), endure.

The meaning is that it stands dependent upon the Vedas. He who knows this suchness of the nature of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*) is alone the knower of the secret of the Vedas, and no other. Of this tree whose form is the body, however, [the name is] *aśvattha*.
The name indeed corresponds to its meaning. Among trees, the Aśvattha is truly the best. Regarding that aspect of the Supreme Self, the wise should not entertain thoughts of inferiority. || 1 ||
Its branches extend below and above, nourished by the gunas and having sense-objects as their sprouts;
and its roots, which bind one to karma, stretch downwards into the world of men.

The branches of this tree, whose sprouts are the objects of the senses— namely, sound and the rest— have reached a state of extreme growth through substances composed of the three *guṇas*; such branches extend in various directions both downwards and upwards,
and thus this tree is vastly expanded by the objects of sense, such as sound and the like.

The meaning is that it exists spreading in various directions. The roots of this tree, which are bound by and connected to karma, remain constantly extended and pervasive both below—in the lower world—and also in the human world. || 2 ||
Its form is not perceived here in that way; it has neither end, nor beginning, nor foundation.
Having cut down this deeply rooted Ashvattha tree with the firm weapon of non-attachment— || 3 ||
Therefore, that Goal must be sought, reaching which they do not return again;
I take refuge in that very Primeval Person from whom the ancient course of emanation has issued forth.

The form of this aforementioned tree of saṃsāra is not perceived here in this world; that is to say, it does not become directly manifest to the transmigrating soul (*saṃsārijīva*) in the manner described. Not only is that so, but its end within is not perceived, nor is its beginning or root perceived, nor is its foundation or support perceived.

Having cut down and destroyed this *aśvattha* tree of *saṃsāra*, which has deeply grown roots and is exceedingly well-established, with the weapon of non-attachment— a firm and powerful instrument consisting of the renunciation of attachment even while remaining in *saṃsāra*— one may thereafter attain that supreme state.

In that very place, within the center of the thousand-petaled lotus at the crown of the head, one must seek out the abode known as the *bhāvaliṅga*, which shines resplendently; one must investigate the appropriate means for its attainment—that supreme state (*paramapada*) having reached which those who have gone do not return again. Such is the [goal].

Regarding the statement "it should be thoroughly sought," he says "that very one," and so forth. Because— from that Supreme Person (paramapuruṣa)— I [seek] the formless Puruṣa, who is the cause of all, known as the *bhāvaliṅga*, namely Paramaśiva.
With the thought "I take refuge," one should seek out that station of the *bhāvaliṅga* by means of taking refuge in Him with undivided devotion. However, if the reading is *prapadyeta*,
then [one should seek] such a Supreme Person, Mahādeva, whose nature consists of the beloved life-force.

The meaning is that one should take refuge—that is, go for shelter—for the sake of liberation preceded by the cutting down of the aforementioned tree of saṃsāra; this is indeed the natural inclination [of the mind]. 3–4.
Free from pride and delusion, having conquered the fault of attachment, ever established in the inner self, with desires turned away,
and liberated from the dualities known as pleasure and pain, the undeluded go to that imperishable state.

Free from pride and delusion—pride being arrogance and delusion being ignorance, they are devoid of these; having conquered the defect of attachment—attachment being association with sense objects, and those by whom the defect dependent upon it has been conquered are "conquerors of the defect of attachment";
ever devoted to the supreme Self—their minds are constantly and always attached to the supreme Self.

Worshipping the external *liṅga* with their bodies and senses through the eightfold ritual services (*aṣṭavidhopacāra*), they simultaneously experience the *prāṇaliṅga* residing within the heart in the stainless mind through the yoga of meditation. Thus, they are devoted to the Supreme Self both externally and internally; for this very reason, their desires have completely ceased.

Those whose desire for sense objects has ceased; those who are liberated from, or have abandoned, the pairs of opposites (dvandvas) characterized by pleasure and pain—such as gain and loss, victory and defeat—and are therefore undeluded and discerning; such persons alone attain that imperishable, eternal state.
They go to the abode of Brahman, which is free from disease, composed of nectar, and attainable through the yoga of Śiva.
By the manifestation of the Supreme Self, whose nature is Being, within even a single object perceived in the world,
the practitioner enters the head— which has become the abode of Brahman— by way of the Suṣumṇā, and there...
He conducts himself with a state of equanimity within the great liṅga of existence; never does he experience suffering.

If those established in the abode of immortality at the head, through the gateway of the heart, should conduct themselves with the nature of Śiva, then the splendor of prosperity, abundance, and majesty would shine forth here with even greater intensity.
In that very same way, those who have experienced the nectar (amṛta) shall experience that same divine nectar as something eternal even at the end of their bodies. || 5 ||
Neither the sun, nor the moon, nor fire illumines that supreme abode of Mine, having gone to which they do not return.

And that state, the abode of immortality, the sun does not illuminate; nor does the moon illuminate it, and likewise fire does not illuminate it. That supreme abode, having gone to which they do not return from there again—do not come back—is [that very place].

"Mine" means belonging to me alone. Within the human body, at the place called Brahmasthāna in the head, there shines a divine light of the brilliance of ten million suns, which is the Bhāvaliṅga. It is the impeller and the illuminator even of the sun, moon, and fire. No one at all is able to go there. Among the six sense organs—

And he who perceives the Lord as the grasper of the sixfold objects through faith, steadfastness, concentration, experience, and realization—this very attainment of the state of immortality is the ultimate fruit of spiritual resolve. Without the experience of this fruit, spiritual resolve itself would be meaningless. || 6 ||
An eternal portion of My very self, having become a living soul in the world of the living,
draws toward itself the senses, with the mind as the sixth, which abide in material nature.

Having beheld Mahādeva dwelling within the body composed of *prakṛti* in the form of pure existence, yogins—even while engaging in worldly affairs like ordinary people—will certainly not be partakers of suffering. Although they remain in the cycle of transmigration (*saṃsāra*), being devoid of egoistic identification, they exist like burnt cloth. Immediately after the vision of Mahādeva—
In response to the doubt, "Would they not take up the path of worldly enjoyment again?", he teaches the reality of the individual self (*jīvātmatattva*) and provides the resolution:

since all individual souls (*jīvas*) are indeed portions of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), the attainment of the whole by its parts is innate. [He says: "In this world of living beings, that which is the eternal one who has become the life-force of living beings..."
The Self, established from beginningless time, exists with its power diminished by connection to *prakṛti*;

it is the direct portion (*aṃśa*) of Me, the formless Supreme Śiva. However, being bound to *prakṛti* due to the influence of beginningless karma, it attracts—that is, draws toward itself—the senses, with the mind as the sixth, which reside within *prakṛti*.
This is also an elliptical indication of the organs of action (karmendriyas).
The meaning is that, in this way, he requires the cooperation of all the sense organs for the sake of experiencing the fruits of his actions.
Whatever body the Lord acquires and whatever [body] he departs from,
he goes taking these [senses] with him, just as the wind carries fragrances from their source.
And he says that this connection with the senses and so forth belongs to him at all times: "The Lord"— the individual soul who is the master of this body—
"whatever body it acquires anew, and whatever body it departs from,
leaving behind, then [it takes] these senses, beginning with the mind, just as the wind or breeze [takes] fragrances from their source, such as flowers, at all times."

Having taken [it] along with itself and having appropriated it, it moves—that is, it goes. When the wind leaves one flower and goes to another, it goes only after taking its fragrance; it moves here and there together with the fragrance. Just as its movement is not possible without the fragrance, so too is it with the individual soul (jīva).
By means of the very senses, it goes from one body to another body. || 8 ||
Presiding over the ear, the eye, the sense of touch, the tongue, and the nose,
as well as the mind, this [self] enjoys the objects of the senses.

Regarding the question of what things the living being (*jīva*) takes with it when departing, he says: the ear, the eye, the sense of touch (the skin), the tongue, and the nose—along with the mind (*manas*). Having presided over and taken recourse to these, this *jīva* enjoys and experiences objects such as sound and the rest. (9)
Whether departing, or staying still, or even enjoying [objects] while endowed with the qualities, the deluded do not perceive Him; those who possess the eye of knowledge perceive Him.

How does this individual soul (jīvātman) depart from this body and go elsewhere? How does it abide within the body? How does it experience objects such as sound and the rest? How does it act when bound by the qualities (guṇas)? Ignorant people do not know these points; only those who possess knowledge of reality (tattvajñānin) know all of this.
They are able to know this very intention which is indicated here: [the self] as it departs— leaving the body and going elsewhere— or as it exists in the body, experiencing,
or as it perceives objects such as sound, or as it is endowed with the qualities (guṇas), namely sattva and the others.
Fools who lack knowledge do not perceive this Self as it truly is; they simply do not know it at all.
However, those wise ones who possess the eye of knowledge—they alone perceive the activity of the individual soul (jīva).

And there is a departure from this tree of saṃsāra. Thus, the meaning is that the individual soul (jīvātman) is extremely subtle and difficult to perceive. How does it dwell in this tree, how does it act, and how does it experience? These aspects are indeed most diverse. Its transition from one body to another is truly extraordinary. Only he who knows that [attains liberation].
That very wise person becomes eternally happy and free from all affliction. || 10 ||
Striving yogis behold Him established within themselves;
yet those of unrefined self, though striving, do not behold Him, being devoid of wisdom.

Yogis, whose minds are concentrated and who delight in the practice of yoga, perceive this individual soul (jīvātman) residing within their very own bodies, as they themselves exert effort and apply themselves. However, those of unrefined self— those whose internal organs (antahkarana) are unpurified and who are mindless or ignorant— even though they exert effort and apply themselves, [do not perceive it].

The individual soul does not see itself; indeed, it is not able to see it. He who, failing to see the Self, perceives only the phenomenal world composed of the five elements, is not capable of beholding the consciousness that is of the nature of light and resides within that very world.
Thus, one who is averse to the vision of the Self becomes a partaker of suffering through delusion regarding phenomenal proliferation (*prapañca*).
Sinking and repeatedly sinking, he remains in the ocean of saṃsāra. Thus, not knowing for himself his own coming and going and so forth, the fool remains seized by fear, grief, and delusion. (11)
That light which, residing in the sun, illumines the entire world, and that which is in the moon and in the fire—know that light to be mine. 12.
Having thus described the nature of the individual soul (jīva), he next explains the nature of himself as the Supreme Self (paramātman):
that which illuminates and manifests the entire world and the whole of phenomenal existence (prapañca)— namely,
that light which exists in the moon and that light which resides in fire— is this very same light.

Know—that is, understand—that "māmaka" means "belonging to me alone. For the divine light residing in the sun, moon, and fire is indeed connected to the Supreme Self; the meaning is that He Himself shines forth by abiding within them as their inner ruler (antaryāmin).
And entering the earth, I sustain all beings by my vital energy;
and becoming the sap-filled Soma, I nourish all herbs.

Having entered— that is, having pervaded— the earth, I alone sustain all beings, that is, all living creatures, by my vital power, which is my own strength. In this very same way, having become Soma, the moon, whose essence is sap and who consists of all flavors—

I alone nourish and sustain all medicinal herbs; for it is well known that the Moon, the lord of herbs (*oṣadhīśa*) and lord of the night, is the master of medicinal plants. All living beings likewise abide by depending solely upon the Supreme Self;
it is by depending on Him alone that they all live. Thus, He is the ground of rest for all.

In the Śiva Āgamas, the Supreme Self is designated by the very term *sthala*. Not only after creation, but even at the time of dissolution (*pralaya*), He alone becomes the place of rest for all individual souls (*jīvas*) and the five elements (*pañcatattva*). Thus, He alone exists before, now, and in the future.

It serves as the substratum and the place of rest for this world consisting of the moving and the unmoving; therefore, its designation as "sthala" (the place) is entirely fitting. Likewise, because it is the locus where the conscious and the unconscious dissolve, it is also studied under the name "liṅga. It is not only by the manifestation of this undivided liṅga that...
But the sun and others, as well as other living beings, also shine forth.
Becoming Vaiśvānara, I have entered the bodies of living beings; joined with the prāṇa and apāna breaths, I digest the four kinds of food.

Becoming Vaiśvānara, the digestive fire within the stomach, and having taken up residence in the bodies of living beings, joined with prāṇa and apāna—accompanied by the out-breath and in-breath—I digest, that is, cook, the fourfold food consisting of the four types of nourishment: what is chewed, eaten, licked, and sucked. 14.
And I am seated within the heart of all; from me come memory, knowledge, and their loss.
I alone am that which is to be known by all the Vedas; I am the author of the Vedānta, and I alone am the knower of the Vedas.
I alone am seated within the heart, in the cave of the heart, as the inner controller (*antaryāmin*) of every class of living beings;

everything indeed comes from me, having me as its cause—I alone am the cause of all this—and they proclaim me alone. I alone am the author of the Vedāntas, the teacher of the Vedāntas; I alone am the knower of the Vedas.
And I alone am the knower of all the Vedas; [I am] one who praises the greatness of the Supreme Self, which is all-pervading and possesses both manifest and unmanifest forms. (p.

The Vedas have already been indicated by the word "leaves" (*parṇa*). Therefore, describing the extraordinary greatness of the Supreme Self, who is distinguished by such wondrous power, the Vedas serve as the supreme authority for the realization of His true nature. || 15 ||
There are these two persons in the world: the perishable and the imperishable.
All beings are the perishable; the unchanging is called the imperishable. (16)
But there is another, the Supreme Person, who is declared to be the Supreme Self—the imperishable Lord who, having entered the three worlds, sustains them. (17)

Thus, by this much, the nature of the conscious being in the form of transmigratory existence has been taught, followed by the fact that the purified individual self (jīvātman) is a portion of the Supreme Self (paramātman), and then the true nature of the Supreme Self itself. As it has been said:
"There are these two Puruṣas: the perishable (kṣara) and the imperishable (akṣara). Among these, all beings—that is, the entire multitude of living creatures—[constitute the perishable]."

The "perishable" (kṣara) refers to those things designated by the term "perishable. The "immutable" (akṣara), however, is the changeless, pure consciousness; it is called the "imperishable. Beyond these two, there is another who is superior and most excellent, proclaimed as the Supreme Self (paramātman).
That Supreme Self is undecaying, eternal, the Lord, the Lord of all, who, having entered even the three worlds, [presides over them].
Pervading the entire world and abiding therein as the inner controller (*antaryāmin*), He sustains and supports all the worlds.

Thus, all living beings are called "perishable" (*kṣara*). However, the individual soul (*jīva*), when well-purified through initiation by the grace of the Guru, is called "imperishable" (*akṣara*). This very [soul] is called a "limb" (*aṅga*) because it serves as the ground for the playful sport of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*).

It is thus designated; that too becomes denoted by the term "Person" (puruṣa). In the same way, the Supreme Self (paramātman), though designated as the "Highest Person" and pervading all worlds, is called the "liṅga" when it dwells within that [body] in the form of the desired state of the vital breaths, its [natural] purity diminished due to contact with primordial nature (prakṛti).

It has been stated more than once that the state of *sāmarasya* (perfect equilibrium), which is the form of unity between these two—the *aṅga* and the *liṅga*—is to be attained within this very body through the cooperation of the senses. || 16–17 ||
Since I transcend the perishable and am superior even to the imperishable, therefore I am celebrated in the world and in the Veda as the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama). || 18 ||
Having thus stated the reason for the superiority of the Supreme Person (puruṣottama) in relation to others, he teaches that "I am He.
For I am that which has transcended— having gone beyond— the perishable and the imperishable as previously described, and I am the highest.
For this very reason, I am renowned and celebrated as Puruṣottama in both the world and the Veda.

The status of Puruṣa belonging to the all-pervading, formless Supreme Śiva is clearly established in the *Puruṣasūkta*. Since there is no other being superior to Him, His status as Puruṣottama is well-known.
It is also heard in scripture that "Rudra, the great seer, is superior to all"; yet Kṛṣṇa speaks thus because of his identity with Śiva. 18.
O Bhārata, he who knows me thus as the Supreme Person without delusion, being all-knowing, worships me with his whole being.

He states the fruit of knowing the meaning thus explained: O Bhārata, Arjuna, he who, being undeluded—that is, free from delusion—and having become a knower of the essence of all things, worships Me with his whole being, thinking through such contemplation, "I alone am everything," in the form of the goal, the sustainer, the lord, the witness, and so forth; and thus, by realizing My true nature—
Thus has this most secret teaching been spoken by me, O sinless one.
By understanding this, O Bhārata, one becomes wise and has accomplished all that is to be done.

Declaring that such knowledge of one's own true nature is the supreme secret and the most worthy of being adopted, He concludes the study: "O sinless Arjuna, this most secret scripture—being of an extremely esoteric nature—has been spoken, that is, taught, by Me. O Bhārata."
Having understood this secret, Arjuna, by that alone a man would become wise; not through any other knowledge.

And by this very knowledge, he would have fulfilled his purpose. Having attained birth as a human, whatever is to be done would then be accomplished at that very moment. Otherwise, however, it would be entirely useless for him.
The absence of restlessness of the sense faculties. || 20 ||
Chapter Sixteen:
Previously, in the ninth chapter, those who have resorted to the divine nature and those who have resorted to the demonic state were described.
By these and other such statements, the two natures—the divine nature and the asuric nature—have been indicated.
Since their true nature must necessarily be known, they are taught in detail in this chapter.
Fearlessness, purity of being, steadfastness in the yoga of knowledge, charity, self-control, sacrifice, study of the scriptures, austerity, and uprightness; (1)
Non-violence, truthfulness, freedom from anger, renunciation, tranquility, absence of malice, compassion toward all beings, lack of greed, gentleness, modesty, and steadiness. (2)
O Bhārata, splendor, forgiveness, fortitude, purity, non-malice, and lack of excessive pride— these belong to one born with a divine nature.
The Blessed Lord said: Fearlessness is the absence of fear; fortitude is the purity of the mind (*sattva*);
self-restraint is the calming of the external senses; sacrifice is the worship of one's chosen deity;
study is the recitation of one's own sacred scripture; austerity is that which will be described later as being of three kinds—bodily, vocal, and mental.

And the mental [virtues] are threefold: straightforwardness (*ārjava*) is always acting with rectitude; non-violence (*ahiṃsā*) is the absence of anger even toward one who has caused harm to living beings; renunciation (*tyāga*) is the relinquishing of mental desires; tranquility (*śānti*) is compassion for those suffering within; and lack of greed (*aloluptva*) is the absence of sensory restlessness even in the presence of sense objects.

Gentleness (*mārdava*) is a heart free from harshness. Modesty (*hrī*) is shame regarding improper actions and the like. Lack of fickleness (*acāpala*) is the steadiness of the mind. Splendor (*tejas*) is majesty. Forbearance (*kṣamā*) is endurance. Fortitude (*dhṛti*) is mental stability, defined as not even noticing physical pain and the like. Purity (*śauca*) is external and internal cleanliness. Non-malice (*adroha*)...

The absence of deceiving others; the absence of excessive pride—*atimāna* being extreme pride or arrogance, its absence [is meant]. O Bhārata, Arjuna, these [qualities belong] to one born facing toward the divine endowment (*daivī saṃpad*).

These qualities arise in the living being (jīva). The meaning is that it should be understood that such a person, possessing these qualities, is worthy of attaining divine sovereignty and other such states. || 1–3 ||
Hypocrisy, arrogance, self-conceit, anger, as well as harshness and ignorance— these, O Pārtha, belong to one born to the demonic nature.

Now, He describes the demonic nature (*āsurī saṃpat*): "Deceit" (*dambha*) means wearing the cloak of righteousness; that is, practicing dharma for the sake of fame and the like. "Arrogance" (*darpa*) is intoxication caused by learning, wealth, and so forth. "Self-conceit" (*abhimāna*) is pride.
"Anger" (*krodha*) is a disposition toward wrath. "Roughness" (*pāruṣya*) is cruelty. "Ignorance" (*ajñāna*) is a lack of discrimination. O Pārtha, O Arjuna!

These qualities belong to a living being who has manifested even the demonic nature (āsurī saṃpat). The meaning is that one possessing such qualities should be understood as being worthy of the demonic state. || 4 ||
The divine endowment is deemed to lead to liberation, while the demonic leads to bondage.
Do not grieve, O Pāṇḍava, for you are born with a divine endowment.
The divine nature is considered conducive to liberation— that is, for the attainment of release— while the demonic nature is considered a cause of bondage,

meaning it yields its respective fruits through repeated binding in saṃsāra. When the Blessed One had spoken thus, Arjuna fell into doubt, wondering, "Am I possessed of the demonic nature or the divine nature?"
O Pāṇḍava Arjuna, you were born having turned toward the divine nature, and not toward the demonic— this was by your own merit.
There are two types of created beings in this world: the divine and the demonic.
The divine has been described in detail; now hear from me, O Pārtha, about the demonic.

Not being satisfied with this brief instruction on the demonic nature (*āsurī-saṃpat*), the Blessed One prepares an introduction in order to describe the true nature of the demonic nature in detail, as it is something that must necessarily be known. "O Pārtha, O Arjuna,
in this world there are two types of creation of beings— that is, two kinds of manifestation of living creatures— the divine (*daiva*) and the demonic (*āsura*)."

Creation has been accomplished. Of those two, the divine creation has already been described in detail by such passages as "Fearlessness, purity of being," and so forth. Now, listen as I describe the demonic—the demonic creation—in detail. 6.
Asuras do not understand what is to be engaged in nor what is to be desisted from; neither purity, nor right conduct, nor truth exists among them. (7)
They say that this world is without truth, without a foundation, and without a Lord;
it is born of mutual union, caused by nothing other than desire. (8)

For those Asuras, being possessed of an Asuric disposition, say that the entire world is unreal and merely false. Thus they say this world is "without foundation," meaning there is nothing such as the Supreme Brahman to serve as its support. For this very reason, they say this world is "without a Lord" (anīśvara), devoid of a ruler. Then, as for the world...

To the question of how they know that activity itself [is without a cause], he says: "Taking hold of this view—that things arise neither from themselves nor from another, nor from both, nor without a cause—those of ruined souls and small intellects, intent on cruel deeds and hostile to the world, arise for its destruction. (9)

Having grasped and relied upon this view—the aforementioned nihilistic intellect—those whose selves are destroyed arise as enemies to their own selves. Being of such demoniacal nature, they thus destroy the world. 9.
Taking refuge in insatiable desire, filled with hypocrisy, pride, and arrogance, they embrace evil dogmas through delusion and proceed with impure vows. (10)

Relying upon desire—that thirst which is impossible to fill—they exist; the meaning is that they have seized those crocodiles of hypocrisy and possess them. For they proceed with impure vows, being intent on unclean conduct;
the meaning is that they always strive to fulfill their own desires. || 10 ||
Resorting to immeasurable anxiety that ends only with death,
they are devoted solely to the enjoyment of desires, convinced that this is all there is.
Bound by hundreds of snares of hope and devoted to desire and anger,
they strive for the sake of sensual enjoyment to amass wealth through unjust means. (12)

And they have resorted to a thought that is immeasurable, limitless, ending only with dissolution, and culminating in total destruction; being devoted solely to the enjoyment of desires, they consider the enjoyment of sense-objects alone to be the supreme goal of human life;
they are convinced that "this is all," and they possess the firm conviction that there is nothing else whatsoever beyond this.
Bound and restrained by hundreds of snares of hope— hope itself being the snares—

they are devoted to desire and anger, being under the sway of desire and anger; having accumulated wealth and gathered material possessions through unjust means, they act solely for the sake of sensual enjoyment and objects of pleasure.
"Today this has been gained by me; I shall attain this desire of my heart.
This is mine, and this wealth also shall be mine again. (13)
"This enemy has been slain by me, and I shall slay others as well;
I am the lord, I am the enjoyer, I am successful, powerful, and happy. (14)
"I am wealthy and of noble birth; who else is equal to me?
I shall sacrifice, I shall give gifts, and I shall rejoice"—thus are they deluded by ignorance. (15)
Perplexed by many thoughts, enveloped in the net of delusion, and attached to the enjoyment of sensual pleasures, they fall into impure hell. 16.

"This wealth and so forth was obtained by me alone today; I shall obtain, indeed I will obtain, this very desire intended by my mind; this belongs to me alone; and this wealth, too, will belong to me again"—such is the restatement of hopes for material gain. "This enemy has now been slain by me alone."

In this very way, I shall also slay others who act against my will. I alone am the Lord, all-powerful; I alone am the enjoyer; I alone am the perfected and accomplished one. I am strong, happy, and full of wealth and other riches. I am of noble lineage, born into an excellent family; there is no other equal to me.

"Who am I? I shall sacrifice, I shall give, I shall rejoice"—this is an imitation [of such thoughts] based on the conviction, "I am capable of doing all this. Thus, deluded by ignorance, they have fallen into a state of lack of discrimination (*aviveka*), possessing many-mindedness.

"Perplexed" means especially deluded by the various kinds of minds previously described. "Enveloped by the net of delusion" means covered by that very delusion which is a net—a means of bondage—having fallen within it. [They are thus bound] amidst the enjoyments of sensual desire.

Attached to the pleasures of the senses—meaning intensely clinging to them and making them their sole refuge—such as these are of demoniacal nature; for in the end, they fall into the impure hell, into perdition. (13–16)
Self-conceited, stubborn, and filled with the intoxication of wealth and pride,
they perform sacrifices under the guise of religion, yet out of hypocrisy and contrary to scriptural injunctions.

Self-conceited: those who, considering themselves superior in all virtues, esteem themselves by their own estimation; stubborn and unsubmissive; endowed with wealth, honor, and pride—that is, possessed of wealth, honor, egoism, and intoxication;
and characterized by hypocrisy, which is the aim of proclaiming one's own fitness and so forth.

Those who perform sacrifices in name only—sacrifices consisting of ostentatious displays and the mere utterance of names—and who do not follow the prescribed rules, being possessed by egoism, power, arrogance, lust, and anger;
envious and hating Me in their own bodies and in the bodies of others. (18)

"I-conceit" (*ahaṅkāra*) is the thorough identification of oneself as being the most excellent; "egoism" (*ahaṅkāra*) refers to that. "Strength" (*bala*) is the strength of the body and so forth. "Arrogance" (*darpa*) is lust and anger. Having resorted to these—meaning existing by depending upon them—they [do not know] Me, who exists everywhere within their own and others' bodies (their own and others' persons) as the inner controller (*antaryāmin*).
Hating and slandering, these envious ones, being under the sway of malice, perform sacrifices under the guise of hypocrisy; such is the connection of the verse. || 18 ||
Those hateful, cruel, and most base among men, I cast perpetually into inauspicious, demonic wombs alone within the cycles of worldly existence. 19.
Having entered the womb of an asura, deluded from birth to birth, they fail to reach Me, O son of Kuntī, and from there they go to the lowest state. 20.

Having thus described the nature of the demonic (āsurī) disposition, he speaks of the destiny of those who possess it: "Hating the path of the righteous, I cast the inauspicious sinners perpetually—always—into demonic wombs, that is, into births. Thus, having entered—that is, attained—a demonic womb, they become deluded fools birth after birth."
Having been so,
O Kaunteya Arjuna, never having attained Me— the Supreme Self— having failed to reach Me from that state, [you fall] from there as well.
This threefold gate of hell, which leads to one's own ruin—namely desire, anger, and greed—one should therefore abandon these three. (21)

Having summarized the demonic endowment (*āsuri-sampad*), he says: "Desire, anger, and greed—this threefold gate of hell is the destroyer and ruin of the self. This triad alone is the root of all misfortune;
therefore, a discerning person devoted to the meditation on Śiva should abandon these three and avoid them from afar.
Otherwise, total destruction itself would surely occur. || 21 ||
O son of Kuntī, a man who is liberated from these three gateways to darkness practices what is beneficial for his own self and thereby attains the supreme goal.

He also states the fruit of abandoning these three: O Kaunteya Arjuna, through the gates of darkness, which are the gates of hell, one becomes fit to practice what is beneficial; thus one becomes intent upon the propitiation of the Blessed One and upon service to the devotees of the Blessed One. By such practice of what is conducive to the highest good—
The meaning is that one goes to, attains, and experiences the supreme goal, the state of immortality, which is the unity of existence and the subtle body (bhāvaliṅga).
He who, casting aside the injunctions of the scriptures, acts according to his own whims,
attains neither perfection, nor happiness, nor the supreme goal.
Therefore, the scripture is your authority in determining what ought to be done and what ought not to be done;
having ascertained what is prescribed by the ordinances of the scripture, you should perform your duty here.
Regarding how it is possible for us to know and experience what is beneficial for ourselves, he says this:

that man who, setting aside the sequence of scriptural injunctions, proceeds and conducts himself according to his own whims and according to the dictates of desire, does not attain *siddhi*, which is the attainment of the goals of human life; for that very reason, he does not attain happiness nor the supreme goal.
And one does not attain a good rebirth. Therefore, for you, in determining what is to be done and what is not to be done—namely, "this is to be done" and "this is not to be done"—[this is the rule].

In matters of final determination, the scripture alone is the authority and nothing else. Therefore, you ought to perform only that action prescribed by the ordinances of the scriptures—such as battle and so forth—which is the duty of a Kṣatriya, and not act according to your own whims.
(Chapter Seventeen)

When the Blessed One has declared, "He who acts according to his own whims, casting aside the injunctions of the scriptures, attains neither perfection, nor happiness, nor the supreme goal," Arjuna, desiring to know their destiny, asked:
"But what is the fate of those who, casting aside the injunctions of the scriptures, perform sacrifice endowed with faith?"
But what, O Kṛṣṇa, is their ultimate state: is it goodness (sattva), or passion (rajas), or darkness (tamas)? || 1 ||

But those who, having cast aside and abandoned the scriptural injunctions—the sequence prescribed by the scriptures—yet worship the gods and others with faith, being endowed with a sense of conviction, O Kṛṣṇa, what is their final state? What is its nature? Is it the nature of *sattva*? Or...

Alternatively, is it *rajas* in the form of *rajas*, or is it *tamas* in the form of *tamas*? Since it was stated that they are "endowed with faith," it is possible that it is also *sāttvika*; such is the intention of the questioner, Arjuna. (1)
The faith of embodied beings is of three kinds, born of their own nature: it is sattvic, rajasic, and tamasic; hear now about that. (2)

The Blessed Lord spoke the answer to the question: "The faith of embodied beings—that is, living creatures—is born of their own nature; it is innate and is of three kinds: sāttvic, rājasic, and tāmasī. Listen to that which is about to be described."
(319) O Bhārata, the faith of every being conforms to its own nature;
this person is made of faith— whatever one's faith is, that indeed one is.

O Bhārata, O Arjuna, for the faith of every living being is in accordance with its own nature (*sattva*); the intention is that faith, by its very nature, is mutually distinct according to the internal disposition of each. For this person is made of faith; this is its explanation: whatever one’s faith, that is, whatever kind of faith one possesses.

He becomes composed of that very same faith; for one whose mind is always fixed on that alone, the attainment of that state is indeed observed. He whose senses always take the Supreme Self as their sole object becomes established in the Supreme Self; such is his [nature].

And when the mind is exclusively attached to that [object], it attains the very nature of that object; the experienced ones declare that the pure mind itself becomes the very form of Mahādeva, like camphor in the presence of fire. || 3 ||
Those of sattvic nature worship the gods; those of rajasic nature worship yakṣas and rākṣasas; and other people of tamasic nature worship ghosts and hosts of spirits.

To the question, "How can this distinction of faith be known? he says: Those who are *sāttvika* worship the *sāttvika* deities; others, namely those who are *tāmasa* and possess *tāmasa* faith, worship the *pretas*, the hosts of *bhūtas*, and the well-known *bhūtas*, *pretas*, *piśācas*, and so forth. Thus, by their very actions, [this distinction is known].

The meaning is that even the essential nature of their faith is to be inferred. Here, however, the Śaraṇas have manifested a noble disposition. Regarding the worship of spirits and ghosts, their perspective is distinct:
there is no such thing as a "Mārī" (demoness) renowned in the world apart from a woman with a squinting eye; she is simply a woman appearing in a different form.

And those who speak thus have declared that the tongue itself is Mārī; for the failure to remember objects that ought to be remembered is indeed Mārī, and for one who abandons this Mārī, there shall be happiness. Thus, the Śaraṇas—who conceive of the worship of the powers of the elements and so forth as a secondary purpose and assert the primacy of virtuous conduct—[speak].
For the sake of abandoning the fault known as "the killer" (māryā) which exists even in all [beings], they teach with speech that is most full of vigor. || 4 ||
Those people who perform terrible austerities not ordained by the scriptures,
being possessed of hypocrisy and egoism, and impelled by the force of desire and attachment; (5)
Those mindless ones who emaciate the collection of elements within the body,
as well as Me who dwells within the body— know them to be of demonic resolve.

Having thus explained the classification of faith, He gives the answer to Arjuna’s present question: "Those who perform austerities not prescribed by the scriptures... [referring to] those people who are joined with hypocrisy and egoism—meaning joined with hypocrisy (*dambha*) and egoism (*ahaṅkāra*).
They are "endowed with the force of desire and attachment" (*kāmarāgabalānvitāḥ*); "desire" (*kāma*) is the longing for objects such as heaven that are desired; "attachment" (*rāga*) is...

It consists of the desire for the enjoyment of those objects. Likewise, "strength" (*bala*) refers to physical strength useful for accomplishing tasks by force. Being endowed with these qualities, they perform austerity (*tapas*). Others, however, [regard] the "group of elements" (*bhūtagrāma*) residing in the body—the collection of instruments existing within their own bodies—as being "within the body" (*antaḥśarīrastha*) by virtue of being the inner controller (*antaryāmin*).
They emaciate and make me—residing within that very body—lean; the sense is that they cause me pain.

Know, O Acetaḥ (O you who lack discernment), that those who thus suffer possess the fierce resolve characteristic of Asuras—that is, they possess a fierce determination associated with the nature of Asuras. Here, by the first verse, those established in *rajas* are described.

By the second verse, those persons who are devoted to darkness (tamas) have been described; the intention is that it follows as a matter of course that those who are free from both these types of defects are indeed those whose devotion is characterized by goodness (sattva). || 5-6 ||
Moreover, the food dear to everyone is also of three kinds;
likewise, sacrifice, austerity, and charity—listen now to this distinction between them.
Thus, just as there is a threefold nature regarding the final goal (*niṣṭhā*), so too there is a threefold nature regarding food and other matters;
he teaches this as a relevant digression. For the entire world, even food is dear in three ways according to its respective suitability.
In the very same way, sacrifice (*yajña*), austerity (*tapas*), and charity (*dāna*)—all these are likewise threefold; of these, this [is the first]:
Listen to the distinctions that are about to be described.
Foods that increase longevity, vitality, strength, health, happiness, and joy; which are savory, unctuous, substantial, and agreeable to the heart—these are dear to those of sattvic nature.

Longevity (*āyus*) is life; vitality (*sattva*) is purity of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*); strength (*bala*) is the capacity for the performance of one's duties; health (*ārogya*) is the absence of disease; happiness (*sukha*) is contentment; and joy (*prīti*) is satisfaction. Of these—

"Vivardhanāḥ" means growth-promoting; "ras-yāḥ" means endowed with flavor; "snigdhāḥ" means possessed of unctuousness; "sthirāḥ" means those that remain in the body for a long time; and "hṛdyāḥ" means heart-pleasing—such foods are dear to the sāttvika and are fit to be enjoyed by sāttvika people. || 8 ||
Bitter, sour, salty, excessively hot, pungent, dry, and burning foods are desired by those of the rajasic nature; they bestow suffering, grief, and disease. (9)

Pungent and bitter; sour and salty; excessively hot; sharp; dry, meaning devoid of oiliness—such foods are burning, producing distress, and bestowing pain, grief, and disease. These are the foods for one of a rajasic nature, whose constitution is characterized by the quality of rajas.
Grief is desired for the body that is the fruit thereof. || 9 ||
Food that is stale, tasteless, putrid, and decomposed, as well as that which is leftover or impure—such food is dear to those of a tamasic nature. (10)

That which is *yātayāma* is insufficiently cooked; *gatarasa* is sapless; *pūti* is foul-smelling; *paryuṣita* is stale; and that food which is *ucchiṣṭa*—meaning trivial and impure—is dear to *tāmasa*, for it is dear to the body whose nature is characterized by the quality of *tamas*. || 10 ||

That sacrifice which is performed according to scriptural injunction by those who do not desire its fruits, with the mind focused on the thought that "sacrifice must indeed be made," is characterized by goodness (sāttvika). 11.

That sacrifice which is performed by men free from desire for fruits— those devoid of longing for results— who, having fixed their minds on the thought "sacrifice must indeed be performed" as prescribed by rule and declared in the scriptures, carry it out with the firm resolve in their hearts, "This is my duty," that sacrifice is said to be *sāttvika*. This is done even without expectation of fruit, through the control of body, senses, and mind.
That sacrifice which is performed through meditation in the form of worshiping the Guru and the Deity is declared to be sāttvika. || 11 ||
But that sacrifice which is performed with a view toward the fruit, and even for the sake of ostentation, O best of the Bharatas— know that sacrifice to be rajasic.

O best of the Bharatas, Arjuna, know that sacrifice to be that which is performed or offered with a view toward fruit— that is, for the sake of a result— either out of hypocrisy or for the sake of fame, desiring reputation and status.

Or, that sacrifice which takes the form of worshiping the Lord but is performed with ostentation for the sake of attaining fruits pertaining to this world, such as sons and so forth, is said to be *rājasa*. (12)

They declare that sacrifice to be of the nature of darkness (tāmasa) which is devoid of prescribed rules, where food is not distributed, which lacks mantras and sacrificial fees, and is bereft of faith.

They declare that action to be *tāmasa* which is devoid of prescribed rules, lacking the sequence of the scriptures, where food has not been properly prepared, which is devoid of mantras, lacks sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*), and is bereft of faith. Such is the worship of the Lord [when performed in this manner].
It would be both meaningless and productive of harm. || 13 ||
Worship of the gods, the twice-born, teachers, and the wise; purity, straightforwardness, celibacy, and non-violence—this is called bodily austerity.

Now he describes the threefold nature of austerity (tapas): the gods, such as Indra and others; the twice-born (dvijas), who have attained a second birth in the form of grace that accomplishes the knowledge of Brahman; the guru, the teacher who instructs in reality;
and the wise one (prājña), the knower of Brahman. Worship of these constitutes purity (śauca), which is complete purification. Straightforwardness (ārjava) is rectitude.
Celibacy, mastery over the senses, and non-violence are said to be bodily austerity (*śārīraṃ tapaḥ*).

Furthermore, even the *Śaraṇas* (devotees), taking their own experience as authoritative, declare that the body has come into being solely for the purpose of worshiping the Lord. Even gladdening the world through contemplation of the Lord is indeed bodily austerity.
Even the removal of the suffering of the miserable, the poor, and the helpless is that very same thing; whatever is done today, all of it is indeed physical austerity (tapa).
Speech that causes no agitation, which is truthful, pleasant, and beneficial, as well as the practice of reciting the sacred texts—this is called austerity of speech. (15)

That speech which causes no agitation to others, which does not produce suffering, and which is truthful, factual, pleasant, and beneficial—that alone is called the austerity of speech (*vāṅmaya-tapas*). Likewise, the study of one's own Veda (*svādhyāya*) should be like a pearl;
likewise, it should be like the luster of a gem; likewise...
That indeed is like a crystal;
it is that very form of consciousness, the unbroken *liṅga*. And this *liṅga* is present within the heart.

"One should indeed speak these words: 'It may be so, it may be so. For if action did not correspond to what has been spoken, the God would never come under the sway of man. Therefore, the harmony of speech, body, and mind is scrutinized by the virtuous, who are like *cātaka* birds.
Thus, that which is spoken for the sake of the welfare of others through the purity of the three organs is itself the austerity (*tapas*) consisting of speech."

Thus it is said by those who have experienced it: such a gift of fearlessness to all, being dear to the Blessed One, is proclaimed as the austerity of speech; this alone reveals the purity of the human heart.
Serenity of mind, gentleness, silence, self-restraint,
and purity of being— this is called mental austerity.

Clarity of mind is the serenity of the mind; gentleness is a state of mental well-being. Silence is the restraint of the mind that serves as the cause for the restraint of speech; self-control is the mastery of the internal organ.
Purity of being is the complete purity of the mind's disposition. All this is called mental austerity. || 16 ||
That threefold austerity which is performed by men with supreme faith, by those who are disciplined and free from desire for rewards, is declared to be *sāttvika*. (17)

Having thus described the threefold nature of austerity according to the divisions of bodily, vocal, and mental, [the text now] states: that threefold austerity— bodily, vocal, and mental— which is performed by men who are sattvic, free from desire for fruits, devoid of expectation for results, disciplined, and composed— that is declared, or spoken of, as "sāttvika austerity."
For the wise, austerity performed with faith even without expectation of fruit is called sāttvika austerity;
such is the meaning. || 17 ||
That austerity which is performed for the sake of honor, respect, and worship, and with hypocrisy, is declared here to be rajasic; it is unstable and impermanent. (17)

For the sake of honor, respect, and worship: "honor" (satkāra) means being placed at the forefront; "respect" (māna) means being treated with esteem; "worship" (pūjā) refers to prostration, ritual adoration, and so forth. Whatever austerity is performed under the pretext of these—with hypocrisy or with the desire for status and the like—out of the three aforementioned types, that austerity is declared to be *rājasa*. And it is said to be both unstable and impermanent.

It is unstable, not firm; it is transient and its fruit is merely occasional. The meaning is that since austerity is performed solely for the sake of honor and the like, once that objective is attained, the austerity itself would naturally cease. || 18 ||
That austerity which is performed with a deluded grasp, causing pain to oneself or for the purpose of destroying another, is declared to be tāmasa.

That austerity which is performed with a deluded grasp— that is, a grasp rooted in a lack of discrimination and accompanied by false pride— for the sake of tormenting oneself, or for the purpose of destroying another or harming others even at the cost of self-injury,
is declared to be *tāmasa* (of the nature of darkness). It has as its fruit the injury of both oneself and others.
The meaning is that asceticism characterized by darkness (tamas) is what is intended. || 19 ||
That gift which is given with the thought "it ought to be given" to one who cannot return the favor,
at the proper place and time and to a worthy recipient, is declared to be *sāttvika*.

"It must be given. This refers to that gift which is bestowed upon one who has not rendered assistance, yet is considered a worthy recipient (*satpātra*), by means of the cultivation of duty (*kartavyabhāvanā*)—thinking, "This is my obligation"—just as in the grammatical usage *phalaṃ pacati* ("he ripens the fruit"). Furthermore, that which is given for the sake of a return favor, or with a view toward a future result, [is not the highest gift]. As it is said: "But that which is given for the sake of a return favor, or again with a view toward a result..."
And that gift which is given with distress is considered to be of the nature of passion (rājasa). || 21 ||
But that gift which is given for the sake of a return favor, or with the aim of a return favor, or with reference to a fruit,
or with the aim of attaining fruits such as merit (puṇya) and the like— given with affliction and preceded by weariness— that gift is declared to be rajasic. || 21 ||
That gift which is given at an improper place and time, to unworthy recipients, without respect and with contempt, is declared to be of the nature of darkness (tāmasa).

"In improper place and time" means in an unsuitable location and at an unsuitable moment; that is to say, in an inauspicious place and at an inauspicious time. That gift which is given to unworthy recipients—meaning those who are not fit vessels—and which is unrefined, lacking in hospitality, or performed with contempt, preceded by insults and derision, is of the nature of darkness (tāmasa).
