Giving has been declared; it has been explained. || 22 ||
"Oṃ tat sat"—this was declared of old as the threefold designation of Brahman;
by it, the Brāhmaṇas, the Vedas, and the sacrifices were ordained in ancient times. (23)

Desiring to instruct on the manner in which sacrifice, charity, austerity, and other such duties are to be performed, he states the introductory framework: "The designation of Brahman—that is, Paramaśiva—as 'Oṃ Tat Sat' is recorded as threefold, of three kinds, by those who have experienced Śiva; it has been declared by the Brāhmaṇas."

The Vedas, such as the Ṛgveda and others, which bear those names, as well as the sacrifices that are means of worshipping the Lord, were ordained and created by Him at the beginning of creation through these threefold designations alone. The Brāhmaṇas, the Vedas, and the sacrifices possess an intimate relationship with Paraśiva; therefore, they are [designated] by the designations of Paraśiva.

The meaning is that they were created by the very words "Oṃ," "Tat," and "Sat. It is well known from such passages as "In the beginning, he fashioned the gods and others from the Vedic words alone" that the creation of the entire universe proceeds from the Vedic words alone. || 23 ||
Therefore, having uttered the syllable "Om," the acts of sacrifice, gift-giving, and austerity, as prescribed by the ordinances, constantly proceed from those who discourse on Brahman. (24)

This is the statement of the purpose for the subject matter already discussed. Therefore, because the word "Oṃ tat sat" is of the nature of a designation for the Supreme Self, all sacrificial, charitable, and ascetic acts—whether prescribed by rule or enjoined by scripture—for those Brahmins who are habituated to speaking of Brahman (brahmavādins), [are indeed] sacrifice... [yajña].
Sacrifice, charity, and austerity—these activities proceed and are practiced constantly and at all times.
The meaning is that the engagement of the knowers in all Vedic rites is seen to occur precisely preceded by the utterance of these three aforementioned words. || 24 ||
Therefore, without aiming for a reward, those who desire liberation perform sacrifices, acts of austerity, and various kinds of giving. (25)

Having stated the general rule, he also states the specific rule: by the word "that" (tat), which denotes Paraśiva, [it is meant that] those desiring liberation—those seeking liberation without aiming for a fruit or without reference to a specific result—perform and carry out acts of giving and ritual action; that is, they do not aim for the fruit prescribed for each respective rite.

All acts such as sacrifice (*yajña*) performed solely for the sake of pleasing the Supreme Self and for the attainment of liberation rooted therein are that very same [worship], because they consist of words denoting Paraśiva.
The meaning is that it must be performed preceded by recitation. || 25 ||
The word *sat* is used in the sense of existence and in the sense of goodness;
likewise, O Pārtha, the word *sat* is applied to a praiseworthy action. (26)

Desiring to explain the application of the word *sat*, [the Lord] first states its meaning: "O Pārtha, O Arjuna, in *sadbhāve*—that is, in the state of being real (*samīcīnabhāve*). Its further explanation is 'the state of being good' (*sādhubhāva*). Indeed, *sadbhāva* is precisely the state of being good; for when referring to a virtuous person (*satpuruṣa*), one observes the worldly usage: "This person is good."

The word "sat" is employed in the sense of existence and in the sense of goodness; likewise, in exactly that same way, the word "sat" is employed for a praiseworthy or excellent action. Just as in the expression "satpuruṣa" (a good person), even an excellent action is designated by the term "sat" in the world. || 26 ||
Steadfastness in sacrifice, austerity, and charity is called "good" (sat); likewise, action performed for their sake is also designated as "good. (27)

In sacrifice, austerity, or charity, the application of the word "sat" (good/true) is said to consist in their being established in form. Because those actions are prescribed by the scriptures, intended for that purpose, and have the satisfaction of the Supreme Lord as their goal, they are likewise called "sat" (good) due to their nature as *sat-karma* (virtuous action). Thus, all actions performed for the sake of pleasing the Blessed One are [to be understood in this way].
It is taught that the designation for virtuous deeds is by means of the three words: "Oṃ," "Tat," and "Sat. || 27 ||

Regarding the question, "What is the state (*niṣṭhā*) of those who, abandoning the injunctions of the scriptures, perform sacrifice endowed with faith?"— after first establishing that those acts performed according to the scriptural sequence are characterized by passion (*rājasa*) and ignorance (*tāmasa*), and then, as an incidental teaching, instructing on the distinctions among sacrifice, charity, and austerity as being *sāttvika* and so forth, [the Lord] concludes:

He concludes that even an action enjoined by the scriptures does not yield fruit if it is devoid of faith: "Whatever is offered in sacrifice, given as a gift, or performed as austerity, if done without faith..."
It is called "non-existent," O Pārtha, for it exists neither hereafter nor in this world.

O Pārtha, O Arjuna, that which has been offered in sacrifice without faith— that is, whatever oblation and so forth has been performed, whatever gift has been given, whatever austerity has been practiced, and whatever else such as praise and prostration has been performed— [that is without fruit].

It is called "non-existent" (asat). It is indeed called "non-existent action" (asatkarma). Non-existent action does not yield its prescribed fruit even after death—that is, in the interval following death—nor does it bear fruit here in this world. Therefore, [the criterion for action] is its being ordained by the scriptures.
Faith is necessary for both; the meaning is that the attainment of the fruit does not occur through either one alone. || 28 ||
Chapter Eighteen:
Thus everything was taught by the Blessed One to Arjuna. However, because the principal subjects are scattered here and there, it is not easy for the mind to focus upon them.
That which can be accomplished—the essence of all the scriptures—is taught in this chapter. And, in accordance with that, for the purpose of introducing the inquiry, Arjuna said:
"O mighty-armed one, I wish to know the true nature of renunciation."
And [tell me] of renunciation, O Hṛṣīkeśa, O slayer of Keśin, separately.

"O mighty-armed one, O slayer of Keśin, O Hṛṣīkeśa"—these are the three vocatives addressed to Kṛṣṇa with an excess of devotion. A story is heard in the Bhāgavata Purāṇa that Kṛṣṇa slew a certain demon named Keśin; therefore, he is called "the slayer of Keśin. I [am] of renunciation...

I wish to know—to understand—the reality, that is, the distinct and unmixed essential nature, of renunciation (*tyāga*) separately. Do renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) and renunciation (*tyāga*) constitute one and the same thing, or are they different?
What, then, is their essential nature? It is with the intent of knowing such matters that I ask; please instruct me on this. || 1 ||
The wise know the renunciation of optional rites to be *saṃnyāsa*;
the discerning declare the abandonment of the fruits of all actions to be *tyāga*.

Thus questioned, the Blessed One said: "The wise, the learned, know *saṃnyāsa*— renunciation— to be simply the abandonment (*tyāga*) of those optional rites (*kāmya-karma*), such as the Agnihotra and others, which have heaven and the like as their fruits."

Furthermore, some wise and learned people declare that *tyāga* (renunciation) is merely the relinquishment of the fruits of all actions— that is, the abandonment of the results of all deeds— but not the total abandonment of the actions themselves. Thus, the renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) of optional rites (*kāmya-karma*) consists precisely in the abandoning of their fruits.
This is the meaning: thus there is a distinction between the two. || 2 ||
Some wise men say that action should be abandoned as being full of fault;
others say that action consisting of sacrifice, gift-giving, and austerity should not be abandoned.

Some wise scholars, however, declare that action—even action in its general sense—must be renounced because it is defective, as it brings about the defect of bondage. Others, who are learned, declare that action consisting of sacrifice, charity, and austerity must not be renounced; it is not at all fit to be abandoned.
With the vision of the welfare of the world, one must indeed perform every action for the satisfaction of the Supreme Śiva. || 3 ||
Hear from me the definitive conclusion regarding renunciation, O best of the Bharatas;
for renunciation, O tiger among men, is proclaimed to be of three kinds. (4)

When the doubt arises as to what, then, is the established conclusion (*siddhānta*) regarding the mutual difference of opinion among the wise, the Blessed One said: "O best of the Bharatas, O Arjuna, hear from me the certainty concerning that aforementioned subject. O tiger among men, O Arjuna, for renunciation..."
It is remembered as being threefold and of three types.
The acts of sacrifice, charity, and austerity are not to be abandoned; they must indeed be performed.
For sacrifice, charity, and austerity are the purifiers of the wise.

Regarding the question "What are those types?", the author—intending to explain the threefold division of obligatory action (*niyata-karman*) into *sāttvika*, *rājasa*, and *tāmasa* through the verse beginning with "But renunciation of the obligatory" (*niyatasya tu saṃnyāsaḥ*)—first states the established conclusion (*siddhānta*): Sacrifice, charity, austerity, and so forth—that which is action—is indeed not to be abandoned; it is not fit to be relinquished, but rather that action must certainly be performed.
If it is asked "Why?", [the answer is: sacrifice, charity, and austerity—these actions are purifiers for the wise, that is, for human beings;
they are sanctifying and destroyers of all sins. Therefore, they must not be abandoned. (5)
"But even these actions, O Pārtha, must be performed after abandoning attachment and the fruits thereof; this is my firm and supreme conviction. (6)

O Pārtha Arjuna, it is my firm conviction and supreme opinion that these aforementioned actions must indeed be performed after abandoning attachment— that is, one's clinging to them— and their fruits. Thus, the performance of action preceded by the renunciation of attachment is absolutely necessary for those actions.
The meaning is that complete renunciation is simply not appropriate. || 6 ||
But the renunciation of obligatory action is not appropriate;
its abandonment through delusion is proclaimed to be of the nature of darkness (tāmasa). || 7 ||

Thus, the renunciation or abandonment of action— which, even in the absence of its fruits, is necessarily one's own duty according to one's particular caste and stage of life (*varṇāśrama*) and is therefore eternally incumbent— is neither possible nor appropriate. Therefore, out of delusion,
thinking "this is painful" or simply out of fear of physical hardship, if one should abandon action...
Having performed a renunciation of the passionate type (rājasa), he would certainly not obtain the fruit of renunciation.

Because affliction arises from performing [action], one who would abandon action out of fear of bodily affliction—that is, out of dread that "bodily affliction will occur"—having made a *rājasa* renunciation, shall not obtain nor attain the fruit of renunciation. The meaning is that the abandonment of action due to laziness and the like is *rājasa*. (8)
O Arjuna, when obligatory action is performed simply because it is duty,
having abandoned attachment as well as the fruit, that renunciation is considered to be of the nature of goodness (sāttvika).

Now, He describes the sattvic renunciation as that which is to be adopted: "O Arjuna, [perform] that action which is *niyata*—that is, obtained through the injunctions of the scriptures—with the mere thought, 'This must be done by me,' having abandoned attachment—the delusion regarding friends, enemies, and so forth—and having relinquished the fruits, the connection with the results of action. Regarding such action:

That renunciation is considered *sāttvika*. Renunciation consisting solely in the abandonment of attachment to fruits is *sāttvika* renunciation; however, the total abandonment of actions is *tāmasa*, while their abandonment due to laziness and the like is *rājasa*. Thus, the threefold nature of renunciation has been explained.
He does not hate unwholesome action nor does he cling to the wholesome;
he is renounced, filled with being, wise, and his doubts are severed. (10)

He praises one whose nature is characterized by such sattvic renunciation: the renouncer (tyāgī), who possesses the aforementioned sattvic disposition, and for that very reason is permeated by *sattva*—endowed with the quality of purity; who is wise (*medhāvī*), possessed of intelligence; and whose doubts are severed, being free from uncertainty regarding what ought to be done—he does not hate even unwholesome action, nor [does he cling] to the wholesome.

Even in action, he does not become attached; he does not become one who clings. Since no attachment whatsoever exists for him, nor even any expectation of results, therefore all his action becomes of a single nature. || 10 ||
For it is not possible for one who bears a body to abandon actions entirely;
however, he who renounces the fruits of action is said to be a "renouncer. (11)

To the question, "Why might the meaning of the word 'renunciation' not be complete renunciation itself? he says: It is simply not possible for a "bearer of the body"—that is, for any living being whatsoever—to renounce everything entirely and completely; for at the very least, activities such as eating and so forth must necessarily be performed for the sake of maintaining the body.
This is accepted by all experience; therefore, he who renounces the fruits of action but does not renounce the action itself is alone designated as a "renouncer."
The threefold fruit of action— unpleasant, pleasant, and mixed—
accrues after death to those who do not renounce, but never to those who have renounced.

Having thus stated that the abandonment of the fruits of action alone is the meaning of the word "renunciation," he also speaks of the censure of those who do not practice such renunciation: for men who are non-renouncers— those who do not perform the aforementioned renunciation and yet continue to carry out actions— the fruit of their action is undesirable, desirable, or mixed.

The fruit indeed comes after death, immediately following the passing away; since they have not performed renunciation, the fruit must necessarily be experienced by them. However, for renunciants who have truly abandoned [action], such attainment of fruit is not possible anywhere at all. Therefore, the meaning is that renunciation alone must be practiced. || 12 ||
O mighty-armed one, learn from me these five causes which are declared in the Sāṃkhya system of final conclusions for the successful accomplishment of all actions. (13)
Thus, it has been stated [in the verse beginning] "Indeed, it is not possible for one who bears a body... (Gītā 3.5), that the complete renunciation of actions cannot be accomplished.
In that context, He describes the nature of agency regarding action: "O mighty-armed one, these... (Gītā 3.27).

Understand—that is, know—from me those causes for the accomplishment of all actions which are to be described; they have been declared in the *Sāṃkhya*, that is, in the established doctrine of Sāṃkhya (*sāṃkhyakṛtānta*).

Even though they are stated in the Sāṃkhya system, [they are to be understood here] according to the maxim: "that which is not inconsistent with the sequence [of the present context] may be taken from elsewhere."

Since these [teachings] are not contradictory even for us Vedāntins, they are indeed to be accepted; however, to indicate that one should never harbor groundless hatred toward anything, the words "in Sāṃkhya and Kṛtānta" were used. || 13 ||
The locus, the agent, and the various instruments, as well as diverse and distinct activities—fate is the fifth among these. (14)

Regarding the question "What are those five?", he says: the substratum is the body (*adhiṣṭhānaṃ śarīram*). For the body is the support for all activity. And that [body] is of various kinds, being manifold. The sense organs (*indriyāṇi*) are indeed eleven. Likewise, there are various, distinct, and diverse movements (*ceṣṭāḥ*), which are the activities of the body.
In this very accomplishment of an action, destiny is said to be the fifth cause. || 14 ||
Whatever action a person undertakes with body, speech, and mind—whether it be righteous or its opposite—these five are its causes. (15)

A person—a human being—undertakes whatever action is appropriate and consistent with dharma, or its opposite, which is of the nature of adharma, by means of body, speech, and mind; that is, through the body, speech, or the mind.
For every kind of such action, these five combined together are the causes that serve as its instrumental factors; they do not [operate individually].
Among these, there may be only a single cause. || 15 ||
This being so, he who, due to his unrefined intellect, perceives the self alone as the sole agent— that person of dull wit does not truly see.

Likewise, regarding the accomplishment of an action, when this is so—that is, when an action is being accomplished by these five in this manner—the fool who perceives, or knows, himself alone as the sole agent is one possessed of a corrupted intellect (*durmati*). For that very reason, he does not see the truth; he does not know it at all. By the five...
The meaning is that if, while an action is being performed, one perceives only oneself as the agent, then such a person is indeed a fool.
He whose state of being is free from egoism, whose intellect is not tainted—
even having slain these worlds, he does not kill, nor is he bound. (17)
He describes the nature of the discriminating person: for that discriminating person whose state of mind— that is, the state of his internal organ—

is not characterized by egoism (not joined with the sense of "I"), and whose intellect is not smeared by those actions— meaning it does not become attached [thinking] "I alone am performing the action"— he, even having slain all these worlds, would be the agent of the slaying.
He does not kill them at all; for that very reason, he is not bound. He does not become subject to the bondage occasioned by those acts.
Since the isolated Self lacks agency, he is not even the doer of the killing. For this same reason, he does not share in the sin occasioned by it—this is the meaning. || 17 ||
Knowledge, the object of knowledge, and the knower—this is the threefold impulse to action.
The instrument, the action, and the agent—this is the threefold aggregate of action. (18)

He states the motivating cause for a person's engagement in actions: knowledge (*jñāna*), the object of knowledge (*jñeya*), and the knower (*parijñātā*)—as well as the "knower" (*jñātā*)—constitute the impulsion toward action (*karmacodanā*).

This impulsion regarding action, or the inclination toward activity, is threefold, consisting of three types. Only when these three are combined does the engagement in actions occur. Likewise, there is also the instrument (*karaṇa*), the action (*karman*), and the agent (*kartṛ*).

The "comprehension of action" (*karmasaṃgraha*)—the inclusion or encompassing of action—is threefold. The meaning is that within these three categories alone, the causality of action is fully accounted for. || 18 ||
Knowledge, action, and the agent—these three are indeed described according to the distinction of the qualities (guṇas) in the enumeration of the qualities; hear them also as they truly are. (19)

Thus, He describes the distinctions of the *sāttvika* and other types regarding such things as knowledge and so forth: "Knowledge, action, and this agent who has been specified—when these are enumerated according to their basis in the qualities (*guṇas*) such as *sattva*, they are declared to be threefold due to the threefold nature of the *sattva* and other qualities. These also shall be explained by Me exactly as they are."
Listen.
That by which one perceives the one undecaying reality in all beings, undivided within the divided— know that knowledge to be *sāttvika*.

First, he describes sattvic knowledge: by means of that knowledge through which one perceives a single, undivided state— a state of equanimity— within all beings and all things, from the unmanifest down to stationary objects, even though they appear divided.

(333) That by which the individual soul (jīva) perceives or sees—that knowledge, know it to be sāttvika. Thus, the meaning is that knowledge which serves as the cause for the cultivation of equanimity toward all things is sāttvika. || 20 ||
But know that knowledge to be rajasic which perceives various distinct entities as separate from one another among all beings. (21)
And that knowledge which perceives, exactly as they appear, all various entities— distinct and mutually different among all beings and all things—
as distinctness itself, know that knowledge to be *rājasa*. That which [perceives] merely by way of its being perceived...
The meaning is that such knowledge is of the nature of passion (rājasa). || 21 ||
But that which is attached to a single effect as if it were the whole, which is causeless, devoid of the true nature of reality, and meager— that is declared to be tāmasa.

That knowledge which, though complete in every respect, is intent upon only one single effect and does not touch anything else even in the slightest degree, but rather terminates right there— arising by chance (*yadṛcchā*) without a cause, that is, without a proper cause— is therefore "insignificant" because it terminates in only one thing; it does not possess the true nature of reality.
And that knowledge which has as its object what is not the true reality is declared to be tāmasa. || 22 ||
Action performed with determination, free from attachment, and devoid of passion and hatred, by one who does not desire its fruit—that is called sāttvika. (23)

Now, he describes the divisions of action, such as that characterized by *sattva* and so forth: "That action which is obligatory—meaning prescribed by scriptural injunctions—and is performed without attachment, without desire for fruit, and without passion or aversion, is said to be *sāttvika*. (23)
Furthermore, that action which is performed with great exertion by one desiring objects of desire, or again, by one possessed of egoism— that is declared to be rājasa.

But that action which is performed by a person who desires objects of longing, who possesses a wish for results, or who is endowed with egoism— that action which involves great exertion and is accompanied by manifold afflictions— is [the action under discussion].
This is declared to be the quality of rajas. || 24 ||
That action which is undertaken out of delusion, without regard for consequences, loss, injury, or one's own human capacity, is said to be tāmasa.

That action which is undertaken out of delusion— that is, through ignorance— without regard for the consequences (anubandha), namely the future result that is harmful, or for one's own ruin (kṣaya) or injury (hiṃsā) arising therefrom, which causes suffering to oneself and others, or even for one's own human capacity (pauruṣa)— that action is said to be tāmasa. || 25 ||
One who is free from attachment, free from egoistic speech, endowed with fortitude and enthusiasm,
and remains unshaken by success or failure— such an agent is said to be of the nature of goodness (sāttvika).
Now he describes the threefold nature of the agent: one who is free from attachment—that is, devoid of the sense of being the doer of actions;
one who does not speak with ego—that is, free from the notion of "I"; one who is endowed with fortitude and perseverance—meaning possessed of both steadfastness and energy;
and likewise, one who remains unchanged in success or failure—that is, free from perturbation whether there is attainment of the fruit or its non-attainment.
An agent who acts with a single-minded consistency is said to be of the nature of sattva. || 26 ||
A doer who is passionate, desirous of the fruits of action, greedy, violent by nature, impure, and possessed by joy and sorrow, is proclaimed to be rajasic. (27)

One who is full of passion (*rāgī*) is possessed of attachment; one who desires the fruits of action (*karmaphalaprepsuḥ*) is one who has expectations regarding the results of action; one who is greedy (*lubdhaḥ*) is possessed of covetousness;

one whose nature is harmful (*hiṃsātmakaḥ*) has the disposition to cause pain to others; one who is impure (*aśuciḥ*) is unclean; one who is beset by joy and sorrow (*harṣaśokānvitaḥ*) is one who is affected by the attainment or non-attainment of results;
one who is undisciplined (*ayuktaḥ*) is vulgar, stubborn, deceitful, malicious, and lazy.
One who is dejected and procrastinating is said to be a doer of tamasic nature. || 28 ||
One who is undisciplined, unconcentrated, vulgar, and of unrefined intellect; who is stubborn, ill-mannered, deceitful, and foolish;

who is malicious, envious, lazy, devoid of effort, despondent, always miserable, procrastinating, and slow in performing his duties—such a doer is said to be of the nature of darkness (tāmasa). || 28 ||
(335) Hear now, O Dhanañjaya, the threefold division of the intellect and of fortitude according to their qualities, as it is being declared by me in its entirety and in detail. 29.

Now, He declares the division of intellect (*buddhi*) and fortitude (*dhṛti*) according to the qualities such as *sattva* and so forth: "O Dhanañjaya Arjuna, listen to the threefold division of intellect and fortitude according to the qualities—*sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*—as it is being proclaimed by Me in its entirety, in full detail, and with distinct characteristics. I—
"I shall speak; listen," the Blessed One says to Arjuna. || 29 ||
O Pārtha, that intellect which understands engagement and withdrawal, what ought to be done and what ought not to be done, fear and fearlessness, as well as bondage and liberation, is sattvic.

O Pārtha Arjuna, [know] *pravṛtti*—the path of active engagement which is the cause of bondage—and *nivṛtti*—the path of withdrawal which is the cause of liberation; likewise, [know] what is to be done and what is not to be done, such that "this is to be done" and "this is not to be done";
and likewise, [know] fear and fearlessness, such that "this is the cause of fear" and "this is the cause of fearlessness."
In this very way, that intellect which understands bondage and liberation as the results of everything, as well as the essential nature of both bondage and liberation, is considered to be *sāttvikī*.
That intellect by which one perceives dharma and adharma, as well as what ought to be done and what ought not to be done, incorrectly, O Pārtha, is rajasic.

O Pārtha Arjuna, that intellect which, out of fear, does not discern with certainty whether something is dharma or adharma, what should be done or what should not be done, nor anything else that has been spoken—such a intellect is rajasic. 31.
O Pārtha, that intellect which, enveloped by darkness, perceives unrighteousness as righteousness and all objects in a perverted manner— that intellect is tāmasī.

O Pārtha, that intellect which is enveloped—covered—by *tamas*, the quality of darkness, perceives all matters in a completely perverted manner, such as mistaking unrighteousness for righteousness and what should not be done for what should be done; that intellect is called *tāmasī*. || 32 ||
That resolve by which one sustains the activities of the mind, the vital breaths, and the senses through unwavering yoga—that, O Pārtha, is sattvic resolve. (33)

336) He speaks of the different types of fortitude (*dhṛti*): by means of which fortitude all the activities of the mind, the vital breath, and the senses—that is, all the activities of the mind, of the fivefold vital breath (*prāṇa*), and of the senses such as sight and the rest—[are sustained].

That fortitude (dhṛti) by which one maintains or establishes actions—that is, their respective activities—through yoga, meaning through the power of yoga, in a manner that is unwavering and uninterrupted, is declared to be sattvic. || 33 ||
But that resolve by which one holds fast to duty, pleasure, and wealth, O Arjuna, while desiring the fruits through attachment—that resolve, O Pārtha, is of the nature of passion (rājasa). (34)

O Pārtha, that fortitude by which one, desiring results and characterized by an expectation of fruit, holds fast to virtue, pleasure, and wealth— the human aims other than liberation— through attachment and preoccupation with them, is declared to be rājasic. 34.
That resolve by which the dull-witted person does not abandon sleep, fear, sorrow, despondency, and even intoxication—that, O Pārtha, is tāmasī resolve. (35)

That resolve by which a person of dull intellect and perverted understanding does not relinquish sleep, sloth, fear, terror, grief, dejection of mind, nor the intoxication and arrogance of the other senses, but remains attached to them— that resolve is considered tāmasī. 35.
But now hear from me, O bull of the Bharatas, about the threefold happiness, wherein one finds delight through practice and reaches the end of suffering. (36)

Now, He declares the classification of happiness: "O Arjuna, bull among the Bharatas, listen now from Me to the threefold happiness, in which—that is, in the experience of which happiness—one finds delight through practice, by the power of habit, and a person reaches the end of suffering, the destruction of sorrow; such is that threefold happiness."
That happiness which is like poison at first but like nectar in its result, born from the serenity of one's own intellect, is declared to be sattvic. (37)
At the beginning, at the start, and in front, it may be like poison or like suffering due to fear; yet in the end, at its conclusion,
it would be like nectar, equal to immortality— born from the clarity of one's own intellect, that is, of the self's understanding.
That happiness which arises from serenity and clarity of mind is designated as sāttvika. || 37 ||
That pleasure which arises from the contact of the senses with their objects, which is like nectar at first but turns out to be like poison in its consequence, is declared to be rajasic.

That pleasure which is initially— first, at the commencement— born from the contact of the sense organs with their objects, such as the connection between the ears and other senses with objects like sound, which is like nectar and resembles ambrosia,
but which in its transformation becomes like poison and consists entirely of suffering— that very pleasure is known as rajasic. (38)
That pleasure which, both at the beginning and in its consequence, deludes the self and arises from sleep,
laziness, and negligence, is declared to be tāmasa.
As for that pleasure which, at its beginning, during its course, and in its conclusion, produces only delusion for the self—
there is no being on earth, nor in heaven among the gods, that is free from these three qualities born of material nature. (40)

And so, having stated the distinctions between *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*, he describes their pervasiveness: whether on earth (*pṛthivī*) in the world of mortals, or in heaven (*divi*) among the gods who have gone to the celestial realm, whatever being exists that is composed of *sattva* alone— even among those, there is not even one that is free from or devoid of these three qualities born of *prakṛti*, beginning with *sattva*.
The meaning is that the connection with the three guṇas is unavoidable for every class of living beings whatsoever. || 40 ||
Thus, because this *saṃsāra* is pervaded by the three *guṇas*, it is unavoidable that there will be corresponding differences [in conduct];
therefore, each individual, having understood their respective duties and acting in accordance with them, shall be liberated from bondage.
Hence, even among humans, according to the distinctions of their respective *sattva* and other *guṇas*...

The duties of the castes and stages of life, such as those of the Brāhmaṇas and others, are established by nature at the time of creation. It is for this very purpose— that the practitioner may become liberated by knowing and performing the duties corresponding to those [castes]— that he declares the duties of the castes:
O scorcher of the foe, the duties of Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras have been distributed according to the qualities arising from their own natures. (41)
O scorcher of foes, Arjuna, for the Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras— where *viśaḥ* means Vaiśyas—
the duties to be performed by these four classes alone are those arising from their own natures, established by birth:
tranquility, self-restraint, austerity, purity, forbearance, and uprightness.
Knowledge, discernment, and faith are the duties of a Brahmin, born of his own nature. (42)

In this context, *śama* is the conquest of the mind; *dama* is the conquest of the external senses; *tapas* is well known; *śauca* is indeed purity; *kṣānti* is forbearance; and *ārjava* is straightforwardness. *Jñāna* is the sattvic knowledge previously mentioned; *vijñāna* is the manifold knowledge produced by the study of the scriptures.

Faith is simply the state of being convinced of the reality [of the scriptures]. Thus, this very action—born of one's own nature and established by innate disposition—is declared to be the "brahminical action," the duty of a Brahmin. || 42 ||
Heroism, majesty, firmness, dexterity, and not fleeing in battle, as well as generosity and lordliness—this is the duty of the kṣatriya, born of his own nature. (43)

Valor is the state of being brave; splendor is innate power; fortitude is steadfastness; and skill is also proficiency. Not fleeing from battle on the field of combat—that is, not turning one's back—and generosity, sovereignty, and self-restraint: this very set of duties, born of one's own nature, is declared to be the *kṣātra-karman*, the duty of a *kṣatriya*.
Agriculture, cattle-rearing, and trade are the duties of a Vaiśya, born of his own nature;
the duty of a Śūdra, also born of his own nature, consists of service. 44.

Agriculture, enterprise, cattle-tending or animal husbandry, and trade or commerce—these are declared to be the natural duties of a Vaiśya, born of his own nature. For a Śūdra, the duty consists of service;
indeed, the classification into Brāhmaṇas and so forth is based solely on those respective differences in innate nature, and is determined by them.
The meaning is that the differentiation of karma is unavoidable. || 44 ||
Devoted to his own particular duty, a man attains perfection;
hear how one who is intent on his own work finds success. 45.

339) Now, he points out the fruit of such instruction: a person who is "abhirataḥ"—that is, devoted with total orientation—toward their own respective duties (karma), that is, toward what has been stated as their own respective obligations, attains perfection, which is liberation. One who is devoted to one's own duty.

I shall now describe that very way by which a man devoted to the duties of his own caste and stage of life attains perfection— liberation in the form of union with Śiva— even during his lifetime; listen, for from Him proceeds the activity of all beings and by Him all this is pervaded.
By worshipping Him through one's own duty, a human being attains perfection. || 46 ||

Since the activity of all beings— that is, of all living creatures— proceeds from that root, and since the entire world is pervaded by that reality called Paraśiva, the practitioner, having worshipped that very Paraśiva through his own action— the performance of the duties specific to his own caste— attains and acquires perfection.

And thus, the meaning is that there is no room for doubt here: even the performance of the duties of the castes and stages of life (varṇāśramadharma) constitutes the worship of Paraśiva, who is the root of the entire universe, and liberation certainly follows from this. || 46 ||
Better is one's own duty, though deficient, than the duty of another well performed.
Performing the action prescribed by one's own nature, one incurs no sin. 47.

Therefore, even if one's own duty (*svadharma*)— that which is obtained by virtue of one's own specific caste and stage of life— is deficient, lacking some quality, it is indeed better and superior to the duty of another (*paradharma*), even if that other duty is well-performed, correctly executed, and endowed with all its qualities. It is to be adopted.

This is the meaning. To the question "Why?", he says "svabhāva" and so forth. A person performing action in accordance with the nature that is innate to creation does not incur *kilbiṣa*, i.e., sin; indeed, he never incurs it.
However, the duty (*dharma*) of another caste, by its very nature as being "other," even if it appears at first glance to be for one's own benefit—
Because it is inconsistent with one's own naturally established qualities, it brings about ruin. || 47 ||
O son of Kuntī, one should not abandon one's innate duty, even if it is flawed;
for all undertakings are enveloped by defect, just as fire is covered by smoke. 48.

He explains this very point: O Kaunteya Arjuna, one should not abandon one's own duty (karma), which is established by one's own nature, even if it is defective or appears to be somewhat lacking in quality; one should not renounce it for that reason alone. For indeed, all actions are necessarily covered or joined with some slight impurity or defect. This is because every object consists of the three *guṇas*.

340) Since even among the three—sattva, rajas, and tamas—the quality of sattva is rendered deficient by portions of rajas and tamas, there is a slight deficiency everywhere; however, this is inherent to the very nature of creation. Therefore, [one should perform] one's own duty (svadharma) to that extent.
The meaning is that a person should never abandon it. In this regard, there is the illustration "like fire by its smoke.
Even though fire is of the nature of light, its quality of smoke is seen to be innate and dependent upon darkness (tamas);
such is the sense. || 48 ||
With an intellect unattached everywhere, self-conquered, and free from longing,
he attains through renunciation the supreme perfection of actionlessness.

Therefore, he says that one should indeed perform action which is innate (*sahaja*). "In all things" means in all objects; "one whose intellect is unattached" means one whose intellect is detached, free from attachment—such a person, being "devoid of longing," meaning having conquered the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) and being "free from desire," meaning devoid of expectation for results, [should act] by means of renunciation (*saṃnyāsa*) of the aforementioned nature.

By performing even one's own duty (*svadharma*), though it may be devoid of qualities (*nirguṇa*), without expectation for its fruit—by means of this renunciation of results described at the beginning of this chapter—the accomplishment of the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*) occurs;
through the arising of the knowledge of Śiva, the destruction of all kinds of impurities and karma is produced. || 49 ||
Learn from me, O son of Kuntī, how one who has attained perfection reaches Brahman;
I shall describe in brief that which is the supreme culmination of knowledge.

He also states the fruit of such perfection in brief: "O Kaunteya, listen—that is, hear—from me the manner in which one who has attained such perfection as that which is the supreme goal, the ultimate limit of knowledge, reaches Paraśiva-Brahman; I shall explain it to you in summary, that is, in brief. (50)
Endowed with pure intellect and having restrained the self with fortitude, one should abandon the objects of the senses, such as sound and the rest, and cast off both attachment and aversion. (51)
Frequenting solitary places, eating light food, with speech, body, and mind restrained, he is constantly devoted to the yoga of meditation and has fully taken recourse to dispassion. || 52 ||
Having abandoned egoism, power, arrogance, desire, anger, and possessiveness, one who is free from the sense of "mine" and tranquil is fit for becoming Brahman. 53.

Endowed with a pure intellect free from defects, and having restrained and subdued the self— that is, the mind— by means of fortitude, which is firm resolve, he should apply it to the objects of Brahman, such as sound and the rest.

Having cast off and eliminated passion, hatred, and the like, he dwells in solitude, delights in seclusion, eats light food, consumes little, and has his speech, body, and mind restrained; with his body, speech, and mind disciplined, he is always intent on meditation and yoga,
devoted to the meditation upon the Supreme Self, and possesses detachment— an absence of passion toward objects other than the Supreme Self.
Having properly resorted [to the Self], having completely relinquished egoism, self-confidence, pride, intoxication, lust, and anger, as well as possessions— the accumulation of external implements—
and being free from the sense of "mine" (nirmama), such a person is therefore peaceful and attains the state of Brahman (brahmabhāva).

It becomes fit; it becomes capable; it becomes worthy to experience the bliss of union with Supreme Śiva. And thus, the meaning is that the supreme culmination of knowledge is indeed the experience of identity with Śiva. (51–53)
Having become Brahman, serene in soul, he neither grieves nor desires;
equal toward all beings, he attains supreme devotion to Me. 54.

Having become Brahman—that is, having attained such a state of identity with Śiva—one whose self is serene and whose mind is tranquil does not desire anything, nor does one even take account of pleasure, pain, and the like. Such a person is equal toward all beings, possessing a state of equanimity; they possess supreme devotion to Me, the highest pinnacle of devotion.

One attains the supreme devotion, which is formless and free from desire, and which accomplishes *kaivalya*—the state of identity with Śiva. Other forms of devotion, however, are like steps; they accomplish worldly fruits. The distinction is that supreme devotion brings about the state of *sāmarasya* (perfect equilibrium) with the *bhāvaliṅga*, whose nature is the space of consciousness (*cidākāśa*), for one who is liberated. This alone...

Devotion (*bhakti*) is employed on the path of worship through the six stages (*ṣaṭsthala*). This devotion consists of specific states of faith (*śraddhā*), which manifest the unfolding of devotion among human beings. Indeed, by practicing devotion—from the stage of faith and devotion up to steadfastness (*niṣṭhā*) and so forth—the devotee proceeds toward the realization of *samarasa-bhakti* (devotion of equal flavor).

When the *prāṇaliṅga* resides in the heart and the *bhāvaliṅga* shines upon the head, having become dissolved through the state of *samarasa* (equilibrium of flavors), one dwells in the world like a burnt cloth. Regarding this matter, more may be seen in the latter part of the *Śaktiviśiṣṭādvaita-darśana*. || 54 ||
Through devotion he comes to know Me as I am in truth, and whatever My nature truly is;
then, having known Me in truth, he enters into Me immediately thereafter.
And by such supreme devotion, the devotee truly knows Me— exactly as I am in reality, in whatever measure, who I am, and of whatever nature; he knows Me correctly.
Immediately thereafter, having known Me alone in reality, for that very reason he enters—that is, he merges—into Me alone.

It was stated previously that "He can be attained through unswerving devotion," and thus the meaning is that the ultimate pinnacle of steadfastness in knowledge is indeed oneness with Paraśiva. || 55 ||
Even while constantly performing all actions, one who takes refuge in me attains through my grace the eternal and imperishable state.

And so, having taught the entire meaning of the scripture by way of its essential summary, He begins to state the conclusion, declaring that this alone is the core essence: "At all times, even while performing all actions, a person who remains taking refuge in Me alone— by My grace [attains perfection]."
Only through my grace does one attain the eternal, imperishable, and indestructible state, which is liberation in the form of the immortal abode. || 56 ||
Renouncing all actions in Me with your mind, regarding Me as the supreme goal, and taking refuge in the yoga of discernment, keep your consciousness ever fixed on Me. 57.

Therefore, you too, having mentally and with your mind renounced—that is, offered—all actions performed by you unto Me, the Supreme Lord; being intent on Me alone (*matpara*), that is, having your sole focus on Me; having resorted to and taken hold of such a yoga of intellect, which is the yoga of knowledge (*jñānayoga*); and being ever-minded of Me (*maccita*), that is, having a mind solely devoted to Me—always, at all times.
Be; abide.
With your mind focused on Me, you shall cross over all difficulties by My grace;
but if, out of egoism, you do not listen, you shall perish.
In this very way, O Arjuna, by my grace alone you shall cross over all difficulties and all that is unfavorable.
But if, out of egoism—the false pride that "I too am indeed omniscient"—you do not listen to what has been said by me, then you will perish; you will meet with destruction. || 58 ||
If, relying on egoism, you think "I will not fight," this resolve of yours is false; your own nature will compel you.

He says that because you do not follow the intention of the Blessed One, your desired goal will not be accomplished: "When you think, 'I shall not strike him,' relying upon egoism, then this resolve of yours—that is, your determination—is indeed false.
It shall come to pass; for your own nature itself will engage you—that is, it will impel you—to the performance of action. The meaning is that, in every way, you will simply have to fight. || 59 ||
Bound by your own karma born of your nature, O son of Kuntī,
you shall do that which you do not wish to do out of delusion, even against your will.

He says this very thing: O Kaunteya Arjuna! Bound by your own action born of your nature, that which you now do not wish to do out of delusion—that is, out of ignorance—you will nonetheless perform all that very same action, being under the sway of *prakṛti* and having no other recourse. This [action] is already attached to you by nature.
You will certainly engage in battle. || 60 ||
The Lord dwells in the heart-region of all beings, O Arjuna,
causing all beings to revolve by His power of illusion, as if they were mounted on a machine.

To the question "Why?", he says: O Arjuna, the Lord, the Supreme Self, who dwells in the region of the heart, causing all beings—even all living entities—to revolve and move by means of His own inconceivable power of illusion (*māyā*), as if they were mounted upon a machine or bound to a mechanical device; therefore, no one can do anything at all by transgressing Him.
It is possible. All worldly transactions proceed spontaneously only in accordance with His will.
At that time, he alone who offers a mango with a heart full of contentment finds happiness;
for this very reason, the Will of the Lord is remembered as the most powerful. || 61 ||
Go to Him alone for refuge with your whole being, O Bhārata;
by His grace you shall attain supreme peace and the eternal abode. 62.

Therefore, He says: "You too, O Bhārata Arjuna, go for refuge to that very Supreme Self alone. Go for refuge with your whole being—that is, with your entire self—not merely from an external perspective, but with your innermost soul as well—to that Supreme Self who resides within your heart and is your impeller.
By His grace alone you shall attain supreme peace and the eternal state;
the meaning is that there is no other path for you than peace.
Thus has this knowledge, more secret than the secret, been declared by Me to you.
Having reflected upon it in its entirety, do as you wish.

In this manner— "I am your disciple; teach me who have come to you for refuge"— this knowledge, which is more secret than the secret, even more hidden than the hidden, the supreme mystery, has been declared by Me to you.
(344) This has been taught. Having reflected upon and deliberated thoroughly and in its entirety upon what I have said, do as you wish, in whatever way pleases you. || 63 ||
Hear again from Me my supreme word, the most secret of all secrets.
Since you are dearly beloved to Me, I shall therefore speak what is for your benefit.

Even though he had spoken thus, the Blessed One, out of compassion, spoke again: "Listen once more to my words, which are the most secret of all secrets, the supreme mystery, and the most profound. Because you are very dear to me—indeed, you are exceedingly beloved to me—I shall speak that which is for your benefit."
I shall speak. Even though you remain silent, it is not possible for me to remain so;
therefore, I instruct you once more. Listen with an attentive mind. 64.
Fix your mind on Me, be devoted to Me, sacrifice to Me, and bow down to Me.
Thus you shall come to Me alone; I promise you this truly, for you are dear to Me. 65.

To the question "What is that?", he says: "Always be one whose mind is fixed on Me; be one whose heart is centered solely on Me. In this way, become My devotee. Even Kaṃsa and others possessed such single-minded devotion toward Him out of fear and so forth; to prevent that [kind of attachment], He says: "Worship Me. Acting in this manner, you will come to Me—that is, you will attain Me, the Supreme Self. And this—
"Truly," thus I promise—that is, I make this vow—to you; and since you are dear to me, the meaning is that I shall certainly not speak an untruth in your presence. || 65 ||
Abandoning all dharmas, take refuge in me alone;
I shall liberate you from all sins—do not grieve.

Thus, if you are unable to perform sacrifices and other such rites, and if you are unable to practice all the duties that have come upon you as your own inherent obligations (*prakṛti-dharma*), then, setting those aside, take refuge in Me alone— the Lord of all worlds, the remover of all sins, the peerless, formless Supreme Lord.

Become one who has come for refuge as my protector. To you who act in this way, I myself—the Lord of all, the All-powerful—shall deliver you from all sins, including incapacity and the abandonment of one's own duty (svadharma), which are the root of all evils.

In passages such as, "The wise man, devoted to his own duty, attains perfection," it is taught that a person should take refuge in the Supreme Self alone according to their respective qualifications. Even in the world, persons who are incapable of protecting themselves protect themselves by taking shelter with another person who is capable; it is exactly like that.

The meaning is that for a person who is unable to practice their own duty (*svadharma*) and so forth, yet desires the protection of the self, the Blessed Lord alone becomes the protector. That this very meaning is the essence of all scriptures is understood from the instruction given at the conclusion. With this very verse, the instruction of the *Gītā* scripture is brought to completion.
By the Blessed One. || 66 ||
This must never be spoken by you to one who lacks austerity, nor to one who is without devotion,
nor to one who is unwilling to listen, nor to one who finds fault with me.

Thus, it is stated that this scripture taught out of compassion must not be imparted to an unworthy recipient. This scripture spoken to you must not be told to a man who lacks austerity—that is, one devoid of the power for spiritual discipline.
Likewise, it must never, at any time, be given to one who is without devotion—that is, one lacking devotion toward me, whose nature consists of both the manifest and the unmanifest.
It should not be spoken thus to one who does not wish to hear—that is, to one devoid of the desire to listen and lacking in respect.
Likewise, it should not be spoken even to one who finds fault with Me—meaning, one who, perceiving Me as an ordinary human being, harbors malice and the like toward Me. || 67 ||
Whoever shall declare this supreme secret among my devotees, having established supreme devotion toward me, will come to me alone, without doubt. (68)

He states the fruit for one who teaches this to a worthy recipient: that man who shall declare—meaning, speak—this supreme secret, this most profound meaning of the scripture, to people who are My devotees, by that very act he shall perform the highest and most excellent devotion toward Me; through that, he shall come to Me—that is, he shall attain Me within his own heart.

It dissolves into me alone, who am the resplendent form shining forth; of this there is no doubt. Even one who has told this to another shall attain firm devotion to me and reach me as its fruit. || 68 ||
And among humans, there shall be no one who does more for me than he;
nor shall there be anyone else on earth dearer to me than he.
Therefore, among men, there is no other person superior to that man who has given this treatise to a worthy recipient.
"He who does what is pleasing to Me and performs My sacrifice—there is no one else at all [who is so]. This means that he alone is the doer of what is dear to Me.
Not only that, but even in the future time, in this world on earth, there shall be no one other than that aforementioned man who will be more beloved to Me; indeed, none shall exist. 69.
And whoever shall study this dialogue of ours concerning Dharma, by him I shall have been worshipped through the sacrifice of knowledge; such is my conviction. (70)
That man who shall study this scripture of the Gītā—which is righteous, endowed with dharma, and consists of our mutual conversation—by him I am worshipped through the sacrifice of knowledge;
such is my conviction and resolve. It is superior to sacrifices consisting of material objects.
It has already been stated previously that this is the sacrifice of knowledge.
Even that man who, possessing faith and free from malice, should merely hear this, shall be liberated and attain the auspicious worlds of those who perform meritorious deeds. || 71 ||

Even if one does not study it at all, or even if one does not study it oneself, whoever hears this with faith and devotion, being free from malice— that is, devoid of the intent to expose faults— even such a person is liberated from sins and, being freed from them, attains the auspicious and meritorious worlds of those who perform virtuous deeds.
"He shall surely attain it"—this is the certainty.
"Has this been heard by you with a one-pointed mind, O Pārtha?
Has the delusion born of ignorance been destroyed within you, O Dhanañjaya? (72)
"O Pārtha Dhanañjaya, have you perhaps heard this which was taught by me with a one-pointed mind?
Has the delusion regarding the discrimination between what ought to be done and what ought not to be done been destroyed? Has your doubt—such as 'should I fight or not'—dissolved? || 72 ||
Delusion has been destroyed and memory regained by me through your grace, O Acyuta;
I stand firm with my doubts dispelled, and I shall do as you have commanded.
Thus, having heard the instruction on reality directly from the mouth of the Blessed One, Arjuna, with his delusion destroyed, said:

"O Acyuta Kṛṣṇa, my delusion has perished; and through your grace—that is, through your favor—right mindfulness, the recollection of the true meaning, has been regained. Now, with my doubts gone, I am free from all uncertainty."
(347) I stand firm. Being dependent on you, I shall carry out and abide by your word alone with satisfaction; however, I shall not utter words of mere intellectual sophistry. || 73 ||
Thus have I heard this wonderful dialogue between Vāsudeva and the high-souled Pārtha, which causes the hair to stand on end. (74)
To Dhṛtarāṣṭra, who had asked, "What did they do on the field of dharma, O Sañjaya?",
Sañjaya recounts that which occurred and concludes: "In this manner,
this wonderful [account] of the high-souled Blessed One, Vāsudeva, who is the form of supreme power, and of Pārtha, Arjuna..."
And he said, "I have now heard this hair-raising dialogue."
By the grace of Vyāsa, I have heard this supreme secret,
the Yoga, directly from Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of Yoga, as he himself was speaking it.

To the question, "How did you hear this scripture of the Gītā while remaining right here?", he replies: "I [heard] this supreme secret yoga directly from Kṛṣṇa himself—the Lord of Yoga (yogeśvara), who is the ultimate goal even for all yogas—as he was speaking it; and by the grace (anugraha) of the great seer Vyāsa, through his favor."
"I am learned," Sañjaya said. || 75 ||
O King, remembering again and again this wonderful and meritorious dialogue between Keśava and Arjuna, I rejoice over and over.

O King Dhṛtarāṣṭra, remembering again and again this wonderful, meritorious, and merit-bestowing dialogue between Keśava and Arjuna—that is, Kṛṣṇa and Arjuna—I rejoice over and over. The meaning is that whenever I remember it, at that very moment I shall be immersed in joy. || 76 ||
And remembering again and again that most wonderful form of Hari, O King, great is my amazement, and I rejoice over and over again. (77)
Furthermore, O King Dhṛtarāṣṭra, as I repeatedly recall that most wonderful universal form (viśvarūpa) of Hari Śrī Kṛṣṇa which was shown to Arjuna,
a great wonder and amazement arise within me; I rejoice again and again, for there is no limit to my joy.
Wherever there is Kṛṣṇa, the Lord of Yoga, and wherever there is Pārtha, the wielder of the bow, there will surely be prosperity, victory, and fortune; this is my conviction. (78)
What need is there for much speaking? In whichever side the Lord of Yoga—

Śrī Kṛṣṇa, the supreme goal of all yogas, composed of compassion, and expert in bestowing grace upon devotees— resides, and in whichever side Pārtha Arjuna, the stainless practitioner bound by initiation, resides, in that very side all prosperity dwells.

It is my conviction and firm resolve that prosperity, stability, and sound policy shall prevail; or rather, the construction is: "My mind is firm and my resolve is steadfast. In that state where, along with the knowledge of the Supreme Lord, the activity that brings about His grace and favor shines forth brilliantly, there [no obstacle remains].

Not only does it manifest worldly happiness, but even the happiness of the hereafter manifests at one and the same time. Thus, for the welfare of all human beings, this Gītā scripture— which accomplishes supreme happiness and peace in this world, establishes the greatness of the body, and increases devotion— should be properly [studied].
Since it is clearly understood, one desists here after having gained firm conviction. || 78 ||
This commentary, composed by me at the command of my father, is indeed in accordance with the Śrī Vīraśaiva tradition;
it is offered for the understanding of the meaning of the Gītā to those great souls whose minds are devoted to the worship of Maheśvara.

This new commentary on the *Bhāṣya*, which establishes the true meaning, was composed by me for the satisfaction of my father—who passed away in his eighteenth year—after he had performed the funeral rites at the appropriate time; may it lead to the gratification of my father in the hereafter.
Thus ends the eighteenth chapter in the Bhagavadgītā-vīraśaiva-bhāṣya.
